### [1] [Exposing the Unsaid: Visualizing Hidden LLM Bias through Stochastic Path Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19344)
*Matteo Pelossi,Rita Sevastjanova,Thilo Spinner,Mennatallah El-Assady*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TreeTracer is a visual analytics tool that aggregates hundreds of stochastic LLM generations into syntax-aligned hierarchical Sankey diagrams, enabling systematic comparison of biases across semantic contexts through ontology-driven perturbation and contrastive counterfactual probability analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLM bias auditing methods—single output inspection and static automated metrics—obscure underlying probability distributions and miss biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. Stochastic generation variability makes representational and syntactic biases difficult to evaluate reliably.

Method: TreeTracer employs a perturbation analysis pipeline that replaces ontology-defined terms in prompts, aggregates hundreds of stochastic generations into syntax-aligned hierarchical structures, and performs classification-aware node merging using an auxiliary language model. Results are visualized through custom Sankey diagrams that juxtapose two ontology-driven trees for direct cross-context comparison. The system additionally applies contrastive inference to compute and display counterfactual token probabilities, mitigating misinterpretation risk.

Result: Case studies comparing GPT-2 XL against constitutionally aligned Apertus models reveal hidden representational harms, including counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization of individuals. A preliminary user study confirms the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and supports effective systemic bias detection.

Conclusion: Visual aggregation of stochastic LLM outputs combined with contrastive counterfactual analysis provides a more reliable and interpretable framework for auditing representational biases than single-output or static-metric approaches, exposing harms that would otherwise remain hidden.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit representational and syntactic biases that are difficult to evaluate due to the stochastic nature of text generation. Standard auditing methods rely on a single output inspection or static automated metrics. These approaches obscure the underlying probability distributions and fail to capture biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. This paper introduces TreeTracer, a visual analytics tool designed to evaluate LLM bias through aggregated comparison. Using a systematic perturbation analysis pipeline, the tool replaces ontology-defined terms in each input prompt, aggregates hundreds of stochastic generations into a syntax-aligned hierarchical structure, and then performs classification-aware node merging with an auxiliary language model. The resulting structure is visualized through a custom Sankey diagram. By juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees, the workspace enables direct comparison between semantic contexts and supports systematic bias detection. Because any visualization reflects only a subset of the model's learned behavior, the system further applies contrastive inference to compute and directly display counterfactual token probabilities across contexts, reducing the risk of misinterpreting the presence of bias. We validate the workspace through case studies comparing an unaligned baseline model GPT-2 XL against the constitutionally aligned Apertus models. The visual aggregation successfully exposes hidden representational harms, such as counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization of individuals. A preliminary user study confirms that the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and effectively supports analysts in detecting systemic biases.

</details>


### [2] [Ensembles of Large Language Models for Identifying EQ-5D Studies in PubMed Based on Their Abstracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19345)
*Zhyar Rzgar K. Rostam,Márta Péntek,János Tibor Czere,Zsombor Zrubka,László Gulácsi,Gábor Kertész*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study proposes a multi-phase framework using ensemble LLMs (Gemini and Gemma) to automate the detection of EQ-5D health-related quality-of-life results in PubMed abstracts, achieving a 0.74 weighted F1-score through few-shot prompting, weight ensembling, and soft stacking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual screening for systematic literature reviews is increasingly resource-intensive, inefficient, and inconsistent due to the rapid growth of scientific publications. Detecting studies reporting EQ-5D data requires high-level clinical interpretation, posing particular challenges for human reviewers.

Method: A multi-phase framework integrating (1) few-shot prompting of nine Google Gemini and Gemma LLMs, (2) weight ensembling aggregation of top-performing models (gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, gemma-3-27b), and (3) a soft stacking meta-classifier. Models were evaluated on a PubMed dataset manually labeled by two domain experts.

Result: The weighted ensemble achieved a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, surpassing all individual model performances. Ensembling improved precision-recall balance, and soft stacking enhanced reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis confirmed that model probability outputs were important for guiding final predictions.

Conclusion: An ensemble-based LLM approach is a reliable, scalable solution for automating study screening in biomedical systematic literature reviews, particularly for detecting EQ-5D reporting in abstracts.

Abstract: The rapid increase in scientific publications leads to the fact that manual study screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) is increasingly resource consuming, inefficient, and inconsistent. Classifying studies that clearly report health-related quality-of-life results, such as EQ-5D data, requires a high level of clinical interpretation and poses challenges for human reviewers. This study investigates the use of Google's Gemini and Gemma large language models (LLMs) in automating EQ-5D detection in the PubMed biomedical database based only on published abstracts. A multi-phase framework is proposed that integrates few-shot prompting, weight ensembling aggregation, and a soft stacking meta-classifier. Nine LLMs are evaluated on a dataset of PubMed studies manually labeled by two experts regarding EQ-5D reporting. The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b obtained a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, exceeding individually attained results. The ensembling of top-performing models improved the balance between precision and recall compared to individual models, while the soft stacking approach provided greater reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis shows that the probability results from the models are important in guiding the final predictions. The findings suggest that an ensemble-based LLM setup is a reliable and scalable approach for automating screening in biomedical research.

</details>


### [3] [Disentangling Linguistic Relatedness from Task Alignment in Cross-Lingual Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19346)
*Ahmed Haj Ahmed,Ruochen Zhang,Alvin Grissom*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fine-tuning LLMs on Arabic improves zero-shot reading comprehension across all languages tested, not just Semitic ones. Gains depend on baseline strength, not language family, and chain-of-thought reasoning produces similar benefits — both mechanisms likely address task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether fine-tuning on a single language (Arabic) yields cross-lingual transfer benefits specifically for genetically related languages (other Semitic languages) versus unrelated controls, challenging the assumption of language-family-based transfer advantages.

Method: Seven LLMs (4B–671B parameters, dense and MoE architectures) were fine-tuned on Arabic reading comprehension and evaluated zero-shot on other Semitic languages (Hebrew, Amharic, etc.) and non-Semitic controls. A chain-of-thought ablation was conducted to compare inference-time reasoning with fine-tuning effects.

Result: No Semitic-specific transfer was found. Weak-baseline models improved substantially across all languages; strong-baseline models showed only marginal gains regardless of language family. Chain-of-thought prompting produced gains mirroring fine-tuning, concentrated in the same models.

Conclusion: Both fine-tuning and chain-of-thought reasoning primarily address task-format alignment rather than facilitating cross-lingual knowledge transfer. Language family relatedness does not confer a transfer advantage in this setting.

Abstract: We study cross-lingual transfer by fine-tuning seven large language models (4B--671B parameters) on Arabic and evaluating zero-shot reading comprehension on Semitic languages and non-Semitic controls. Across dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, we find no evidence of Semitic-specific transfer: models with weak baselines improve dramatically across all languages, while strong-baseline models show only marginal gains regardless of language family. A chain-of-thought ablation reinforces this finding -- the same models that benefit most from fine-tuning benefit equally from inference-time reasoning, suggesting both mechanisms address task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual knowledge transfer.

</details>


### [4] [How LLMs Fail and Generalize in RTL Coding for Hardware Design?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19347)
*Guan-Ting Liu,Chao-Han Huck Yang,Chenhui Deng,Zhongzhi Yu,Brucek Khailany,Yu-Chiang Frank Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Frontier LLMs plateau at ~90.8% on VerilogEval due to unsolvable functional errors rooted in pretraining knowledge gaps; alignment only teaches models to compile, while repeated sampling patches solvable errors but cannot overcome fundamental RTL reasoning limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate why LLMs struggle to translate sequential programming knowledge into parallel hardware description logic (RTL), and to characterize the empirical performance ceiling observed on VerilogEval through a cognitively-grounded error taxonomy.

Method: The authors introduce a four-category error taxonomy (syntactic, semantic, solvable functional, unsolvable functional) based on problem solvability and cognitive theory. They evaluate frontier LLMs on the VerilogEval benchmark, analyze the distribution of error types, and test the effects of test-time compute scaling, repeated sampling, and alignment techniques on each category.

Result: Frontier models plateau at 90.8% initial pass rate, with unsolvable functional errors defining the ceiling. Optimization eliminates syntax errors but simultaneously worsens deeper functional failures (surface convergence gap). Repeated sampling resolves solvable functional errors, but unsolvable functional errors remain immune to test-time compute scaling, indicating bounded RTL capacity constrained by pretraining knowledge.

Conclusion: Alignment interventions merely teach models to compile rather than reason. Advancing LLM-based hardware generation requires focusing on genuine model reasoning capabilities, not alignment or sampling strategies, as RTL coding capacity is fundamentally bounded by pretraining knowledge.

Abstract: Translating sequential programming priors into the parallel temporal logic of hardware design remains a crucial bottleneck for large language models(LLM). To investigate this, we introduce a new error taxonomy grounded in problem solvability, inspired by cognitive theory. Our taxonomy categorizes failures into syntactic, semantic, solvable functional, and unsolvable functional types. Evaluations reveal a strict empirical ceiling on the VerilogEval benchmark, as frontier models plateau at a 90.8% initial pass rate. These plateaus are defined by unsolvable functional errors, exposing persistent knowledge gaps immune to test time compute scaling. Furthermore, we expose a striking surface convergence gap: optimization readily eliminates syntax errors but concurrently exacerbates deeper functional failures. Our findings demonstrate that alignment techniques merely teach models to compile. While repeated sampling strategies can patch solvable errors, register-transfer level(RTL) coding capacity remains strictly bounded by pretraining knowledge. Addressing challenges in the current LLM based hardware generation pipeline requires more studies in model reasoning rather than alignment interventions.

</details>

Pan,Zongqing Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DeepSeek-V4 introduces two MoE models (Pro: 1.6T/49B activated; Flash: 284B/13B activated) with 1M-token context, featuring hybrid CSA+HCA attention, manifold-constrained hyper-connections, and the Muon optimizer, achieving SOTA open-model performance with dramatically improved long-context efficiency (27% FLOPs, 10% KV cache vs. V3.2).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To push the frontier of open-source language models by improving long-context efficiency, training stability, and inference cost, enabling routine use of million-token contexts for long-horizon tasks and test-time scaling.

Method: The DeepSeek-V4 series employs a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with three key innovations: (1) a hybrid attention mechanism combining Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) for long-context efficiency; (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) to enhance residual connections; and (3) the Muon optimizer for faster convergence and training stability. Models are pre-trained on 32T+ tokens and undergo a comprehensive post-training pipeline. The Pro variant offers a "Pro-Max" maximum reasoning effort mode.

Result: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max achieves state-of-the-art results among open models on core tasks. In million-token contexts, DeepSeek-V4-Pro uses only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache compared to DeepSeek-V3.2, enabling routine long-context processing.

Conclusion: DeepSeek-V4 represents a significant advance in open-weight LLMs, combining scale (up to 1.6T total parameters) with architectural innovations that dramatically reduce long-context inference costs, making million-token contexts practically feasible for the first time in this model class.

Abstract: We present a preview version of DeepSeek-V4 series, including two strong Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models -- DeepSeek-V4-Pro with 1.6T parameters (49B activated) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash with 284B parameters (13B activated) -- both supporting a context length of one million tokens. DeepSeek-V4 series incorporate several key upgrades in architecture and optimization: (1) a hybrid attention architecture that combines Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) to improve long-context efficiency; (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) that enhance conventional residual connections; (3) and the Muon optimizer for faster convergence and greater training stability. We pre-train both models on more than 32T diverse and high-quality tokens, followed by a comprehensive post-training pipeline that unlocks and further enhances their capabilities. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max, the maximum reasoning effort mode of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, redefines the state-of-the-art for open models, outperforming its predecessors in core tasks. Meanwhile, DeepSeek-V4 series are highly efficient in long-context scenarios. In the one-million-token context setting, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of KV cache compared with DeepSeek-V3.2. This enables us to routinely support one-million-token contexts, thereby making long-horizon tasks and further test-time scaling more feasible. The model checkpoints are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.

</details>


### [6] [Where to Place the Query? Unveiling and Mitigating Positional Bias in In-Context Learning for Diffusion LLMs via Decoding Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19349)
*Zhengheng Li,Panrui Li,Xuyang Liu,Puzhi Xia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper reveals that query position is a critical first-order variable in Diffusion LLMs for In-Context Learning, driven by a spatial "Recency Effect" in attention and task-dependent decoding shifts. It proposes Average Confidence, a novel metric for query optimization, and Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically places queries to approach oracle-level performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) use bidirectional attention, unlike autoregressive (AR) LLMs, yet current ICL practices blindly inherit AR-style trailing-query templates. This structural mismatch overlooks the spatial flexibility dLLMs offer for query placement. The authors aim to systematically understand whether and how query position matters in dLLM-based ICL.

Method: The authors conduct an empirical decoupling analysis, isolating the effect of query position from example semantic quality on generation performance. They analyze internal mechanisms, identifying a spatial "Recency Effect" in attention flow and task-dependent decoding trajectory shifts. They further diagnose that standard single-step confidence (C_decoded) is unreliable for dLLMs, and instead propose Average Confidence (C̄), a metric that tracks confidence over the full iterative decoding process. Leveraging these spatial ICL baselines, they develop Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically selects optimal query placement per instance.

Result: Query position variance impacts generation quality at a level comparable to example semantic quality. The proposed Average Confidence metric effectively captures decoding quality without ground-truth labels. Auto-ICL robustly approaches oracle performance across diverse reasoning and perception tasks, outperforming fixed-position baselines.

Conclusion: Query position is a first-order design variable in dLLM-based ICL that has been systematically overlooked. Auto-ICL provides a practical, training-free solution to dynamically optimize query placement, advancing the understanding and application of ICL within diffusion language models.

Abstract: While In-Context Learning (ICL) is extensively studied in Autoregressive (AR) LLMs, its mechanism within Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) remains largely unexplored. Unlike AR models restricted by unidirectional causal masking, dLLMs intrinsically utilize bidirectional attention, offering extensive spatial flexibility for query placement. Unfortunately, current practices conventionally inherit AR-style trailing-query templates, often overlooking the structural paradigm shift. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis unveiling that query position is actually a first-order variable in dLLMs. Through empirical decoupling, we demonstrate that positional variance impacts generation quality on par with example semantic quality. Internally, this positional sensitivity stems from a spatial ``Recency Effect'' in attention flow and task-dependent shifts in decoding trajectories. To mitigate this instability without ground-truth labels, we reveal that traditional single-step confidence ($C_{decoded}$) fails in dLLMs. Instead, we propose Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$), a novel metric tracking the iterative decoding process. By establishing the foundational spatial ICL baselines, we introduce Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically optimizes query placement, robustly approaching oracle performance across heterogeneous reasoning and perception tasks.

</details>


### [7] [Pruning via Causal Attribution Preserves Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19350)
*Amogh Sheth,Biruk Assefa,Yi Wen Huang,Andrew Lin,Yuhao Ge*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CAP is a training-free pruning method that uses causal attribution of attention heads to guide weight-level pruning, outperforming correlational methods like Wanda on reasoning benchmarks at moderate sparsity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are strong at multi-step reasoning but suffer from high inference cost. Existing pruning methods rely on magnitude or activation correlations, which fail to capture the functional causal contribution of attention heads to reasoning tasks.

Method: CAP measures each attention head's causal impact by masking it during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems, estimating expected performance degradation. These head-level causal scores are converted to weight-level importance values for projection matrices, guiding fine-grained structured pruning without any training.

Result: CAP achieves up to 61% relative accuracy improvement over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. Evaluated on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct across GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge at 10%, 20%, and 50% sparsity, CAP outperforms Wanda in most configurations at 10–20% sparsity, with particularly large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3.

Conclusion: Head-level causal attribution better preserves reasoning performance than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, though coarse MLP attribution limits effectiveness at 50% sparsity.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning but incur substantial inference cost. We introduce Causal Attribution Pruning (CAP), a training-free method that identifies critical attention heads by measuring their causal impact on reasoning tasks and uses these head-level scores to guide fine-grained weight pruning. For each attention head, CAP estimates the expected performance degradation when the head is masked during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems. These causal scores are then converted into weight-level importance values for the corresponding projection matrices. Unlike magnitude-only or activation-based criteria, CAP's interventional measurement directly captures each head's functional contribution, yielding relative accuracy gains of up to 61% over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. We evaluate CAP on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct at 10%, 20%, and 50% sparsity. At moderate sparsity (10-20%), CAP improves over Wanda in most model-benchmark configurations. with especially large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3. Our results suggest that attention-head-level causal attribution can better preserve reasoning performance on downstream benchmarks than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, while remaining limited by coarse MLP attribution at 50% sparsity.

</details>


### [8] [Detecting Hallucinations for Large Language Model-based Knowledge Graph Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19351)
*Xinyan Zhu,Yaoqi Liu,Yue Gao,Huadong Ma,Cheng Yang,Chuan Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LUCID is a hallucination detection method for LLM-based KG reasoning that combines LLM attention scores with KG structural information via a graph neural network, achieving state-of-the-art performance across nine datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs hallucinate even when supplied with relevant KG knowledge during reasoning, and existing hallucination detection methods ignore KG structural information, leading to suboptimal detection performance.

Method: LUCID extracts node and edge features from LLM attention scores and semantic similarities, then integrates these with KG structure using a graph neural network (GNN) for hallucination detection. The authors also constructed manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation.

Result: LUCID achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to 15 baselines across nine benchmark datasets.

Conclusion: Jointly leveraging LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information via a GNN effectively addresses hallucination detection in LLM-based KG reasoning, significantly outperforming methods that ignore structural signals.

Abstract: Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning infers new knowledge from existing facts and is widely applied in question answering, recommendation, and decision support. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks have become increasingly popular by leveraging retrieved KG information. However, hallucinations in LLMs remain a critical issue. Even when relevant KG knowledge is incorporated, models may still generate incorrect outputs, leading to misinformation and unreliable decisions. Existing hallucination detection methods either focus on LLM internal states or verify consistency with retrieved contexts, but both overlook the structural information in KGs, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this gap, we propose LUCID, the first halLUcination deteCtIon method for LLM-based knowleDge graph reasoning frameworks. LUCID jointly leverages LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information. Specifically, it extracts node and edge features from attention scores and semantic similarities, and integrates them with KG structure using a graph neural network. We also construct manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation. Experiments on nine datasets show that LUCID achieves state of the art performance compared to 15 baselines.

</details>


### [9] [Sign-Language Datasets at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey on Resources, Benchmarks, and Annotation Standards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19352)
*Yiming Ni,Zhi-Qi Cheng,Jiayu Li,Wei Cheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey indexing 120 sign-language datasets across 35 sign languages, analyzing challenges like modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias, and proposing a standardized 24-field datasheet for future dataset design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite progress in sign-language recognition, translation, and production, current benchmarks suffer from fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Systematic analyses of these limitations are lacking, hindering development of technologies that reflect real-world communication needs of DHH communities.

Method: The authors conducted a comprehensive survey compiling an index of 120 sign-language resources across 35 sign languages. They systematically analyzed key challenges (modality imbalance, annotation granularity, signer bias) and introduced a standardized 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet for consistent dataset documentation, along with a public GitHub repository for reproducible evaluation.

Result: The survey catalogs 120 datasets spanning 35 sign languages, identifies persistent issues including modality imbalance, coarse annotation granularity, and signer bias across existing resources, and delivers a standardized datasheet framework plus an open-source repository to support the community.

Conclusion: The work provides a unified, practical foundation for developing more inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies by promoting standardized documentation, reproducible benchmarking, and awareness of dataset design considerations for real-world applications.

Abstract: Sign languages are expressive visual languages used by Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) communities. Despite substantial progress in sign-language recognition, translation, and production, advances remain constrained by fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Existing benchmarks often fail to reflect real-world communication needs, and systematic analyses of these limitations remain limited. In this survey, we present a comprehensive index of sign-language datasets, covering 120 resources across 35 sign languages. We analyze key challenges such as modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias, and outline considerations for future dataset design. We also introduce a 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet and release a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/Ginqwerty/Open-Sign-Language) to support standardized documentation and reproducible evaluation. Overall, our work provides a unified and practical foundation for developing inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies in real-world applications.

</details>


### [10] [Quantifying Aleatoric Uncertainty of In-Context Learning for Robust Measure of LLM Prediction Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19353)
*Jinseok Chung,Minkyoung Song,Hyunji Jung,Namhoon Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces "self-function vectors," a Bayesian framework leveraging internal LLM representations to decompose and estimate aleatoric uncertainty in In-Context Learning, along with a rigorous evaluation protocol. The method outperforms existing alternatives and enables applications like hallucination detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ICL reliability is undermined by sensitivity to prompt design and model comprehension. Existing uncertainty decomposition methods fail for ICL because they rely on input/output manipulations unsuitable for its dynamics. The authors aim to separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty in ICL to better diagnose failure sources.

Method: The authors propose self-function vectors grounded in Bayesian principles and mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors capture the latent concept learned during prompting from internal representations, enabling direct aleatoric uncertainty estimation without brittle input or decoding manipulations. They also introduce a controlled evaluation protocol using synthetic and real-world data to quantify uncertainties separately.

Result: The proposed self-function vector methodology measures ICL prediction uncertainty more reliably than existing methods. It also demonstrates practical utility for trustworthiness tasks like hallucination detection.

Conclusion: The work establishes a new direction connecting quantitative uncertainty estimation with mechanistic understanding of LLM behavior, offering both theoretical and practical advances for trustworthy ICL.

Abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) allows LLMs to adapt to new tasks from a few demonstrations, but its reliability remains a concern: predictions are highly sensitive to both prompt design and the model's ability to understand the context, obscuring whether failures arise from data properties or model limitations. Uncertainty decomposition-separating aleatoric from epistemic sources-is particularly crucial in this setting, yet existing methods, designed for standard generation tasks, fail to capture the unique dynamics of ICL. To address this, we introduce a concept of self-function vectors, built upon Bayesian views and the mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors leverage internal model representations to model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting, thereby enabling a direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework and circumventing the reliance on brittle input or decoding manipulations. Given the lack of established benchmarks and suitable evaluation protocols, we also propose the first and rigorous evaluation protocol, in which data is manipulated in controlled ways so as to quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely and separately from epistemic uncertainty. With this new evaluation framework, initially grounded in synthetic tasks for conceptual development and subsequently extended to real-world datasets, we show that our proposed methodology can measure uncertainty of LLM predictions made under ICL more reliably than existing alternative methods. Moreover, we show it can be used as a practical tool for trustworthy-related applications, such as hallucination detection. Our findings pave a new direction for connecting the quantitative view of uncertainty with the mechanistic understanding of model behavior.

</details>


### [11] [Granularity-Regulated Adaptive Computational Efficiency for Optimal Verification in Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19354)
*Ardit Krasniqi,Luan Vejsiu,Elira Dervishi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GRACE is a theoretical framework that identifies optimal verification granularity for test-time scaling as a function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. The paper proves a phase transition: fine-grained verification (PRMs) is optimal for hard problems or large compute budgets, while coarse-grained verification (ORMs) is optimal for easy problems or small budgets. An adaptive strategy achieves the Pareto frontier, with up to 3.1% improvement on math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on test-time scaling uses either coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) or fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) for verification, but neither is compute-optimal across all regimes. The fundamental question of what granularity of verification is optimal under a given compute budget remains unanswered.

Method: The authors propose GRACE, a unified theoretical framework that models optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of three variables: problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. They mathematically prove a phase transition between fine-grained and coarse-grained regimes, unify Best-of-N, beam search, and step-level MCTS under a single Pareto-optimality analysis, and derive an adaptive granularity strategy that switches between verification levels based on instance-level characteristics.

Result: Empirical validation on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks confirms all four theoretical claims. The adaptive granularity strategy outperforms fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1% accuracy at matched compute budgets.

Conclusion: There is no universally optimal verification granularity; optimal granularity depends systematically on problem difficulty, verifier quality, and compute budget. An adaptive strategy that dynamically adjusts granularity can provably achieve the compute-performance Pareto frontier, offering a principled approach to test-time scaling.

Abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs) by investing additional compute at inference time. A central component of TTS is the \emph{verifier}, which selects or scores candidate solutions to guide the search process. While prior work has explored the benefit of verification, a fundamental question remains underexplored: \emph{what is the optimal granularity of verification under a given compute budget?} Coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) and fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) represent two extremes, yet neither alone achieves compute-optimality across all regimes. In this paper, we establish a unified theoretical framework, called \textbf{GRACE} (\underline{G}ranularity-\underline{R}egulated \underline{A}daptive \underline{C}omputational \underline{E}fficiency), that characterizes the optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. We prove that there exists a phase transition: fine-grained verification dominates when either the compute budget is large or the problem is hard, whereas coarse-grained verification is preferred in the low-budget, easy-problem regime. Our theory unifies Best-of-$N$, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality framework, and motivates an adaptive granularity strategy that provably achieves the compute-performance Pareto frontier. Empirical results on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks corroborate all four theoretical claims, with our adaptive strategy outperforming fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1\% accuracy at matched compute.

</details>


### [12] [Trustworthy Multi-Agent Systems: Mitigating Semantic Drift with the Argent Signaling Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19356)
*Anantha Sharma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP) introduces structured quality signals (certainty, grounding, stochasticity, assumption index) into LLM outputs, enabling controllers to distinguish repairable failures from irredeemable ones. Evaluated on a legal document QA benchmark, ASP significantly improves pass rates and term coverage across multiple models, and in multi-agent mode blocks 100% of ungrounded outputs from propagating downstream.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multi-agent LLM systems treat all failures uniformly with naive retry strategies, without distinguishing between repairable failures (incomplete but grounded) and containment failures (ungrounded). This leaves human supervisors unable to determine whether retrying is appropriate or the system should halt.

Method: The Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP) is a compact machine-readable header accompanying AI-generated responses. It encodes four structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index that classifies the evidentiary basis of each claim. A controller uses these signals to route repairable failures to retry and containment failures to halt. Evaluated in two modes: (1) standalone — 27-question document-grounded QA over a legal contract, comparing baseline prompts vs. ASP-instrumented controllers across three local GGUF models (Qwen 0.8B, Dobby 8B, SmolLM3 3B); (2) multi-agent — an ASP sidecar placed between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent to filter ungrounded outputs.

Result: Standalone mode: Qwen 0.8B pass rate improved from 11.1% to 33.3%, mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; Dobby 8B achieved 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; SmolLM3 3B alternated between repair and containment per question. Aggregate passes rose from 12/81 to 21/81. Multi-agent mode: the ASP sidecar blocked 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs (24/27 blocked, zero ungrounded propagations).

Conclusion: ASP provides an effective, lightweight mechanism for distinguishing failure modes in LLM outputs, enabling targeted repair of salvageable answers while preventing ungrounded responses from propagating, thereby improving both overall system reliability and human oversight efficiency.

Abstract: When multi-agent LLM systems produce bad answers, not all failures are equal: some answers are grounded in the right material but incomplete, while others are simply ungrounded and should be stopped. Current retry strategies treat both cases identically (try again and hope for the best), leaving human supervisors unable to tell whether a retry was warranted or whether the system should have halted instead.
  We introduce the Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP), a compact machine-readable header that accompanies every AI-generated response with structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index that classifies the evidentiary basis of each claim. These signals enable a controller to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures and route each case differently.
  We evaluate ASP in two modes. In standalone mode, a 27-question document-grounded QA benchmark over the Array BioPharma/Ono license agreement compares baseline prompts against ASP-instrumented controller actions across three local GGUF models. On Qwen~(0.8B), ASP improves pass rate from 11.1% to 33.3% and mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; on Dobby~(8B), ASP produces 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; on SmolLM3~(3B), ASP alternates between repair and containment per question. Aggregate improvement is meaningful (12/81 to 21/81 passes). In multi-agent mode, an ASP sidecar sits between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent; the sidecar blocks 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs from reaching the downstream agent (24/27 blocked, 0 ungrounded propagations).

</details>


### [13] [When Does Streaming Tool Use Help? Characterizing Tool-Intent Stabilization in Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20113)
*Elroy Galbraith*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Streaming RAG hides tool latency by issuing speculative queries during user input; this paper quantifies "tool-intent stabilization" — the point where speculative retrieval converges to the correct result — on the CRAG benchmark. At realistic settings (L=600ms, δ=3w/s), 73.9% of queries admit substantial latency hiding, with early stabilization predictable by question type, providing a model-agnostic framework for optimizing streaming RAG without training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work reports only aggregate latency gains for Streaming RAG, but the benefit is fundamentally query-intrinsic: speculation only helps when the correct tool query becomes determinable before input ends. The authors aim to isolate, measure, and bound this property — tool-intent stabilization — to understand when and why streaming speculation succeeds, without requiring model training or specialized hardware.

Method: Using the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions), the authors: (1) measure the distribution of tool-intent stabilization points across queries; (2) derive a model-agnostic upper bound H on hidable latency as a function of tool latency L, input cadence δ, and a confidence threshold θ; (3) validate against a working streaming pipeline to confirm realized savings meet/exceed the bound; and (4) conduct statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis, epsilon-squared effect size) to identify query properties (specifically question type) that predict early vs. late stabilization. The analysis runs on commodity CPU.

Result: At operating point L=600ms, δ=3 words/second, θ=0.8: 73.9% of all CRAG queries admit substantial latency hiding. This blends two regimes — on the 21.3% of questions where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable, 95.2% are streamable (φ_suf bracketed to [0.26, 0.281], indicating early stabilization). On the remainder, a grounding-free top-1-settling fallback applies. Question type yields a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, ε²=0.04), informing cost-benefit analysis for learned speculative triggers.

Conclusion: Tool-intent stabilization is measurable and predictable without training. The derived bound H provides a principled ceiling on streaming RAG's latency-hiding potential. The bimodal distribution of stabilization (favorable vs. unfavorable queries) and the predictive signal from question type suggest that lightweight, model-agnostic routing — triggering speculation only when early stabilization is likely — can optimize the cost-latency tradeoff in production streaming RAG systems.

Abstract: Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Streaming RAG) reduces user-perceived latency by issuing tool queries in parallel with ongoing user input, before the utterance is complete. Reported gains are aggregate, yet the mechanism's benefit is fundamentally query-intrinsic: speculation can only help when the correct tool query becomes determinable before the user stops speaking or typing. We isolate and measure this property -- tool-intent stabilization, the point in the input stream at which a speculative query's retrieval converges to the answer-bearing result. On the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions) we (i) measure the distribution of stabilization, (ii) derive a model-agnostic bound H on the portion of tool latency that can be hidden behind the user's remaining input, as a function of tool latency L and input cadence δ, (iii) validate against a working streaming pipeline that realized savings meet or exceed this bound, and (iv) identify which query properties predict early versus late stabilization. The study requires no model training and runs on commodity CPU hardware. We find that at a realistic operating point (L=600ms, δ=3w/s, θ=0.8), 73.9% of queries across the full benchmark admit substantial latency hiding -- a blended figure that mixes sufficiency stabilization on the 21.3% of questions where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable (95.2% streamable on this favorable slice) with a grounding-free top-1-settling fallback on the remainder. On the favorable slice, φ_suf is bracketed to [0.26, 0.281] by exact and relaxed grounding -- both early. Question type produces a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, epsilon^2=0.04), directly informing when a learned speculative trigger is worth its cost.

</details>


### [14] [Characterizing Narrative Content in Web-scale LLM Pretraining Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19468)
*Teagan Johnson,Elliott Ash,Andrew Piper,Maria Antoniak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: First large-scale fine-grained analysis of narrative features (agency, setting, events) in LLM pretraining corpora, using a custom-trained RoBERTa model (NarraBERT) on 3M passages from the Dolma corpus, revealing measurable multidimensional narrative structure that is unequally distributed across sources and topics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite narrative being a fundamental mode of human communication, the narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora has remained largely unexplored. Current data curation practices fail to measure or account for narrative qualities, leaving a critical gap in understanding how pretraining data composition affects downstream narrative reasoning capabilities.

Method: The authors design a framework grounded in narrative theory covering three core elements — agency, setting, and events — operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. They sample and manually annotate 400 diverse passages, then fine-tune NarraBERT (RoBERTa-based) on these annotations. NarraBERT is applied to 3 million passages from the Dolma corpus to produce NarraDolma, a large-scale dataset of narrative feature predictions.

Result: Three key findings: (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across highly heterogeneous web data; (ii) a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlies web text, rather than discrete categories; (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics, a factor current curation practices neither measure nor account for.

Conclusion: The framework, NarraDolma dataset, and NarraBERT model provide a foundation for analyzing narrative quality distributions in LLM pretraining data and for investigating how data composition influences narrative reasoning performance. All artifacts are publicly released.

Abstract: The narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored even though narrative is a fundamental mode of human communication. We present the first fine-grained study of narrative features in Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open pretraining corpus. Drawing on narrative theory, we design a framework spanning three core narrative elements (agency, setting, and events) operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. After sampling and annotating a diverse set of 400 passages, we finetune and validate NarraBERT, a RoBERTa-based model for fine-grained narrative prediction. We apply NarraBERT to 3M passages, resulting in a new dataset, NarraDolma. We find (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data, (ii) we uncover a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlying web text, and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics in ways that current curation practices neither measure nor account for. Our framework, dataset, and analyses provide a foundation for understanding how narrative qualities are distributed in LLM pretraining data and for studying how data composition affects narrative reasoning tasks. We publicly release NarraDolma and NarraBERT.

</details>


### [15] [Creating Multilingual Mental Health Dialogue Datasets: Limits of Persona-Based Localization via Nationality and Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19640)
*Yunkai Xu,Saeed Abdullah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper examines whether English-centric clinical persona generation methods can be adapted for multilingual mental health datasets (Mandarin, Bengali, Hindi). Results show that simply modifying nationality and language parameters introduces clinical inconsistencies, and LLM judges exhibit accuracy degradation in non-English depression severity assessment, highlighting the need for culturally responsive data generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a critical shortage of high-quality multilingual datasets for training and evaluating AI/LLM-based mental health support systems. While synthetic clinical persona generation is increasingly used to address data scarcity, existing validated approaches are predominantly English-centric, leaving a gap in understanding whether these methods generalize across languages and cultural contexts.

Method: The authors modified nationality and language parameters in existing clinical personas to generate synthetic mental health dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. They then evaluated how different LLMs perform as judges when assessing depression severity in these multilingual datasets, using English as the baseline for comparison.

Result: Simply adding nationality and language parameters proved inadequate, introducing clinical inconsistencies across languages. LLM judge models exhibited inaccuracies when evaluating depression severity in non-English texts, with performance varying significantly across different models, exposing systemic limitations of English-centric persona approaches in multilingual contexts.

Conclusion: There is an urgent need for culturally responsive data generation methodologies rather than superficial parameter adjustments. Equitable global mental health AI systems require approaches that fundamentally account for linguistic and cultural differences, rather than simply extending English-centric frameworks to other languages.

Abstract: AI and large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools to address global mental health challenges. Despite the global nature of these challenges, there remains a critical shortage of high-quality datasets for training and evaluating such systems. To mitigate this gap, researchers increasingly generate synthetic clinical personas to simulate user data and test digital mental health support systems. However, most validated personas rely on English-centric contexts. This paper investigates whether similar persona-based methods can be used to generate multilingual mental health datasets. We modified nationality and language parameters in personas to generate clinical dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. We then examined how different LLMs perform when evaluating the depression severity of these generated multilingual datasets against the baseline in English. Our findings indicate that just adding nationality and language parameters in personas might not be adequate, as it can introduce clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judge models often exhibit inaccuracies in assessing depression severity in non-English texts, with performance varying across different models. This exposes the systemic limitations of applying English-centric personas to multilingual contexts. Ultimately, our work highlights the urgent need for culturally responsive data generation to ensure equitable mental health systems globally.

</details>


### [16] [Reliability without Validity: A Systematic, Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge Models Across Agreement, Consistency, and Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19544)
*Justin D. Norman,Michael U. Rivera,D. Alex Hughes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A large-scale evaluation of 21 LLM judges reveals that standard exact-match agreement overstates performance; Cohen's kappa drops 33–41 pp, judge rankings shift up to 14 positions, and a consistency–bias paradox emerges where high test–retest reliability coexists with severe position bias. The authors propose a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge is widely adopted, but validation relies on exact-match agreement, which fails to correct for chance and inflates perceived discriminative ability. There is no rigorous, standardized validation protocol, risking unreliable judge selection in practice.

Method: The authors conduct the largest systematic evaluation to date: 21 judges from 9 providers, tested across MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench. Three protocols are applied — agreement (exact match vs. Cohen's kappa), consistency (test–retest reliability), and bias audit (position bias, verbosity bias) — totaling 118 runs and ~541,000 individual judgments.

Result: Four key findings: (1) kappa deflation is universal (33–41 pp drop on MT-Bench); (2) judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks; (3) two production-deployed judges exhibit a consistency–bias paradox: test–retest reliability >0.95 yet position bias >0.10; (4) verbosity bias is small (<0.011) under a single pairwise rubric.

Conclusion: Exact-match agreement systematically overstates judge quality. A Minimum Viable Validation Protocol incorporating Cohen's kappa, multi-benchmark ranking, test–retest reliability, and bias auditing is essential for trustworthy LLM judge evaluation and deployment.

Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for language models, but judge validation in practice relies on exact-match agreement, a metric that does not correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability. We present the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge to date: 21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench, evaluated under three protocols (agreement, consistency, bias audit) over 118 runs and approximately 541,000 individual judgments. Four findings emerge, consistent across the full cohort, including the April 2026 frontier: kappa deflation between exact match and Cohen's kappa is universal (33--41 pp on MT-Bench), judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks, high test--retest reliability (>0.95) coexists with severe position bias (>0.10) in two production-deployed judges (instantiating a consistency--bias paradox), and verbosity bias is small (<0.011) across our cohort under a single pairwise rubric. We distill these into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.

</details>


### [17] [Beyond Uniform Forgetting: A Study of Sequential Direct Preference Optimization Across Preference Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19744)
*Pranav Bhandari,Nicolas Fay,Amitava Datta,Usman Naseem,Mehwish Nasim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether sequential DPO training uniformly degrades earlier-learned preferences. Across four settings with varying objective relationships, it finds no single forgetting pattern: outcomes range from degradation to stability or positive transfer, depending on objective compatibility, signal strength, and training order. Mechanistic analysis reveals near-orthogonal gradients between stages, suggesting gradient opposition is not the primary driver of forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practical alignment of language models often requires multiple behavioural objectives applied sequentially via DPO. However, it is unclear whether later training uniformly degrades earlier preferences or whether the effect depends on the relationship between objectives. The paper aims to characterise this relationship systematically.

Method: The authors conduct sequential DPO experiments using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters across four preference settings: distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. All objectives are evaluated after every stage using a fixed base-model reference. Analysis includes aggregate metrics, pair-level length-normalised policy margins, quartile decomposition, and mechanistic diagnostics examining gradient and adapter update orthogonality between stages.

Result: Sequential DPO does not produce a uniform forgetting pattern. Depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order, outcomes include partial degradation, stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer. Pair-level analysis reveals that aggregate metrics mask heterogeneous changes; high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve by setting. Mechanistic diagnostics show Stage 2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective, providing little evidence that direct gradient opposition drives forgetting.

Conclusion: Future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength rather than assuming later objectives uniformly affect earlier preferences. The absence of gradient opposition as a primary driver suggests other mechanisms underlie preference forgetting in sequential DPO.

Abstract: Aligning language models with human preferences often requires optimising multiple behavioural objectives. A practical approach is to apply these objectives sequentially using preference optimisation methods such as Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO), but it remains unclear whether later training uniformly degrades preferences learned earlier or whether the effect depends on the relationship between objectives. We study sequential DPO across four preference settings covering distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters, we evaluate all objectives after every stage with a fixed base-model reference. We find that sequential DPO does not produce a single forgetting pattern; preference change ranges from partial degradation to stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order. Pair-level analysis using length-normalised policy margins shows that aggregate metrics can mask heterogeneous changes across preference pairs, whereas quartile decomposition reveals that high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve depending on the setting. Mechanistic diagnostics show that Stage~2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective across all settings, providing little evidence that direct gradient opposition is the primary driver. These findings suggest that future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength, rather than assuming that later objectives affect earlier preferences uniformly.

</details>


### [18] [LaViSA: A Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19552)
*Lee Sangmyeong,Shun Inadumi,Koichiro Yoshino*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LaViSA is a new benchmark for evaluating how well Vision-Language Models (VLMs) resolve structural ambiguity in sentences using visual context. Testing across seven ambiguity categories reveals that while VLMs show some ability, they still struggle with subtle semantic distinctions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structural ambiguity—where a sentence has multiple valid syntactic parses—poses a fundamental challenge for language understanding. Visual scenes can disambiguate such sentences, yet no standardized benchmark exists to measure how well VLMs leverage visual context for this purpose.

Method: The authors introduce LaViSA, a curated benchmark containing ambiguous sentences paired with their disambiguated counterparts and corresponding images, spanning seven ambiguity categories. They evaluate a diverse set of VLMs—both proprietary and open-source, across parameter scales and reasoning capabilities—on this benchmark.

Result: VLMs demonstrate some capacity to use visual scenes for structural disambiguation, but performance remains limited, particularly on certain ambiguity types and cases requiring fine-grained visual-semantic distinctions.

Conclusion: Current VLMs still exhibit significant limitations in resolving structural ambiguity via visual cues, highlighting the need for further advances in multimodal semantic understanding.

Abstract: Structural ambiguity arises when a single sentence admits multiple valid interpretations due to its syntactic structure, posing a fundamental challenge for language understanding. Visual scenes serve as useful cues for resolving such ambiguity, and Vision and Language Models (VLMs) need to be capable of deriving possible semantic interpretations from visual scenes. We introduce Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity (LaViSA), a benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of VLMs to resolve structural ambiguity leveraging visual scenes. LaViSA consists of ambiguous sentences, their disambiguated sentences, and corresponding images of these disambiguated sentences across seven ambiguity categories. Using LaViSA, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of diverse VLMs, including both proprietary and open-source models with varying parameter scales and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that although recent VLMs can leverage visual scenes to resolve structural ambiguity to a some extent, they still struggle with certain ambiguity types and visually subtle semantic distinctions, indicating remaining limitations in resolving structural ambiguity using visual scenes.

</details>


### [19] [A BART-based approach with hierarchical strategy for Vietnamese abstractive multi-document summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19591)
*Vu Nguyen Nguyen Xuan,Huy Ngo Quang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a hierarchical approach for Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization, introducing a novel golden-summary-driven document shortening strategy. It achieves a ROUGE2-F1 of 0.2468 on the VLSP 2022 shared task and releases additional training data for the community.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization introduced in the VLSP 2022 shared task, with a focus on improving the correlation between the document condensing and summarization stages in hierarchical approaches, and mitigating the data scarcity problem for Vietnamese.

Method: A hierarchical approach with two stages: (1) condense each individual document, (2) aggregate the condensed documents and generate a summary. The key innovation is a novel document shortening strategy that uses the golden (reference) summary to guide which content to retain, ensuring high semantic correlation between the two stages. External data sources are also leveraged to augment the training dataset.

Result: The method achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP public test set and produces fluent, concise summaries.

Conclusion: The proposed golden-summary-driven shortening strategy effectively bridges the gap between document encoding and summary generation in hierarchical summarization. The release of additional training data further supports Vietnamese multi-document summarization research.

Abstract: In this technical report, we focus on solving the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization, introduced in the International Workshop on Vietnamese Language and Speech Processing (VLSP) 2022. We choose to follow the popular hierarchical approach, i.e. condensing each document followed by aggregation and summarization. We propose a novel yet simple strategy to shorten documents that is driven by the golden summary, thus ensuring high correlation between stages of the hierarchical approach. Our method achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP's public test set, and can produce fluent and concise summaries. Additionally, we utilize external sources for extra data, which greatly enhances the quantity of data for Vietnamese multi-document summarization. The additional data is made available for the community.

</details>


### [20] [Where Does Social Reasoning Come From? Capability Provenance in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19625)
*Glenn Matlin,Chandreyi Chakraborty,Saehee Eom,Mika Okamoto,Rayan Castilla,Louis Jaburi,Alvin Deng,Taywon Min,Lucia Quirke,Stella Biderman,Mark Riedl*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper uses training-data attribution to map which regions of the pretraining corpus support social reasoning versus STEM reasoning in OLMo3-7B, finding qualitatively distinct corpus regions for each, with sharper contrast at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior training-data attribution work emphasizes factual knowledge rather than reasoning, and document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities. The authors aim to bridge this gap by using attribution as an interpretable tool for discovering which pretraining data regions support distinct reasoning capabilities.

Method: Gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) is computed over a working set from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix. Influence is aggregated across WebOrganizer's 24-format × 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins). A 2×2 design contrasts benchmark pairs varying domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA & MMLU Social Sciences vs. ARC-Challenge & MMLU STEM. Targeted machine unlearning is used for partial causal validation.

Result: Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, with the contrast sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted unlearning of high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines.

Conclusion: Training-data attribution can serve as an effective interpretable tool for capability discovery, revealing that different reasoning capabilities rely on distinct pretraining data regions. All code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints are open-sourced.

Abstract: We use training-data attribution as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, mapping which regions of the pretraining corpus support social-reasoning versus STEM-reasoning in OLMo3-7B. Training-data attribution measures how strongly each training document influences a model's predictions on a benchmark, but document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities, and prior work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning. We compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) over a working set drawn from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix, aggregate influence across WebOrganizer's 24-format x 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins), and contrast benchmark pairs in a 2x2 design that varies domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences against ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, and the contrast is sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted machine unlearning provides partial causal validation: forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, and we open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

</details>


### [21] [Your Mouse and Eyes Secretly Leak Your Preference: LLM Alignment using Implicit Feedback from Users](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20482)
*Haw-Shiuan Chang,Jeffrey Gomez,Mehul Patwari,Aryan Sajith,Hamed Zamani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces IFLLM, a dataset capturing implicit human feedback (mouse trajectories, eye gaze) during LLM interactions, and demonstrates that incorporating this implicit feedback into reward models improves preference prediction accuracy from 55% to 64% and nearly triples DPO-based response quality gains across eight LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM alignment methods rely on explicit human feedback, which is expensive to collect and rarely provided by users in practice. Moreover, these methods fail to leverage implicit feedback signals (e.g., gaze patterns, cursor movements) that major Internet platforms already exploit. The authors aim to quantify the alignment value of such implicit behavioral signals.

Method: The authors built IFLLM, a dataset of 1,336 multi-turn questions collected from 59 Mechanical Turk workers. During interactions, they recorded mouse trajectories and webcam-based eye-gazing points as users read LLM responses. They then trained a reward model incorporating these implicit signals alongside text-based features and evaluated it using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) across eight LLMs.

Result: The implicit-feedback-based reward model improved preference prediction accuracy from 55% (text-only) to 64%. When used with DPO, it nearly tripled the relative improvement in response quality across eight LLMs. The dataset also revealed substantial diversity in users' gazing behaviors and mouse trajectory patterns.

Conclusion: Implicit human feedback — specifically eye gaze and mouse trajectories — carries significant signal for LLM alignment, substantially outperforming text-only reward models. This suggests that leveraging passively collected behavioral data can be a cost-effective and powerful complement to explicit human annotations for aligning LLMs.

Abstract: To align a Large Language Model (LLM), most existing methods collect explicit human feedback and train a reward model to predict the human preference based on the response text. These existing methods have two key limitations. First, the users rarely provide explicit feedback for LLM responses, which makes the high-quality preference annotation expensive to collect. Second, the methods do not leverage implicit human feedback, which has proven vital to the economic moats of Internet giants. To quantify the value of implicit feedback, we build a new dataset called IFLLM, which collects 1336 multi-turn questions from the 59 Mechanical Turk workers, their mouse trajectories, and eye gazing points to the LLMs' responses from their webcams. IFLLM shows that the users have very diverse types of gazing behavior and mouse trajectories. Our reward model based on the implicit user feedback boosts the accuracy of the text-based reward model from 55% to 64% and nearly triples the relative response quality improvements after applying the DPO to eight LLMs, demonstrating the value of implicit feedback in the wild. Our data collection website, dataset, and codes can be found at https://github.com/themehulpatwari/llm-implicit-feedback/.

</details>


### [22] [Before the Labels: How Dataset Construction Shapes Suicidality Detection in Clinical Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19637)
*Priyanshi Garg,Ishita Rao,Jieqiong Ding,Amandalynne Paullada*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EHR-based suicidality datasets embed specific operational assumptions about suicidality — who documents it, how episodes are defined, and how ambiguity is handled. Using the ScAN dataset as a case study, the authors demonstrate that governance, cohort selection, annotation practices, and aggregation strategies produce labels that obscure heterogeneous clinical framings, urging the NLP community to critically examine these assumptions before treating such labels as ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical NLP treats EHR-derived suicidality labels as reliable ground truth, but this uncritical acceptance masks the constructed nature of these labels. The authors seek to surface how dataset design choices embed a particular operationalization of suicidality that may not reflect clinical reality, using ScAN (built on MIMIC-III) as a concrete case study.

Method: A qualitative, argument-driven case study of the ScAN dataset. The authors examine four layers of construction: (1) governance constraints shaping what data is available, (2) ICD-code-based cohort selection, (3) single-annotator labeling practices, and (4) hospital-stay-level aggregation. They complement this with a linguistic analysis of the labeled data, showing how identical labels encompass divergent clinical framings that differ along dimensions of temporality, negation, and uncertainty.

Result: The analysis reveals that ScAN labels reflect clinician-documented judgments rather than direct patient reports, treat suicidality as a bounded episode delimited by hospital stay, and assume intent can be reliably inferred from documentation. The linguistic analysis demonstrates that identical labels subsume heterogeneous framings, including negated mentions, historical events, uncertain statements, and hypotheticals — all collapsed into the same label.

Conclusion: Clinical NLP must move beyond treating EHR-derived suicidality labels as transparent ground truth and instead interrogate the assumptions embedded in dataset construction. Failure to do so risks building models that reproduce narrow, institutionally-shaped operationalizations of suicidality rather than capturing its clinical complexity.

Abstract: Clinical NLP increasingly relies on electronic health record (EHR) data to detect suicidal behaviors, treating clinical documentation as more reliable ground truth than social media. We argue that this framing obscures how EHR-based suicidality datasets encode a particular operationalization of suicidality, shaped by who authors the data, how episodes are bounded, and how ambiguity is resolved. We ground this argument in a case study of the ScAN dataset, built over MIMIC-III clinical notes. We show how governance constraints, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling, and hospital-stay-level aggregation produce labels that reflect clinician-documented judgments, treat suicidality as a bounded episode, and assume that intent can be reliably inferred from documentation. A linguistic analysis demonstrates that identical labels subsume heterogeneous clinical framings differing in temporality, negation, and uncertainty. We argue that clinical NLP should examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before interpreting their labels as ground truth.

</details>


### [23] [MiqraBERT: Regression-Based Sentence-BERT Finetuning for Biblical Hebrew Parallel Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19638)
*David M. Smiley*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MiqraBERT is a Sentence-BERT model finetuned on Biblical Hebrew verse pairs for semantic similarity, improving distributional separation 2.7-fold over baselines and achieving 87.1% recall@10 for narrative parallels, though poetic parallels remain challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing computational methods for detecting textual reuse in the Hebrew Bible rely on lexical overlap and fail when parallels involve paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. A semantics-aware model is needed to capture these non-literal parallels.

Method: MiqraBERT finetunes AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) into a Sentence-BERT architecture using a training set of 1,650 labeled verse and half-verse pairs (825 true parallels from Chronicles synoptic material and poetic parallelism studies, balanced with 825 random negatives). Training uses cosine-similarity regression. Evaluation employs Wasserstein distance and overlap coefficient across ten random seeds to measure distributional separation between parallel and non-parallel pair embeddings.

Result: MiqraBERT yields a 2.7-fold improvement in distributional separation over the pre-trained baseline and reduces the ambiguous overlap region from ~24% to ~6%. Narrative synoptic parallels achieve 87.1% recall@10, while poetic parallels remain under 9% recall.

Conclusion: The model is reliable for narrative textual reuse detection but not for poetic parallels, revealing a genre-dependent asymmetry. The authors release MiqraBERT publicly on Hugging Face.

Abstract: Textual reuse pervades the Hebrew Bible, yet the computational methods used to detect it still rest largely on lexical overlap, and they falter once a parallel involves paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. This paper introduces MiqraBERT, a Sentence-BERT model finetuned from AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) for verse-level semantic similarity in Biblical Hebrew. The training set comprises 1,650 labeled verse and half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels drawn from the Chronicles synoptic material and from foundational studies of poetic parallelism, balanced against 825 randomly sampled negatives. Through cosine-similarity regression, the model learns an embedding space in which parallel verses cluster together and unrelated verses move apart. We evaluate separation with distribution-based metrics, Wasserstein distance and the overlap coefficient, across ten random seeds. MiqraBERT improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over the pre-trained baseline and reduces the ambiguous overlap region from roughly 24% to about 6%. Narrative synoptic parallels reach a recall@10 of 87.1%; poetic parallels remain difficult, below 9%. This genre-dependent asymmetry confines the model's reliable scope to narrative textual reuse. MiqraBERT is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/davidmsmiley/MiqraBERT

</details>


### [24] [From 50K to 8.2 Million in 24 Hours: Vozinha's Algorithmic Consecration and the Multilingual Making of World Cup Visibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19647)
*Vinicius Covas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A multilingual discourse analysis of how four languages differently framed the viral rise of Cape Verdean goalkeeper Vozinha after a 2026 World Cup draw, treating the follower-count leap ("50k to 8M") as a narratable linguistic object and introducing a reproducible frame-annotation pipeline with LLM-assisted suggestion and human validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To examine how distinct languages construct divergent narratives around the same algorithmic consecration event — a peripheral athlete's sudden platform visibility — and to provide a structured, reproducible methodology for cross-lingual computational discourse analysis that treats follower counts as circulating linguistic objects rather than neutral metrics.

Method: The authors built a multilingual corpus (Portuguese, Spanish, English, French) and developed a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based frame annotation. They used an LLM-assisted suggestion pipeline combined with human validation for annotation. The follower-growth timeline was reconstructed conservatively as a phased structure (not a continuous API stream), with each datapoint typed by value class, confidence, and evidence type. Only one exact anchor point (8,235,652 followers at a precise UTC timestamp) was scraped directly; all other figures are estimated ranges or thresholds.
