Result: Distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese discourse emphasized mobilization, Spanish discourse focused on crisis, English discourse centered on nation-making, and all languages shared a platform-metric spectacle frame through which peripheral athletic performance achieved global visibility. The study releases the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline as a v0.1 pilot.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates the viability of treating platform metrics as narratable linguistic objects in cross-lingual discourse analysis, while acknowledging it as a pilot study that defers full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement to planned future work.

Abstract: We present a multilingual computational discourse analysis of how language constructed the algorithmic consecration of Vozinha, the 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper, after Spain 0-0 Cape Verde at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The study contributes a multilingual corpus in Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French; a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based frame annotation; a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestion with human validation; and an analysis of cross-lingual narrative diffusion across discourse phases. We treat the platform follower count itself, narrated as "50k to 8M", as a linguistic object: a circulating and narratable proof of visibility rather than a mere measurement. The follower-growth timeline is used only as contextual metadata: we reconstruct a conservative phase structure, not a continuous API-native series, and type every datapoint by value class, confidence, and evidence type. The only exact primary scraper anchor is 8,235,652 followers at 2026-06-16 15:47 UTC; all other figures are reported as estimated ranges or thresholds, including an estimated pre-match baseline of 45k-56k. Findings suggest that distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese mobilization, Spanish crisis, English nation-making, and a shared platform-metric spectacle through which peripheral athletic performance became globally visible. As a v0.1 pilot, the paper releases the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline, while flagging full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement as planned work.

</details>


### [25] [SAGE-OPD: Selective Agent-Guided Intervention for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19659)
*Yuhang Zhou,Lizhu Zhang,Yifan Wu,Mingyi Wang,Bo Peng,Jiayi Liu,Xiangjun Fan,Zhuokai Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SAGE-OPD introduces a selective intervention framework for multi-turn on-policy distillation that uses teacher judgment to decide when to intervene, weights distillation by teacher confidence, and normalizes loss to improve agent performance, achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement on ALFWorld.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) is designed for single-turn settings and becomes brittle in multi-turn agent scenarios, where early errors compound, dense token-level supervision over-penalizes valid alternatives, reinforces local degeneracies, and propagates unreliable teacher guidance on off-distribution histories.

Method: SAGE-OPD is a verifier-free framework with three components: (1) turn-level selective intervention using environment feedback and teacher judgment to decide whether to skip or intervene on each student response; (2) teacher confidence weighting to reduce influence of uncertain distributions on corrupted/ambiguous histories; (3) loss normalization that preserves overall loss scale while retaining selective turn-level weighting.

Result: SAGE-OPD consistently improves over baselines, achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablations confirm that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization each provide complementary benefits.

Conclusion: Effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy but allocate teacher supervision selectively to turns where intervention is both necessary and reliable.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves student models by training them on trajectories induced by their own policy, making it a promising approach for mitigating exposure bias in agent training. However, most OPD studies focus on single-turn settings, while realistic LLM agents interact with environments over multiple turns. In this regime, early errors can alter future observations and compound across the trajectory, and standard dense token-level OPD becomes brittle, as it may over-penalize semantically valid alternatives, reinforce local degeneracies such as repeated actions, and propagate unreliable teacher supervision on off-distribution histories. We propose SAGE-OPD, a verifier-free selective intervention framework specifically designed for multi-turn OPD. Instead of applying teacher supervision uniformly across all turns, SAGE-OPD first observes environment feedback and uses teacher judgment to decide whether each student response should be skipped or intervened on. To further address compounding errors, SAGE-OPD weights token-level distillation by teacher confidence, reducing the influence of uncertain teacher distributions on corrupted or ambiguous histories. Finally, SAGE-OPD applies loss normalization to preserve the overall loss scale of standard OPD while retaining selective turn-level weighting. Experiments on agent tasks show that SAGE-OPD consistently improves over baselines, achieving up to a 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies further demonstrate that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization provide complementary benefits. Our results suggest that effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision should be selectively allocated to turns where intervention is necessary and reliable.

</details>


### [26] [CacheWeaver: Cache-Aware Evidence Ordering for Efficient Grounded RAG Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19667)
*Kaizhen Tan,Rong Gu,Mingyuan Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CacheWeaver is a lightweight prompt-layer method that reorders retrieved evidence to maximize prefix cache reuse in RAG systems, achieving 20–33% reduction in time-to-first-token without degrading answer quality, by greedily scheduling evidence sequences based on a prefix tree of recently served requests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG improves factual accuracy but increases prompt length and prefill cost. Existing prefix caching (e.g., vLLM) only works when requests share identical token prefixes. In practice, adjacent RAG queries retrieve overlapping evidence sets but in different orders, so the set-level overlap fails to translate into reusable prefix overlap. The gap between evidence overlap and cache reuse motivates a scheduling layer that reorders evidence for cache locality.

Method: CacheWeaver maintains a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences. For each incoming query with retrieved evidence, it performs a greedy walk on this tree to select an evidence ordering that maximizes the length of the shared prefix with previously cached sequences. The serving engine and the retrieved evidence set remain unchanged; only the order of evidence chunks in the prompt is rearranged.

Result: Across three vLLM configurations, CacheWeaver reduces median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by approximately 20–33% relative to retrieval-order prefix caching. The greedy policy achieves 97.5% of the median TTFT gain attainable by an oracle ordering, demonstrating that most reusable prefix locality is recoverable. Answer quality in QA evaluations remains unaffected.

Conclusion: A simple, non-invasive scheduling layer placed between retrieval and inference can recover most of the prefix-cache reuse potential lost due to arbitrary evidence ordering. CacheWeaver demonstrates that reordering evidence for cache locality is both effective and orthogonal to the underlying serving engine, offering a practical path to lower prefill latency in RAG pipelines.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual grounding, but it also lengthens prompts and raises prefill cost. Prefix caching in serving engines such as vLLM reduces this cost only when requests share the same token prefix. In grounded generation, however, adjacent queries may retrieve overlapping evidence in different orders, so set overlap does not become reusable prefix overlap. We present CacheWeaver, a lightweight prompt-layer method for cache-aware evidence ordering. The method keeps a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences and uses a greedy walk to place the most reusable prefix first, while leaving the serving engine and retrieved evidence set unchanged. Across three vLLM configurations, the method lowers median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by about 20-33 percent relative to retrieval-order prefix caching, without hurting answer quality in our QA tests. The greedy policy reaches 97.5 percent of the median TTFT gain from oracle ordering, indicating that most reusable prefix locality can be recovered by a simple scheduling layer between retrieval and inference.

</details>


### [27] [Code-Switching Reveals Language Anchoring in Multilingual LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19668)
*Jeonghyun Park,Seunghyun Yoon,Yonghyun Jun,Hwanhee Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Multilingual LLMs degrade on code-switched inputs. The paper introduces Anchor Bias, a geometric measure showing that target-framed code-switching shifts representations away from the source language, causing larger QA drops. The proposed CANVAS method steers target-language hidden states toward source anchors during inference, recovering performance across models and CS conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual LLMs exhibit performance degradation when processing code-switched (CS) inputs compared to monolingual inputs, but the representational mechanisms underlying this degradation are poorly understood. The authors aim to diagnose and mitigate this failure mode.

Method: (1) Grammar-forced CS is used as a controlled diagnostic setting. (2) Anchor Bias, a geometric measure quantifying whether a CS hidden state is closer to its source- or target-language counterpart, is introduced. (3) CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering) is proposed as an inference-time intervention that extracts a source-side anchor from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward it during prefill.

Result: Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS remains source-anchored, while target-framed CS shifts target-ward and exhibits larger QA degradation. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across diverse MLLMs and CS conditions.

Conclusion: Internal anchoring signals, as captured by Anchor Bias, provide a geometrically interpretable and actionable target for mitigating code-switching inference failures in multilingual LLMs, demonstrating that representation-level steering can effectively address this robustness gap.

Abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to handle Code-Switched (CS) inputs, yet mixing languages frequently degrades performance relative to source- or target-language monolingual counterparts. To understand this degradation, we use grammar-forced CS as a controlled diagnostic setting for locating CS representations relative to their source and target counterparts. We introduce Anchor Bias, a geometric measure that quantifies language anchoring, whether a CS hidden state aligns closer to its source or target language counterpart. Across diverse MLLMs, Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS stays source-anchored, whereas target-framed CS shifts target-ward and shows larger Question Answering (QA) degradation. Motivated by this representational pattern, we propose CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering), an inference-time intervention that extracts a source-side canvas from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during prefill. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across MLLMs and CS conditions, showing that internal anchoring signals provide an actionable target for mitigating CS inference failures.

</details>


### [28] [What sentiment analysis can't see: Measuring whether customers were helped, and what went wrong, across 70,000 support conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19698)
*Jason Potteiger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that LLM-based annotation (GPT-5.4) of customer support conversations can capture customer satisfaction and problem flags far more accurately than traditional sentiment analysis, revealing that tone and satisfaction disagree 44% of the time and uncovering a large "tolerated friction" segment invisible to sentiment-based dashboards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sentiment analysis, the industry standard for analyzing customer support at scale, measures linguistic tone rather than actual customer satisfaction or whether problems were resolved. This creates a fundamental blind spot: tone and satisfaction often diverge, and sentiment-based metrics cannot surface actionable business intelligence about fixable problems or customer states beyond emotional valence.

Method: The authors analyzed 70,450 support conversations from an online fundraising platform using three readings: (1) traditional sentiment analysis (tone), (2) GPT-5.4-estimated customer satisfaction, and (3) GPT-5.4-flagged concrete problem reports. All three were validated against ground-truth 1-to-5 customer ratings on rated conversations. Correlational and false-alarm analyses compared satisfaction estimates against sentiment baselines, and disagreement patterns between tone and satisfaction were catalogued.

Result: Satisfaction estimates correlated with customer ratings at 0.47 vs. 0.36 for sentiment, with substantially fewer false positives in flagging unhappy customers. Tone and satisfaction disagreed in 44% of conversations — a single "Neutral" sentiment label conflates quietly satisfied customers with those who quietly gave up. The largest identified group was "tolerated friction": customers who were satisfied yet still reported a fixable problem, a cohort invisible to sentiment-based dashboards.

Conclusion: LLM-based annotation moves beyond linguistic tonality to capture customer state (satisfaction) and problem causality directly from raw textual data, enabling new classes of business metrics — satisfaction grounded in outcomes rather than affect, and structured problem taxonomies extracted from interactions and feedback.

Abstract: Most companies read their customer support data at scale using sentiment analysis, which measures how customers sound rather than whether they were satisfied with the result. We tested a richer alternative on 70,450 support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform: alongside tone, we used GPT-5.4 to estimate each customer's satisfaction and to flag whether they reported a concrete problem, then validated all three readings against the 1-to-5 ratings customers left on the conversations they rated. The satisfaction estimate tracked those ratings far better than sentiment did, correlating at 0.47 against 0.36 and flagging unhappy customers with far fewer false alarms. The structured read also sees what sentiment cannot: tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of conversations, a single "Neutral" label hides everything from quietly satisfied customers to ones who quietly gave up, and the largest group of all is "tolerated friction," customers who are satisfied but still reporting a fixable problem, a standing issue that no sentiment-based dashboard can surface. The broader finding is that LLM-based annotation can capture far more than the tonality of a customer's language, offering strong potential for new business metrics grounded instead in the customer's state (whether they were satisfied) and the cause of their problem extracted directly from the raw textual data of interactions and feedback.

</details>


### [29] [TerraMARS: A Domain-Adapted Small-Language-Model Pipeline for Mars Terraforming Literature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19700)
*Jyotsna Singh,Ash Black,Jeff Larsen,Scott R. Saleska*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TerraMARS is an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that uses a QLoRA fine-tuned Gemma 3 1B Small Language Model to convert unstructured Mars scientific literature into structured JSON outputs and answer terraforming-related questions, supporting downstream applications like habitability modeling and digital twins.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Comprehensive knowledge of Mars' atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation, and spatial features is needed for habitability assessment and terraforming studies. This knowledge is scattered across unstructured scientific literature, requiring automated extraction into machine-readable formats for use in quantitative models.

Method: The TerraMARS pipeline collects open-access Mars papers, processes them through a multistage retrieval and chunking framework, and employs Google Gemma 3 1B fine-tuned with QLoRA on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The model outputs both natural language answers and structured JSON representations.

Result: The pipeline produces promising structured outputs from Mars scientific literature, though further improvements are needed to increase extraction accuracy and factual consistency.

Conclusion: TerraMARS demonstrates a viable foundation for integrating scientific knowledge into downstream applications like digital twins and habitability modeling, but requires continued refinement to meet accuracy and factual consistency standards.

Abstract: Researchers are interested in learning about Mars so that it may eventually become habitable for humans. To achieve this, there is a need for comprehensive knowledge of the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation environment, and spatial features through the scientific literature. These contain valuable information and meaningful quantitative constraints that can be used in other models and studies, such as habitability assessment and future terraforming studies. We present TerraMARS, an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that combines a domain-adapted Small Language Model to answer Mars terraforming-related questions and convert unstructured Mars science text into machine-readable structured outputs in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. A corpus of open-access papers is collected and processed using a multistage retrieval and chunking framework. Google Gemma 3 1B was adapted to the domain using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets. The resulting pipeline generates both types of output and provides a foundation for integrating knowledge from scientific literature into downstream applications like digital twins and habitability modeling for Mars. The output from this pipeline looks promising, but further improvements are needed to increase extraction accuracy and factual consistency.

</details>


### [30] [FineREX: Fine-Tuned NER-RE for Human Smuggling Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19710)
*Elijah Feldman,Dipak Meher,Carlotta Domeniconi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FineREX is a knowledge graph construction pipeline using a fine-tuned LLM for NER-RE on legal documents about human smuggling, outperforming larger general-purpose models by 15.50% entity F1 and 31.46% relation F1 while halving processing time and reducing legal noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal court documents contain valuable evidence about human smuggling networks, but information extraction is hindered by unstructured, jargon-heavy text. General-purpose LLMs lack domain-specific entity/relation definitions needed for accurate knowledge graph construction in this domain.

Method: FineREX is a streamlined knowledge graph construction pipeline centered on a fine-tuned LLM for joint named entity recognition and relationship extraction (NER-RE). The model is fine-tuned on a manually annotated dataset of 512 text chunks from legal documents. The pipeline eliminates document rewriting and redundant extraction stages present in prior approaches.

Result: Compared to a larger general-purpose baseline, FineREX achieves +15.50% entity F1 and +31.46% relation F1. It reduces legal noise by nearly half, lowers node duplication on long documents from 17.78% to 11.17%, and cuts end-to-end processing time by 50.0%.

Conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning substantially outperforms larger general-purpose models for knowledge graph construction in illicit network analysis, improving both extraction quality and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Court proceedings contain valuable evidence about human smuggling networks, but this information is often buried within unstructured, jargon-heavy legal documents. While large language models (LLMs) can support knowledge graph construction through automated information extraction, existing approaches rely on general-purpose models that are not tailored to the entity and relationship definitions required in this domain. We introduce FineREX, a streamlined knowledge graph construction pipeline built around a fine-tuned LLM for named entity recognition and relationship extraction (NER-RE). Using a manually annotated dataset of $512$ text chunks, FineREX achieves absolute improvements of 15.50% and 31.46% in entity and relationship F1-score, respectively, compared to a larger general-purpose baseline. These gains translate into higher-quality knowledge graphs, reducing legal noise by nearly half and lowering node duplication on long documents from 17.78% to 11.17%. By eliminating document rewriting and redundant extraction stages, FineREX also reduces end-to-end processing time by 50.0%. Our results demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning can substantially outperform larger general-purpose models while improving both the quality and efficiency of knowledge graph construction for illicit network analysis.

</details>


### [31] [NRITYAM: Language Models Meet Art and Heritage of Dance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19727)
*Punit Kumar Singh,Niladri Ghosh,Advait Joshiınst,Shailee Choudhary,Michael Färber,Haiqin Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NRITYAM is a multilingual, multicultural benchmark of 9,260 QA pairs across 12 languages for evaluating language models' understanding of global dance traditions, created with native artists and speakers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models lack nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts, which limits their global effectiveness. Existing benchmarks do not adequately assess cultural comprehension in domain-specific performing arts like dance.

Method: The authors constructed NRITYAM from scratch through collaboration with native dance artists and native speakers across 12 languages, who authored and validated culturally relevant QA pairs. They evaluated a broad spectrum of models: large language models, small language models, multimodal large language models, and small multimodal language models.

Result: The paper presents NRITYAM as the largest dataset dedicated to cultural knowledge in dance. Detailed evaluation results across the spectrum of model types are provided, though specific performance metrics are not detailed in this abstract.

Conclusion: NRITYAM establishes a new standard for evaluating AI systems' ability to understand and reason about traditional performing arts, addressing a critical gap in culturally grounded evaluation benchmarks.

Abstract: Language models have become essential tools in shaping modern workflows. However, their global effectiveness hinges on a nuanced understanding of local socio-cultural contexts. To address this gap, we present NRITYAM, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the cultural comprehension capabilities of language models in the context of global dance traditions. NRITYAM comprises 9,260 carefully curated question-answer pairs spanning 12 languages, making it the largest dataset dedicated to evaluating cultural knowledge in dance. The dataset has been developed from the ground up through close collaboration with native dance artists and native speakers of the languages, who authored and validated culturally relevant questions specific to their regions. We evaluate a broad set of models, including large language models, small language models, multimodal large language models, and small multimodal language models. As a multilingual and multicultural benchmark, NRITYAM sets a new standard for evaluating the ability of AI systems to understand and reason about traditional performing arts. Detailed dataset samples are available at~\url{https://github.com/niladrighosh03/NRITYAM}.

</details>


### [32] [Clusters are All You Need: Pre-Training the Tsetlin Machine with Semantic Clusters from Language Models for Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19815)
*Jiechao Gao,Rohan Kumar Yadav,Yuangang Li,Yuandong Pan,Jie Wang,Ying Liu,Michael Lepech*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A semantic pre-training framework transfers knowledge from BERT-like models into Tsetlin Machines without embeddings, using cluster-based pre-training with enhanced feedback to learn interpretable semantic keywords that achieve near-BERT performance while remaining fully interpretable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language models like BERT achieve high text classification accuracy but are opaque "black boxes." The Tsetlin Machine (TM) offers full interpretability through clause-based reasoning but captures limited semantic information. Existing TM-LM hybrids rely on static word embeddings that lack contextual meaning. The motivation is to bridge this gap by transferring deep semantic knowledge into an interpretable TM framework without sacrificing transparency.

Method: The proposed framework uses K-means or Top2Vec to group text samples into semantically coherent clusters. These cluster-sample pairs are then used to pre-train a non-negated Tsetlin Machine with enhanced Type I feedback. This pre-training stage allows the TM to learn interpretable semantic keywords from the clustering structure. The pre-trained TM is subsequently fine-tuned on downstream classification tasks. Critically, no word embeddings are used in the knowledge transfer.

Result: Evaluated across five datasets, the proposed method substantially outperforms both vanilla TMs and embedding-based TM variants. It achieves classification performance competitive with BERT while maintaining full interpretability.

Conclusion: Semantic pre-training via clustering enables Tsetlin Machines to capture rich semantic information without relying on embeddings, yielding a model that is both highly accurate and fully interpretable, making it suitable for high-stakes applications requiring transparency.

Abstract: Pre-trained language models such as BERT achieve strong text classification performance but lack transparency, limiting their use in high-stakes settings. The Tsetlin Machine (TM) offers fully interpretable, clause-based reasoning but captures little semantic information, and prior attempts to bridge the two rely on static word embeddings that miss contextual meaning. We propose a semantic pre-training framework that transfers knowledge from a pre-trained language model into a TM without using embeddings. Text samples are grouped into semantically coherent clusters with K-means or Top2Vec, and the resulting cluster-sample pairs pre-train a non-negated TM with enhanced Type I feedback. The TM thereby learns interpretable semantic keywords that are fine-tuned on downstream tasks. Across five datasets, our method substantially outperforms vanilla and embedding-based TMs and reaches performance competitive with BERT while remaining interpretable.

</details>


### [33] [CREDENCE: Claim Reduction for Decomposition & Enhanced Credibility -- Semantic Metrics and Convergence Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19819)
*Phuong Huu Vu Tran,Thuan Duc Mai,Bach Xuan Le*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Credence, a claim decomposition framework that replaces Jaccard-based evaluation with a semantic similarity metric (Semantic-F1 using BGE-large), provides formal convergence analysis of rule-based and LLM-based repair loops, and benchmarks across three domains, showing Semantic-F1 outperforms Jaccard-F1 by 15–32pp and rule-repair reduces atomicity violations by 47–100%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing claim decomposition systems suffer from two key limitations: (1) token-overlap metrics like Jaccard systematically underestimate decomposition quality when claims are paraphrased rather than verbatim extracts, and (2) the repair loop used to fix atomicity violations lacks formal termination guarantees, leaving its convergence behavior uncharacterized.

Method: The authors propose Credence, consisting of: (1) Semantic-F1 — a BGE-large cosine similarity fidelity metric replacing Jaccard, plus downstream fact-checking accuracy validation; (2) formal convergence theorems proving rule-based repair is monotone and finitely terminating under an oracle parser, while LLM-based self-repair is non-monotone and requires an early-exit guard; (3) three evaluation benchmarks (SocialClaimSplit, WikiSplitBench, ClaimDecompBench); and (4) multi-model benchmarking across four decomposers (3.8B–12B parameters) plus a closed API model, using metrics such as EPR (Edge Preservation Ratio) and AVR (Atomicity Violation Rate).

Result: Semantic-F1 outperforms Jaccard-F1 by +15–32 percentage points across all benchmarks. Edge Preservation Ratio (EPR) ranges from 0.94 to 1.00 on SocialClaimSplit and WikiSplitBench, while ClaimDecompBench shows lower EPR (down to 0.824) due to harder news-domain constructions. Rule-based repair reduces the Atomicity Violation Rate (AVR) by 47–100% relative to the base model without degrading fidelity.

Conclusion: Credence establishes that semantic similarity metrics are superior to token-overlap metrics for evaluating claim decomposition, formal termination analysis is essential for reliable repair pipelines, and rule-based repair offers monotone, terminating improvements over LLM-based self-repair, which requires guard mechanisms to prevent divergence.

Abstract: Decomposing compound sentences into atomic, verifiable claims is a prerequisite for reliable automated fact-checking. Prior work has relied on token-overlap (Jaccard) metrics that systematically underestimate decomposition quality for paraphrastic claims, and has lacked formal termination analysis for the repair loop. We present Credence, a revised claim decomposition and evaluation framework addressing both shortcomings. Our contributions are: (1) Semantic-F1: we use BGE-large cosine similarity fidelity metric that resolves Jaccard's penalisation and improves downstream fact-checking accuracy; (2) Convergence theorems: we formally characterise four properties of the repair pipeline, establishing that rule-based repair is monotone and finitely terminating under an oracle parser assumption; LLM-based self-repair is provably non-monotone and requires an early-exit guard; (3) Three evaluation benchmarks spanning social-media, encyclopaedic, and news domains for cross-domain generalisation measurement; (4) Multi-model benchmarking across four decomposer models (3.8B-12B) and a closed API model. Experiments on SocialClaimSplit, WikiSplitBench, and ClaimDecompBench show that Semantic-F1 outperforms Jaccard-F1 by +15-32pp. EPR ranges from 0.94 to 1.00 on SocialClaimSplit and WikiSplitBench, while ClaimDecompBench includes lower base EPR cases (down to 0.824) due to harder news-domain constructions, and rule-repair reduces the Atomicity Violation Rate (AVR) by 47-100% relative to the base model without degrading fidelity.

</details>


### [34] [Leverage Is Not Reach: A Control-Window Law for Single-Neuron Steering in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19831)
*Hongliang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper develops a theoretical framework—budget-normalized control windows—for understanding when and why single-neuron steering of language models succeeds or fails, revealing that coherent control depends on a coherence budget (residual norm divided by write norm), a universal saturation curve, and a ceiling-collapse distinction that predicts intervention outcomes with high accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite empirical evidence that sparse feed-forward neurons gate behaviors like refusal and language routing in aligned LMs, no theory predicts when single-neuron intervention produces coherent control versus output collapse. Practitioners rely on anecdotal dose-response curves without understanding the underlying principles.

Method: The authors develop a budget-normalized control window framework that reduces neuron steering to a single control coordinate: alignment between residual stream and write direction, governed by a universal saturation curve parameterized by a coherence budget (residual norm / write norm). Coherent control exists when a behavior trigger lies below a collapse ceiling. The ceiling is predicted from weights and one generic forward pass; triggers are measured at rollout. A forward-only contrastive screen is derived from the window to recover controllers missed by gradient attribution.

Result: On 15 held-out neurons, predicted ceiling achieves mean absolute error of 0.14 (≈0.07 in bulk layers), with committed open/closed verdicts correct on 11 vs. a 10/15 majority baseline. Three failure modes explain closed cases: collapse before trigger, insufficient depth, and normalization caps. Gradient attribution anti-predicts control because true controllers write off the readout axis with near-zero first-order gradients. For refusal, intervention success is typed rather than scalar: coherent bypass and actionable reach are separate; only 3 of 6 audited Llama pivots show genuine actionable reach, and only at later rollout horizons.

Conclusion: Single-neuron steering is a budgeted, typed audit of controllability rather than a fixed-dose anecdote. The framework explains why attribution methods fail, provides a principled screening method, and demonstrates that refusal interventions require distinguishing between coherent bypass and genuine actionable reach.

Abstract: Aligned language models gate behaviors such as refusal and language routing through sparse feed forward neurons, yet no theory predicts when a single neuron intervention controls a behavior coherently rather than collapsing the output. We develop a budget normalized control window framework for single neuron steering. A dose along one write direction reduces to one control coordinate: the alignment between the residual stream and the write, driven along a universal saturation curve in units of a coherence budget set by the residual norm divided by the write norm. Coherent control exists when a behavior trigger lies below the collapse ceiling. The same coordinate governs benign mode switches and refusal; the ceiling follows from weights and one generic forward pass, while triggers are measured at rollout. On fifteen held out neurons, the predicted ceiling has mean absolute error 0.14, about 0.07 in bulk layers, and the committed open or closed verdict holds on eleven against a ten of fifteen majority baseline. Closed cases expose three failure modes rather than violations: collapse before trigger, too little depth to propagate, or a normalization that caps how far one neuron can push. The law explains why local gradient attribution anti predicts control: true controllers write off the readout axis and carry a near zero first order gradient. A forward only contrastive screen made precise by the window recovers controllers that attribution misses. On refusal, the hardest case, intervention success is typed, not scalar: coherent bypass and strict actionable reach separate, so a neuron can flip refusal in fluent, on task text with no actionable content, and genuine actionable reach appears only for three of six audited Llama pivots and only at later rollout horizons. Single neuron steering is therefore a budgeted, typed audit of controllability rather than a fixed dose anecdote.

</details>


### [35] [AtomMem: Building Simple and Effective Memory System for LLM Agents via Atomic Facts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19847)
*Yanyu Yao,Shangze Li,Zhi Zheng,Hui Zheng,Qi Liu,Tong Xu,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AtomMem is a long-term memory system for LLMs that extracts atomic facts from interactions, organizes them hierarchically, and uses an associative memory graph for retrieval, achieving SOTA on the LoCoMo benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have fixed context windows that prevent effective long-term information accumulation across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems suffer from coarse, unstable memory construction with inefficient representations and unconstrained updates.

Method: AtomMem consists of three components: (1) a Fact Executor that selectively extracts high-value atomic facts from long-form interactions; (2) a hierarchical organization scheme that structures facts into event hierarchies and temporal profiles to capture episodic context and evolving user attributes; (3) an associative memory graph activated during retrieval to connect fragmented memories.

Result: AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks on the LoCoMo benchmark.

Conclusion: AtomMem provides a scalable, economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents with effective long-term memory capabilities.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning and generation abilities, but their fixed context windows limit long-term information accumulation and reuse across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems often construct memory in a coarse and unstable manner, relying on inefficient memory representations or unstable unconstrained updates. To address these challenges, we propose AtomMem, a long-term memory system designed for value-dense storage and stable memory evolution. AtomMem introduces a Fact Executor, which selectively extracts high value atomic facts from long form interactions to serve as highly efficient memory representations. Subsequently, AtomMem organizes these facts into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, capturing coherent episodic contexts and tracking dynamically evolving user attributes over time. During retrieval, the system activates an associative memory graph to connect fragmented memories. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark confirm that AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks, offering a scalable and economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents.

</details>


### [36] [Prompt, Plan, Extract: Zero-Shot Agentic LLMs Workflows for Lung Pathology Extraction from Clinical Narratives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19852)
*Aman Pathak,Cheng Peng,Mengxian Lyu,Ziyi Chen,Reema Solan,Sankalp Talankar,Yasir Khan,Hiren Mehta,Aokun Chen,Yi Guo,Yonghui Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A zero-shot agentic workflow using open-source LLMs extracted 13 synoptic fields from lung pathology reports, achieving Micro-F1 of 0.893 (GPT-OSS-20B) versus 0.960 for a supervised GatorTron baseline, offering a low-cost alternative without task-specific training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual extraction of structured cancer data from narrative pathology reports is labor-intensive and error-prone. Supervised NER-RE pipelines require expensive annotation and suffer from cascading errors when upstream entities are missed. The authors aim to explore whether zero-shot generative LLMs can bypass these limitations.

Method: Five open-source generative LLMs were evaluated in a zero-shot, agentic workflow to populate 13 CAP synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. Performance was compared against a supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline using a novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework. The primary metric was Micro-F1, with analysis of recall and precision on complex relations such as Pathologic Stage.

Result: The supervised GatorTron baseline achieved Micro-F1 of 0.960. The best zero-shot model, GPT-OSS-20B, achieved Micro-F1 of 0.893 with recall of 0.949, successfully extracting complex relations including Pathologic Stage without any task-specific fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs represent a viable, low-cost solution for extracting structured lung pathology information, approaching the performance of supervised methods while eliminating the need for manual annotation and mitigating cascading error propagation.

Abstract: Information extraction from pathology reports is essential for cancer staging, tumor registry population. Yet key data remains embedded in narrative reports, making manual extraction labor-intensive and error-prone. Traditional supervised Natural Language Processing pipelines address this through fully supervised Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction, but require expensive manual annotation and suffer cascading failures when upstream entities are missed. In this study, we developed a zero-shot, agentic workflow, and evaluated five open-source generative Large Language Models (LLMs) to populate 13 College of American Pathologists synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. We compared them against a state-of-the-art supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline using a novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework. The baseline achieved Micro-F1of 0.960, while the best zero-shot model (GPT-OSS-20B) achieved Micro-F1 of 0.893 (recall: 0.949), accurately extracting complex relations like Pathologic Stage without task-specific training. These results suggest that open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs are a low-cost solution for extracting lung pathology information.

</details>


### [37] [Large Language Models Do Not Always Need Readable Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19857)
*Jiayi Zhu,Haoxuan Peng,Junxi Wang,Liang Ke,Chen Zhang,Linfeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces BabelTele, a class of compact, non-standard textual representations that sacrifice human readability but preserve semantic recoverability for LLMs, achieving 99.5% semantic fidelity at 27.9% of original text length, with applications in reducing context overhead in multi-agent and agent memory scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are typically prompted with human-readable natural language even when communicating with other models. The authors investigate whether semantic information can be encoded in compact, model-centric textual forms that decouple human readability from machine recoverability, potentially reducing context overhead in LLM systems.

Method: The authors empirically probe LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret non-standard textual representations (BabelTele). They evaluate these representations through: (1) readability diagnostics, (2) model likelihood measures, (3) human questionnaires, and (4) downstream task evaluations. They further test semantic robustness in cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication settings.

Result: BabelTele can substantially depart from ordinary natural language while preserving core semantics for instruction-tuned LLMs. It demonstrates 99.5% semantic fidelity when text volume is condensed to 27.9% of original length. Effectiveness depends on the compressor-reader pair and task setting, but it generally maintains reliable downstream performance while reducing context overhead.

Conclusion: Human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled. This opens a path toward model-native representations for future LLM systems, where inter-model communication need not conform to human-readable conventions.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly prompted and interfaced with human-readable natural language, even when the intended reader is another model. This paper investigates whether semantic information can be encoded in compact, non-standard textual forms that sacrifice human readability while remaining recoverable by LLMs. We refer to this class of model-centric textual representations as BabelTele, approached here not as a fixed protocol but as an empirical probe into LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret such representations. Through readability diagnostics, model likelihood measures, human questionnaires, and downstream task evaluations, we find that BabelTele can substantially depart from ordinary natural language while preserving core semantics for instruction-tuned LLMs. As a task-agnostic representational paradigm, BabelTele demonstrates high information density, maintaining 99.5% semantic fidelity even when the text volume is condensed to 27.9% of its original length. We further evaluate its semantic robustness in cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication. Results suggest that BabelTele can reduce context overhead while generally maintaining reliable downstream performance, although its effectiveness depends on the compressor-reader pair and task setting. These findings indicate that human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled, opening a path toward model-native representations in future exploration of LLM systems.

</details>


### [38] [The Almost Intelligent Revolution: Options for Scaling Up Deliberation and Empowering People with AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19864)
*Serge Sharoff*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This chapter examines how Large Language Models (LLMs) can scale up and democratise public deliberation, particularly for marginalised groups, using Systemic-Functional Linguistics to analyse how socio-demographic and communicative variations shape participation. It advocates balancing optimism with caution and outlines future research directions with ethical safeguards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While red teaming addresses specific risks of LLMs in public discourse, broader challenges remain — including linguistic constraints, biases, and sycophancy. The chapter is motivated by the need to understand how LLMs can foster more inclusive deliberation and empower marginalised groups, rather than merely mitigating harms.

Method: The chapter draws on Systemic-Functional Linguistics (SFL) as an analytical framework to examine how variation across language users (socio-demographic groups) and language use (communicative functions) influences participation in AI-supported deliberation. It reviews AI-driven deliberation studies and assesses their capacity to scaffold argumentation, improve access, and counteract exclusionary linguistic norms embedded in prestigious registers.

Result: The analysis finds that LLM-supported deliberation can scaffold argumentation, enhance access for marginalised groups, and reduce the influence of exclusionary linguistic norms. However, the chapter warns against both overclaiming (creating unrealistic expectations) and underclaiming (missing opportunities), advocating for a measured, evidence-based approach.

Conclusion: Maximising the democratic potential of AI-assisted participation requires embedding ethical safeguards to counteract the reproduction of linguistic inequalities. Future research should pursue these directions while maintaining a balanced perspective on LLM capabilities and limitations.

Abstract: The increasing prominence of Large Language Models (LLMs) in public discourse presents both opportunities and challenges for democratic deliberation. While red teaming strategies help mitigate specific risks, broader concerns persist regarding linguistic constraints, biases, and the sycophantic tendencies of LLMs. This chapter explores how LLMs can be used to significantly scale up and democratise deliberation, particularly in fostering inclusivity and empowering traditionally marginalised groups. Drawing on concepts from Systemic-Functional Linguistics, the chapter examines how variations across language users (for example, with respect to socio-demographic groups) and across language use (for example, with respect to communicative functions) shape participation in AI-supported deliberation. The chapter presents AI-driven deliberation studies and assesses their potential to scaffold argumentation, enhance access, and reduce the influence of exclusionary linguistic norms and biases which are embedded in prestigious registers. At the same time, the chapter cautions against both overclaiming, which leads to unrealistic expectations, and underclaiming, which risks missed opportunities for AI-assisted engagement. The chapter concludes by identifying future research directions to maximise the democratic potential of AI-assisted participation while embedding ethical safeguards to counteract the reproduction of linguistic inequalities.

</details>


### [39] [REDACT: A Systematically Controlled Multilingual Benchmark for Personal Information Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19881)
*Guneesh Vats,Anubha Agrawal,Shikha Singhal,Ajita Dash,Praison Selvaraj,Vidhan Jhawar,Ranga Prasad Chenna,Bharadwaj Y M G*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: REDACT is a multilingual PII detection benchmark with 13,427 records across 25 languages and 51 entity types, generated via a covering-array sampler controlling nine axes. Evaluation of five detectors reveals that aggregate F1 masks critical failure patterns: rule-based systems fail on high-sensitivity and non-verbatim data, while LLM-based detectors prove more robust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PII detection benchmarks are limited in entity type coverage, rely on ad hoc generation, and fail to reveal which surface conditions cause detector failures. There is a need for systematic, controlled evaluation across diverse linguistic and structural axes.

Method: The authors construct REDACT using a strength-2 covering-array sampler controlling nine generation axes (domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, co-occurrence). Three entity-level metadata fields — disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier — enable stratified evaluation. Five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6) are evaluated on a locked, language-stratified 1,000-record sample. A reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment using three models corroborates findings.

Result: Aggregate F1 conceals architecture-dependent failure structures. The rule-based Presidio detector achieves only 0.07 recall on HIGH-sensitivity categories and struggles with non-verbatim disclosure forms. LLM-based detectors (GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6) are more robust, with the HIGH sensitivity tier emerging as their strongest slice. Sensitivity-tier assignment is identified as the hardest evaluation axis.

Conclusion: Systematically controlled benchmarking is essential for exposing PII detector weaknesses. REDACT provides a rigorous evaluation framework, and its metadata-rich schema enables fine-grained failure analysis that aggregate metrics mask. The benchmark, schema, prompts, and evaluation harness are publicly released.

Abstract: Benchmark infrastructure for personally identifiable information (PII) detection remains limited: existing corpora cover few entity types, use ad hoc generation conditions, and do not show which surface conditions cause detector failures. We present REDACT, a systematically controlled multilingual PII benchmark with 13,427 records, 324,078 entity annotations, 51 entity types, 4,127 surface-form patterns, and 25 languages across 9 scripts. A strength-2 covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes: domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, and co-occurrence. Three entity-level metadata fields (disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier) enable stratified evaluation beyond aggregate or per-type F1. From the full benchmark, we evaluate five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, the OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,000 records. Aggregate F1 masks an architecture-dependent failure structure: the rule-based detector performs poorly on the highest-stakes data, including HIGH-sensitivity categories (recall 0.07) and non-verbatim disclosure forms, while the LLM detectors remain more robust, with the HIGH tier as their strongest sensitivity slice. A three-model reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment corroborates that sensitivity-tier assignment is the task's hardest axis. We release the benchmark, schema, prompts, and stratified evaluation harness.

</details>


### [40] [Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19910)
*Syeda Faiza Ahmed Sara,Shammur Absar Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A pronunciation assessment framework using only native speech for training, combining SSL-based token surprisal with text-guided DTW alignment, achieving near-supervised performance on SpeechOcean762 (PCC 0.66).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional automated pronunciation assessment depends on expensive labeled learner error data or non-native corpora. The authors aim to bypass this by leveraging only readily available native speech resources, making pronunciation assessment more accessible and scalable.

Method: The framework has three components: (1) An SSL encoder with K-means codebook discretizes learner speech into acoustic tokens; a token LM trained on native speech computes surprisal as a phonotactic deviation signal. (2) A Text2DUnit-DTW module predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens via DTW, extracting error-sensitive features. (3) Surprisal and alignment features are fused through simple regression. The system operates unsupervised or with light calibration from a small set of scored utterances.

Result: On SpeechOcean762, Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) improves from 0.60 (unsupervised) to 0.66 with transcript guidance, approaching supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent improvements, demonstrating generalization.

Conclusion: A lightweight, native-only training paradigm can achieve competitive pronunciation assessment performance. The combination of unsupervised surprisal-based phonotactic deviation detection with text-guided alignment provides complementary error signals that together rival supervised methods.

Abstract: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit--DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.

</details>


### [41] [GEMS: Geometric Constraints Enable Multi-Semantic Superposition in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19946)
*Yu Deng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Activation steering breaks when multiple semantic directions are superposed. The authors decompose this collapse into distributional deviation and directional interference, then propose GEMS — a training-free method using norm-preserving weighted superposition, targeted attention-pathway injection, and real-time orthogonalization — to enable robust multi-directional steering without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing activation steering methods only handle single-direction injection; when multiple semantic directions are combined without constraints, model behavior collapses. The authors aim to understand why this collapse occurs and to develop a principled, training-free solution for concurrent multi-directional steering.

Method: The authors first decompose multi-directional collapse into two independent sources: (1) distributional deviation — additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers, pushing activations outside the training distribution; (2) directional interference — non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually attenuate when superposed. They then propose GEMS, which addresses each source with a geometric constraint: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted injection into attention pathways to mitigate distributional deviation, and real-time orthogonalization (e.g., Gram-Schmidt) to eliminate directional interference. They evaluate on GSM8K (3 concurrent non-mathematical directions) and Wikitext-2, with layer-level probes verifying signal propagation and ablation studies isolating each constraint's causal role.

Result: On GSM8K, GEMS preserves accuracy at 98% with 3 concurrent steering directions (baseline 92%), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%. On Wikitext-2, the same multi-directional injection incurs only a 2.2% perplexity increase. Component ablation confirms each constraint (norm preservation, attention-pathway targeting, orthogonalization) is causally necessary. Layer-level probes show orthogonalized signals survive through FFN pathways and reach the output distribution with maintained semantic specificity. Qualitative steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B parameters.

Conclusion: Multi-directional activation steering collapse arises from two separable, independently acting mechanisms. By enforcing geometric constraints that directly counteract these mechanisms — norm preservation, targeted pathway injection, and orthogonalization — training-free multi-directional steering becomes feasible and robust, enabling simultaneous control over multiple semantic axes without retraining or degradation in model performance.

Abstract: Activation steering controls model behavior by modifying intermediate hidden states at inference time without retraining. Existing methods handle only single-direction injection; when multiple semantic directions are superposed without constraints, the model collapses. We show that this collapse decomposes into two independently acting sources: distributional deviation, where additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers and drive activations outside the training distribution, and directional interference, where non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen when superposed. These two sources define the design constraints that any training-free multi-directional intervention must address. As one instantiation of these principles, we propose GEMS, a training-free method that maps each source to a corresponding geometric constraint: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted attention-pathway injection for distributional deviation, and real-time orthogonalization for directional interference. On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserves accuracy at 98% (baseline 92%), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%; on Wikitext-2, the same injection incurs only 2.2% PPL increase. Component ablation isolates the causal role of each constraint, and layer-level probes confirm that orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Qualitative steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B.

</details>


### [42] [Source-Grounded Data Generation for Text-to-JSON Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20072)
*Sunghee Ahn,Guijin Son,Youngjae Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: STAGE is a data generation pipeline that creates text-to-JSON training data grounded in spreadsheets, using LLMs for synthesis while validating against source data. It significantly improves structured extraction accuracy, boosting Qwen3-4B exact match from 31.37% to 74.27%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legacy industries rely on long, unstructured documents containing high-value information. Extracting this into structured JSON is critical for automation, but building reliable, scalable text-to-JSON training data is challenging due to hallucination and lack of ground-truth anchors.

Method: STAGE is a source-grounded data generation pipeline that synthesizes reports and JSON schemas using LLMs, while validating extracted ground-truth values against an underlying spreadsheet to ensure fidelity. A benchmark called STAGE-Eval (851 examples) is also introduced for evaluation.

Result: STAGE-generated training data significantly outperforms existing approaches: Qwen3-4B exact match improves from 31.37% to 74.27%, and value accuracy rises from 45.46% to 90.69%.

Conclusion: Grounding synthetic data generation in spreadsheet sources provides a scalable, reliable method for producing high-quality text-to-JSON training data, enabling substantial gains in structured extraction performance.

Abstract: From financial filings to clinical records, legacy industries rely heavily on long, unstructured documents to store high-value information. Reliably extracting this information into structured, machine-readable representations is a key prerequisite to making the contents accessible to automated systems. JSON is a natural target for such structured extraction, yet constructing reliable and scalable text-to-JSON training data remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration), a source-grounded data generation pipeline that constructs reports and JSON schema by using LLMs for scalable synthesis while validating ground-truth values against the underlying spreadsheet. Evaluations on STAGE-Eval, our source-grounded benchmark with an 851-example test set, show that STAGE produces stronger training data than existing approaches. This improves Qwen3-4B exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.

</details>


### [43] [IHUBERT: Vector-Based Semantic Deduplication and Domain-Balanced Pretraining for Persian Resources](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20089)
*Arash Ghafouri,Mahdi Firouzmandi,Hossein Saberi,Mohammad Reza Hasani Ahangar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: IHUBERT is a monolingual Persian PLM (RoBERTa-base, 125M parameters) trained from scratch on a semantically deduplicated 45 GB corpus. It achieves state-of-the-art results on Persian extractive QA and NLI, with competitive performance across NER, sentiment, and topic classification, while structured relation extraction remains a challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persian PLMs are limited by (1) scarcity of large-scale, high-quality pretraining corpora and (2) narrow evaluation confined to standard classification and NER tasks. This motivates building a high-quality corpus and a robust Persian PLM evaluated across diverse NLU benchmarks.

Method: (1) Corpus curation: 45 GB from Sepahr-Danesh collection (~7-8B tokens) processed through multi-stage pipeline—normalization, exact/near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for domain/register balancing. (2) Tokenizer: 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer trained on the full corpus to handle Persian morphology. (3) Model: RoBERTa-base encoder (125M) trained from scratch. (4) Evaluation: seven Persian NLU tasks—NER, sentiment, topic classification, NLI, extractive QA, relation extraction—using entity-level F1, Macro-F1, and EM/F1.

Result: IHUBERT ranks 1st on PQuAD (F1 88.35) and ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.10) for extractive QA, and best on FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). Competitive on NER (ParsTwiNER F1 0.8308) and topic classification (DigiMag Macro-F1 0.7953). Relation extraction remains the weakest area (PERLEX Macro-F1 0.6684). BPE tokenizer ablation showed lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size.

Conclusion: Semantically curated large-scale pretraining with BPE tokenization advances Persian language modeling, yielding strong gains especially in comprehension-oriented tasks like extractive QA and NLI, while structured relation extraction remains an open challenge for future work.

Abstract: Persian pretrained language models (PLMs) are still limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality pretraining corpora and by insufficient evaluation beyond standard classification and NER tasks. We present IHUBERT, a monolingual Persian PLM trained from scratch with the RoBERTa-base encoder (125M parameters) on a 45 GB curated subset of the Sepahr-Danesh collection (about 7-8B tokens). To improve corpus quality and reduce redundancy, we employ a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline that includes normalization, exact and near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for distribution balancing control across domains and registers. We additionally train a 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer on the full pretraining corpus to better capture Persian morphology and orthographic variation. IHUBERT is evaluated on seven Persian NLU benchmarks covering NER, sentiment analysis, topic classification, NLI, extractive question answering, and relation extraction, using task-standard metrics (entity-level F1, Macro-F1, EM/F1). IHUBERT achieves its strongest gains on extractive QA, ranking first on both PQuAD (F1 88.3542) and ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.0987), and attains the best result on FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). On NER and topic classification, it remains competitive (e.g., 0.8308 F1 on ParsTwiNER; 0.7953 Macro-F1 on DigiMag), while relation extraction remains the main remaining gap (0.6684 Macro-F1 on PERLEX). A controlled tokenizer ablation on the IHUBERT pretraining corpus shows that BPE yields slightly lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size, supporting our tokenization design. Overall, IHUBERT advances Persian language modeling through semantically curated large-scale pretraining and broad evaluation across both classification and comprehension-oriented tasks.

</details>


### [44] [Self-Preference Is Weak or Absent in Verifiable Instruction-Following Revision: A Four-Model Test Under Genuine Authorship](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20093)
*William Guey,Pierrick Bougault*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit a self-preference bias when evaluating corrections to their own writing, using a deterministic verifier (IFEval) to establish ground truth. Across 85 comparisons, authors reject verified-good fixes at nearly the same rate as fresh models, with a non-significant gap of -5.1 pp. The main finding is null: no robust self-preference bias was detected, though effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work documents that LLMs prefer their own generations when acting as judges. This paper extends that question to revision: do models resist valid corrections to their own writing? The key distinction is using a deterministic verifier rather than another model's judgment to establish what constitutes a "valid" correction, eliminating confounds from evaluator subjectivity.

Method: The authors use IFEval, an instruction-following benchmark with a deterministic rule-based checker. The pipeline: (1) a model writes a draft, (2) the IFEval checker confirms a constraint violation and verifies a candidate edit fixes it, (3) the model evaluates whether to accept/reject the edit either as the original author or as a fresh model seeing the draft neutrally. Four mid-tier model families (85 author-vs-fresh comparisons) are tested. A smaller pilot also explored a self-skepticism hint.

Result: No statistically significant self-preference bias was found: the author-vs-fresh rejection gap is -5.1 percentage points (95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). The self-skepticism hint from the pilot did not replicate. Qualitatively, when authors do reject verified-good fixes, 97% of stated reasons involve flaw-catching (e.g., claiming the fix introduces new errors) rather than mere preference for their own text. The sample size limits the ability to detect effects below ~13 pp.

Conclusion: Contrary to documented self-preference in judging tasks, LLMs do not exhibit a robust self-preference bias when evaluating verified corrections to their own writing. The nature of rejections is dominated by (potentially spurious) flaw-catching rather than preference-based resistance. The study highlights a meaningful dissociation between self-preference in rating/judging and in revision acceptance, though effects smaller than ~13 pp remain unexcluded.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly review and revise text, including their own. A documented self-preference bias (models favoring their own generations when acting as judges) raises the question of whether models also resist valid corrections to their own writing. We test this in a setting where "valid" is decided not by another model but by a deterministic verifier: instruction-following revision on IFEval. A model writes a draft; the official IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it; the model then accepts or rejects that edit either as the genuine in-context author or as a fresh model that sees the draft neutrally. Across four mid-tier model families and 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons, we find no detectable self-preference: authors reject verified-good fixes to their own drafts at essentially the same rate as fresh models judging the same drafts (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). A self-skepticism hint from a smaller pilot did not replicate at scale. The one robust observation is qualitative: when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of their stated reasons are flaw-catching rather than preference, that is, about the character of rejections, not an elevated rate. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded at this sample size.

</details>


### [45] [HydraHead: From Head-Level Functional Heterogeneity to Specialized Attention Hybridization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20097)
*Zhentao Tan,Wei Chen,Jingyi Shen,Yao Liu,Xu Shen,Yue Wu,Jieping Ye*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HydraHead proposes hybridizing Full Attention and Linear Attention at the head level rather than the layer level, using interpretability-driven selection to preserve FA only for retrieval-critical heads and a scale-normalized fusion module to reconcile distributional gaps, achieving superior long-context performance with minimal training overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The quadratic complexity of Full Attention bottlenecks long-context processing. Existing layer-wise hybrid attention designs struggle to effectively integrate Linear Attention with Full Attention. The authors observe that attention heads within the same layer exhibit functional specialization (heterogeneity) despite layer-wise block similarity, suggesting the head dimension as a more principled granularity for attention hybridization.

Method: HydraHead introduces: (1) An interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and retains FA only for those heads, while other heads use LA. (2) A scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs. Training uses a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and knowledge distillation to minimize overhead.

Result: Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs on long-context tasks while maintaining general reasoning capability. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Trained on only 15B tokens, HydraHead achieves over 69% improvement over the baseline at 512K context length, approaching the performance of Qwen3.5 (a model with 256K native context).

Conclusion: Head-level hybridization is a promising and scalable design paradigm for attention mechanisms. By exploiting head-level functional specialization, HydraHead achieves an efficient and effective balance between Full Attention's retrieval capability and Linear Attention's efficiency, with strong scaling potential for ultra-long contexts.

Abstract: The quadratic complexity of attention poses a critical bottleneck for long-context processing, spurring interest in hybrid attention designs. Most open-source hybrid models adopt a layer-wise strategy. Yet, prior work has noted the inherent difficulty of integrating Linear Attention (LA) with Full Attention (FA), suggesting that the design space of attention hybridization remains underexplored. To probe this space, we conduct interpretability analysis and observe that layers exhibit block-wise functional similarity, while individual heads within the same layer display distinct functional specialization despite sharing input features. This head-level heterogeneity suggests that the head dimension provides a natural and principled granularity for fusing heterogeneous attention signals. Building on this insight, we introduce HydraHead, a novel architecture that hybridizes FA and LA along the head axis. HydraHead features two key innovations: (1) an interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and preserves FA only for them, and (2) a scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs. By leveraging a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and distillation, we achieve high-performance hybrid models with minimal training overhead. Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs in long-context tasks while maintaining strong general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Crucially, trained on only 15B tokens, HydraHead achieves over 69% improvement over the baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5, a leading model of comparable size with a native context length of 256K. This highlights the significant scaling potential of head-level hybridization.

</details>


### [46] [From Texts to Scores: Tracing the Emergence of Essay Quality Representations in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20152)
*Jiaxu Zuo,Mu You,Kaixin Lan,Tao Fang,Yujia Huo,Henghua Shen,Lidia S. Chao,Derek F. Wong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Analysis of LLM hidden representations for automated essay scoring reveals that essay quality is encoded in a linearly accessible, progressively emerging form across layers, with identifiable "essay scoring neurons" that respond to intervention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the transformative impact of LLMs on automated essay scoring (AES), the internal mechanisms by which these models encode and assess essay quality remain poorly understood. This work aims to open the "black box" of LLM-based AES through systematic interpretability analysis.

Method: The authors analyzed hidden representations of eight LLMs across two English datasets (ASAP++, CSEE) and one Portuguese dataset (ENEM). They employed linear probing, cross-prompt generalization tests, dimensionality reduction (PCA), and neuron-level analyses, including identification of "essay scoring neurons" and targeted intervention experiments.

Result: Key findings: (1) Essay quality is linearly decodable from LLM representations — nonlinear probes offer only marginal gains. (2) Quality representations emerge progressively across layers. (3) Representations are robust to different prompting strategies. (4) Cross-prompt transfer occurs despite rubric differences. (5) Individual neurons strongly correlate with scores and are sensitive to intervention. (6) Neuron distribution shifts with essay length — longer essays rely more on deeper layers.

Conclusion: LLMs encode structured, linearly accessible representations of essay quality. The identification of interpretable "essay scoring neurons" and the progressive layer-wise emergence of quality signals provide new mechanistic insights into LLM-based AES, advancing both interpretability and potential system improvements.

Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have substantially transformed Automated Essay Scoring (AES), yet the internal mechanisms underlying LLM-based scoring remain poorly understood. In this work, we systematically analyze the hidden representations of eight LLMs across two English essay datasets (ASAP++, CSEE) and one Portuguese dataset (ENEM). Using linear probing, cross-prompt generalization, dimensionality reduction, and neuron-level analyses, we find consistent evidence that essay quality information is encoded in a linearly accessible form within LLM representations. These representations emerge progressively across layers, remain robust across prompting strategies, and partially transfer across essay prompts despite differences in scoring rubrics. In addition, nonlinear probes provide only marginal and inconsistent improvements over linear probes, suggesting that most essay quality information is already linearly decodable. We further identify individual ``essay scoring neurons'' whose activations strongly correlate with essay scores and whose behavior is sensitive to targeted intervention. Moreover, the layer-wise distribution of these neurons systematically shifts with essay length, with longer essays relying more heavily on deeper layers. Overall, our findings provide evidence that LLMs encode structured representations related to essay quality and offer new insights into the interpretability of LLM-based AES systems.

</details>


### [47] [MedRLM: Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence for Long-Context Clinical Reasoning, Sensor-Guided Screening, Evidence-Grounded Decision Support, and Community-to-Tertiary Referral Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20164)
*Aueaphum Aueawatthanaphisut*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MedRLM proposes a recursive multimodal AI framework that treats patient cases as external environments to be iteratively inspected and synthesized, using specialized agents and a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory to enable longitudinal, sensor-guided, uncertainty-aware clinical decision support rather than single-step QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
