Motivation: Current medical LLMs and RAG systems rely on single-step prompting/retrieval, which fails when clinical evidence is scattered across longitudinal EHRs, imaging, sensor streams, guidelines, and referral constraints. Real-world clinical decision support demands reasoning over heterogeneous, temporally distributed patient information.

Method: MedRLM employs a recursive architecture that treats the patient case as an external clinical environment, coordinating specialized agents (clinical text, longitudinal EHR, imaging, physiological sensors, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, referral planning). A Clinical Evidence Graph Memory links patient observations with retrieved evidence, biomarkers, and referral criteria. Sensor-guided recursive triggering activates deeper reasoning upon detecting abnormal patterns, and uncertainty-gated refinement flags high-risk or low-confidence cases for clinician review.

Result: This is a framework/proposal paper; no empirical results are reported. The authors outline a planned real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes.

Conclusion: MedRLM aims to shift medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, workflow-aware clinical decision support by enabling recursive inspection, evidence grounding, and clinician-in-the-loop uncertainty management.

Abstract: Real-world clinical decision support requires reasoning over heterogeneous and longitudinal patient information rather than answering isolated medical questions. However, current medical large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems often rely on single-step prompting or retrieval, which can be fragile when clinical evidence is distributed across long electronic health records, medical images, sensor streams, guidelines, and referral constraints. This paper proposes MedRLM, a Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence framework for long-context clinical reasoning, sensor-guided screening, and community-to-tertiary referral support. Instead of compressing all patient information into one prompt, MedRLM treats the patient case as an external clinical environment that can be recursively inspected, decomposed, retrieved, verified, and synthesized. The framework coordinates specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, medical imaging, physiological sensor signals, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning. It further introduces a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory to connect patient-specific observations with retrieved evidence, standardized definitions, sensor-derived biomarkers, and referral criteria. A sensor-guided recursive triggering mechanism activates deeper reasoning when abnormal physiological or behavioral patterns are detected, while uncertainty-gated refinement supports clinician review for high-risk or low-confidence cases. We also outline a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. MedRLM aims to move medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, and workflow-aware clinical decision support.

</details>


### [48] [ReNikud: Audio-Supervised Hebrew Grapheme-to-Phoneme Conversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20179)
*Maxim Melichov,Yakov Kolani,Morris Alper*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReNikud introduces a novel G2P approach for Modern Hebrew that uses weak audio supervision from ASR pseudo-labeling and a character-aligned pseudo-vocalization architecture, outperforming prior methods on both existing and new spoken Hebrew benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern Hebrew G2P is difficult due to its abjad writing system (missing vowels), scarce vocalization data, and the gap between formal grammatical nikud and everyday spoken pronunciation. Existing methods either rely on limited manual vocalization or struggle with direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction.

Method: ReNikud combines: (1) weak audio supervision via an ASR-based pseudo-labeling pipeline trained on thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio to generate natural phonemic transcriptions without manual annotation; (2) a pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias.

Result: ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and the newly introduced MILIM benchmark, which specifically targets spoken Hebrew pronunciation.

Conclusion: By leveraging weak audio supervision and character-aligned prediction, ReNikud effectively bridges the gap between written and spoken Hebrew, enabling better TTS and speech technologies. Code and models will be publicly released.

Abstract: Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion for Modern Hebrew is needed for applications like text-to-speech (TTS), but is challenging due to the language's abjad writing system, which leaves vowels largely unwritten, creating substantial ambiguity. Standard approaches first predict vowel diacritics (nikud) to produce International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcriptions, but this is limited: vocalization data is scarce and laborious to produce, it does not specify features such as lexical stress, and it reflects formal grammatical rules rather than everyday spoken pronunciation. Direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction, meanwhile, struggles on limited data and fails to exploit the character-level alignment characteristic of abjads. Our method, ReNikud, overcomes these limitations with two key insights: (1) Weak audio supervision via a phoneme-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) pseudo-labeling pipeline on thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio, yielding phonemic transcriptions that reflect natural spoken norms without manual annotation. (2) A pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias. Results on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and the new targeted MILIM benchmark for spoken Hebrew show that ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods. We will release our code and trained models to support further work on Hebrew TTS and speech technologies.

</details>


### [49] [Pitch Spelling Jazz Lead Sheets, Solo Transcriptions, Classical Piano and Monophonic Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20198)
*Augustin Bouquillard,Florent Jacquemard*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A two-stage algorithm for joint pitch spelling and key estimation from MIDI-like input: a "modal" stage infers local scales per bar via shortest-path optimization to minimize accidentals, followed by a "tonal" stage that derives global key signatures and note names. Evaluated across diverse datasets (jazz, classical, monophonic), with novel inter-scale distances defined for jazz scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To support music transcription pipelines—particularly building digital collections of jazz solos from audio recordings for analysis, teaching, and cultural heritage preservation—by accurately converting MIDI pitch data into readable, musically correct notation with appropriate key signatures and note spellings.

Method: A two-stage optimization framework: Stage 1 ("modal") uses shortest-path search to assign the most probable local scale to each bar, minimizing accidental counts in the resulting notation. Stage 2 ("tonal") leverages these local scale assignments to jointly estimate a global Key Signature and final note names that yield optimal notation across the entire piece. Novel inter-scale distances between common jazz scales are defined to support the process.

Result: The algorithm was evaluated on diverse datasets including jazz lead sheets (Real Book), transcriptions of jazz solos and bass lines, traditional tunes, and classical scores for both piano and monophonic instruments, demonstrating robust performance across varied musical styles.

Conclusion: The joint optimization of local scales, global key signature, and note names effectively automates pitch spelling and key estimation. The method is valuable for music transcription workflows and broader music notation processing tasks. The newly defined jazz-scale distances also hold musicological interest.

Abstract: We present an algorithm for pitch spelling and key estimation. Given an input in MIDI-like format, containing information on note pitches (expressed in semitones relative to the lowest reference note) and bar boundaries, it estimates the appropriate note names, a global Key Signature, and a local scale for each bar. This related information elements are evaluated jointly during two stages of optimisation. During an initial 'modal' stage, a probable scale is proposed for each bar, minimising the number of accidentals to be printed in the printed score with a shortest-path search. Then, during a second stage called 'tonal', these local scales are used to estimate the Key Signature and note names that would result in the best musical notation for the entire piece. We present evaluations conducted on datasets comprising a variety of digital musical scores: jazz lead sheets taken from the Real Book, transcriptions of recordings of jazz soli and bass lines, traditional tunes, as well as classical scores for piano and monophonic instruments. Our procedure was originally designed for use in music transcription, specifically for building digital collections of jazz solos transcribed from audio recordings, for the purposes of music analysis, teaching and the preservation of cultural heritage. This method should also prove useful for other tasks related to the processing of musical notation. Furthermore, to this end, we have defined new distances between various common jazz scales, which may be of some interest to musicological studies.

</details>


### [50] [CzechDocs: A Multiway Parallel Dataset of Formatted Documents for Minority Languages in Czechia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20212)
*Josef Jon,Ondřej Bojar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CzechDocs is a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, PDF) in Czech and minority languages, designed to benchmark format-preserving machine translation systems, with a publicly released validation split and a held-out test set reserved for a future shared task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current machine translation evaluation largely overlooks document formatting preservation (e.g., retaining HTML tags, DOCX styles, PDF layout), which is crucial for practical deployment. There is a lack of publicly available, multi-format, multi-language parallel datasets specifically designed to assess how well MT systems maintain formatting during translation.

Method: The authors construct CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset covering three document formats (HTML, DOCX, PDF) across Czech and several minority languages (primarily Ukrainian and English, plus Vietnamese, Russian, and others). They provide a validation subset and an evaluation toolkit, and compare the most common format-preserving MT approaches on this validation split. A held-out test split is reserved for a future shared task.

Result: The paper reports a comparative evaluation of common format-preserving machine translation approaches on the validation subset of CzechDocs. The dataset and evaluation toolkit are publicly released to facilitate further research.

Conclusion: CzechDocs fills a critical gap in MT evaluation by providing a structured, multi-format, multi-language benchmark for format-preserving translation. The public release of the validation split and toolkit, along with a planned shared task on the held-out test set, aims to spur progress in document-level translation with formatting fidelity.

Abstract: We present CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, and PDF) covering Czech and minority languages used in Czechia-primarily Ukrainian and English, with smaller portions of Vietnamese, Russian and other languages. The dataset is designed to support the evaluation of machine translation systems that aim to preserve document formatting during translation. We provide a comparison of the most common approaches to format-preserving machine translation on a validation subset of the dataset. This validation split, together with the evaluation toolkit, is publicly released for further research. A held-out test split will be reserved for a future shared task focused on document-level translation with formatting preservation.

</details>


### [51] [Actionable Activation Directions for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Misalignment Across Language Model Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20225)
*Abdul Rafay Syed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Fine-tuning on insecure code causes misalignment with a linear direction in activation space. Within-model steering by subtracting this direction is causally specific; cross-model transfer works but lacks specificity, revealing a two-tier structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether emergent misalignment from fine-tuning on insecure code corresponds to a causally actionable activation-space direction, and whether this direction is shared across model architectures.

Method: Four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) were identically fine-tuned on insecure code. Difference-in-means between aligned and misaligned activations at the final layer was computed. Causal steering tested by subtracting this direction. Cross-architecture transfer used ridge regression mapping between model activation spaces, with random and orthogonal directions as specificity controls.

Result: Difference-in-means achieved 99.6% linear separability at each model's final layer. Within-model steering reduced code spillover by 21–51 points with content specificity confirmed via a secure-code control. Cross-architecture transfer achieved up to 46-point suppression but failed specificity controls: random and orthogonal directions performed comparably. An asymmetric transfer topology emerged: Gemma and Qwen act as geometric donors, Llama as a receiver.

Conclusion: There is a two-tier specificity structure: within-model misalignment directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. This defines limits of linear cross-architecture correction, and the authors recommend within-model probing for auditing purposes.

Abstract: Fine-tuning language models on insecure code induces emergent misalignment with poorly understood internal structure. We investigate whether this misalignment corresponds to a causally actionable activation-space direction shared across architectures. Across four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) finetuned identically, a difference-in-means direction achieves 99.6% separation of aligned and misaligned activations at each model's final layer. Causal steering by subtracting this direction reduces code spillover by 21-51 points, while a secure-code control confirms content specificity. Cross-architecture transfer via ridge regression maps yields large behavioral suppression (up to 46 points) but fails specificity controls as random and orthogonal directions perform comparably. We identify a two-tier specificity structure: within-model directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. An asymmetric transfer topology emerges, with Gemma and Qwen acting as geometric donors and Llama as a receiver. These findings define the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for auditing.

</details>


### [52] [The Register Gap: A Meaning Intelligence Framework for Nigerian Public Discourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20255)
*Celestine Achi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MIF, a nine-dimension framework for annotating Nigerian public discourse that distinguishes surface sentiment from pragmatic intent. It demonstrates that providing the MIF schema to a language model dramatically improves performance across multiple dimensions, with register classification accuracy jumping from 33.3% to 73.3%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Nigerian-language sentiment benchmarks (NaijaSenti, AfriSenti) reduce analysis to three-way polarity, but the dominant AI failure mode on Nigerian discourse is context failure — not translation failure. The same utterance can carry opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situational context, which polarity-only approaches cannot capture.

Method: The authors designed the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF) with nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. They built a 30-item calibration dataset spanning Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers. They evaluated Gemini 2.5 Flash under zero-shot and schema-informed prompting conditions, computing a composite Meaning Intelligence Score and dimension-level comparisons.

Result: The key result is the "Register Gap": zero-shot register classification accuracy was 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) when the model received the MIF schema in-context. The composite Meaning Intelligence Score increased from 73.2 to 78.6 (+5.4 points). The largest practical gains occurred in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points).

Conclusion: Context-aware schema prompting dramatically improves model understanding of Nigerian discourse across all dimensions. The MIF framework provides a more nuanced alternative to simple sentiment polarity. The authors release the framework specification, annotation guidelines, and the 30-item calibration set publicly, while retaining a private holdout corpus for contamination-protected future evaluation.

Abstract: We introduce the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation and evaluation schema for Nigerian public discourse that separates surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Existing benchmarks for Nigerian languages, including NaijaSenti and AfriSenti, treat sentiment classification as a three-way polarity task (positive, negative, neutral). We argue that the dominant failure mode of AI systems on Nigerian discourse is not translation failure but context failure: the same utterance carries opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situation. The MIF operationalises this insight across nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. We construct a 30-item calibration dataset spanning Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers, and evaluate a frontier language model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) under zero-shot and schema-informed prompting conditions. The headline finding is the Register Gap: zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) when the model receives the MIF schema in-context. The composite Meaning Intelligence Score increases by 5.4 points (73.2 to 78.6) under schema-informed prompting, with the largest practical gains in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points). We release the framework specification, annotation guidelines, and the 30-item public calibration set to support reproducibility, while retaining a private holdout corpus for contamination-protected evaluation.

</details>


### [53] [PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287)
*Wei Xia,Jin Wu,Haoran Shi,Xiangyu Wang,Chanjin Zheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PsyScore integrates neural IRT-based automated essay scoring with ability-adaptive feedback generation, using a shared latent trait to bridge diagnostic assessment and instructional scaffolding, achieving competitive scoring and pedagogically aligned feedback on ASAP++.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AES systems fragment scoring and feedback: neural scoring models lack interpretability, while LLM-generated feedback ignores learner proficiency levels. The authors aim to unify these through a psychometrically grounded framework.

Method: PsyScore has three modules: (1) Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer, embedding the Graded Partial Credit Model (GPCM) into a neural network for ability estimation with psychometric interpretability; (2) ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator, which conditions multi-agent feedback on diagnosed ability (Zone of Proximal Development); (3) Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation, using pairwise preference judgments and student revision simulations to assess feedback quality.

Result: Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset show PsyScore achieves competitive scoring accuracy and produces feedback that is more pedagogically aligned compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Integrating psychometric models with neural and LLM-based approaches via a shared latent ability representation effectively unifies scoring and feedback, yielding both reliable assessment and proficiency-sensitive instructional support.

Abstract: Effective Automated Essay Scoring (AES) are expected to support both reliable assessment and actionable instructional feedback. However, existing approaches often treat scoring and feedback as separate components: neural scoring models provide limited interpretability, while Large Language Model (LLM)-based feedback is typically insensitive to learners proficiency levels. To address this fragmentation, this work proposes PsyScore, a psychometrically-aware framework that integrates diagnostic assessment with instructional scaffolding through a shared latent ability representation. PsyScore comprises three key modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer that incorporates the Graded Partial Credit Model (GPCM) into a neural architecture, enabling the precise estimation of student ability while maintaining psychometric interpretability, a ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator, which conditions multi-agent feedback strategies on the diagnosed ability parameter to adapt instructional focus across different proficiency levels, and a Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy that assesses feedback quality via pairwise preference judgements and student revision simulations. Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset demonstrate that PsyScore achieves competitive scoring performance while providing more pedagogically aligned feedback.

</details>


### [54] [CATCH-ME if you RAG: a dataset of Contextually Annotated multi-Turn Counterspeech against Hate and Misinformation Exchanges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20369)
*Helena Bonaldi,Genoveffa Martone,Marco Guerini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces the first large-scale, multilingual, expert-curated dialogue dataset addressing the intersection of online hate speech and misinformation. The dataset spans five languages, targets hate against seven marginalized groups, features multi-turn dialogues, and is anchored in verified external knowledge (fact-checking articles, NGO reports) with span annotations for RAG systems, enabling training of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hate speech and misinformation frequently co-occur online, yet NLP research treats them separately. While LLMs can generate counterspeech at scale, zero-shot outputs tend to be repetitive and vague, creating a need for high-quality exemplars. Existing counterspeech datasets are scarce, limited to single-turn English dialogues, and fail to capture the multi-turn, multilingual nature of real-world interactions at the intersection of hate and misinformation.

Method: The authors construct an expert-curated, multilingual dataset of dialogues specifically targeting the overlap of hate speech and misinformation. Dialogues are grounded in verified external knowledge sources—fact-checking articles and NGO reports—and include both document-level and chunk-level span annotations. The resource covers five languages and seven marginalized groups, and is designed for direct integration with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.

Result: The paper presents the dataset as a novel resource; specific experimental results are not detailed in the abstract. The resource enables training and evaluation of counterspeech models that are expected to be more persuasive and factually grounded due to the multi-turn structure and verified knowledge anchoring.

Conclusion: The dataset fills a critical gap by providing multi-turn, multilingual, knowledge-grounded training data for counterspeech at the intersection of hate and misinformation, paving the way for more effective and factually reliable counterspeech generation models, particularly in RAG-based architectures.

Abstract: Online hate speech and misinformation frequently overlap, yet NLP research has mainly treated them in isolation. While LLMs represent a scalable solution for assisting humans in the generation of counterspeech for both threats, zero-shot models frequently generate repetitive and vague responses, underscoring the need for high-quality examples to steer model generation. However, existing counterspeech datasets against the overlap of hate and misinformation are scarce and limited to single-turn English dialogues, while real-life interactions span across multiple turns and languages. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dataset of dialogues tackling the intersection of hate and misinformation. To ensure factual grounding, the dialogues are also anchored in verified external knowledge (i.e., fact-checking articles and NGO reports) and include document- and chunk-level span annotations, making it directly applicable for RAG systems. Covering five languages and targeting hate directed at seven marginalized groups, this novel resource enables the training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models.

</details>


### [55] [Beyond Global Replanning: Hierarchical Recovery for Cross-Device Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20487)
*Shu Yao,Yuhua Luo,Qian Long,Jingru Fan,Zhuoyuan Yu,Yuheng Wang,Lin Wu,Yufan Dang,Huatao Li,Chen Qian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: H-RePlan introduces a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents that separates device-local strategy recovery from global replanning via a cross-layer failure abstraction. Evaluated on HeraBench, a fault-injected benchmark spanning Linux and Android, it significantly outperforms coarse-grained baselines in completion, instruction adherence, and token efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-device agent systems handle failures coarsely—retrying, reassigning subtasks, or revising global plans—without systematically modeling the device-local strategy space. This prevents them from distinguishing failures solvable within the current device from those needing cross-device replanning, limiting robustness in heterogeneous, fault-prone environments.

Method: The authors propose H-RePlan, a hierarchical replanning framework with unified API–CLI–GUI execution. Each device is equipped with interchangeable execution strategies. A compact cross-layer failure abstraction enables device-local strategy recovery to operate independently from orchestrator-level global replanning, ensuring scope-aware recovery. They also introduce HeraBench, a fault-injected benchmark that constructs cross-device workflows over Linux and Android and injects both strategy-level and device-level failures.

Result: Experiments on HeraBench show H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines, achieving higher task completion rates, better instruction adherence, more perfect-pass outcomes, and lower token cost for reliable end-to-end success.

Conclusion: Scope-aware hierarchical recovery is essential for robust multi-device agent execution. Decoupling device-local recovery from global replanning enables more precise failure handling, improving both reliability and efficiency.

Abstract: Real-world computer-use tasks often span multiple applications and devices, requiring agents to coordinate heterogeneous environments under dynamic runtime failures. Existing multi-device agent systems support task decomposition and cross-device assignment, but recovery remains largely coarse-grained: when execution fails, they typically retry the same strategy, reassign the subtask, or revise the global plan, without systematically modeling the device-local strategy space. This limits their ability to distinguish failures that can be repaired within the current device from those that require cross-device replanning. We propose \textbf{H-RePlan}, a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents with unified API--CLI--GUI execution. H-RePlan equips each device with interchangeable execution strategies and separates device-local strategy recovery from orchestrator-level global replanning through a compact cross-layer failure abstraction. To evaluate this capability, we introduce \textbf{HeraBench}, a fault-injected benchmark that constructs cross-device workflows over Linux and Android devices and injects strategy- and device-level failures. Experiments show that H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines, achieving higher completion, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rates while reducing the token cost required for reliable end-to-end success. These results demonstrate that scope-aware hierarchical recovery is essential for robust multi-device agent execution.

</details>


### [56] [StylisticBias: A Few Human Visual Cues Drive Most Social Biases in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20527)
*Shaghayegh Kolli,Timo Cavelius,Nafiseh Nikeghbal,Samantha Dalal,Jana Diesner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: StylisticBias introduces a controlled benchmark of ~25K images varying single visual attributes on fixed identities to measure social bias in MLLMs, finding that a small set of cues (age, body type, fashion) drive most judgment shifts, especially in socioeconomic evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior bias evaluations in MLLMs conflate identity differences with appearance effects by comparing different individuals. There is a need to isolate how specific visual attributes independently shift model judgments while holding identity constant.

Method: 500 photorealistic base faces are generated, then ~50 single-attribute variations per face are created (e.g., changing only age, body type, or fashion style), yielding ~25K images. Six MLLMs are evaluated across 25 binary social judgment scenarios, measuring how each attribute shifts responses relative to the base face.

Result: Age and body type dominate identity-level effects, while fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. Approximately 15 attributes account for nearly 80% of total variation. Sensitivity is strongest in judgments semantically aligned with appearance, particularly socioeconomic and style-related judgments.

Conclusion: Social bias in MLLMs is concentrated in a small set of visual attributes, and attribute-level analysis offers finer-grained insight than identity-level comparisons. The StylisticBias benchmark is released to support targeted bias evaluation and mitigation.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in personally and societally consequential settings, yet the visual cues that shape how these models judge people remain poorly understood. Prior work often compares different (groups of) individuals, making it difficult to separate appearance effects from identity differences. We introduce StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute-level social bias in MLLMs. We generate 500 photorealistic base faces and create about 50 single-attribute variations per face, producing about 25K images. This design keeps identity fixed and changes one visual attribute at a time. It lets us measure how specific cues shift model judgments. We evaluate six MLLMs across 25 binary social judgment scenarios. We find that age and body type dominate identity-level effects, while fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. We further find that about 15 attributes account for nearly 80\% of the total variation, showing that bias is concentrated in a small set of visual cues. Sensitivity is strongest in judgments that are semantically aligned with appearance, especially socioeconomic and style-related judgments. We release StylisticBias as a benchmark for fine-grained bias evaluation in multimodal models. Code and dataset: https://github.com/timo-cavelius/StylisticBias and https://hf.co/datasets/shaghayegh/stylistic-bias-dataset.

</details>

### [57] [Supporting Design Decisions in Rule-Based Model Transformations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19342)
*Dejan Stojimirovic,Sinisa Neskovic*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes an approach to externalize design decisions from model transformation code using four interconnected models (decision, binding, configuration, and trace) with a formal mathematical framework, enabling flexibility, reusability, and traceability in rule-based model transformations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In traditional model-driven engineering, design decisions governing how source model elements map to target artifacts are hard-coded within transformation rules. This embedding limits flexibility (cannot easily switch mapping strategies), reusability (decisions cannot be shared across similar transformations), and traceability (rationale behind mappings is opaque).

Method: The approach introduces three separation mechanisms: (1) a decision model capturing design decisions and their options independently of source metamodels; (2) a binding model connecting decisions to specific metamodel concepts, enabling cross-language reuse; (3) a configuration model recording chosen options per source element with automatic defaults. At execution time, variability points in transformation rules resolve dynamically against configured choices, with a trace model recording rule-to-target-element provenance. A formal mathematical framework defines variability-based transformation concepts and proves key properties. A practical architecture of four interconnected artifact models realizes these concepts, demonstrated by extending an existing embedded DSL for MDE.

Result: The work establishes formal definitions and proofs for variability-based transformations. It delivers a practical architecture composed of four artifact models (decision, binding, configuration, trace) and demonstrates feasibility through an extended embedded DSL with a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling design decisions separately from transformation logic significantly improves flexibility, promotes reuse of design knowledge across similar modeling languages, and provides fine-grained traceability. The formal framework ensures correctness guarantees for the variability-based transformation approach.

Abstract: Model Driven Engineering relies on model transformations to automate the derivation of target models or source code from source models. However, the design decisions that govern how source elements are mapped to target artifacts typically remain embedded in the transformation source code, limiting flexibility, reusability, and traceability. This paper proposes an approach to explicitly model and manage design decisions in rule-based model transformations. Design decisions are separated from transformation implementation through three mechanisms. First, a decision model captures design decisions and their options independently of any source modeling language for a given transformation domain. Second, a binding model connects these decisions to specific metamodel concepts in a given source modeling language, enabling reuse of the same design knowledge across transformations from similar languages. Third, a configuration model records the specific option chosen for each applicable source model element, with defaults pre-selected automatically. During execution, variability points in transformation rules are resolved dynamically according to configured choices. A trace model records which rules and options were applied to produce each target element. We establish a formal mathematical framework that defines the core concepts of variability-based transformations and proves key properties of the resulting transformations. The formal concepts are realized in a practical architecture of four interconnected artifact models. We demonstrate practical feasibility by extending an existing embedded domain-specific language for model-driven engineering with variability support and illustrate the approach with a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example.

</details>


### [58] [AgentArmor: A Framework, Evaluation, \& Mitigation of Coding Agent Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19380)
*Kenneth Ge,Andre Assis*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper identifies three failure modes in AI coding agents—underspecification, capability errors, and agent harness errors—evaluates them across 8 evaluations with 20 coding environments, and proposes AgentArmor, a harness modification with safeguards (extended prompts, command classifier, "3 strikes" policy, guardrails, self-editing tools) that significantly improves safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI coding agents are increasingly deployed in real-world software engineering tasks, rare but highly destructive failures are emerging. These failures are not well-categorized or systematically mitigated, motivating a structured taxonomy and practical countermeasures.

Method: The authors taxonomize failures into three mechanisms: (1) underspecification (unsafe default behaviors), (2) capability errors (model bias or limitations prevent correct action), and (3) agent harness errors (failure to execute safe actions through the tooling layer). They design 8 evaluations inspired by real deployment incidents, covering 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. AgentArmor is then proposed as a harness-level defense combining an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a "3 strikes" execution policy, deterministic guardrails, and tools enabling the agent to modify its own context window.

Result: AgentArmor demonstrates statistically significant safety improvements across the evaluated samples, effectively reducing failures from all three error categories.

Conclusion: Concrete, harness-level mitigations can substantially reduce destructive failure modes in AI coding agents. The paper offers both immediate practical fixes and a design philosophy for building safer agent harnesses in the future.

Abstract: Software engineering and deployment are increasingly being delegated to AI coding agents. The scale of their adoption is surfacing rare, but highly destructive, failure modes. In this paper, we study these failure modes as stemming from three distinct mechanisms: underspecification, where default model behavior is unsafe; capability errors, where the safe action is available but the model does not adhere to it due to bias or capability limitations; and agent harness errors, where the model fails to execute the safe action through the harness. We evaluate these across 8 different evaluations, each inspired by real-life deployment failures, totaling 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. Based on this evaluation, we propose AgentArmor, an agent harness modification, to mitigate these errors. By adding an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a ``3 strikes'' policy, deterministic guardrails, and tools for the agent to edit its own context, we show that AgentArmor is safer across a statistically significant number of samples. Thus, we suggest concrete mitigations for current coding agents and a design philosophy for future agent harness features.

</details>


### [59] [DynAMO:Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration via Topological Multi-Agent Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19382)
*Kanishk Kushwaha,Vikrant Vinod Bansode,Harsh Vardhan,Dhaval C. Patel*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: DynAMO is a deployment-ready LLM agent orchestration engine for Industry 4.0 that uses a Plan-then-Execute architecture with verifiable workflow graphs. It supports both sequential and parallel execution, achieving 1.6–1.8× latency reduction while maintaining safety and correctness under fault injection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-powered agents for industrial asset lifecycles face deployment barriers including high latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks in real-world Industry 4.0 settings. Existing solutions lack a practical engine that balances efficiency gains from parallelism with verifiable correctness and safety guarantees.

Method: DynAMO employs a Plan-then-Execute architecture that generates verifiable workflow graphs. It supports two execution modes: SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency with dynamic identification of independent tasks). The system incorporates structured context pruning (≈30% inference latency reduction) and controlled reasoning overlap to preserve structural correctness. Evaluation uses the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark across six controlled experiments, including latency decomposition analysis and controlled fault injection for robustness testing.

Result: Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6× over sequential orchestration, reaching 1.8× on highly parallelizable workflows. LLM reasoning and orchestration account for >90% of execution time after instrumenting realistic external tool latencies. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by ~30%. DynAMO maintains correct functional behavior (task completion, agent sequencing, output quality) with graceful degradation under fault injection. Reproducibility analysis confirms stable execution with reduced latency variance under parallel scheduling.

Conclusion: DynAMO provides a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware LLM agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines, demonstrating that dependency-aware parallelism can significantly improve efficiency without compromising correctness or safety.

Abstract: While LLM-powered agents offer end-to-end automation for industrial asset lifecycles, real-world Industry 4.0 deployment is hindered by latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks. We present DynAMO (Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration), a deployment-ready engine using a Plan-then-Execute architecture to generate verifiable workflow graphs. DynAMO supports both SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency). By dynamically identifying independent tasks, DynAMO preserves structural correctness and safety while significantly improving efficiency through controlled reasoning overlap.
  Across six controlled experiments on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark, DynAMO demonstrates substantial performance and robustness gains. Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6x over sequential orchestration, rising to 1.8x on highly parallelizable workflows. After instrumenting external tool calls with realistic latencies, a latency decomposition shows that LLM reasoning and orchestration still account for more than 90% of execution time, identifying model inference as the primary system bottleneck. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by approximately 30%, and DynAMO maintains correct functional behaviour (task completion, agent sequencing, and output quality) while exhibiting graceful degradation under controlled fault injection. Reproducibility analysis further confirms stable execution under repeated runs, with parallel scheduling reducing latency variance. These findings establish DynAMO as a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines. Code is available at: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO

</details>


### [60] [Bistable by Construction: Wall-Clock-Calibrated State Monitors Have No Moment-Detection Regime at Agent Cadence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19386)
*Manvendra Modgil*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitor (affect engine) trapped in constant-alarm or silent regimes on agent streams due to variable inter-action timing. The trap is a general property of wall-clock calibration, not the specific engine. Sample-time methods (CUSUM) are dt-invariant; rising-edge triggers with hysteresis avoid the trap but fail to match human intervention timing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Correct a previously published error (Modgil 2026) where an affect-based runtime monitor exhibited near-constant alarms on SWE-bench debugging agents. The root cause — dt=0 between actions preventing exponential decay — was misattributed. The authors reframe the flaw as an experiment to investigate a deeper structural issue: whether monitor dynamics calibrated in wall-clock time versus sample time behave differently on agent streams with highly variable inter-action intervals.

Method: Pre-registered sweep over uniform dt intervals (0–600s) across 20 trajectories, testing a wall-clock leaky-integrator threshold trigger. Compared against: (1) a minimal wall-clock accumulator on raw error, (2) a sample-time CUSUM on identical streams, and (3) a rising-edge trigger with hysteresis. Real agent latency measured (median 1.53s, p90 2.33s).

Result: The wall-clock trigger exhibits two regimes: constant alarms at dt ≤ 1s (20/20 trajectories, median 18 firings) and complete silence at dt ≥ 60s. All critical dt values fall in (1,30]s — precisely where real agent coding cadence sits. The minimal wall-clock accumulator reproduces the same cliff, confirming the property belongs to the calibration class. Sample-time CUSUM is exactly dt-invariant (20/20 across all dt). Rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires only 0–3 times per trajectory in every condition.

Conclusion: Wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime where they function as moment detectors on agent streams. Transition detection (rising-edge with hysteresis) escapes the trap at every cadence but cannot recover human intervention timing. The findings provide a structural diagnostic for designing runtime monitors on autonomous agent streams.

Abstract: Runtime monitors for autonomous agents commonly threshold an accumulated internal state - a behavioural baseline, a drift statistic, or, in our prior work, a modelled affective state. We previously reported a State Saturation Trap: threshold-on-state triggers over a continuous affect engine become near-constant alarms on SWE-bench debugging agents (Modgil 2026). A post-release audit found the engine received dt=0 between actions, so its exponential decay never operated: the published trap is a pure-accumulator result. We correct the record (erratum, v2) and treat the flaw as an experiment. The key variable it exposes is whether a monitor's dynamics are calibrated in sample time (per observation, as in CUSUM) or wall-clock time (half-lives in seconds, as in affect models and EMA baselines). On fixed-rate streams these coincide; on agent streams, where inter-action time varies by orders of magnitude, they do not. A pre-registered sweep over uniform intervals (dt in {0..600}s) on 20 trajectories shows the wall-clock level trigger has two regimes: at dt<=1s a constant alarm (20/20; median 18 firings); at dt>=60s silent. Every critical dt lies in (1,30]s. Real agent runs measure latency at median 1.53s (p90 2.33s); real coding cadence sits inside the trap regime, vindicating the empirical finding under a corrected mechanism. The structure is a property of the calibration class, not the engine: a minimal wall-clock accumulator over the raw error stream reproduces the same cliff, while a sample-time CUSUM over the identical stream is exactly dt-invariant (20/20). A rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires 0-3 times per trajectory in every condition. We conclude that wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime in which they act as moment detectors on agent streams; transition detection escapes the trap at every cadence, but does not recover human intervention timing.

</details>


### [61] [Interpretable and Verifiable Hardware Generation with LLM-Driven Stepwise Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19387)
*You Li,Samuel Mandell,David Z. Pan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A framework that combines LLMs with formal methods to generate correct RTL hardware designs by iteratively applying verified transformation rules from specifications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs show promise for software development but suffer from hallucinations (semantic/logical errors), which is unacceptable in high-stakes chip design. Hardware engineers remain reluctant to trust LLMs for RTL generation due to the need for absolute correctness.

Method: A hybrid framework where an LLM agent iteratively applies a set of predefined transformation rules—covering various design decisions and hardware features—to convert a design specification into an RTL program. Formal methods ensure correctness guarantees throughout the transformation process.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate the framework is both effective at generating RTL designs and efficient in its execution, with guaranteed correctness via formal methods.

Conclusion: Combining LLM creativity with formal method rigor offers a viable path toward trustworthy RTL generation, potentially overcoming hardware engineers' reluctance to adopt LLM-assisted chip design workflows.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in software development. However, they are susceptible to hallucinations, meaning that they can introduce subtle semantic and logical errors. Due to the high stakes in chip design and manufacturing, hardware engineers are still reluctant to rely on LLMs for register-transfer level (RTL) generation. In this paper, we propose a hardware generation framework that combines the creativity and broad knowledge of LLMs with the explainability and mathematical rigor of formal methods. Specifically, we devise a set of transformation rules that cover various design decisions and hardware features. By iteratively applying these rules, an LLM agent can convert a design specification into an RTL program with guaranteed correctness. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the framework.

</details>


### [62] [Before the Pull Request: Mining Multi-Agent Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19616)
*Dipankar Sarkar*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Autonomous coding agents face a coordination problem: concurrent agents duplicating work leads to low PR acceptance rates. The paper introduces "grite," a git-native, serverless, append-only event log that serves as a coordination substrate. It eliminates redundant work (78% → 0%), triples useful throughput, ensures strong log convergence, and enables automatic recovery from concrete failure modes (conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close) by mining the coordination log.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale studies show autonomous coding agents produce pull requests faster but with lower acceptance rates, a coordination and trust gap unexplained by PR-level telemetry. The core problem is not visible at the PR level — it occurs beforehand, in how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work. Existing tools lack a reliable, shared coordination fabric to capture this pre-PR process.

Method: The authors build "grite," an open-source coordination substrate with no central server. It stores coordination records directly inside git as an append-only, signed event log, ensuring every agent converges to the same state without silently dropped writes (unlike file-based trackers). The system is evaluated by measuring duplicate work reduction, throughput gains, log convergence properties, and the ability to automatically mine and recover from failure modes with full provenance.

Result: (i) Duplicate/redundant work dropped from 78% to 0%, while useful throughput more than tripled. (ii) Every agent's log copy converges identically with no lost writes, whereas a file-based tracker loses concurrent writes. (iii) The log enables automatic recovery with provenance for failure modes — conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close — several of which are invisible in PR history alone.

Conclusion: The pre-PR coordination process is the critical missing signal for understanding and improving multi-agent coding workflows. A git-native, append-only event log like grite provides a reliable, mineable coordination fabric that eliminates redundant work, ensures convergence, and surfaces otherwise invisible failure modes. The dataset, harness, and mining toolkit are publicly released.

Abstract: Autonomous coding agents now open millions of pull requests, yet large-scale studies find their PRs are produced faster but accepted less often - a coordination and trust gap that pull-request-level telemetry cannot explain. We argue the missing signal lives before the PR, in how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work. We study this process through grite, our open-source coordination substrate that needs no central server and stores its records inside git itself, so its append-only, signed event log captures the coordination process directly. We show that (i) this shared substrate reduces duplicate and conflicting work at bounded overhead - the share of work that merely re-does a teammate's task falls from 78% to 0% while useful throughput more than triples; (ii) every agent's copy of the log converges to the same state with no write silently dropped, where a file-based tracker loses concurrent writes; and (iii) the log is a mineable artefact from which concrete failure modes - conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close - are automatically recoverable with provenance, several invisible in pull-request history. We release the dataset, harness, and mining toolkit.

</details>


### [63] [Beyond the GUI Paradigm: Do Mobile Agents Need the Phone Screen?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19388)
*Li Gu,Zihuan Jiang,Linqiang Guo,Zhixiang Chi,Ziqiang Wang,Huan Liu,Yuanhao Yu,Tse-Hsun Chen,Yang Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper argues that mobile command-line interfaces (CLI) deserve equal attention alongside GUI-based mobile agents. Using off-the-shelf coding agents without mobile-specific training, CLI agents (especially Claude Code with Opus 4.7) significantly outperform all reproducible GUI baselines on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks, while using substantially fewer steps. The authors also introduce the CLI-Advantage Task Suite covering tasks beyond GUI scope and provide oracle solutions establishing performance ceilings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile agent research is overwhelmingly dominated by the GUI paradigm, despite mobile platforms also exposing CLIs that provide direct access to device services and data. The authors aim to demonstrate that CLI-based agents are not only competitive but can outperform GUI agents, and that CLI enables task categories fundamentally beyond GUI reach.

Method: Three coding agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) are evaluated across four model APIs on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks, without any mobile-specific post-training. These are compared against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). Oracle CLI solutions establish performance ceilings. A novel CLI-Advantage Task Suite with 45 templates across five categories (bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, hidden device state) is introduced to cover intents beyond GUI scope.

Result: Claude Code (Opus 4.7) achieved 71.8% on AndroidWorld and 51.9% on MobileWorld, outperforming all GUI baselines (69.3/68.1/57.8% on AndroidWorld; 43.2/26.3/13.3% on MobileWorld). Every other CLI configuration remained competitive. Oracle CLI solutions reached 88.8% on AndroidWorld (103/116 tasks CLI-solvable) and 86.3% on MobileWorld (101/117 tasks CLI-solvable). CLI agents outperformed GUI baselines in all five CLI-Advantage categories with fewer steps per task (10.7 vs. 18.6).

Conclusion: CLI-based mobile agents represent a promising and underexplored paradigm that can outperform GUI agents on existing benchmarks and uniquely handle task categories beyond GUI reach. Substantial headroom remains for improvement toward oracle performance. The authors will open-source all implementations and infrastructure to support future research.

Abstract: Recent advances in mobile agents are dominated by the GUI paradigm, in which agents perceive UI information and emit screen interactions. However, mobile platforms also expose a command-line interface (CLI) that provides direct access to device services and data. We argue CLI deserves first-class consideration alongside GUI. We evaluate three coding agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) across four model APIs on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld without any mobile-specific post-training, comparing against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). Claude Code (Opus 4.7) reaches 71.8\% and 51.9\%, outperforming every reproducible GUI baseline (69.3/68.1/57.8\% on AndroidWorld; 43.2/26.3/13.3\% on MobileWorld), while every other CLI configuration remains competitive. To establish the paradigm's ceiling, we provide oracle CLI solutions that reach 88.8\% on AndroidWorld (103/116 tasks CLI-solvable) and 86.3\% on MobileWorld (101/117 tasks CLI-solvable), indicating substantial room for future improvement. To cover everyday user intents beyond the GUI scope, we introduce the \textbf{CLI-Advantage Task Suite}, comprising 45 templates across five categories: bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, and hidden device state. Every CLI agent outperforms every GUI baseline in all five categories, with substantially fewer steps per task (10.7 vs.\ 18.6). To support future research on mobile CLI agents, we will open-source agent implementations, oracle solutions, the CLI-Advantage suite, and evaluation infrastructure.

</details>


### [64] [Execution-bound advisory automation for agentic AI: a reproducible AIBOM-driven CSAF-VEX framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19390)
*Petar Radanliev,Omar Santos,Carsten Maple,Kay Atefi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A framework that links SBOM/AIBOM artefacts with deterministic environment capture and runtime telemetry to compute exploitability, generate signed CSAF VEX advisories, and validate through deterministic replay, evaluated on ~10,000 components in Agentic AI workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond static vulnerability scanning by combining declared software/AI bill of materials (SBOM/AIBOM) with runtime evidence, enabling more accurate exploitability assessment and automated generation of verifiable vulnerability exploitability exchange (VEX) advisories.

Method: A protocol-driven framework that: (1) binds SBOM and AIBOM artefacts to deterministic environment snapshots and structured runtime telemetry; (2) computes exploitability using declared artefacts, observed activation conditions, and enforced execution policies; (3) generates CSAF-format VEX advisories from combined static and runtime evidence; (4) cryptographically signs advisories; and (5) validates findings through deterministic replay.

Result: The framework was evaluated on approximately 10,000 component entries across synthetic Agentic AI workloads ranging from 50 to 5,000 components, incorporating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets. Results demonstrate the feasibility of deterministic environment capture and replay for verifiable exploitability assessment.

Conclusion: The proposed protocol-driven approach effectively bridges static SBOM/AIBOM analysis with runtime telemetry, enabling more precise exploitability computation and trustworthy, cryptographically verifiable VEX advisories suitable for AI-driven and conventional software supply chains.

Abstract: A protocol driven framework is presented that binds SBOM and AIBOM artefacts to deterministic environment capture and structured runtime telemetry. Exploitability is computed from declared artefacts, observed activation conditions, and enforced execution policies. CSAF VEX advisories are generated from combined static and runtime evidence, cryptographically signed, and validated through deterministic replay. Evaluation uses approximately 10000 component entries across synthetic Agentic AI workloads 50 to 5000 components, incorporating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets.

</details>


### [65] [Library-Aware Doubles and Iterative Repair for Large Language Model-Generated Unit Tests in OpenSIL Firmware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19725)
*Ma Toan Bach,Yuchi Zheng,Haingo Razafindranto,Tanvir Alam,Aric Leather,Ranveer Sandhu,Jitesh Arora*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An LLM-guided multi-agent pipeline automates unit test generation for AMD's openSIL firmware, using iterative compile-dispatch repair with line-coverage feedback. Across 76 functions, 73 achieved compilable tests, reaching up to 98.8% mean line coverage, demonstrating substantial efficiency gains in constrained embedded environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Validating low-level C firmware changes is expensive due to fragile unit tests under strict build constraints — missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently block compilation and linking. Manual test authoring in this environment is labor-intensive and error-prone, motivating automation.

Method: An automated multi-agent pipeline combining: (1) LLM-guided generation of test scaffolds; (2) library-aware creation/reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes; (3) an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop driven by build logs and line-coverage feedback. Evaluated in configurations with and without vector-database retrieval augmentation.

Result: Out of 76 functions under test, 73 produced compilable unit tests. Without line-coverage guidance or retrieval, mean line coverage reached 73.9%. On a 48-function subset, line-coverage guidance alone achieved 98.8% mean coverage; adding vector-database retrieval yielded 94.7%.

Conclusion: Automated generation-and-repair pipelines substantially improve unit test creation efficiency and coverage for constrained firmware environments, significantly reducing manual debugging effort while maintaining high compilation success rates.

Abstract: Validating changes in low-level C firmware is expensive because unit tests (UTs) are fragile under strict build constraints, where missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently prevent compilation and linking. This study introduces an automated UT authoring workflow for the Open-Source Silicon Initialization Library (openSIL) firmware codebase maintained by Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) that reduces manual effort through a large language model (LLM) guided multi-agent pipeline. The workflow combines automated generation of test scaffolds, library-aware creation or reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes, and an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop driven by build logs and line-coverage feedback. We evaluate the approach using compilation success, repair iterations, dispatch success, and line coverage, with time, cost, and token usage as secondary measures. Across 76 functions under test, the workflow generated compilable UTs for 73 functions. In a configuration without line coverage guidance or retrieval augmentation, mean line coverage reached 73.9%. On a 48-function subset evaluated under both configurations, mean line coverage reached 98.8% with line-coverage guidance alone and reached 94.7% when combined with vector-database retrieval. Results show that automated generation-and-repair pipelines can substantially improve UT creation efficiency and coverage for constrained firmware environments while reducing manual debugging effort.

</details>


### [66] [DevOps and General Developers: Insights from Stack Overflow's 2023 Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19395)
*Hasan Abdulla,Fatema AlJazeeri,Fawzi AlBalooshi,Jaflah Al-Ammary*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study compares DevOps specialists and general software developers using Stack Overflow 2023 Survey data, finding no significant differences in tool/technology preferences—both groups use Docker and Kubernetes extensively. Demographic trends show younger general developers versus mid-career DevOps professionals, with both adapting to remote/hybrid work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically differentiate DevOps specialists from general software developers in terms of tool usage, technologies, methodologies, and demographics, addressing a gap in understanding their distinct roles, contributions, and challenges in modern software development.

Method: Quantitative comparative analysis of the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey data using Python's Pandas library, focusing on technological preferences, demographic variables, and professional experiences between the two groups.

Result: No significant difference in tool and technology preferences between groups; both heavily use Docker and Kubernetes. General developers employ a more diverse tool set. DevOps specialists tend to be mid-career, while general developers skew younger. Both groups show strong adaptation to remote and hybrid work models.

Conclusion: DevOps specialists and general developers play complementary rather than distinct roles, with converging tool ecosystems. The research underscores DevOps' growing importance and provides a data-driven snapshot of role evolution valuable to both academia and industry.

Abstract: Purpose: To investigate the distinct roles of DevOps specialists and general software developers, examining their varying use of tools, technologies, methodologies, and demographics in the current software development environment. In addition, to differentiate these two professional groups regarding their unique contributions and challenges in the field.
  Design/Methodology/Approach: The research uses a quantitative approach to analyze data from the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey. It focuses on a comparative analysis of technological preferences, demographic information, and professional experiences between DevOps specialists and general developers, highlighting key trends and differences. The data analysis was conducted using Python's Pandas library for data analysis.
  Findings: The research indicates no significant difference in the tool and technology preferences between DevOps specialists and general software developers, highlighting their complementary roles. DevOps specialists and general software developers use tools like Docker and Kubernetes, emphasizing efficiency and automation. While general developers employ diverse tools for various role demands, demographic trends show younger general developers and mid-career DevOps professionals. This age range reflects growing experience in DevOps, and both groups are adapting to remote and hybrid work models in the evolving tech industry.
  Practical Implications: This research offers perspectives on the dynamic roles within software development, emphasizing the growing importance of DevOps. It is a valuable resource for academic and industry professionals to understand the evolving dynamics in software development roles.
  Originality/Value: This research fills a significant gap in the existing literature regarding the evolving dynamics of software development roles.

</details>


### [67] [JustDiag!: A Diagnostic Justification Engine for Accountable Root Cause Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19407)
*Tingzhu Bi,Xinrui Jiang,Xun Zhang,Pengcheng Su,Congjie He,Jinglin Li,Ping Wang,Meng Ma*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: JustDiag is a diagnostic justification engine for root cause analysis (RCA) that maintains explicit process state over evidence, hypotheses, conflicts, and checks. Tested on 66 real incidents, it outperformed a non-justification baseline on outcome and process quality, with slightly lower completion rates due to calibrated non-closure — demonstrating that accountable RCA requires justification artifacts, not just fluent answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can generate fluent RCA answers, but fluency alone does not constitute accountability. In high-stakes incident response, engineers need transparency into what evidence supported a diagnosis, which alternatives were considered, where contradictions remain, and whether uncertainty was preserved or prematurely resolved. Existing approaches lack explicit diagnostic justification.

Method: The authors developed JustDiag, a system that maintains an explicit process state tracking evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks during RCA. They evaluated it on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer evaluation protocol: one scoring final-answer quality (outcome) and another scoring diagnostic process quality. Performance was compared against a matched control system lacking diagnostic justification capabilities.

Result: JustDiag achieved stronger scores on both outcome quality and process quality relative to the matched control. It had a slightly lower terminal completion rate due to more calibrated non-closure — i.e., it appropriately refrained from closing cases when evidence was insufficient, rather than producing overconfident answers.

Conclusion: Accountable RCA demands explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation methods, not merely fluent final answers from language models. Calibrated non-closure is a feature, not a flaw, in high-stakes diagnostic systems.

Abstract: Large language models can produce fluent root cause analyses, but fluent final answers alone are insufficient evidence for accountability in high-stakes operations. In real incident response, engineers need to know what evidence supported a diagnosis, which alternatives were considered, where contradictions remained, and whether the system resolved the case or preserved uncertainty. We address this gap with JustDiag, a diagnostic justification engine for RCA that maintains an explicit process state over evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks. We evaluated the system on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer protocol that separately scores final-answer quality and process quality. Relative to a matched control without diagnostic justification, JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores, while accepting slightly lower terminal completion due to more calibrated non-closure. These results suggest that accountable RCA requires explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not only fluent final answers.

</details>


### [68] [OpenRath: Session-Centered Runtime State for Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19409)
*Fukang Wen,Zhijie Wang,Ruilin Xu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: OpenRath introduces a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent systems centered on a first-class runtime abstraction called Session — a branchable, inspectable, replayable value that unifies fragmented runtime state (transcripts, tool effects, memory, provenance) into a single composable entity, enabling explicit fork/merge/replay operations rather than external trace reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern agent systems suffer from fragmented runtime state — transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded separately across different subsystems, making them difficult to inspect, reproduce, or audit coherently. This fragmentation undermines debuggability, reproducibility, and compositional reasoning about agent behavior.

Method: OpenRath adopts a PyTorch-like programming model (analogous in providing a central first-class runtime abstraction, not in tensor computation) where Session serves as the core runtime value passed between agents and workflows. Session records conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence while defining where memory interactions enter the runtime record. The framework defines six additional abstractions: Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector — with Selector converting control flow into runtime-routed decisions. Because state is carried by the same value used during execution, fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations. The paper also presents an evidence protocol and audited milestones.

Result: The paper presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. Claims are explicitly limited to controlled runtime properties; broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are deferred to follow-on evaluation.

Conclusion: The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition, unifying previously fragmented state into a single branchable, inspectable, replayable, and composable abstraction that makes fork, merge, and replay explicit runtime operations.

Abstract: Modern agent systems often suffer from fragmented runtime state: transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded separately and become difficult to inspect or reproduce. OpenRath addresses this issue with a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent, multi-session systems. The analogy concerns the role of a central first-class runtime abstraction, not tensor computation. Its core abstraction is Session, the runtime value passed between agents and workflows. A Session is branchable, inspectable, replayable, backend-aware, and composable. It records conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence, while defining where memory interactions enter the runtime record. Since this state is carried by the same value used in program execution, fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations rather than states reconstructed from external traces. OpenRath further defines Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector, with Selector turning control flow into runtime-routed decisions. This report presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. Its claims are limited to controlled runtime properties, while broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are left for follow-on evaluation. The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition.

</details>


### [69] [FAPO: Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization of Multi-Step LLM Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19605)
*Paul Kassianik,Baturay Saglam,Huaibo Zhao,Blaine Nelson,Supriti Vijay,Aman Priyanshu,Amin Karbasi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: FAPO is an autonomous optimization framework that improves multi-step LLM pipelines by diagnosing and fixing bottlenecks across retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps—escalating from prompt edits to structural changes only when necessary. It outperforms the GEPA baseline in 15 of 18 comparisons, with particularly large gains (+33.8 pp) on tasks requiring structural fixes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail due to complex interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps. Prompt-only optimization overlooks structural bottlenecks in the chain, motivating a fully autonomous approach that can both tune prompts and restructure the pipeline when needed.

Method: FAPO operates within a standardized codebase using Claude Code to iteratively: (1) evaluate a pipeline against a score function, (2) inspect intermediate step outputs, (3) diagnose failures via attribution, (4) propose scoped changes—starting with prompt edits and escalating to chain-structure modifications only when prompt optimization proves insufficient. This cycle repeats until convergence.

Result: FAPO beats baseline GEPA in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons; 11 wins have non-overlapping mean ± trial-SD ranges. Mean FAPO-GEPA gain is +14.1 pp overall. On HoVer and IFBench where structural changes were triggered, FAPO wins all 6 comparisons with +33.8 pp mean gain. On CTIBench-RCM security task, prompt-only FAPO improves accuracy by +4.0 pp (GPT-5), +7.1 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct), and +2.0 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning).

Conclusion: FAPO represents state-of-the-art pipeline optimization for both general-purpose and security-focused LLM tasks, demonstrating that autonomous, attribution-driven diagnosis combined with hierarchical intervention (prompts first, structure second) yields substantial and reliable performance gains.

Abstract: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail through interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, so prompt-only optimization can miss bottlenecks in the chain. We present FAPO (Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization), a framework that lets Claude Code optimize an LLM pipeline inside a standardized codebase. FAPO evaluates a pipeline, inspects intermediate steps, diagnoses failures, proposes scoped changes, and validates variants repeatedly to optimize against a score function. It first tries prompt edits and, only when prompt optimization appears insufficient, changes chain structure within the permitted scope when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck. Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the baseline GEPA in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. In 11 model-benchmark comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean $\pm$ trial-standard-deviation ranges, and the mean FAPO-GEPA gain is +14.1 pp. In the six HoVer and IFBench comparisons where prompt-first search escalated to structural changes, FAPO wins all six with a mean gain of +33.8 pp. FAPO also improves performance on security tasks: on CTIBench-RCM, a security CVE-to-CWE task, prompt-only FAPO lifts test accuracy by +4.0 pp on GPT-5, +7.1 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct, and +2.0 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning.
