These results position FAPO as a state-of-the-art pipeline optimization technique for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks.

</details>


### [70] [StaminaBench: Stress-Testing Coding Agents over 100 Interaction Turns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19613)
*Vlad Sobal,Shuo Yang,Yuting Zhang,Wei Xia,Stefano Soatto*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: StaminaBench is a new benchmark for evaluating coding agents' ability to handle long sequences of consecutive change requests (up to 100 turns), revealing that current agents fail within 5-6 turns without test feedback, but providing test feedback and retry mechanisms improves performance by up to 12x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding benchmarks use fraction-of-tasks-solved metrics that don't capture real-world "vibe-coding" sessions where agents must sustain performance over dozens or hundreds of consecutive modification turns. There is a need to measure agent stamina — how long they can maintain correctness across many sequential changes — rather than just one-shot task completion.

Method: StaminaBench procedurally generates 100-turn scenarios where agents implement and iteratively modify a REST API server (up to ~6,000 lines). Tests are generated fully programmatically (no LLM involvement) for reproducibility. Change requests come from either a hardcoded or LLM-driven sampler, constrained to a structured action space. The agent and server run in an isolated environment communicating via HTTP, making evaluation fully black-box and language-agnostic. Six harnesses with seven open-source LLMs are evaluated across 20 scenarios.

Result: Key findings: (1) All tested models fail within 5-6 consecutive turns without test feedback, confirming that vibe-coding without testing produces bugs. (2) Passing test feedback back to the agent with retry capability increases passed turn count by up to 12x. (3) Harness quality significantly impacts performance — stronger models show up to 6x gap between best and worst harness; weaker models fail regardless of harness.

Conclusion: Current coding agents lack the stamina needed for extended multi-turn development sessions. Test feedback loops and well-designed agent harnesses are critical for sustained performance. StaminaBench provides a reproducible, language-agnostic framework for advancing research into multi-turn coding agent behavior.

Abstract: We introduce StaminaBench, a benchmark that measures the stamina of coding agents: how many consecutive interaction turns (change requests) they can handle before failing. Unlike the prevailing fraction-of-tasks-solved metric, this matches real vibe-coding where sessions run dozens or hundreds of turns. In StaminaBench, agents implement a REST API server and modify it across a tunable number of procedurally generated follow-up change requests - 100 in our experiments, resulting in codebases of up to 6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically without LLM involvement, ensuring reproducibility and reliability; change sequences are drawn from either a hardcoded or LLM-driven sampler, both constrained to a structured action space to ensure changes are valid. The agent and the server run in an isolated environment and communicate with the benchmark through HTTP, making testing fully black-box and language-agnostic. We evaluate six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each and find that: (1) all the tested models fail within 5-6 turns, confirming that vibe-coding-style programming without thorough testing produces bugs; (2) passing test feedback back to the agent and allowing it to retry improves passed turn count by up to 12x; and (3) a good harness is required for strong performance: stronger models exhibit up to a 6x gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail with any harness. We release the benchmark and the generated tasks to enable further research into multi-turn coding agent behavior. Benchmark code and data: github.com/amazon-science/StaminaBench.

</details>


### [71] [Phoenix: Safe GitHub Issue Resolution via Multi-Agent LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20243)
*Kipngeno Koech,Muhammad Adam,Baimam Boukar Jean Jacques,Joao Barros*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Phoenix is a multi-agent LLM system with six specialized agents and seven safety controls that resolves GitHub issues end-to-end, achieving 75% oracle-resolution on a curated SWE-bench Lite slice and 100% correctness preservation on a pilot of 42 real issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated issue resolution systems face deployment challenges including safety risks (code regressions, flaky CI), localization failures, and integration friction. The authors aim to build a production-ready system that safely resolves real GitHub issues while preserving correctness and handling real-world failure modes.

Method: Phoenix uses a label-based GitHub webhook state machine to coordinate six specialized agents: Planner, Reproducer, Coder, Tester, Failure Analyst, and PR Agent. Seven layered safety controls are embedded throughout the pipeline, including baseline-aware test evaluation where every change is checked against a baseline test run before a PR is opened.

Result: On a 24-instance curated slice of SWE-bench Lite (production webhook path): 75% oracle-resolution rate with zero pass-to-pass regressions. A pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories: 100% correctness preservation (mean 122s on hard tier). Manual inspection showed ~50% of PRs were well-targeted fixes; the rest suffered from planner localization errors (code placed at incorrect paths). Deployment failure modes identified: WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, and flaky CI.

Conclusion: Phoenix demonstrates that multi-agent LLM systems can safely and effectively resolve real GitHub issues, though planner localization remains a key limitation. The layered safety controls effectively prevent regressions, and retrieval-based improvements are planned to address localization failures.

Abstract: We present Phoenix, a multi-agent LLM system that resolves GitHub issues from triage through pull-request creation, combining seven layered safety controls with a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy. Phoenix decomposes the work across six specialized agents. Planner, reproducer, coder, tester, failure analyst and Pull Request (PR) agent, all coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Every change is checked against a baseline test run before a pull request is opened. On a 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite. run on the production webhook path, Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% of instances with no pass-to-pass regressions on successful runs; this curated slice is not directly comparable to full-split leaderboard results, and we discuss the limits of the comparison. A complementary pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories yields 100% correctness preservation (CP; mean 122s on the hard tier). Manual inspection shows that about half of the resulting pull requests are well-targeted fixes. The other half place code at incorrect paths, a planner localization limitation we are addressing with retrieval. We also report the deployment failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI) that motivated each safety mechanism.

</details>


### [72] [Prompt Quality and Pull Request Outcomes: A Stage-Based Empirical Study of LLM-Assisted Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19644)
*Richard Sserunjogi,Daniel Ogenrwot,John Businge*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how prompt structure (Context, Specificity, Verification) in developer-ChatGPT interactions influences outcomes in open-source pull requests. Analyzing 265 validated interactions, the authors find that prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects: Specificity and Context drive actionable code generation, Verification predicts code adoption, and Context most strongly influences integration depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLM-powered tools are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering, prior work has focused narrowly on conversational helpfulness or coarse adoption metrics, leaving the role of prompt structure in collaborative integration behavior poorly understood. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically examining how prompt design choices shape downstream PR outcomes.

Method: The study analyzes 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions from self-admitted ChatGPT usage in open-source pull requests. Prompt structure is operationalized along three dimensions — Context, Specificity, and Verification — building on prior prompt engineering and developer-facing artifacts research. The authors first evaluate LLM-assisted annotation reliability against human judgments, then use the validated hybrid human-LLM annotation framework to regress prompt dimensions against three outcomes: actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth.

Result: LLM annotation agreement with humans varies substantially: Specificity shows the most stable agreement; Context is systematically underscored by the LLM; Verification is difficult to assess consistently, motivating a hybrid strategy. In downstream analysis, Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification is the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context.

Conclusion: Prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows. Contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues differentially influence generation, adoption, and integration stages, providing actionable insights for both prompt design and tool support in collaborative development.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering workflows, yet little is known about how prompt structure influences downstream pull request (PR) outcomes. Prior studies primarily examine conversational helpfulness, productivity, or coarse-grained adoption metrics, leaving the role of prompt structure in collaborative integration behavior insufficiently understood. We analyze 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions derived from self-admitted ChatGPT usage in open-source pull requests. Building on prior research on developer-facing artifacts and prompt engineering, we operationalize prompt structure using three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification. We first evaluate whether LLM-assisted annotation can reliably reproduce human judgments of prompt structure, finding substantial variation across dimensions and workflow contexts. Specificity shows the most stable agreement with human judgments; Context is systematically under-scored by the LLM; and Verification remains difficult to assess consistently, motivating a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy. Using this validated framework, we then examine how prompt structure influences actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth across AI-assisted PR workflows. Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification emerges as the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context. Overall, our findings show that prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows, influencing downstream adoption and integration through contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues.

</details>


### [73] [Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19795)
*Jiawei Liu,Peiyi Han,Yuntao Lu,Su Zheng,Fengyu Yan,Bei Yu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This survey introduces "handoff validity" as a framework for evaluating LLM-based agents in EDA workflows. It classifies 82 systems into Stage-Bound, Flow-Bound, and Organization-Bound classes, analyzing how each manages handoff contracts, objects, and coordination. The paper proposes a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP) as a foundation for trustworthy agentic EDA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EDA workflows are multi-stage and involve frequent handoffs across tools, sessions, and organizational boundaries. Each handoff carries explicit and implicit requirements that stage-local checks alone cannot guarantee. As LLM-based agents increasingly invoke EDA tools, generate scripts, and pass state across stages, their outputs condition downstream decisions. Without systematic handoff validity, errors, missing context, or unverifiable provenance can propagate, undermining trust in agentic EDA.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic survey of 82 LLM-based EDA systems. They propose "handoff validity" as the organizing concept: a handoff is valid when the transferred object satisfies consumer acceptance conditions and carries sufficient context, evidence, and provenance. Systems are classified into three boundary classes — Stage-Bound (validity within a single EDA stage), Flow-Bound (coherent state across tools and sessions), and Organization-Bound (source grounding and provenance across knowledge/authority boundaries). Each class is analyzed along dimensions of handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. From this analysis, they derive a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP).

Result: The survey reveals that most current systems are Stage-Bound, focusing on isolated verification tasks. Flow-Bound systems introduce mechanisms for state persistence and cross-tool coordination but lack standardized contracts. Organization-Bound systems are the least mature, grappling with provenance, IP protection, and authority boundaries. The proposed EACP addresses these gaps across five layers: agent discovery, agent messaging, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security/IP protocols. Critical open questions remain around contract formalization, evidence chains, and cross-organizational trust.

Conclusion: Handoff validity provides a unifying lens for evaluating and designing trustworthy agentic EDA systems. The three boundary classes expose progressive challenges in contract enforcement, context preservation, and provenance. The EACP offers a concrete communication architecture to address these challenges, establishing a common vocabulary and research agenda for the field.

Abstract: Electronic design automation (EDA) is inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy. Design artifacts, flow scripts, and engineering decisions cross tool, session, and organizational boundaries before final implementation, signoff, or release. Each transfer carries explicit and implicit requirements that may not be fully captured by stage-local checks. LLM-based agents now invoke EDA tools directly, embed retrieved knowledge in executable scripts, and hand off state across sessions and stages. Once their outputs condition downstream engineering decisions, the transferred object must satisfy a handoff contract and meet the assumptions of its next consumer. This survey introduces handoff validity as its organizing principle. A handoff is valid when the transferred object satisfies the consumer's acceptance conditions and carries sufficient context, evidence, and provenance for downstream use. We review 82 systems and classify them into three boundary classes. Stage-Bound systems establish validity within a single EDA stage or bounded verification task. Flow-Bound systems preserve coherent workflow state across tools, invocations, and sessions. Organization-Bound systems maintain source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries. For each class, we analyze handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. These analyses motivate a five-layer EDA agent communication protocol (EACP), covering the agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security and IP protocols. We aim to provide a common vocabulary and research agenda for trustworthy agentic EDA.

</details>


### [74] [The Hidden Environmental Cost of Poor Coding Practices in TensorFlow and Keras Applications: A Study on Resource Leaks and Carbon Emissions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19799)
*Bashar Abdallah,Gustavo Santos,Rola Al Bataineh,Alain Abran,Mohammad Hamdaqa*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents an initial empirical investigation showing that two common resource-leak smells in TensorFlow/Keras — Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR) — increase electricity consumption by ~32% and ~46% respectively, with proportional CO₂ emission increases, providing statistically significant evidence that resource leaks degrade ML sustainability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While efficiency and sustainability are critical in ML development, empirical evidence quantifying the environmental impact of resource leaks in ML code remains limited. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing quantitative data on how resource-leak smells affect energy consumption and carbon emissions.

Method: Controlled experiments were conducted for two resource-leak smells (IMR and UTR) in TensorFlow and Keras workloads. Each smell was tested by executing identical training tasks and comparing energy consumption and CO₂ emissions against a smell-free baseline. Paired statistical tests were applied to assess significance.

Result: IMR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32% and UTR by approximately 46%, with proportional increases in CO₂ emissions. Paired statistical tests confirmed these differences are systematic and statistically significant.

Conclusion: Resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and environmental sustainability. The findings emphasize the need to integrate resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development practices.

Abstract: Efficiency and sustainability are critical considerations in the development and deployment of machine learning (ML) applications. Among the factors influencing sustainability, resource leaks in ML code can introduce hidden inefficiencies that elevate energy consumption and CO2 emissions. Despite this, empirical evidence quantifying their environmental impact remains limited. This emerging results paper presents an initial empirical investigation of two common resource-leak smells, namely Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR), and their impact on energy consumption and CO2 emissions in TensorFlow and Keras workloads. Controlled experiments were conducted for each smell by executing identical training tasks while comparing against a smell-free baseline. Our preliminary results show that both smells consistently increase estimated electricity usage and carbon emissions. IMR and UTR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32% and 46%, respectively, with proportional increases in CO2 emissions. Paired statistical tests indicate that these differences are systematic and statistically significant, providing initial empirical evidence that resource-leak smells may degrade ML energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. These findings suggest that resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and sustainability, emphasizing the importance of integrating resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development.

</details>


### [75] [CoRaCommit: A VS Code Extension for Commit Message Generation with Exemplar Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19814)
*Chaoran Cai,Bo Xiong,Chong Wang,Lulu He,Peng Liang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CoRaCommit is a VS Code extension that improves commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate generation, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback, outperforming existing extensions on standard metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual commit message authoring is time-consuming and yields inconsistent quality. Existing VS Code extensions directly invoke LLMs on code diffs without leveraging similar commit exemplars or supporting user feedback-driven LLM recommendation, leaving room for improvement in generation quality and adaptability.

Method: CoRaCommit employs a retrieval-augmented approach: (1) it retrieves similar commit exemplars from a dataset to serve as prompt context, (2) invokes multiple LLMs in parallel to generate candidate commit messages, and (3) incorporates a dynamic LLM recommendation mechanism based on user feedback. The system is implemented as a VS Code extension and evaluated on 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset.

Result: CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics on the ApacheCM dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.

Conclusion: Retrieving similar commit exemplars as prompt context and incorporating user feedback-driven LLM recommendation significantly enhance commit message generation quality over direct LLM invocation approaches, offering a practical improvement for developer workflows in VS Code.

Abstract: Commit messages are essential textual artifacts that describe the intent behind code changes, and play a critical role in version control, code review, and historical tracking. However, in practice, commit messages are primarily authored manually, which is time-consuming and often results in inconsistent quality and non-uniform expression. Existing VS Code extensions for commit message generation typically directly invoke large language models based on the code diff, without leveraging similar commit exemplars as references, and rarely support user feedback-driven LLM recommendation. To address these limitations, this paper presents CoRaCommit, a VS Code extension that enhances commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as prompt context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate commit message comparison, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback. Experimental results on 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset show that CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.

</details>


### [76] [JAMER: Project-Level Code Framework Dataset and Benchmark on Professional Game Engines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19830)
*Jianwen Sun,Chuanhao Li,Zizhen Li,Yukang Feng,Fanrui Zhang,Yifei Huang,Yu Dai,Kaipeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: JamSet and JamBench are the first project-level game code dataset and benchmark built on a professional game engine (Godot), sourced from Game Jam competitions. Using deterministic verification pipelines, 8,133 verified projects were curated. Benchmarking 9 frontier models reveals a dramatic capability drop as project scale increases (runtime pass rates from 80.4% to 5.7%), with Code Agents improving compilation but not runtime quality — indicating the bottleneck is architectural design, not syntax.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-driven game development lacks project-level code engineering benchmarks on professional game engines due to the absence of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. Game Jam competitions — where developers build complete games under time pressure — provide a rich, underexploited source of open-source projects that can fill this gap.

Method: The authors leverage the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode to build a deterministic verification pipeline covering file integrity and runtime behavior collection. From over 240,000 repositories, they distill 8,133 verified projects (JamSet), with 300 manually verified projects forming JamBench. JamBench defines two tasks: theme-driven generation and code completion. Evaluation uses compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS).

Result: Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a "capability cliff": runtime pass rates drop from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large projects (Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates but not runtime behavioral quality. JamSet proves effective as training data.

Conclusion: The bottleneck in AI-driven project-level game code generation lies in architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. JamSet and JamBench provide critical infrastructure for advancing this research direction, and all data and code are publicly released.

Abstract: Current AI-driven game development has made substantial progress in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based game coding, yet project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains largely unexplored due to the absence of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. We present JamSet and JamBench, the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on a professional game engine. Our key insight is that Game Jam competitions, community events where developers build complete games under tight time constraints, yield thousands of open-source projects suitable for this purpose. Building on the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode, we design a deterministic verification pipeline from file integrity to runtime behavior collection, distilling 8,133 verified projects from over 240,000 repositories. Of these, 300 manually verified projects form JamBench; the rest constitute JamSet. JamBench defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated through a pipeline combining compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a capability cliff as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates dropping from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large ones (Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates yet yield no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating that the bottleneck lies in architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. Experiments validate JamSet as effective training data. All data and code are publicly available.

</details>


### [77] [Repository-Level Solidity Code Generation with Large Language Models: From Prompting to Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19988)
*Shi Chen,Rongcun Wang,Yuan Tian,Xiaoyuan Xie,Wei Song,Rubing Huang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SolidityBench introduces a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts with natural language descriptions and SolidityScore, a domain-aware semantic metric. Evaluating multiple LLMs across five strategies reveals that supervised fine-tuning with high-quality domain data most effectively improves repository-level smart contract generation, while general-purpose models exhibit structural deficiencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs excel at general-purpose code generation but remain underexplored in specialized, high-stakes domains like Solidity smart contracts, which demand strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks and metrics are insufficient for repository-level generation where complete contracts must be synthesized from natural language requirements.

Method: The authors construct SolidityBench (5,470 repository-level Solidity contracts with NL descriptions) and propose SolidityScore, a semantic metric weighting domain-critical constructs (security modifiers, contract declarations, Solidity-specific keywords). They evaluate Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama under five strategies: zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Result: General-purpose models show systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, RAG performs best, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. SFT achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters.

Conclusion: High-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts. The study provides a comprehensive benchmark and demonstrates that domain-specific adaptation is essential for repository-level Solidity code generation.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in general-purpose code generation, but their effectiveness in specialized software domains remains underexplored. Solidity smart contracts represent a high-stakes domain where generated code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks and metrics remain insufficient for repository-level Solidity generation, where models must synthesize complete contracts from natural language requirements. To address this gap, we introduce SolidityBench, a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts paired with natural language descriptions. We also propose SolidityScore, a Solidity-aware semantic metric that emphasizes domain-critical constructs such as security modifiers, contract declarations, and Solidity-specific keywords. Using this benchmark, we evaluate representative code LLMs, including Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama, across zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and supervised fine-tuning. The results show that general-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, retrieval-augmented generation performs best, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. Supervised fine-tuning achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive benchmark for repository-level Solidity code generation and shows that high-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts.

</details>


### [78] [Beyond Static Endpoints: Tool Programs as an Interface for Flexible Agentic Web Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19992)
*Mugeng Liu,Shuoqi Li,Yixuan Zhang,Yun Ma*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ToolPro is a framework that encodes LLM agent tool interactions as executable programs, replacing step-by-step API calls with optimized multi-step workflows. It uses constraint-guided program construction, effect-aware replay for safe idempotency, and a profile-driven execution policy, achieving up to 53.4% latency reduction and 96.1% traffic reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current web service interfaces for LLM agents are static endpoints ill-suited for long-horizon workflows involving loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. Stepwise calling incurs high latency and network overhead. There is a need for a more expressive and efficient paradigm that captures agent tool intent as compact, executable representations.

Method: ToolPro introduces three core mechanisms: (1) constraint-guided program construction that compiles agent intent into executable tool programs with explicit effect types; (2) effect-aware replay ensuring exactly-once execution of state-modifying calls; and (3) a profile-driven policy to decide when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. The system is instantiated over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing for safe execution.

Result: Evaluated on diverse real-world workflows, ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1%, with larger gains observed under higher network latency and greater workflow complexity.

Conclusion: Representing agent tool intent as executable programs rather than stepwise API calls yields substantial performance improvements, particularly as workflows grow more complex and network conditions degrade. The approach demonstrates a viable path toward more efficient agentic web service interactions.

Abstract: In the agentic web era, LLM-based agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, yet most interfaces remain \emph{static endpoints} that poorly express long-horizon workflows with loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. We present ToolPro, which represents an agent's tool intent as an \emph{executable tool program} that compactly encodes multi-step service interactions with explicit effect types. ToolPro combines constraint-guided program construction, effect-aware replay for exactly-once state-modifying calls, and a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. We instantiate ToolPro over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing and evaluate it on diverse workflows of real-world applications. ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4\% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1\%, with larger gains under higher network latency and workflow complexity.

</details>


### [79] [When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20023)
*Kaiyue Yang,Yuyan Bu,Jingwei Yi,Yuchi Wang,Biyu Zhou,Juntao Dai,Songlin Hu,Yaodong Yang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM agents frequently choose over-privileged tools when lower-privilege alternatives suffice, especially after transient failures. General safety alignment fails to transfer to least-privilege selection, but a privilege-aware post-training defense significantly reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents autonomously select tools with varying privilege levels, over-privileged selection poses a safety risk (e.g., choosing a sudo-level tool when a user-level tool would suffice). Prior work only examines safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving privilege-sensitive choices unexplored. This gap motivates studying how agents behave when faced with tools of differing privilege levels.

Method: The authors introduce ToolPrivBench, a benchmark spanning 8 domains and 5 recurring risk patterns, evaluating both initial tool selection and escalation behavior after transient tool failures. They test mainstream LLM agents, assess whether general safety alignment transfers to least-privilege choices, evaluate prompt-level controls, and propose a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary.

Result: Over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is amplified by transient failures. General safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice. Prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. The proposed privilege-aware post-training defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.

Conclusion: Over-privileged tool selection is a prevalent and underexplored safety issue in LLM agents. Standard safety measures are insufficient; dedicated privilege-aware training is necessary to enforce the principle of least privilege in agent tool selection, and the proposed post-training defense offers an effective solution.

Abstract: As LLM agents increasingly select tools autonomously, their choices among tools with different privileges become safety-relevant. However, prior tool-selection studies focus on safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving privilege-sensitive choices underexplored. To address this gap, we study over-privileged tool selection, in which an agent selects or escalates to a higher-privilege tool despite a sufficient lower-privilege alternative. We introduce ToolPrivBench to evaluate whether agents choose higher-privilege tools despite sufficient lower-privilege alternatives, measuring both initial selection and escalation after transient tool failures. Across eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, we find that over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is further amplified by transient failures. We further find that general safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice, while prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. We therefore introduce a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary. Our mitigation experiments show that this defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.

</details>


### [80] [The Correctness Illusion in LLM-Generated GPU Kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20128)
*Dipankar Sarkar*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Existing LLM-generated GPU kernel benchmarks rely on fixed-shape, small-sample allclose-style checks that fail to catch systematic bugs. The authors construct a controlled corpus of 24 kernels (15 correct, 9 buggy) and demonstrate that op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with fp64 CPU reference achieves perfect detection (9/9 bugs caught, 15/15 correct passed). Results replicate identically across five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100, H100) on an extended 26-op corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) evaluate LLM-generated GPU kernels using correctness checks that are too narrow — fixed input shapes, small sample counts, fixed dtypes, and fixed tolerances. This risks certifying buggy kernels as correct (illusions), undermining the reliability of LLM-based kernel generation. The work aims to expose these deficiencies and propose a more rigorous evaluation protocol.

Method: The authors constructed a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU stand-in kernels: 15 correct controls and 9 buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors. They then applied op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with a high-precision (fp64) CPU reference oracle using per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The protocol was extended to 26 ops (adding flash-attention) and tested across five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL). All failures are deterministically replayable via stored seeds.

Result: The seeded fuzzing oracle achieved perfect discrimination: 9/9 buggy kernels flagged, 15/15 correct controls passed with zero precision cost on controls. This held identically across all five GPU classes on the extended corpus: 10/10 illusions caught, 16/16 controls clean. The allclose-on-one-shape oracle, by contrast, certifies some buggy kernels as correct.

Conclusion: Fixed-shape, small-sample allclose checks are insufficient for validating LLM-generated GPU kernels. Op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with an fp64 CPU reference provides reliable, reproducible, GPU-agnostic correctness discrimination, and every flagged failure is byte-for-byte replayable, making it suitable for benchmark use.

Abstract: Benchmarks for LLM-generated GPU kernels (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) score correctness through fixed-shape, small-sample allclose-style checks. The number of inputs varies between benchmarks. The shape, dtype, and tolerance are fixed for each kernel. We test that oracle empirically. We construct a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU stand-in kernels (15 correct controls and 9 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors) and re-evaluate it under op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with a high-precision (fp64) CPU reference and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The seeded oracle flags 9 of 9 buggy kernels and passes 15 of 15 correct controls, at zero precision cost on controls. We extend the corpus to 26 ops (adding a flash-attention pair) and re-run the same protocol on five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL). The verdicts are identical across all five GPUs: 10 of 10 illusions caught and 16 of 16 controls clean. The corpus result is about LLM-style transcription bugs that the allclose-on-one-shape oracle certifies as correct, not about the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM. Every flagged failure replays byte-for-byte from a stored seed.

</details>


### [81] [Learning Critical Testing Literacy Through Puzzles: an Experience Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20129)
*Niels Doorn,Bart Th. Knaack,Tanja E. J. Vos,Beatriz Marín*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper reports on using puzzle-based activities to teach Critical Testing Literacy (CTL), based on the P4TEST framework. Across thirteen workshops with diverse participants, puzzles fostered experimentation and sensemaking. Key findings include differences in solution strategies between students and professionals, the role of think-aloud sessions in revealing reasoning, and the importance of the full solve-debrief-reflect sequence rather than puzzles alone. An open-source web app with analytics was developed to support workshop customization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software testing is a critical yet challenging subject to teach. The authors aim to address this pedagogical gap by exploring puzzle-based learning activities grounded in a model of critical tester's cognition, encapsulated in the P4TEST framework, to foster Critical Testing Literacy (CTL).

Method: The authors conducted thirteen workshops with diverse participants (students, professional testers, teachers, primary school pupils). Eleven workshops used a semi-structured format with variations in puzzles, materials, and timing. Two additional workshops introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions to capture richer learning data. Data were gathered through observations, written reflections, and verbal think-aloud protocols.

Result: Participants consistently perceived puzzle-solving as experimentation. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring beyond the answer. Emotions were visibly expressed during activities but rarely surfaced in written reflections. Think-aloud sessions captured immediate reasoning, whereas written reflections elicited more meta-cognitive insights. The overarching theme of "Sensemaking / reflection-in-action" characterized how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.

Conclusion: Puzzles alone are insufficient; the full pedagogical intervention comprises solving, debriefing, and reflecting. Future work lies in deliberately designing this integrated sequence. An open-source web application with built-in analytics was developed to support customizable workshop delivery.

Abstract: In this paper, we report our experiences and takeaways from workshops using puzzles to learn CTL.
  Background: Software testing is important yet difficult to teach. We introduced a BoK of puzzle-based learning activities to teach CTL, based on a model of critical tester's cognition, leading to the pedagogical framework P4TEST. We conducted thirteen workshops with students, testers, teachers, and primary school pupils to assess puzzle-based teaching of critical testing literacy.
  Experience: Across eleven workshops, we used a semi-structured approach, varying puzzles, materials, and timing. In two additional workshops, we introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions to gather more data on the learning experience.
  Observations: Participants consistently perceived themselves as experimenting while solving puzzles. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring. Emotions were visible in behaviour but hard to surface through written reflection alone. Think-aloud sessions revealed immediate reasoning; written reflections elicited more meta-cognitive reflection. The theme Sensemaking / reflection-in-action captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
  Reflections: Puzzles are not the intervention: the entire sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is. Designing that sequence more deliberately is the work ahead. We also developed an open-source web application with built-in analytics to customise workshops.

</details>


### [82] [N-Version Programming with Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20158)
*Javier Ron,Benoit Baudry,Martin Monperrus*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper revisits N-version programming using modern AI coding agents, replicating the Knight-Leveson experiment. It finds that while common-mode failures persist (often tied to specification ambiguity), diversity across agents, models, and languages provides substantial practical benefit: three-version majority voting reduces mean failures from ~387 to ~131, with nearly 12,000 triples showing zero failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether the classical N-version programming paradigm—originally studied by Knight and Leveson—remains relevant in the era of AI coding agents, and whether diversity across agent systems, language models, and implementation languages can mitigate common-mode failures.

Method: Using the Knight-Leveson Launch Interceptor Program specification, 48 agent-generated implementations were produced across diverse agents, models, and programming languages. These were evaluated against a shared oracle using a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. Three-version majority-voting units were constructed and analyzed for failure counts.

Result: Substantial common-mode failure was observed, often traced to ambiguous or difficult parts of the specification. However, diversity yielded practical gains: mean failure count dropped from 387.44 (single-version) to 130.99 (three-version majority vote). Out of all three-version units, 11,844 exhibited zero observed failures across the test campaign.

Conclusion: This represents the strongest evidence to date that N-version programming with AI coding agents is a useful engineering strategy, despite persistent common-mode failures linked to specification quality.

Abstract: This paper revisits the classical concept on N-version programming in the setting of contemporary AI coding agents. Revisiting the seminal Knight-Leveson experiment, we study whether diversity across agent systems, models, and implementation languages creates diverse failure modes. Using the Knight-Leveson's, Launch Interceptor Program Specification, we evaluate 48 agent-generated implementations on a shared oracle and a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. The results show substantial common-mode failure, along the findings of Knight-Leveson. Further analysis that many of those co-occuring failures can be traced to where is specification is particularly hard or ambiguous. We also demonstrate that diversity from coding agents provides practical benefit: across majority voting three-version units, the mean failure count drops from 387.44 for single versions to 130.99 for triples, and 11,844 N-version units exhibit zero observed failures. Our original results is the strongest evidence to date that N-Version Programming with coding agents is a useful engineering strategy.

</details>


### [83] [Qiskit Code Migration with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20173)
*Jose Manuel Suarez,Luis Mariano Bibbo,Joaquin Bogado,Alenandro Fernandez*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a hybrid LLM + Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach using a taxonomy of migration scenarios to automate Qiskit code migration across versions, demonstrating that taxonomy-guided retrieval reduces hallucinations and improves migration quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rapid evolution of Quantum Development Kits (QDKs) creates API obsolescence and technical debt that compromises code maintainability. General-purpose LLMs produce unreliable results due to scarce training data and high framework volatility in Quantum Software Engineering (QSE).

Method: A hybrid approach combining LLMs with RAG, using an automatically generated taxonomy of migration scenarios as a structured, version-specific knowledge source. Evaluated two LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5 and OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) under two retrieval schemes: unconstrained and restrictive.

Result: The taxonomy-based RAG architecture significantly reduced hallucinations and improved descriptive quality. The restrictive retrieval scheme outperformed unconstrained. Google Gemini Flash-2.5 showed superior performance in detecting complex refactoring scenarios.

Conclusion: The data-centric taxonomy-RAG methodology holds strong potential for fostering technological independence, providing robust intelligent assistants that mitigate API obsolescence and flatten the learning curve in QSE.

Abstract: The rapid evolution of Quantum Development Kits (QDKs) introduces a specific form of technical debt that compromises code maintainability and hinders software reuse. In the specialized domain of Quantum Software Engineering (QSE), this challenge is intensified by the scarcity of high-quality training data and the high volatility of emerging frameworks, which often lead general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce unreliable or hallucinated results. This paper proposes a hybrid approach integrating LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to automate the migration of Qiskit code across versions. The proposed methodology enhances the precision and reliability of migration suggestions by leveraging an automatically generated taxonomy of migration scenarios as the structured, version-specific knowledge source to guide the models. The approach is implemented through an automated, extensible workflow evaluating LLMs (Google Gemini Flash-2.5 and OpenAI Gpt-oss-20b) under different retrieval schemes (unconstrained and restrictive). Results demonstrate that the taxonomy-based RAG architecture, particularly under the restrictive scheme, significantly reduces hallucinations and improves descriptive quality, with Google Gemini Flash-2.5 showing superior performance in detecting complex refactoring scenarios. These findings confirm the potential of this data-centric methodology to foster technological independence and provide robust, intelligent assistants that mitigate API obsolescence, ensuring the long-term availability of quantum algorithms within a rapidly shifting ecosystem and flattening the learning curve within Quantum Software Engineering (QSE).

</details>


### [84] [SysML Modeling of Digital Twins for Renewable Energy Communities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20230)
*Mohammad Samadi,Luís Miguel Pinho,Andrey Sadovykh,Gabriela Lucas*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Proposes a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for Renewable Energy Community (REC) Digital Twins using SysML, identifies four semantic gaps, and suggests importing the SAREF4ENER ontology to close them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Engineering digital twins of Renewable Energy Communities is challenging due to the heterogeneity of devices, contracts, and runtime data. Existing approaches lack a structured, model-based methodology that can handle this diversity, and the combination of SysML with semantic ontologies for smart-energy digital twins remains unexplored.

Method: Starting from an industrially-validated REC domain model, the authors re-express a representative house subset in SysML v2 using the open-source Modelio tool, producing two Block Definition Diagrams (a device taxonomy and a community organizational view). They then analyze four semantic gaps in plain SysML and sketch how importing the SAREF4ENER ontology as a reference package could address them.

Result: Two SysML Block Definition Diagrams were generated: one capturing a device taxonomy and another representing the community organizational structure. Four semantic gaps were identified where plain SysML falls short, and a preliminary mapping to SAREF4ENER was outlined as a bridging solution.

Conclusion: Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins is a promising but largely unexplored direction. This paper represents an initial step, with significant work remaining to fully integrate semantic ontologies into the MBSE workflow for REC digital twins.

Abstract: Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) are emerging as a key organizational model for local and global sharing of renewable generation, storage, and flexible loads. Engineering Digital Twins of RECs is made difficult by the heterogeneity of devices, contracts, and runtime data involved. In this paper, we take a first step toward a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow for REC's Digital Twins. Starting from an industrially-validated REC domain model, we re-express a representative house subset in SysML using the open-source Modelio tool, yielding two Block Definition Diagrams - a device taxonomy and a community organizational view. We then discuss four semantic gaps that plain SysML leaves open and sketch how the SAREF4ENER ontology could be imported as a reference package to close them. Combining SysML with SAREF-based semantics for smart-energy Digital Twins remains largely unexplored, and we position this paper as a first step along that line.

</details>


### [85] [Token-Operations-Oriented Inference Optimization Techniques for Large Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20295)
*Shiguo Lian,Kai Wang,Zhaoxiang Liu,Wen Liu,Minjie Hua,Yutong Liu,Jiangze Yan,Xin Wang,Cong Wang,Yilin Zhang,Yi Shen,Jieyun Huang,Fang Zhao,Huanlin Gao,Ping Chen,Xinyu Yang,Kaikai Zhao,Yao Zhao,Xinggang Wang,Huishuai Zhang,Dongyan Zhao,Junping Du,Tao Chen,Xiang Gao,Qinghuai Ma*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Proposes a four-layer technical architecture (Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, Compute-Network-Model Fusion) for token-oriented large model inference optimization, systematically reviewing key technologies across these layers and their real-world business value in reducing cost, improving efficiency, and ensuring service stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large model services require scalable, low-cost, and highly stable inference infrastructure. Current approaches lack a unified architectural framework for token-oriented optimization. There is a pressing need to transition large model services from being merely "callable" to being truly "operable" at production scale.

Method: The paper proposes a novel four-layer token-oriented inference optimization architecture: (1) Multi-model Fusion — combining multiple models for synergistic inference; (2) Model Optimization — improving individual model efficiency; (3) Compute-Model Fusion — co-optimizing computation and model design; (4) Compute-Network-Model Fusion — jointly optimizing computation, networking, and model execution. The paper systematically reviews key technologies and industry practices at each layer.

Result: The paper presents a comprehensive technical framework for reducing token production costs, improving token service efficiency, and ensuring the stability of token supply. It validates the application value of the four-layer architecture in real-world business scenarios and provides a practical technology roadmap.

Conclusion: The proposed four-layer architecture offers a systematic and practical pathway for large model inference optimization. It enables the transition of large model services from basic usability (callable) to production-grade operability, addressing cost, efficiency, and stability challenges in token-oriented service delivery.

Abstract: Large model inference optimization serves as a key foundation for supporting the scalable, low-cost, and highly stable operation of large model services. Centered on token-oriented inference optimization technology, this paper proposes for the first time a four-layer technical architecture consisting of Multi-model Fusion, Model Optimization, Compute-Model Fusion, and Compute-Network-Model Fusion. It systematically reviews the key technologies and current industry status across these four levels and analyzes the application value of related technologies in real-world business scenarios. This paper provides a practical technical path for reducing token production costs, improving token service efficiency, ensuring the stability of token supply, and driving the transition of large model services from being merely callable to being operable.

</details>


### [86] [A Model-Driven Approach for Developing Families of Reinforcement Learning Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20324)
*Xiaoran Liu,Istvan David*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Proposes a model-driven approach using a hybrid genetic algorithm to automatically generate families of RL training environments, demonstrated in wildfire mitigation and curriculum learning scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual development of environment variants for realistic RL training is labor-intensive, error-prone, and unscalable. An automated, principled approach is needed to generate families of similar but slightly different environments efficiently.

Method: A model-driven approach with a hybrid genetic algorithm combining population-based global search and heuristic local search. Mutations and constraints are expressed as model transformations and executed by a model transformation engine. A prototype tool implements the approach.

Result: The approach was demonstrated in a wildfire mitigation scenario and curriculum learning, showing soundness of the method.

Conclusion: Model-driven engineering combined with hybrid genetic search effectively automates the generation of RL environment families, addressing scalability challenges in realistic multi-environment training paradigms.

Abstract: Virtual training environments are software-intensive systems in which reinforcement learning (RL) agents learn, adapt, and demonstrate meaningful behavior. Virtual training environments offer a safe and cost-efficient alternative to training agents in real-world settings. However, to converge, most realistic RL problems require training in multiple, mostly similar but slightly different environments - i.e., families of environment variants. The typical development process of environment families is a labor-intensive and error-prone manual endeavor that does not scale well. To alleviate these issues, in this paper, we propose a model-driven approach for developing families of RL training environments. To obtain the family of environments, we develop an approach and prototype tool. In our approach, a hybrid genetic algorithm - a combination of population-based global search and heuristic local search - generates environment families. Mutations and constraints are expressed as model transformations and are operationalized into a search process by a state-of-the-art model transformation engine. We demonstrate the soundness of our approach in a wildfire mitigation scenario and curriculum learning - a particular learning paradigm that relies on environment families.

</details>


### [87] [AutoPass: Evidence-Guided LLM Agents for Compiler Performance Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20373)
*Zepeng Li,Jie Ren,Zhanyong Tang,Jie Zheng,Zheng Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AutoPass is a multi-agent LLM-based framework for compiler performance tuning that exposes compiler internals to LLMs, enabling iterative optimization guided by runtime feedback without training, achieving up to 1.117× speedup over LLVM -O3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs show promise for code tasks but struggle with runtime performance tuning due to complex microarchitectural effects and noisy measurements. Existing autotuning methods treat the compiler as a black box, missing valuable internal optimization state information.

Method: AutoPass uses a multi-agent framework where LLMs query compiler-internal optimization states and analyze intermediate representation (IR). The search process iteratively refines optimization configurations using measured runtime feedback to diagnose regressions and guide edits. Operates inference-only without offline training or task-specific fine-tuning.

Result: On server-grade x86-64 and embedded ARM64 systems, AutoPass achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.043× and 1.117× over LLVM -O3, respectively, outperforming expert-tuned heuristics and classical autotuning methods.

Conclusion: Opening compiler internals to LLM-driven multi-agent search enables effective and generalizable runtime performance tuning without requiring offline training, making AutoPass readily applicable to new benchmarks and platforms.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for code compilation tasks, but applying them to runtime performance tuning is difficult due to complex microarchitectural effects and noisy runtime measurements. We present AutoPass, a multi-agent framework for compiler performance tuning that uses compiler and runtime evidence to guide LLM-generated optimization decisions. Rather than treating the compiler as a black box like prior auto-tuning schemes, AutoPass opens up the compiler to the LLM, enabling it to query compiler-internal optimization states and analyze the intermediate representation to orchestrate compiler options. The search process iteratively refines optimization configurations using measured runtime feedback to diagnose regressions and guide latency-improving edits. AutoPass operates in an inference-only, training-free setting and requires no offline training or task-specific fine-tuning, making it readily applicable to new benchmarks and platforms. We implement AutoPass on the LLVM compiler and evaluate it on server-grade x86-64 and embedded ARM64 systems. AutoPass outperforms expert-tuned heuristics and classical autotuning methods, achieving geometric-mean speedups of 1.043x and 1.117x over LLVM -O3 on x86-64 and ARM64, respectively.

</details>


### [88] [Probe-and-Refine Tuning of Repository Guidance for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20512)
*Asa Shepard,Jeannie Albrecht*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Probe-and-refine tuning iteratively improves AGENTS.md repository guidance files using synthetic bug-fix probes, boosting coding agent resolve rates by directing agents to correct files rather than improving patch quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM coding agents need high-level repository context (subsystem locations, test commands, failure-prone workflows) not present in source code. While engineers use AGENTS.md files to supply this, prior studies disagree on whether LLM-generated guidance helps or harms agent performance. The authors hypothesize that the method of producing guidance is the decisive factor.

Method: Probe-and-refine tuning: a procedure using synthetic bug-fix probes to iteratively diagnose and patch a repository's guidance file through single-shot LLM calls, without agent loops or tool use during tuning. Evaluated on SWE-bench Verified across four independent trials using Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 200 steps, with additional step-budget and cross-model (NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B) experiments.

Result: Probe-and-refine achieved 33.0% mean resolve rate vs. 28.3% for the static knowledge base and 25.5% for unguided baseline (p < 0.001 for both contrasts). The improvement came from coverage: refined guidance produced evaluable patches for 14.5 pp more instances, while per-patch precision remained statistically constant (~59%, p = 0.119). A step-budget experiment showed guidance enables productive use of larger step budgets. Cross-model experiments revealed tuning degrades when the model cannot generate sufficiently diagnostic output, though per-patch precision still remains constant.

Conclusion: How guidance is produced is decisive for LLM coding agent performance. Probe-and-refine tuning improves coverage (reaching the right files) rather than precision (quality of changes), and requires a model capable of diagnostic output during tuning. Guidance unlocks productive use of larger inference-time compute budgets.

Abstract: LLM-based coding agents need higher-level operational knowledge about a repository (which files house which subsystems, how to run the test suite, which workflows have historically led to wrong fixes) that does not exist in the code itself. Engineers typically maintain \texttt{AGENTS.md} files to supply this context as instructions for coding agents, but whether they help is contested: recent studies disagree on whether LLM-generated guidance improves or harms agent performance. In this paper we show that how the guidance is produced is the decisive variable, and introduce \emph{probe-and-refine tuning}: a procedure that uses synthetic bug-fix probes to iteratively diagnose and patch a repository's guidance file through single-shot LLM calls, with no agent loop or tool use during tuning. On SWE-bench Verified across four independent trials with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 200 steps, probe-and-refine achieves 33.0\,\% mean resolve rate vs.\ 28.3\,\% for the static knowledge base used to initialize it and 25.5\,\% for an unguided baseline ($p < 0.001$ for both probe-and-refine contrasts). The improvement comes from coverage rather than precision: refined guidance produces evaluable patches for 14.5 percentage points (pp) more instances while per-patch precision remains statistically constant ($\sim$59\,\%, $p = 0.119$), showing that improved guidance helps agents reach the correct file rather than improving the quality of the changes they make. Further, a step-budget experiment shows that guidance is what lets the agent use a larger step budget productively, and a cross-model experiment with NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B finds that the tuning loop degrades when the model cannot generate sufficiently diagnostic output, though per-patch precision remains constant even then.

</details>

### [89] [Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19464)
*Anupam Joshi,Tim Finin,Karuna Pande Joshi,Lalana Kagal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-driven autonomous agents require governance beyond permit/prohibit — including obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning. The authors propose AgenticRei, a deontic policy framework built on OWL/Rei that enforces these richer constraints at runtime via an external logic engine, governing both tool invocations and agent-to-agent messages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current policy engines (XACML, Rego, Cedar) only handle permit/prohibit binary decisions. Autonomous LLM agents introduce governance needs — obligations (e.g., notify CISO after certain actions), dispensations (waiving obligations under specific conditions), meta-policy conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning over domain hierarchies (healthcare, cybersecurity, privacy) — that these engines cannot express or manage.

Method: AgenticRei employs a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed in OWL (Web Ontology Language). Policies are evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine operating entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages, and composes with industry frameworks like A2AS.

Result: Through examples, the authors demonstrate that deontic policies can capture governance constraints around security and privacy that are largely inexpressible in current production policy engines.

Conclusion: A deontic, ontology-based approach to agent governance fills a critical gap left by existing policy engines. AgenticRei provides a comprehensive governance layer — permits, prohibitions, obligations, dispensations, and conflict resolution — suitable for the regulatory and operational complexity of real-world agentic AI deployments.

Abstract: Autonomous agentic AI systems driven by Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new class of security, privacy, and compliance challenges: an agent that can invoke tools, manipulate data, install software, and coordinate with peer agents across organizational boundaries must be constrained not just by authentication and access control, but by the full structure of enterprise governance. This includes specifying what agents are permitted and prohibited from doing, what they areobliged to do after certain actions (e.g., notify the CISO), under what conditions a standing obligation may be waived, and which rules take precedence when policies conflict. This governance problem exceeds what current policy engines provide. Systems such as XACML, Rego, and Cedar address only the permit/prohibit subset of this governance structure. They do not provide obligation lifecycle management, meta-policy conflict resolution, dispensations that waive obligations in specific circumstances, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies commonly found in applications such as healthcare, cybersecurity, or data privacy. We propose AgenticRei, which realizes key governance requirements such as obligations, dispensations, policy conflict resolutions, and reasoning over policies, as well as the basic permit/prohibit constraints. We use a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed as OWL (Web Ontology Language) and evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages. We show through examples that deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production engines. Our approach composes naturally with industry-standard frameworks like A2AS.

</details>


### [90] [Measuring Curriculum Alignment across Topical Coverage, Competency, and Cognitive Depth: A Longitudinal Framework Applied to CS2013 and CS2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19469)
*Sherzod Turaev,Mary John,Saja Aldabet,Mamoun Awad,Nazar Zaki,Khaled Shuaib*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A human-in-the-loop pipeline maps a CS program's curriculum coverage against CS2013 and CS2023 guidelines using semantic retrieval and human validation, finding coverage remains ~50% across a decade but competency depth gaps emerge under the newer, more demanding CS2023 standard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CS programs lack a reliable, reproducible method to measure how completely they cover international curricular guidelines (like CS2013/CS2023) and how coverage shifts when guidelines are restructured. Existing approaches lack automation and rigorous validation.

Method: A retrieve-then-confirm pipeline: (1) both the program and curricular guidelines are represented as structured corpora; (2) candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches are generated via semantic retrieval (seven retrievers benchmarked, with reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble performing best); (3) matches are confirmed through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition; (4) validated by an independent second rater using Cohen's kappa; (5) extended to analyze competency articulation and cognitive depth alignment.

Result: The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units — near-constant coverage across a decade. The ensemble retriever outperformed a long-context model. Inter-rater reliability was κ=0.64 (CS2023) and κ=0.69 (CS2013). Competency is articulated for ~88% of covered units under both guidelines, but recommended cognitive depth is met for only 76% of CS2023 units vs. 95% for CS2013, reflecting raised expectations in the newer standard. Persistent structural gaps identified: parallel/distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, and systems fundamentals.

Conclusion: The pipeline provides a reusable, validated instrument for longitudinal curriculum-to-standard mapping. It disentangles persistent program gaps from shifts attributable to evolving curricular standards. The tool is available upon request and can inform evidence-based curriculum revision.

Abstract: Undergraduate computer science is governed by international curricular guidelines revised about once a decade, yet programs lack a reliable, reproducible way to measure how completely they cover the current guidelines and how that coverage shifts when the guidelines are restructured. We address this with a human-in-the-loop pipeline that measures a program's coverage of an external body of knowledge, applied longitudinally to one accredited BSc in Computer Science against Computer Science Curricula 2013 (CS2013) and 2023 (CS2023). The pipeline represents the program and each guideline as structured corpora, generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches by semantic retrieval, and confirms them through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition. Of seven benchmarked retrievers, a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble was strongest, and a reputed long-context model underperformed a small sentence model, so retriever choice must be measured. Both maps were validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's kappa 0.64 for CS2023, 0.69 for CS2013). The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units, near-constant across a decade. Extending the same retrieve-then-confirm design to competency articulation and cognitive depth shows that the program articulates the competency for ~88% of covered units under each guideline, yet delivers it at the recommended depth for 76% of present units under CS2023 against 95% under CS2013, a gap reflecting the newer guideline's raised expectations, not the program. The longitudinal comparison separates persistent structural gaps (parallel and distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, systems fundamentals), uncovered against both guidelines and ABET, from differences that reflect the standard's evolution. The instrument is reusable and available from the authors on request.

</details>


### [91] [Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19475)
*Thomas Bertolani,Davide Bucciarelli,Leonardo Zini,Marcella Cornia,Lorenzo Baraldi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic experimental comparison of eight state-of-the-art Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) across eight benchmarks, evaluating both generation quality and computational efficiency while analyzing key inference-time factors like denoising steps, context length, and unmasking strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of diverse DLM architectures has created a fragmented landscape where inconsistent evaluation protocols, datasets, and hyperparameters make meaningful comparison impossible. There is a need for a unified, controlled analysis to understand the trade-offs DLMs offer relative to each other and to autoregressive LLMs.

Method: Systematic evaluation of eight state-of-the-art DLMs on eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving. The study explicitly measures both generation quality and computational efficiency, analyzes inference-time factors (denoising steps, context length, block size, parallel unmasking strategies), and includes controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions.

Result: DLM behavior is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct performance-efficiency trade-offs. The analysis highlights specific strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets.

Conclusion: Contemporary DLMs present viable but nuanced alternatives to autoregressive LLMs, with their effectiveness depending heavily on task type and inference configuration. The study offers practical guidance for understanding and deploying DLMs.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized language modeling through autoregressive generation, enabling strong performance across a wide range of tasks. Recently, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as an alternative paradigm that generates text through iterative denoising rather than next-token prediction, allowing parallel refinement of entire sequences. While numerous diffusion-based architectures have been proposed, differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters make it difficult to compare their capabilities and understand the trade-offs they offer. In this work, we present a systematic experimental analysis of modern DLMs. Specifically, we evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving, while explicitly considering both generation quality and computational efficiency. Beyond downstream evaluation, we analyze the impact of key inference-time factors, including denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies, and complement large-scale experiments with controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets. We show that the behavior of DLMs is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. Overall, our study provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs.

</details>


### [92] [Hidden Anchors in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19494)
*Apurba Pokharel,Ram Dantu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper models multi-agent LLM deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent has a hidden internal belief ("anchor") that persistently pulls its opinions. This explains how group confidence can exceed any initial individual confidence, violating classical consensus models. The anchor can be recovered from deliberation data, and its generalization across held-out runs serves as a diagnostic test for the model's explanatory power.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM deliberation improves reasoning accuracy, but lacks formal modeling of why it works. Existing opinion-dynamics models (DeGroot, Friedkin-Johnsen) capture the "herd effect" but fail to account for each agent's persistent internal belief. The authors seek to explain the phenomenon where group deliberation produces confidence exceeding any individual's starting point—a behavior forbidden by classical models.

Method: The authors formulate multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent possesses a hidden internal belief (anchor) that exerts a continual pulling force on its opinions, independent of neighbors' influence. They demonstrate that this anchor can be recovered solely from deliberation trajectories and propose a generalization test: checking whether the recovered anchor predicts held-out runs. The approach is validated across three open-weight LLM families.
