Result: The anchor-driven closed-loop model successfully explains why agent confidence can surpass the convex hull of initial beliefs—a phenomenon classical consensus rules cannot account for. Across three model families, anchor influence strength is roughly equal, but anchor position varies. Deliberation escapes the initial belief hull only when the anchor sits far from initial opinions, at which point the full closed-loop model becomes necessary.

Conclusion: Multi-agent LLM deliberation is best understood as an anchor-driven closed-loop system rather than classical consensus dynamics. The recoverable anchor serves as both an explanatory mechanism and a diagnostic tool, revealing that anchor influence exists on a spectrum across models and that hull-escaping behavior occurs specifically when anchors are positioned far from initial opinions.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM deliberation, where agents exchange and revise answers over several rounds, is increasingly used to improve reasoning and accuracy, yet how and why it works is rarely modelled. Such deliberation mirrors how humans reach decisions. As social animals we are pulled both by the group, the herd effect that classical opinion-dynamics models such as DeGroot and Friedkin--Johnsen capture, and by our own internal belief, which they do not. We model multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system in which each agent carries a hidden internal belief, its anchor, that continually pulls its opinion regardless of its neighbours. We show this anchor can be recovered from the deliberation alone, and that it explains a behaviour classical consensus rules forbid: an agent's confidence in the correct answer can climb past where any agent started, escaping the space (convexhull) formed by the initial beliefs. Checking whether the recovered anchor also predicts held-out runs (generalizes) gives a simple test for when a model is truly driven bysuch an anchor. Across three open-weight model families this is a spectrum, not all-or-nothing. All anchors' influence are about equally strongly, but they differ in where the anchor sits, and only when it sits far from the initial opinions does deliberation escape the hull and need the full closed-loop model.

</details>


### [93] [DeXposure-Claw: An Agentic System for DeFi Risk Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19501)
*Aijie Shu,Bowei Chen,Wenbin Wu,Cathy Yi-Hsuan Chen,Fengxiang He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeXposure-Claw is an agentic supervision system for decentralized finance that uses a graph time-series foundation model to forecast exposure networks, then routes LLM decisions through structured evidence, monitors, and confidence gates to generate auditable supervisory tickets with low false-intervention rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose LLM agents perform poorly in DeFi supervision: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions. Existing evaluations lack regulator-aligned metrics for measuring false alarms, creating a gap for a structured, forecast-grounded approach.

Method: DeXposure-Claw integrates three components: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model that forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios that convert forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates that constrain escalation before emitting auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. Evaluation uses DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis harness with a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate.

Result: Experiments on five years of weekly real-world DeFi data demonstrate that the system fully supports its design claims, achieving effective supervision with controlled false-intervention rates.

Conclusion: Structuring LLM agent decisions through forecast-grounded evidence, deterministic monitors, and confidence gating enables effective and auditable DeFi supervision, overcoming the limitations of general-purpose LLM agents and the absence of regulator-aligned evaluation frameworks.

Abstract: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks. General-purpose LLM agents fit this setting poorly: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations offer no regulator-aligned way to measure the resulting false alarms. We introduce DeXposure-Claw, a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios then turn those forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation before DeXposure-Claw emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. We further develop DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis evaluation harness, whose decision axis scores tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate. Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support our system. Code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw.

</details>


### [94] [LLM Doesn't Know What It Doesn't Know: Detecting Epistemic Blind Spots via Cross-Model Attribution Divergence on Clinical Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19509)
*Akshat Dasula,Prasanna Desikan,Jaideep Srivastava*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs exhibit poor epistemic self-awareness on structured clinical data: verbalized confidence is uninformative and constant, but cross-model attribution divergence with XGBoost enables super-additive interventions (few-shot + SHAP) and a calibrator that reduces ECE from 0.254 to 0.080 without model internals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed on structured clinical prediction tasks, yet it is unknown whether they can recognize the boundaries of their own knowledge (epistemic uncertainty). This gap poses safety risks in high-stakes medical settings where overconfident wrong predictions are unacceptable.

Method: The authors compare Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a structured clinical prediction task using cross-model attribution divergence analysis. They introduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) to quantify divergence between LLM and XGBoost feature attributions. They test three interventions: (1) few-shot examples, (2) SHAP-derived feature evidence, and (3) their combination. A cross-model calibrator maps attribution divergence signals to patient-specific reliability estimates without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference.

Result: Four key findings: (1) LLM verbalized confidence ranges narrowly (0.856–0.937) regardless of accuracy (49%–75.3%), tracking prompt format not prediction quality. (2) Inverse difficulty effect: LLM accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs 73.1%) under moderate XGBoost uncertainty. (3) Few-shot + SHAP interventions are super-additive, reducing ADS from 1.54 to 0.38 and boosting accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. (4) The cross-model calibrator reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080.

Conclusion: The findings are framed as a cold start problem for LLMs on structured data. The authors argue that genuine epistemic self-awareness in LLMs requires moving beyond verbalized confidence toward cross-model attribution signals, outlining a practical path for safer clinical deployment.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to structured clinical data, yet whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge on such tasks remains unexplored. We study this question through the lens of cross-model attribution divergence with the goal of reducing epistemic uncertainty for structured tasks, comparing Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a prediction task via attribution divergence analysis. We report four findings. First, LLM verbalized confidence is epistemically vacuous, it outputs a near-constant (0.856-0.937) regardless of whether accuracy is 49% or 75.3%, tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. Second, the LLM exhibits an inverse difficulty effect: accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) when it is moderately uncertain. Third, few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions: they reduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) from 1.54 to 0.38 and improve accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. Fourth, a cross-model calibrator that determined LLM reliability using attribution divergence signals reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080, replacing uninformative verbalized confidence with patient-specific reliability estimates, without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference. We frame these findings as a cold start problem for LLMs on structured data and outline a path toward genuine epistemic self-awareness.

</details>


### [95] [Exit-and-Join Dynamics for Decentralized Coalition Formation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19683)
*Quanyan Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Coalition formation is modeled as a decentralized dynamical process where agents make unilateral exit-and-join decisions based on the Aumann-Drèze value. The paper establishes equilibrium characterizations, identifies conditions for Lyapunov/potential representations, and analyzes how switching and acceptance costs affect local stability, with numerical experiments validating the framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional coalition formation models often rely on globally negotiated coalition structures and cooperative solution concepts. This paper seeks to bridge cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response dynamics by modeling coalition formation as a decentralized process driven purely by individual incentives, providing a more realistic account of how coalitions emerge and stabilize through local, self-interested decisions.

Method: The authors model coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical system where agents unilaterally decide to exit their current coalition and join another. Payoffs are computed using the Aumann-Drèze value, which evaluates each agent's share within its current coalition rather than across a global coalition structure. A terminal partition is defined as a coalition structure admitting no individually profitable exit-and-join deviation. The analysis establishes equilibrium characterizations, derives conditions for scalar Lyapunov functions and exact-potential representations, incorporates switching and acceptance costs, and tests the dynamics via numerical experiments including a convex-game benchmark.

Result: The paper provides equilibrium characterizations linking cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior. Conditions are identified under which the dynamics admit scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations, guaranteeing convergence. The analysis further reveals how switching costs and acceptance costs shape local stability properties. Numerical experiments demonstrate finite-time stabilization, sensitivity to cost parameters, and performance on a convex-game benchmark.

Conclusion: The Aumann-Drèze value provides a natural bridge between cooperative and noncooperative approaches to coalition formation. The decentralized exit-and-join dynamics, when augmented with switching and acceptance costs, yield rich stability properties and can be analyzed through Lyapunov and potential-game techniques. The framework offers both theoretical insights and practical tools for understanding emergent coalition structures.

Abstract: This paper studies coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process driven by unilateral exit-and-join decisions. Agents evaluate local moves using the Aumann-Dreze value, so payoffs are computed within the agent's current coalition rather than through a globally negotiated coalition structure. The resulting model links cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior: a terminal partition is precisely a coalition structure with no admissible, individually profitable exit-and-join deviation. We establish equilibrium characterizations, identify conditions under which the dynamics admit scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations, and analyze how switching and acceptance costs shape local stability. Numerical experiments test finite-time stabilization, cost sensitivity, and a special convex-game benchmark.

</details>


### [96] [REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision-Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer's Disease Risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19522)
*Ethan Elio Meidinger,Seowung Leem,Zeyun Zhao,Ruogu Fang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a continuous, learnable formulation of phenotypic similarity for vision-language contrastive learning, replacing rigid discrete groupings with soft, differentiable weighting. Applied to retinal imaging and clinical risk narratives for Alzheimer's disease prediction, it outperforms discrete group-based and standard baselines on UK Biobank data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vision-language alignment methods for AD prediction (e.g., REVEAL) use discrete phenotypic grouping—hard cluster assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. This fails to capture the continuous, spectrum-like nature of neurodegenerative disease risk.

Method: The authors introduce: (1) a continuous phenotypic structure formulation where inter-subject similarity is modeled as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and clinical risk profiles; (2) a continuous aggregation operator that defines soft multi-positive relationships; and (3) a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure end-to-end, treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal.

Result: Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident Alzheimer's disease prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms both discrete group-based contrastive learning approaches and standard vision-language baselines.

Conclusion: Treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule provides a more principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

Abstract: The retina offers a noninvasive window into neurodegenerative disease, capturing subtle structural patterns associated with a risk of future cognitive decline. Vision-language alignment frameworks such as REVEAL have shown that pairing retinal fundus images with structured clinical risk narratives improves early prediction of Alzheimer's disease (AD). A key design choice in these approaches is the use of phenotypic grouping, where individuals with similar risk profiles are treated as multi-positive pairs during contrastive learning. However, existing methods operationalize phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct, relying on hard group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. We propose a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure within contrastive learning. Rather than assigning samples to fixed clusters, we model inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships through a continuous aggregation operator, enabling graded supervision that reflects the spectrum nature of disease risk. We further introduce a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines. By treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule, our approach provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

</details>


### [97] [Emergent Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19527)
*Martin Kolář*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a "conscience step" where an LLM reviews its own outputs for ethical alignment, combined with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), enabling online self-alignment across training, fine-tuning, and inference without external judges — achieving what the authors term "Emergent Alignment" as a counterpoint to previously observed "Emergent Misalignment."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work identified "Emergent Misalignment," where fine-tuning LLMs on narrow tasks (e.g., code hacking) induces unethical behaviors. The authors aim to address whether LLMs can self-detect and self-correct such misalignment without relying on external (weaker or stronger) judges, instead using introspection — a frozen copy of the model reviewing its own outputs.

Method: The method adds a "conscience step": the LLM reviews its own reasoning and outputs for ethical alignment. This is paired with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), extending the training loss with an alignment component that penalizes non-ethical outputs. The technique is online, works across training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot settings, and uses a frozen copy of the model as the alignment reference rather than an external judge. A single high-level introspective question is used to steer training.

Result: Under the same code-hacking scenario that previously produced Emergent Misalignment, the proposed conscience + DPO method instead yields "Emergent Alignment" — the model self-steers toward ethical behavior. The approach proves effective across diverse settings: training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning.

Conclusion: LLMs can discern when their own outputs are ethically misaligned and can self-correct through introspection combined with DPO-based alignment. This provides a scalable, judge-free online alignment technique that transforms emergent misalignment into emergent alignment, suggesting a viable path toward more ethically robust models without external oversight infrastructure.

Abstract: Can Large Language Models (LLMs) discern when their own outputs are misaligned with human ethics? And can they self-correct? We endow an LLM with a conscience step that reviews its own reasoning and outputs, and we extend the training loss with an alignment component using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to steer the model away from non-ethical outputs. The result is an online technique to align models in a wide range of applications: training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning. It does not require a weaker or stronger judge, relying instead on a frozen copy of itself. In previous work, the Emergent Misalignment scenario showed a range of emergent unethical behaviors from fine-tuning the model to hack code. Instead, we empirically show how to achieve Emergent Alignment: a single high-level introspective question steers training toward an ethical model under the same code hacking scenario.

</details>


### [98] [ITNet: A Learnable Integral Transform That Subsumes Convolution, Attention, and Recurrence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19538)
*Ashim Dhor,Rasel Mondal,Pin Yu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified neural architecture built around a learnable integral transform with a kernel that jointly depends on positions and features. Convolutions, self-attention, and recurrent networks all emerge as special cases of ITNet under appropriate parameterizations. With practical optimizations (tiled kernel fusion, Monte Carlo integration, low-rank factorization), a single ITNet matches or exceeds specialized models across diverse benchmarks including ImageNet-1K, GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA v2, and NLVR2.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers have remained mathematically distinct since their inception, each encoding different inductive biases (locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction). The authors argue this fragmentation reflects incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object — a learnable integral transform — rather than fundamental diversity in signal processing. The goal is to unify these three dominant architectural paradigms under one framework.

Method: The core of ITNet is a learnable kernel implemented as a small MLP that models pairwise interactions and depends jointly on both positions and features. Specific parameterizations recover: (1) convolution via translation-invariant, compactly supported kernels; (2) self-attention (including multi-head) via content-dependent dot-product kernels; (3) autoregressive recurrence (LSTM, GRU, S4, Mamba) via causal, state-space-style kernels. For scalability, the authors introduce tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization. The architecture uses a shared ITNet operator with lightweight modality-specific encoders.

Result: A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K (vision), GLUE (language understanding), ModelNet40 (3D point clouds), VQA v2 and NLVR2 (vision-language). This demonstrates that one learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three architectural families — convolution, attention, and recurrence — purely from data.

Conclusion: The fragmentation among convolutions, attention, and recurrence is not fundamental; all three are special cases of a learnable integral transform. ITNet provides a practical unified architecture that can learn which inductive bias to apply, achieving competitive performance across modalities. This suggests the field may benefit from moving beyond hand-designed architectural inductive biases toward learned interaction mechanisms.

Abstract: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers each encode different inductive biases -- locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction -- and have remained mathematically distinct since their inception. We show that this fragmentation reflects not a fundamental diversity in how signals should be processed, but rather incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object: a learnable integral transform. We introduce the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified architecture built around a learnable kernel that depends jointly on positions and features. This kernel is implemented as a small neural network, specifically an MLP, that models pairwise interactions, enabling the model to adapt its behavior from data. We show that convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (including LSTM, GRU, S4, and Mamba) arise as special cases under appropriate parameterizations, and that ITNet is a universal approximator of continuous operators. To make this practical, we develop tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization, enabling efficient and scalable computation. A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K , GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA\,v2 and NLVR2. The results demonstrate that a single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three architectural families from data.

</details>


### [99] [Denoising Implicit Feedback for Cold-start Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19658)
*Gaode Chen,Shicheng Wang,Shikun Li,Rui Huang,Xinghua Zhang,Yunze Luo,Shipeng Li,Shiming Ge,Ruina Sun,Yinjie Jiang,Jun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DIF is a model-agnostic denoising method for cold-start recommendation that leverages content-similar warm items to generate confidence-weighted pseudo-labels, then uses relative entropy and cold-start status to adaptively correct noisy implicit feedback labels at the sample level.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Implicit feedback (e.g., clicks) is inherently noisy due to clickbait and position bias, and cold items are disproportionately affected. Existing denoising methods rely on heuristic patterns (e.g., high loss) and lack adaptability, rendering them ineffective for cold-start scenarios where the significance of denoising is often overlooked.

Method: DIF operates in three stages: (1) inferring pseudo-labels for cold items by leveraging stable user content preferences via content-similar warm items; (2) improving pseudo-label accuracy by modeling confidence based on content similarity and aggregating multiple pseudo-labels per sample; (3) explicitly estimating label uncertainty using relative entropy and the item's cold-start status to adaptively guide pseudo-label correction of noisy labels at the sample level.

Result: DIF is supported by theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. It has been deployed on Kuaishou, a billion-user short video platform, achieving significant improvements across multiple commercial metrics in cold-start scenarios.

Conclusion: DIF provides an effective, theoretically grounded, and model-agnostic solution for denoising implicit feedback in cold-start recommendation, validated by both offline experiments and large-scale industrial deployment.

Abstract: Implicit feedback is widely used in recommender systems due to its accessibility and generality, yet it usually presents noisy samples (e.g., clickbait, position bias). Meanwhile, recommenders inevitably face the item cold-start problem due to the continuous influx of new items. We identify that cold items are more prone to noisy samples due to the aforementioned factors, and researchers often overlook the significance of denoising implicit feedback for cold items. Previous denoising studies usually identify noisy samples based on heuristic patterns, such as higher loss values, and mitigate noise through sample selection or re-weighting. However, these methods have limited adaptability and are ineffective in cold-start scenarios. To achieve denoising implicit feedback for cold-start recommendation, we propose a model-agnostic denoising method called DIF. First, user preferences for content remain stable, which allows us to infer pseudo-labels indicating whether a user is interested in a cold item through content-similar warm items. Furthermore, to improve pseudo-label accuracy, we model the confidence of pseudo-labels based on the content similarity between the cold item and warm items, and then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels for each sample. Finally, we explicitly estimate the uncertainty of the noisy sample label by considering its relative entropy and the cold-start status of the item, which adaptively guides the role of pseudo-labels to correct the noisy labels at the sample level. DIF's superiority is supported by both theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The method has been deployed on a billion-user scale short video application Kuaishou and has significantly improved various commercial metrics within cold-start scenarios.

</details>


### [100] [ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20122)
*Zhibang Yang,Xinke Jiang,Yuzhen Xiao,Ruizhe Zhang,Yue Fang,XinFei Wan,Zhengxing Song,Yuxuan Liu,Yuheng Huang,Xu Chu,Junfeng Zhao,Yasha Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ScaffoldAgent introduces a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research, modeling outline evolution as a structured decision process with Expansion, Contraction, and Revision operations. A utility signal combining retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality guides outline updates, improving long-form report generation and factual grounding over fixed-outline and heuristic baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OEDR systems suffer from scaffold drift: fixed outlines cannot adapt to information accumulated during multi-round retrieval, while heuristic-based refinement lacks principled feedback for evaluating whether outline modifications are beneficial. There is a need for a mechanism that dynamically optimizes the outline based on downstream utility.

Method: ScaffoldAgent frames outline evolution as a structured decision process with three atomic operations (Expansion, Contraction, Revision). A utility-guided feedback mechanism estimates the value of each operation using three signals: retrieval gain (information acquired), structural coherence (logical consistency of the scaffold), and trial-generation quality (preview of generated text quality). This utility score drives node selection, operation scheduling, and termination decisions during inference.

Result: Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym demonstrate that ScaffoldAgent consistently outperforms existing deep research agents in both long-form report quality and factual grounding.

Conclusion: Dynamic outline optimization with utility-guided feedback effectively mitigates scaffold drift, enabling more coherent and factually grounded long-form report generation in open-ended deep research settings.

Abstract: Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.

</details>


### [101] [Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19559)
*Gregory Matsnev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a prompt-based method that decomposes an LLM agent's output into action confidence and request uncertainty, enabling proactive clarification-seeking when task specifications are ambiguous. Evaluated on two new clarification-augmented benchmarks across five LLM backbones, the decomposition significantly outperforms existing uncertainty estimation baselines (ReAct+UE and UAM), with gains generalizing across models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty frameworks are inadequate for interactive LLM agents, which need underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations. Practical deployment constraints (black-box APIs, latency budgets, no labeled trajectories) rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, making prompt-based estimation the only viable option for surfacing uncertainty signals at deployment time.

Method: A simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u). When request uncertainty is high (indicating ambiguous task specification), the agent proactively asks for clarification. Evaluation uses two newly introduced clarification-augmented benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification) where 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified, plus standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection. Systematic comparison against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones: GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, and GPT-OSS-120B.

Result: Averaged across five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and 36% over UAM. It leads clarification F1 on every backbone for WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones for ALFWorld-Clarification, demonstrating generalization beyond a single LLM.

Conclusion: Prompt-based decomposition of action confidence and request uncertainty effectively enables LLM agents to detect underspecified tasks and seek clarification. The approach is model-agnostic, compatible with black-box deployment constraints, and generalizes across diverse LLM backbones and benchmarks.

Abstract: Recent position papers argue that the classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty framework is insufficient for interactive large language model (LLM) agents and call for underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations that can unlock new agent capabilities such as proactive clarification seeking and shared mental-model building. Practical deployment constraints -- black-box APIs, interactive latency budgets, and the absence of labeled trajectories -- rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based estimation as the most viable family for surfacing such signals at deployment time. We answer this call with a simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u), enabling the agent to ask for clarification when the task specification is ambiguous. To evaluate it, we introduce two clarification-augmented benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification) in which 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified, and systematically compare the proposed decomposition against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B) on these variants together with the standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection. Averaged across the five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM, and leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, indicating that the gains generalize beyond a single LLM.

</details>


### [102] [RACL: Reasoning-Agent Control Layers for Continuous Metaheuristic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20142)
*Antón Asla Manzárraga*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RACL introduces a reasoning-agent control layer that sits atop existing metaheuristic optimizers, using an LLM (Codex) to observe, reason about, and dynamically intervene in the optimizer's search behavior — improving solution quality without modifying the underlying algorithm or constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metaheuristics often rely on hand-tuned, static control policies that cannot adapt to instance-specific or runtime-specific conditions. The authors seek to replace brittle manual tuning with an adaptive, reasoning-driven control layer that learns and consolidates effective intervention policies during execution.

Method: RACL operationalizes a reasoning loop: the agent observes the optimizer's operational memory, reasons over historical behavior, formulates bounded hypotheses, tests interventions, evaluates outcomes, applies guardrails, and consolidates successful policies. In the proof-of-concept, Codex serves as the in-the-loop reasoning agent. A policy proxy is later used for reproducible quantitative evaluation. The testbed is vehicle routing (ALNS-based).

Result: RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21/21 feasible cases and the Stagnation-Triggered Policy (STP) in 18/21 cases, with an average cost delta of -0.641% vs STP. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% vs Fixed and -1.605% vs STP, with negligible computational overhead.

Conclusion: A reasoning agent can effectively discover, validate, consolidate, and explain algorithmic control rules for metaheuristics, yielding consistent improvements over static policies without altering the underlying optimizer or constraints.

Abstract: This paper introduces RACL, a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer for metaheuristics. RACL places a reasoning agent above an existing optimizer. The agent does not replace the optimizer and does not modify business constraints. Instead, it controls the optimizer's internal search behavior by observing operational memory, reasoning over past behavior, formulating bounded hypotheses, testing interventions, evaluating outcomes, applying guardrails, consolidating useful policies and explaining its decisions. The experiment uses vehicle routing as a testbed, but the contribution is not a new routing solver, a particular ALNS configuration or a specific set of routing rules. The contribution is the RACL method: a way for a reasoning agent to discover, validate, consolidate and explain algorithmic control rules for a metaheuristic. In the current experimental setting, RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21 of 21 feasible cases and improves or ties a non-reasoning Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18 of 21 feasible cases, with an average RACL vs STP cost delta of -0.641%. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% versus Fixed and -1.605% versus STP without showing material computational overhead. During the proof-of-concept, Codex was used as an in-the-loop reasoning agent observing executions, interpreting logs and proposing live bounded interventions. The policy proxy was later used only to make quantitative evaluation reproducible.

</details>


### [103] [Analyzing the Narration Gap in LLM-Solver Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19588)
*Zunchen Huang,Songgaojun Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates the soundness vulnerability in LLM-solver hybrid pipelines, specifically the "narration gap" — where a formally verified solver output can be subverted by prompt injection when the LLM translates it into natural language for the user. Through formal modeling as a verified decision procedure and empirical evaluation of five open-source models, the authors show that while certificate gating preserves soundness, adversarial prompt injection can invert conclusions, and hardened prompts mitigate but cannot eliminate this risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used with SAT/SMT solvers for safety-critical reasoning. While solvers provide sound, verifiable outputs, prior work has ignored the "narration" step where the LLM converts solver output into user-facing answers. This gap creates a soundness vulnerability: an adversary can manipulate the LLM's narration to invert or corrupt the verified conclusion, undermining the entire pipeline's trustworthiness.

Method: The authors (1) formally model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure with three components (formalization, decision, narration); (2) empirically evaluate five open-source models (including Llama and Mistral variants) under prompt injection attacks targeting the narration step; (3) test two defenses: certificate gating (embedding verification tokens) and hardened prompts; and (4) analyze adaptive attacks that circumvent hardened prompts across different phrasings and communication channels.

Result: Certificate gating successfully preserves solver verdict soundness. However, without gating, adversaries can invert verified conclusions across diverse phrasings and channels. Hardened prompts significantly reduce injection success but fail to eliminate it entirely and remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. The core finding: robustness does not extend to the final answer the user reads.

Conclusion: The LLM-solver loop suffers from a fundamental soundness gap at the narration stage that is not closed by current mitigations. Verified solver outputs do not guarantee trustworthy user-facing answers when an LLM mediates the final communication, calling for new architectural or procedural safeguards in safety-critical LLM-tool pipelines.

Abstract: Formal tools such as SAT and SMT solvers are increasingly embedded in language model reasoning pipelines when a safety or security critical question can be formulated in logic. Unlike chain of thought whose steps are sampled from the model distribution without formal guarantee, a solver produces a sound and independently verifiable answer. However, the soundness guarantee can be lost in the interaction between the solver and the model. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work has studied the formalization and decision, but not narration, which is the step that turns a formal tool's output into the user answer. To fill the narration gap, we first model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure. We further evaluate five open-sourced models under prompt injection, and we find certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, while an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. We study the mitigation through hardened prompt that reduces injection significantly but cannot eliminate it and still suffers under adaptive attack. Combining the formal analysis and empirical studies, we show in the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not reach to the answer that the user finally reads.

</details>


### [104] [Multi-Agent Transactive Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19911)
*To Eun Kim,Xuhong He,Dishank Jain,Ambuj Agrawal,Negar Arabzadeh,Fernando Diaz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MATM proposes a shared memory framework where LLM agents contribute task execution trajectories to a communal repository and retrieve relevant past experiences, improving downstream task performance and efficiency in interactive environments without requiring coordination or joint training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents operating across diverse tasks typically discard their execution trajectories after a single use, forcing new agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions. Just as search engines organize human artifacts for reuse, agent-generated artifacts (particularly trajectories encoding procedural knowledge) should be retrievable across heterogeneous agent populations to avoid redundant problem-solving.

Method: MATM introduces a population-level storage and retrieval system for agent trajectories. Producer agents contribute their execution trajectories to a shared repository. Consumer agents query this repository to retrieve relevant trajectories, which are then incorporated into their decision-making process via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The framework operates without centralized coordination or joint training between agents.

Result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebArena (interactive environments with long, procedurally rich trajectories) show that retrieving from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces the number of interaction steps required, compared to agents operating without shared memory access.

Conclusion: MATM establishes a viable design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems, enabling heterogeneous agents to benefit from collective procedural knowledge without explicit coordination.

Abstract: The decentralized deployment of LLM agents with diverse capabilities across diverse tasks motivates infrastructure for knowledge sharing across heterogeneous agent populations. Just as search engines index human-generated artifacts to support human problem solving, retrieval systems can organize agent-generated artifacts for reuse across agent populations. We extend retrieval-augmented generation - which demonstrates the value of human-authored artifacts to individual agents - to retrieval of agent-generated artifacts supporting a population of agents. In particular, agent trajectories encode reusable procedural knowledge, yet these artifacts are typically discarded after a single use or retained only by the producing agent, forcing newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover existing solutions. We propose Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of agent-generated trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. We focus on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena), where trajectories are long and encode especially rich procedural structure. Our experiments demonstrate that retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces interaction steps without coordination or joint training. These results position MATM as a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems.

</details>


### [105] [A Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20236)
*Federica Filippini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAMO decouples reward weight selection from task execution in constrained RL by treating weight selection as a multi-agent learning problem, enabling autonomous adaptation of the cost-constraint trade-off in dynamic environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In Lagrangian-inspired RL for constrained optimization, the learned policy's behavior critically depends on manually chosen penalty weights, making it difficult to balance primary objective optimization with constraint satisfaction—especially in non-stationary environments where the relative importance of costs and constraints may shift over time.

Method: MAMO formulates reward weight selection as a learning problem using a multi-agent RL framework, decoupling task execution from objective design so that weights are adaptively learned rather than manually tuned.

Result: MAMO provides a first step toward more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization in dynamic environments.

Conclusion: Decoupling weight selection from policy learning via multi-agent RL offers a promising direction for handling the cost-constraint trade-off autonomously in non-stationary constrained optimization problems.

Abstract: Many decision-making problems in computing and networking systems can be naturally formulated as cost-minimization problems under performance constraints. In dynamic environments, reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to solve such problems at runtime by embedding both costs and constraint violations into a single scalar reward through weighted penalty terms, following a Lagrangian-inspired formulation. However, in this context the behavior of the learned policy critically depends on the choice of these weights, which are typically selected manually. This makes it difficult to identify an appropriate trade-off between optimizing the primary objective and effectively avoiding constraint violations, particularly in non-stationary environments where their relative importance may change. This paper presents MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization), an approach to tackle this balancing problem through multi-agent RL. MAMO decouples task execution from objective design by formulating the selection of reward weights as a learning problem, providing a !rst step towards more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization problems in dynamic environments.

</details>


### [106] [Configurable Clinical Information Extraction with Agentic RAG: What Works, What Breaks, and Why](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19602)
*Osman Alperen Çinar-Koraş,Marie Bauer,Sameh Khattab,Merlin Engelke,Moon Kim,Stephan Settelmeier,Shigeyasu Sugawara,Fabian Freisleben,Felix Nensa,Jens Kleesiek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ACIE is an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline deployed at University Medicine Essen that reasons over complete patient contexts (hundreds of documents, thousands of data points), grounds every answer in source passages, and achieves 96.5% clinician acceptance across 7,326 judgments in a lymphoma registry study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Patient records contain vast amounts of heterogeneous documents and structured data, but the document-level metadata needed for AI retrieval and triage is missing or incomplete. Standard RAG fails due to poor temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and absent metadata — motivating a system that can reason over complete patient contexts with verifiable provenance.

Method: ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) — an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that processes complete patient contexts, employs agent-based reasoning to handle temporal and cross-document dependencies, and grounds every extracted value in cited source passages for clinician verification. Evaluation is conducted via an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study where nuclear-medicine physicians verify each extraction against its sources.

Result: Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5% of extractions, with per-type acceptance rates ranging from 80% to 99%.

Conclusion: An agentic RAG architecture that reasons holistically over patient contexts with source grounding can achieve high clinician trust and extraction accuracy, overcoming the metadata gap and cross-document reasoning failures that plague standard RAG in clinical settings.

Abstract: Patient contexts span hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, yet the document-level metadata that AI systems need for retrieval and triage is absent or incomplete. Standard retrieval-augmented generation fails on this data, mishandling temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata. We deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) at University Medicine Essen: an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in source passages for clinician verification. We quantify the metadata gap, trace the architectural decisions it shaped, and evaluate extraction alongside an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study, in which nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources. Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5\% of extractions, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80\% to 99\%.

</details>


### [107] [Which Pairs to Compare for LLM Post-Training?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19607)
*Jiangze Han,Vineet Goyal,Will Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes comparison curation in preference-based post-training (specifically DPO) as a sampling-design problem. It provides matching upper and lower bounds showing that the choice of labeled comparison pairs affects downstream policy quality through a design-dependent information matrix, yielding an explicit optimization criterion for selecting the most informative pairs from large completion pools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human preference labels are expensive relative to generating completions, yet standard practice labels a small set of completions per prompt. The authors argue that for a fixed labeling budget, it is more efficient to generate many completions but label only the most informative comparison pairs.

Method: The authors formulate comparison curation as a sampling-design problem and evaluate designs by final policy quality under the DPO objective. They derive matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap, revealing a design-dependent information matrix that connects label allocation to parameter estimation error. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for selecting informative pairs, motivating practical sampling designs.

Result: Theoretical analysis provides matching upper and lower bounds on DPO policy suboptimality. Experiments on synthetic settings and LM post-training benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.

Conclusion: Comparison curation matters significantly for preference-based post-training. The derived information-matrix criterion enables principled selection of informative pairs, leading to better policies under fixed labeling budgets compared to standard heuristics.

Abstract: Preference-based post-training has become a central paradigm for aligning language models. A common data-collection strategy is to generate a small set of completions for each prompt and label the resulting comparison pairs. However, human preference labels are often much more expensive than generating additional completions, suggesting a different use of the same labeling budget: generate a larger pool of completions, but label only the most informative comparison pairs. This paper studies which pairs should be compared in preference-based post-training. We formulate comparison curation as a sampling-design problem and evaluate designs by the quality of the final policy under the preference-based post-training objective. We instantiate this framework for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), analyzing how the choice of labeled pairs propagates through DPO training to downstream policy performance. Our main results provide matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap of the DPO-trained policy. The bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream performance through a single design-dependent information matrix, which links label allocation to parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation and motivates practical sampling designs for selecting informative pairs from large generated completion pools. Experiments on synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks show that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.

</details>


### [108] [Toten: Knowledge-Based Ontological Tokenization Of Physical Quantities And Technical Notation In Brazilian Portuguese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19626)
*Antonio de Sousa Leitão Filho; Allan Kardec Duailibe Barros Filho; Fabrício Saul Lima; Selby Mykael Lima dos Santos; Rejani Bandeira Vieira Sousa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TOTEN is a knowledge-based tokenization framework that uses a formal engineering ontology (OEE) instead of statistical Byte-Pair Encoding to preserve the integrity of technical entities like quantities, units, and symbolic expressions. It significantly outperforms SOTA baselines on ontological atomicity and numerical reconstruction across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization, while efficient for vocabulary compression, is semantically blind: it fragments structured technical entities (physical quantities, numbers, units, symbols) into arbitrary subwords. This undermines downstream tasks in scientific and engineering NLP where preserving such entities intact is critical.

Method: TOTEN is formalized as a triple: an ontology (OEE) defining types, composition, and invariants; a classification function mapping raw text to typed regions; and an instantiator family producing structured self-descriptive representations. Robustness is ensured via deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional analysis), the Unicode Character Database (typographic classification), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology).

Result: On internal benchmark EngQuant (N=800), TOTEN achieves 0.780 numerical reconstruction vs. 0.340 for the best baseline (Quantulum3). On four external Brazilian Portuguese corpora (N=1,771), reconstruction ranges 0.775–0.904 vs. 0.627–0.703 for Quantulum3. TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with the Pint oracle.

Conclusion: TOTEN demonstrates that declarative, ontology-grounded tokenization decisively outperforms statistical approaches for technical entity preservation. By inheriting dimensional authority from Pint and achieving statistical parity with it, TOTEN provides a robust, verifiable-by-construction alternative to BPE-style tokenizers for scientific and engineering text.

Abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization is statistically efficient for vocabulary compression, but semantically blind to structured technical entities, fragmenting physical quantities, numbers, units, and symbolic expressions into lexically arbitrary subwords. We present TOTEN, a knowledge-based ontological tokenization framework that replaces statistical derivation with declarative classification grounded in a formal ontology of engineering entities (OEE). We formalize TOTEN as the triple <O, classify, {inst_tau}>: the ontology gathers types, structural principles, composition relations, and preservable invariants; the classification function maps raw text into typed regions; and the instantiator family yields a self-descriptive structured representation. Robustness derives from deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional), Unicode Character Database (typographic), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Intrinsic evaluation covers four properties verifiable by construction -- ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction -- over an internal, physically validated benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1771 eligible cases). We also report detection recall, distinguishing coverage from conditional atomicity. Against eight state-of-the-art baselines, TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts and numerical reconstruction of 0.775-0.904 on external corpora, vs. 0.627-0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity of the control benchmark. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint, the oracle from which the system inherits dimensional authority.

</details>


### [109] [AI4SE and SE4AI Exploration: A Decade Looking Back and Forward](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19630)
*H. Sinan Bank,Daniel R. Herber,Thomas Bradley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A retrospective on the AI and Systems Engineering research community's evolution through three phases, combined with a human-AI agreement study of 2,600+ publications, identifying five critical research gaps and providing an interactive web tool for relevance assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To trace the maturation of the AI4SE/SE4AI research community since the landmark March 2020 INSIGHT special issue and to systematically identify remaining research gaps through a large-scale literature review augmented by both human expertise and AI models.

Method: The authors conducted: (1) a qualitative synthesis of the field's core papers organized into three developmental phases — foundational, applied, and LLM inflection; and (2) a human-AI agreement literature review in which six AI models and human experts independently rated the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. An interactive web application (AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer) was developed to share agreement data.

Result: Five critical research gaps were identified. The three-phase progression (foundational → applied → LLM inflection) captures the community's convergence points. The AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer tool enables readers to benchmark their relevance judgments against both human and AI raters.

Conclusion: While the AI and SE research community has grown substantially and converged on several fronts, significant gaps persist in AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation within systems engineering. The open-source agreement data and explorer tool provide a foundation for continued collaborative research.

Abstract: The March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and Systems Engineering (SE) became the most downloaded issue in the publication's history and launched a research community that now draws over 250 registrants to its annual workshop. In this article, we trace the progress in AI and SE across three phases (labeled here foundational, applied, and LLM inflection) based on the authors' reading of the field's core papers, and describe our opinions of where the community has converged and where critical gaps remain. Separately, a human-AI agreement literature review leveraging both human expertise and six AI models was performed to assess the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. The results identify five critical research gaps and offer guidance for practitioners navigating AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE. We share the agreement data and the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application so readers can compare their own relevance judgments with the human and AI raters.

</details>


### [110] [Learning to Prompt: Improving Student Engagement with Adaptive LLM-based High-School Tutoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20138)
*Po-Chin Chang,Nicholas Hogan,Aske Plaat,Michiel T. van der Meer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An adaptive LLM tutoring system using subject-aware prompt routing (based on 14 pedagogical features) outperforms static baselines in simulation and real-world A/B testing, with a stochastic router achieving a 28.1% exercise conversion rate vs. 19.6% for the baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current static-prompt LLM tutoring systems fail to adapt across diverse academic disciplines, limiting their instructional effectiveness. There is a need for systems that dynamically adjust tutoring strategies based on real-time pedagogical signals.

Method: The authors extract 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) from raw transcripts. They train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment, then deploy it online with high-school students. They compare a greedy router and a stochastic (sampling-based) router against two static baselines using simulation benchmarks and A/B testing (N=656 conversations, 359 students).

Result: In simulation, the router significantly outperforms static baselines (0.694 vs. 0.647 and 0.640, p<0.001). In real deployment, the adaptive system switches between analytical and scaffolding strategies, reduces interactions by ~3 turns (p=0.007), and maintains pedagogical quality. The greedy router matches baseline exercise conversion (19.1% vs. 19.6%), while the stochastic router substantially improves it (28.1%).

Conclusion: Adaptive, subject-aware prompt routing enables more efficient and effective LLM-based tutoring across disciplines. Stochastic strategy sampling yields better student exercise conversion than deterministic greedy selection, suggesting exploration benefits instructional outcomes.

Abstract: LLMs can personalize education, although current static-prompt tutoring systems struggle to adapt to diverse academic disciplines. We develop and test a system with subject-aware prompting, based on 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) extracted from raw transcripts. We first train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment, and then deploy it for online adaptation with actual high-school students. The simulation benchmark shows the router outperforming two static baselines ($0.694$ vs. $0.647$ and $0.64$, $p<0.001$). A/B testing ($N=656$ conversations from 359 students) shows sim-to-real transfer where the model switches from analytical to scaffolding learning strategies. Our adaptive prompt selection mechanism improves instructional efficiency, maintains pedagogical quality and reduces interactions by around 3 turns ($p=0.007$). While a greedy router achieves a comparable exercise conversion rate with the baseline ($19.1\%$ vs. $19.6\%$), a stochastic router that samples strategies leads to a higher conversion rate ($28.1\%$).

</details>


### [111] [BrainG3N: A Dual-Purpose Tokenizer for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19651)
*Max Van Puyvelde,Ibrahim Gulluk,Wim Van Criekinge,Olivier Gevaert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a 3D brain MRI tokenizer for latent diffusion models that decouples a frozen masked-autoencoder (MAE) encoder from a CNN decoder. The MAE encoder—pretrained on 35,309 volumes across 18 cohorts—produces clinically informative embeddings that excel on downstream tasks (outperforming SOTA on 21/23 linear-probing benchmarks), while the dedicated decoder enables anatomically faithful reconstruction. A conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on these embeddings supports both conditional generation and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting, establishing a unified embedding space for clinical tasks and controllable generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing latent diffusion models for 3D brain MRI face a trade-off: reconstruction-driven tokenizers produce anatomically faithful volumes but yield embeddings that lack clinical utility for downstream tasks. The authors aim to resolve this tension by decoupling the encoder and decoder, enabling a single embedding space that simultaneously supports both high-quality reconstruction/generation and strong performance on clinical benchmarks.

Method: A fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) serves as the encoder, pretrained on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts (4 modalities, 10 disease categories, 200+ sites) and then frozen. A dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of the MAE embeddings. A conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) is trained on these embeddings for generation. Evaluation uses a 23-task linear-probing benchmark and conditional generation/simulation experiments across six variables with patient-specific longitudinal forecasting.

Result: The frozen MAE encoder outperforms or matches state-of-the-art models (BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 linear-probing tasks. The conditional DiT trained on these embeddings successfully performs conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting.

Conclusion: Decoupling the encoder and decoder in a 3D brain MRI tokenizer resolves the clinical-utility vs. reconstruction-fidelity trade-off, yielding a single embedding space that serves both discriminative downstream tasks and controllable generative modeling. This unified representation has broad potential for data augmentation, disease simulation, and privacy-preserving data sharing in neuroimaging.

Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) brain MRI is central to clinical neurology and neuro-oncology, where generative models could augment under-represented cohorts, simulate disease trajectories, and support privacy-preserving data sharing. Latent diffusion has been the go-to solution for modeling imaging data, but it places two competing demands on the tokenizer: encoder embeddings must retain the clinical information that downstream tasks act on, and the decoder must reconstruct anatomically faithful volumes. Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers achieve the second at the expense of the first. To address this, we introduce a fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) based tokenizer for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion, decoupling encoder and decoder: a frozen 3D MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. We pretrain the encoder on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts spanning four modalities, ten disease categories, and 200+ acquisition sites, and demonstrate its dual utility in two settings. First, on a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (i.e., BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, and MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 tasks. Second, a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on these clinically informative embeddings supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Together these results establish a single 3D brain-MRI embedding space capable of both downstream clinical tasks and controllable generation.

</details>


### [112] [Apparent Psychological Profiles of Large Language Models are Largely a Measurement Artifact](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20205)
*Jelena Meyer,David Garcia,Dirk U. Wulff*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Psychological profiles assigned to LLMs via human-designed instruments are largely measurement artifacts driven by directional response bias, not genuine traits. Bias accounts for 81-90% of between-model variance (vs. 9-16% in humans), declines with model capability but persists, and allows profiles to be manufactured through item selection. The paper calls for dedicated LLM assessment tools centered on response orthogonality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human psychological instruments are increasingly used to assign stable personality profiles to LLMs for usability, safety assessment, and as human proxies in research. The authors question whether these profiles reflect genuine model properties or measurement artifacts arising from the instruments themselves.

Method: A formal psychometric framework was applied. A battery of personality and risk-preference instruments (self-reports and behavioral tasks) was administered to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples. Variance decomposition was used to partition between-model variation into trait-driven vs. response-bias-driven components. A novel metric—response orthogonality—was introduced to quantify the proportion of items where trait and bias pull in opposite directions.

Result: Four key findings: (1) 81-90% of between-model variance is attributable to directional response bias (vs. 9-16% in humans). (2) Bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated. (3) Apparent instrument reliability is almost entirely predicted by response orthogonality. (4) A model's apparent psychological profile shifts with item selection and can be arbitrarily manufactured.

Conclusion: The apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the measurement instruments, not intrinsic model properties. Since instruments from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may lack validity for LLMs, the authors call for dedicated assessments designed around response orthogonality rather than borrowing human-centric tools.

Abstract: Psychological instruments designed for humans are increasingly used to assign large language models (LLMs) stable psychological profiles that affect their usability, safety assessment, and use as proxies for human participants in research. Using a formal psychometric framework, we show that these profiles are largely a measurement artifact. Administering a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments spanning self-reports and behavioral tasks to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples, we report four findings. First, differences between models are driven not by the traits an instrument targets but by a directional response bias, a tendency to respond toward one end of the scale, or one labeled option, regardless of item content; a variance decomposition attributes 81-90% of between-model variation to this bias, against 9-16% in humans. Second, the bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated by it. Third, because bias rather than trait drives responding, an instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality, a term we coin for the proportion of items for which trait and bias point in opposite directions. Fourth, the profile a model appears to have shifts with the items used and can be manufactured through item selection. These results demonstrate that the apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the instrument used to measure them, not properties of the models themselves. As instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, we call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

</details>


### [113] [Beyond Static Leaderboards: Predictive Validity for the Evaluation of LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19704)
*Dhaval C. Patel,Kaoutar El Maghraoui,Shuxin Lin,Yusheng Li,Tianjun Feng,Chun-Yi Tsai,Yihan Sun,Wei Alexander Xin,Akshat Bhandari,Tanisha Rathod,Aaron Fan,Sanskruti Vijay Shejwal,Tomas Pasiecznik,Sagar Chethan Kumar,Tanmay Agarwal,Rohith Kanathur,Sam Colman,Amaan Sheikh,Dev Bahl,Ann Li,Krish Veera,Alimurtaza Mustafa Merchant,Shambhawi Baswaraj Bhure,Sajal Kumar Goyla,Chengrui Li,Kirthana Natarajan,Rui Li,Thomas Ajai,Rujing Li,Vivek G. Iyer,Sanjaii Vijayakumar,Yitong Bai,Ayal Yakobe,Darief Maes,Yassine Jebbouri,Tianyang Xu,Thai Quoc On,Vera Mazeeva,Winston Li,Yuval Shemla,Yeshitha Bhuvanesh,Rushin Bhatt,Siddharth Chethan Gowda,Alisha Vinod,Caroline Cahill,Shriya Aishani Rachakonda,Yunfeng Chen,Aryaman Agrawal,Aman Upganlawar,Mao Le Jonathan Ang,Yubin Sally Go,Madhav Rajkondawar,Yang-Jung Chen,Trisha Maturi,Ananya Kapoor,Andrew Li,Shrey Arora,Mana Abbaszadeh,Shen Li,Charles Xu,Byeolah Kwon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper aggregates fourteen parallel implementation studies of an MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark, argues that aggregate-score leaderboards fail to predict deployment performance (with empirical evidence of rank instability), and proposes evaluating benchmarks by predictive validity rather than mean scores, operationalized through three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent benchmarks are narrow, each covering only four or five deployment-relevant dimensions. Aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify evaluation and produce rankings that do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings, making them unreliable for real-world deployment decisions.

Method: The authors conduct fourteen parallel implementation studies of an MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark spanning new asset classes, orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation probes. These are consolidated with seven prior benchmarks. They propose "predictive validity" — the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank — as the primary metric for benchmark quality, and develop a twelve-tier measurement apparatus. Three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds are formulated.

Result: Aggregate-score leaderboards exhibit rank instability in out-of-distribution settings, confirmed by retrospective analysis of public-to-hidden competition data. The twelve-tier apparatus exposes deployment-relevant dimensions that benchmarks like HELM and its successors collapse. Existing evidence partly supports the proposed criteria but is insufficient to confirm them.

Conclusion: The field should shift from optimizing for in-sample mean scores to optimizing for predictive validity. The authors provide a pre-registered pilot design and a vision for next-generation agentic benchmarks that report on deployment-relevant dimensions with transparent out-of-distribution robustness.

Abstract: Agent benchmarks are growing fast, but no single benchmark touches more than four or five of the dimensions that deployment exposes. This paper aggregates the largest coordinated deep-dive of one MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark to date: fourteen parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes (including a multi-modal visual extension), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes. Consolidating those studies with seven prior agent benchmarks, we argue that aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation. Rankings derived from aggregate scores do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings; recent public-to-hidden competition retrospectives provide direct empirical evidence of this rank instability. We propose ranking configurations by predictive validity, the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank, rather than in-sample mean, and report a twelve-tier measurement apparatus that exposes the deployment-relevant dimensions HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. The position is operationalized through three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds; existing evidence partly supports it but is too thin to confirm. We close with a pre-registered pilot design and a field-level vision for what the next generation of agentic benchmarks should report.

</details>


### [114] [GLARE: A Natural Language Interface for Querying Global Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19735)
*Bhavan Vasu,Rajesh Mangannavar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An LLM-based interactive interface that translates natural language questions into SQL queries over local explanation data, enabling flexible, statistics-augmented exploration of global explanations for black-box image classifiers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global explanations are crucial but complex and monolithic, hindering practical exploration. Users need targeted answers to specific questions rather than static explanation artifacts.

Method: An LLM mediates between users and structured local explanation data by translating natural language questions into SQL queries. The system outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses paired with intent-aligned visualizations and local explanations.

Result: The system was evaluated on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. Results demonstrate substantial improvements in accessibility and usability of global explanations.

Conclusion: LLM-mediated querying significantly enhances the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered explainable AI (XAI).
