Abstract: While global explanations are crucial for understanding vision models across datasets, classes, and decision contexts, their complex and monolithic nature often hinders practical exploration. Because users typically seek targeted answers to specific questions rather than static artifacts, we present an LLM-based interactive interface that provides natural language access to global explanations for black-box image classifiers. The system's core LLM acts as a mediator, translating natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data. This enables flexible aggregation without exposing users to low-level representations. For each query, the interface outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses, supporting local explanations, and intent-aligned visualizations. We evaluate the system on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. Our results demonstrate that LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.

</details>


### [115] [Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19741)
*Haocheng Duan,Yuxin Guo,Jieyi Bi,Anqi Xie,Sirui Li,Yining Ma,Cathy Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EPB is the first framework for interpreting neural combinatorial optimization models by distilling them into evolving, human-readable program portfolios using LLM-guided program evolution with hybrid textual-numerical gradients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) models are black-box, hindering deployment and scientific understanding. Existing interpretability tools like Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) fail for NCO because NCO decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack a predefined concept vocabulary.

Method: EPB iteratively evolves a bank of programs (each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck) using two blocks: Block I uses a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent — numerical gradients update a student router, textual gradients guide LLM-based program revision, all under fixed capacity; Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning.

Result: Extensive experiments show distilled program portfolios largely match the original black-box NCO performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as compositions of classic heuristic variants.

Conclusion: EPB advances interpretable NCO and establishes itself as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models, providing both faithful distillation and scientific insights into NCO policy behavior.

Abstract: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, yet its black-box nature remains a key roadblock to deployment and scientific diagnosis. Standard interpretability tools, such as Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), are ill-equipped for NCO, whose decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack proper concept vocabulary definition. To close this gap, we introduce Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), to our knowledge, the first framework for interpreting NCO policies by distilling black-box NCO models into human-readable program portfolios. EPB employs an LLM to autonomously evolve a bank of programs, where each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck. EPB works through an iterative framework: Block I fixes program bank capacity and introduces a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme that couples numerical gradients for student router updates and textual gradients for LLM-based program revision; Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate EPB's effectiveness and broad applicability, where the distilled program portfolios largely match original performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models.

</details>


### [116] [A Comparative Study of Pretrained Transformer Models for Quranic ASR: Speech Representations, Label Formats, and Dataset Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19747)
*Nabil Mosharraf Hossain,Riasat Islam,Unaizah Obaidellah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic study fine-tuning pretrained Transformer-based self-supervised speech models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on 870+ hours of Quranic recitations achieves state-of-the-art WER of 0.08–0.11, outperforming Citrinet by ~5 percentage points while cutting training time from 140 to 40 hours.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Quranic ASR models suffer from high Word Error Rates on user-recited verses and incomplete Quranic corpus coverage, limiting practical applications like memorisation aids and search engines.

Method: Fine-tuning pretrained self-supervised Transformer models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on a filtered dataset of 870+ hours of professional and user recitations. Ablation studies examine feature extractors, output label formats (with/without diacritics), training strategies, and clip durations. Compared against Citrinet baseline.

Result: Best configuration (Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53, Arabic without diacritics) achieves WER of 0.08 on EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on EveryAyah+Tarteel combined — a ~5 percentage point improvement over Citrinet (WER 0.163). Training time reduced from 140 to 40 hours.

Conclusion: Self-supervised Transformer models fine-tuned on domain-specific Quranic data significantly outperform prior approaches. Diacritic-free Arabic text yields optimal results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest representations. Future work will target improved dataset quality and Tajweed-sensitive phoneme-aware models.

Abstract: Quran Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) aims to convert Quranic recitation into text, enabling applications such as aided memorisation tools and Quranic search engines. However, existing ASR models often exhibit high Word Error Rates (WER) on user-recited verses and lack full coverage of the Quranic corpus. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of domain-specific fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer-based models for Quranic ASR, using advanced speech feature extraction methods: Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, and XLS-R. These models apply self-supervised learning by masking portions of input audio and using Transformer architectures to learn context-aware speech features. The pretrained models are fine-tuned on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours of professional and user recitations. Through comprehensive ablation studies across feature extractors, output label formats, training strategies, and clip durations, we identify the key factors that affect transcription accuracy in this domain. Our best-performing configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on the EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on the combined EveryAyah+Tarteel setting, representing roughly a five-percentage-point gain over the Citrinet baseline (WER = 0.163) while reducing combined-model training time from 140 hours to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall representation. Future work includes improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models to extract deeper speech feature representations for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

</details>


### [117] [Benchmarking Agentic Review Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19749)
*Dang Nguyen,Wanqing Hao,Yanai Elazar,Chenhao Tan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Evaluates AI-based peer review systems (OpenAIReview, coarse, Reviewer3) across six LLMs, finding they track paper quality well (83% pairwise accuracy), catch 71.6% of injected errors, and receive positive user feedback, though false positives and nitpicking remain issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted research is placing pressure on traditional peer review systems, and a new class of agentic AI review systems is emerging as a potential remedy. However, there is no established methodology for evaluating these systems, making it unclear how well they perform or how to improve them.

Method: Two-pronged evaluation: (1) Measuring whether AI reviews on ICLR/NeurIPS papers correlate with paper quality signals (citations, acceptance decisions) via pairwise accuracy; (2) Constructing a perturbation benchmark that injects four error categories into papers across eight arXiv subject classes, then measuring detection recall. Additionally, a real-world deployment study of OpenAIReview with public users was conducted to gather qualitative feedback and comment sentiment.

Result: All systems beat chance on pairwise accuracy; OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 achieved 83.0% accuracy. On injected error detection, the best configuration achieved 71.6% recall, with a six-model union reaching 83.3% recall, indicating complementary error detection across models. In the public deployment, user votes skewed positive (1.44:1), with common complaints being false positives and minor nitpicks.

Conclusion: AI review systems backed by state-of-the-art models can already track human quality judgments, catch important errors in papers, and earn positive user feedback. However, substantial room for improvement remains, particularly through better ensemble designs that leverage complementary detection strengths across different models.

Abstract: A new class of agentic review systems are emerging as a remedy to the pressure placed on peer review systems by AI-assisted research, but it is unclear how they should be evaluated. We evaluate two open-source systems (OpenAIReview and coarse), one proprietary system (Reviewer3), and a zero-shot baseline, across six LLMs spanning frontier and efficient models. First, we study whether AI reviews on ICLR/NeurIPS papers track with papers' quality as approximated by external signals such as citations and acceptance decisions. Every system performs above chance in pairwise accuracy, and the best is OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 at 83.0%. Second, to test whether systems can catch errors with known ground truth, we construct a perturbation benchmark that injects four categories of errors into papers across eight arXiv subject classes and measure detection recall. The strongest configuration (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) catches 71.6% of injected errors, leaving substantial room for improvement. The union of detections across six models reaches 83.3% recall, suggesting different models detect different errors and better harness design can potentially increase performance. Beyond these benchmarks, we study a public deployment of OpenAIReview with real users. Votes on its comments skew positive at 1.44 to 1, and the most common complaints are about false positives and minor nitpicks. Together, by evaluating full review systems backed by state-of-the-art models on real research papers, we show that while AI reviews still have room for improvement, they can already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive feedback from real users.

</details>


### [118] [Grounded Inference: Principles for Deterministically Encapsulated Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19753)
*Marty O'Neill*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a foundational framework of four primitives for integrating generative AI into traditional computational systems to achieve deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models, and identifies two common anti-patterns to avoid.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the high costs incurred by early adopters of generative AI integration, the field lacks foundational frameworks to systematically de-risk incorporating AI into traditional software systems.

Method: Defines four architectural primitives for AI-blended systems that enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models, and identifies two overarching anti-patterns commonly observed across industry.

Result: The framework provides a structured approach for integrating AI into traditional systems, with specific primitives and documented anti-patterns serving as both guidance and caution for practitioners.

Conclusion: The proposed framework establishes a foundation for successful AI integration and offers a basis for generative model providers to build next-generation interfaces.

Abstract: The incorporation of generative models into traditional computational systems presents both enormous opportunity and tremendous peril. Although many early adopters have realized these perils at great expense, the field still requires foundational frameworks to de-risk incorporation of AI into traditional systems. This manuscript establishes this foundation through the definition of four specific primitives of AI blended architecture, designed to enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models. It further establishes two overarching anti-patterns broadly represented across industry to serve as warnings for engineers in this field. This framework was designed to enable successful integration of AI into traditional systems while providing a foundation upon which generative model providers could build the next generation of generative model interfaces.

</details>


### [119] [Optimal Scheduling in a Question-Answering Forum of Knowledge Workers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19759)
*Rohit Negi,Mustafa Yilmaz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper models a future QA forum with paid knowledge workers and designs scheduling algorithms that achieve maximum system capacity while maintaining stability, also exploring how expert collaboration can further increase throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current QA forums rely on volunteers, but a future model may employ paid knowledge workers with varying expertise across topics. Efficient scheduling of incoming questions to these experts is critical for maximizing system throughput while preventing instability (e.g., unbounded queue growth).

Method: The authors model the QA forum as a queuing system where requests arrive for different topics, and experts have heterogeneous expertise levels (i.e., varying service rates per topic). They analyze system capacity — the maximum request arrival rate under which the system remains stable — and design scheduling policies that achieve this capacity. Collaboration between experts on single requests is also investigated as a means to boost capacity.

Result: The paper derives the capacity region of the system and proposes schedulers that achieve this capacity, ensuring the queuing system remains stable. It also demonstrates that collaboration among experts can potentially increase overall system capacity beyond what is achievable with independent work.

Conclusion: Properly designed scheduling algorithms are essential for maximizing throughput in knowledge-worker-based QA forums. Allowing collaboration between experts can further enhance system capacity, suggesting that future paid QA platforms should incorporate both intelligent scheduling and collaborative answering mechanisms.

Abstract: As individuals turn to the Internet to find answers to questions they may have, several Question Answering (QA) forums have evolved, where users knowledgeable in certain topics can contribute their expertise to answering these requests for information. While these are currently volunteer based, we consider a future version employing knowledge workers who are experts in certain topics. In such a system, the request-answer processes forming the queuing system may utilize schedulers that assign requests in different topics to the experts in the forum, who may be able to answer them according to their expertise levels in different topics. With this model, we calculate the capacity of the system for handling the requests while keeping the system stable, and design schedulers that achieve capacity. We also investigate how collaboration between experts in answering requests can potentially increase capacity.

</details>


### [120] [Beyond Entropy: Learning from Token-Level Distributional Deviations for LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19771)
*Xuanzhi Feng,Zhengyang Li,Zeyu Liu,Haoxi Li,Yuming Jiang,Bing Guo,Jingcai Guo,Jie Zhang,Song Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RLVR training of LLMs suffers from a stability trade-off: uniform updates cause entropy collapse (premature convergence), while entropy maximization causes entropy explosion (incoherent exploration). The ICT framework resolves this by selectively updating only tokens with distinctive distributional patterns (identified via JS divergence), theoretically proven to balance Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy. Updating the top 10% unique tokens yields up to 14.9% pass@4 improvement over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR faces a fundamental optimization dichotomy: uniform token updates lead to entropy collapse and premature convergence to suboptimal strategies, while aggressive Shannon entropy maximization triggers entropy explosion, resulting in blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning chains. Existing methods lack principled mechanisms to balance exploration-exploitation at the token level, motivating the need for a distribution-aware token selection strategy.

Method: The ICT framework shifts optimization from scalar uncertainty to distributional properties of token logits. It computes the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logit distributions to identify tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points. Theoretically grounded in both Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy, ICT proves that selective updating on these tokens reduces overall distribution uncertainty (Shannon) while controlling probability concentration (Rényi), stabilizing training. In practice, only the top 10% of unique tokens are updated.

Result: On Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, 7B), updating only the top 10% unique tokens achieves an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58% and a maximum gain of 14.9% over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines, evaluated across seven benchmarks covering math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level problems.

Conclusion: ICT effectively resolves the entropy collapse-explosion dichotomy in RLVR-based LLM reasoning by introducing token-level, distribution-aware selective updates. The strong empirical gains across diverse benchmarks and model scales demonstrate that principled token selection via JS divergence stabilizes RL training and improves reasoning performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has significantly advanced Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning; however, it faces a fundamental optimization instability: uniform token updates precipitate entropy collapse, leading to premature convergence to suboptimal strategies, whereas excessive Shannon Entropy maximization can cause entropy explosion, driving blind exploration toward incoherent reasoning chains. To resolve this dichotomy, we introduce the Independent Combinatorial Tokens (ICT) framework, which shifts the optimization focus from scalar uncertainty to the distributional properties of token logits. By leveraging the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between token logits distributions, ICT identifies tokens with distinctive distributional patterns as critical branching points for guiding effective exploration in LLM reasoning. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in both Shannon and second-order Rényi entropy, proves that selectively updating on these tokens regulates policy concentration: it reduces the overall distribution uncertainty measured by Shannon entropy, while controlling probability concentration captured by second-order Rényi entropy. This dual effect prevents over-concentrated token generation from weakening exploration and effectively stabilizes the training landscape. Empirical results demonstrate that updating only the top 10% of unique tokens on Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B) models yields an average pass@4 improvement of 4.58%, with a maximum gain of 14.9%, over GRPO, 20-Entropy, and STAPO baselines across seven benchmarks spanning math, commonsense, and Olympiad-level problems.

</details>


### [121] [AgentFinVQA: A Deployable Multi-Agent Pipeline for Auditable Financial Chart QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19782)
*Aravind Narayanan,Shaina Raza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentFinVQA is a multi-agent financial chart QA pipeline that achieves strong accuracy gains over baselines while providing full auditability via per-sample traceable Model Evaluation Packets, and supports on-premise deployment with open-weights models without severe accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial chart QA in regulated settings requires two features absent from existing agents: (1) auditability so practitioners know which answers to trust, and (2) on-premise deployability to maintain data residency. Existing chart-QA agents are accuracy-focused, opaque, and assume proprietary API access.

Method: A multi-agent pipeline decomposing each query into planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification stages. Every step is recorded in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP) per sample. The verifier also produces a confidence signal for human-in-the-loop review routing. Both proprietary (Gemini-3 Flash) and open-weights (Qwen3.6-27B-FP8) backbones are evaluated.

Result: On FinMME, AgentFinVQA improves +7.68 pp over matched zero-shot baseline with Gemini-3 Flash (71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar p≈1.1×10⁻¹⁶), and +4.84 pp with locally-served Qwen3.6-27B-FP8. The verifier's verdict provides a useful confidence signal: 68.2% vs. 55.6% exact accuracy on confirmed vs. revised answers. Error analysis reveals question misunderstanding, legend confusion, and extraction error account for ~2/3 of failures and are least detected by the verifier.

Conclusion: Auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical. The open-weights system retains most accuracy gains while enabling full data residency, presenting clear directions for future improvement in the error categories least detected by the verifier.

Abstract: Financial chart question answering in regulated settings demands more than accuracy: practitioners must know which answers to trust before acting on them, and many institutions cannot send client data to external model providers. Yet existing chart-QA agents are accuracy-focused and opaque, and most assume proprietary API access; to our knowledge, none combines auditability with on-premise deployability without significant accuracy compromise. We present AgentFinVQA, a multi-agent pipeline that decomposes each query into planning, OCR, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification, recording every step in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet (MEP) per sample. On FinMME, AgentFinVQA improves $+7.68$ pp over a primary-backbone matched zero-shot baseline with a proprietary backbone (Gemini-3 Flash; 71.24% vs. 63.56%, McNemar $p \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-16}$), and $+4.84$ pp with open-weights Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 served locally. The verifier's verdict also serves as a useful confidence signal (68.2% vs. 55.6% exact accuracy on confirmed vs. revised answers), enabling human-in-the-loop review routing. Error analysis shows that question misunderstanding, legend confusion and extraction error account for nearly two-thirds of failures and are the categories least detected by the verifier, identifying clear directions for future work. Together these results show that auditable, on-premise financial chart QA is practical and that the open-weights system keeps most of the accuracy gains while enabling full data residency. We release our code to support reproducible evaluation.

</details>


### [122] [ORAgentBench: Can LLM Agents Solve Challenging Operations Research Tasks End to End?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19787)
*Jiajun Li,Mingshu Cai,Yixuan Li,Yu Ding,Ran Hou,Guanyu Nie,Xiongwei Han,Wanyuan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ORAgentBench is an execution-grounded benchmark with 107 human-reviewed end-to-end OR tasks. The best of 14 frontier agent-model configurations passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks. Failures stem from strategic weaknesses — missed rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible solutions, and insufficient improvement — rather than coding errors, indicating agents are far from reliable OR practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current OR evaluations decouple modeling from solving, use pre-formalized or text-only instances, and fail to test the full workflow from operational artifacts to validated decisions. The authors aim to assess whether LLM agents can realistically perform end-to-end operations research work in executable environments.

Method: ORAgencyBench: 107 human-reviewed tasks across diverse operational scenarios, each with an isolated environment containing a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a required submission schema. Agents must write and execute solution code; hidden validators then score submissions on schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Fourteen frontier agent-model configurations are evaluated.

Result: The best agent achieves only 35.51% pass rate overall and 20.59% on hard tasks. Many feasible submissions still fall below the quality threshold. Failure analysis reveals errors are dominated by strategic weaknesses: missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills improve hard-task feasibility but not solution quality or pass rate reliably.

Conclusion: Progress in OR agents requires moving beyond generating plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making. Procedural skills alone are insufficient; agents must develop robust strategic reasoning for real-world OR tasks.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for multi-step tasks in executable environments, yet their ability to perform realistic operations research (OR) work remains unclear. Existing OR evaluations often decouple modeling from solving, rely on pre-formalized or text-only instances, and rarely test the full workflow from operational artifacts to validated decisions. In this work, we introduce ORAgentBench, an execution-grounded benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents on challenging end-to-end operations research tasks. It contains 107 human-reviewed tasks across diverse operational scenarios, each packaged in an isolated environment with a natural-language brief, multi-file data, configuration artifacts, and a required submission schema. Agents must write and run solution code, and their submissions are evaluated by hidden validators for schema validity, hard-constraint feasibility, and normalized objective quality. Experiments with fourteen frontier agent-model configurations show that current agents remain far from reliable OR practice. The best agent passes only 35.51% of all tasks and 20.59% of hard tasks, and many feasible submissions still fall below the required quality threshold. Failure analysis further shows that errors are dominated by strategic weaknesses, including missed operational rules, brittle formulations, weak feasible-solution construction, and insufficient solution improvement. OR-specific procedural skills increase hard-task feasibility, but do not reliably improve solution quality or pass rate. These results suggest that progress in OR agents requires moving beyond plausible optimization code toward dependable, high-quality operational decision-making.

</details>


### [123] [CombEval: A Framework for Evaluating Combinatorial Counting in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19788)
*Yuxu Zhou,Ondřej Kuželka,Yuyi Wang,Yuanhong Wang,Yi Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CombEval is a dynamic benchmark for evaluating LLMs on combinatorial counting problems, featuring solver-verified answers and systematic variation of problem parameters. Evaluation of 11 LLMs reveals persistent brittleness in ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relative-positional constraints, and nested dependencies, with errors in constraint interpretation and counting principles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for combinatorial reasoning in LLMs are static collections that do not permit controlled, systematic variation of problem dimensions (object type, entity scale, constraint count, reasoning depth). This limits diagnostic insight into precisely when and why models fail at combinatorial counting.

Method: CombEval formulates each counting problem as a typed Cofola specification comprising entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints. From these formal specifications, natural-language problem statements are automatically generated, and exact answers are verified via a solver. The framework supports independent variation of object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth to create a diagnostic, multidimensional benchmark.

Result: Evaluation of 11 LLMs under direct and code-augmented settings shows models struggle with ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relatively positional constraints, and nested object dependencies. Error analysis identifies two principal failure modes: misinterpretation of constraints and flawed application of fundamental counting principles.

Conclusion: CombEval serves as an effective diagnostic testbed for isolating the specific conditions under which LLMs fail at combinatorial reasoning, highlighting targeted areas for improvement in model training and prompting strategies.

Abstract: We present CombEval, a dynamic benchmark for evaluating combinatorial counting in large language models. CombEval represents each problem as a typed Cofola specification over entities, combinatorial objects, object dependencies, and constraints, enabling controlled generation of natural-language counting problems with exact solver-verified answers. Unlike static collections, CombEval supports systematic variation of object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth. We evaluate 11 LLMs under direct and code-augmented settings and find that models remain brittle on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relatively positional constraints, and nested object dependencies. Error analysis further identifies failures in constraint interpretation and counting principles. CombEval provides a diagnostic testbed for studying when and why LLMs fail at combinatorial reasoning. The code and generated benchmark suites are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/YuxuZhou-CN/combination-problem-generation}.

</details>


### [124] [Think Again or Think Longer? Selective Verification for Budget-Aware Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19808)
*Sajib Acharjee Dip,Dawei Zhou,Liqing Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SEVRA, a serving-layer controller that selectively invokes verification for reasoning models based on recoverability predictions, reducing token costs and harmful answer flips while maintaining accuracy—but tuning the initial solve budget often proves more cost-effective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test-time reasoning (verification, self-correction) is increasingly used as a serving-time control, but extra reasoning is not uniformly beneficial: it can fix failures, waste compute on already-correct answers, or introduce harmful flips. Current approaches treat this as a verifier-design problem, whereas the authors frame it as a deployment allocation problem—deciding when to invoke verification rather than how to verify better.

Method: The authors propose SEVRA (Selective Verification for Reasoning Allocation), a controller that uses a frozen Qwen3-4B solver and logs intervention outcomes to train recoverability-aware gating models. These gates operate on serving-visible attempt state (e.g., confidence signals, completion features) to decide per-instance whether to preserve the initial answer or invoke active verification. The method is evaluated on MATH500, GSM8K, and CommonsenseQA, comparing against always-verify baselines, longer initial solve budgets, and Self-Consistency@5.

Result: On MATH500, SEVRA achieves 76.3% accuracy (vs. 75.5% always-verify), reduces post-generation tokens by 26.8%, and cuts harmful flips from 2.2% to 1.0%. However, an 8,192-token initial solve reaches 76.0% with 28% fewer total tokens. On GSM8K, the selective policy verifies only 3.0% of examples, improves accuracy from 93.4% to 94.5%, and reduces verification tokens by 91.2% vs. always-verify; again, longer initial solves match this at lower cost. On CommonsenseQA, always-on verification hurts accuracy, while Self-Consistency@5 improves accuracy at ~5× token cost. The deployment rule: tune the initial budget first, then use selective recovery when explicit checks, bounded retries, auditability, or regression-risk control matter.

Conclusion: Selective verification is useful as a safety net, audit mechanism, or regression guard, but it is not a cost-efficient substitute for allocating more compute to the initial solve. The recommended deployment strategy is to first optimize the initial reasoning budget, then apply selective recovery for scenarios requiring explicit verification, bounded retries, or risk control.

Abstract: Test-time reasoning is increasingly used as a serving-time control knob, but extra reasoning is not uniformly valuable: it can repair failed attempts, waste compute on already-correct answers, or introduce harmful answer changes. We study this as a deployment allocation problem rather than a new-verifier problem. We introduce \sevra, Selective Verification for Reasoning Allocation, a serving-layer controller that decides whether to preserve a frozen solver's initial answer or invoke active verification. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B solver, we log intervention outcomes and train recoverability-aware gates from serving-visible attempt state. On \mathfive, selective verification reaches 76.3\% accuracy, compared with 75.5\% for always verifying, while reducing post-generation tokens by 26.8\% and harmful flips from 2.2\% to 1.0\%. However, an 8,192-token initial solve reaches 76.0\% accuracy with 28\% fewer total model tokens, showing that selective recovery is useful but not the best tested cost frontier. In frozen transfer to \gsm, the selective policy verifies only 3.0\% of examples, improves accuracy from 93.4\% to 94.5\%, and reduces verification tokens by 91.2\% relative to always verifying; again, a longer initial solve matches its accuracy with fewer realized tokens. On CommonsenseQA, always-on verification hurts, while Self-Consistency@5 improves accuracy at about five times the realized token cost. The resulting deployment rule is: tune the initial budget first, then use selective recovery when explicit checks, bounded retries, auditability, or regression-risk control matter.

</details>


### [125] [Human-on-the-Loop Orchestration for AI-Assisted Legal Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19812)
*Anushree Sinha,Srivaths Ranganathan,Abhishek Dharmaratnakar,Debanshu Das*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents in e-discovery risk "trajectory collapse" where early errors compound across multi-step reasoning. The paper proposes a failure taxonomy, a four-layer verification architecture, and shows via simulation that Human-on-the-Loop escalation with calibrated uncertainty thresholds reduces privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% while routing under 25% of documents to human review.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous LLM agents deployed in electronic discovery (e-discovery) face a critical failure mode termed "trajectory collapse," where an early misclassification in multi-step reasoning chains silently propagates and invalidates the entire privilege review. This presents legal malpractice risk that is not adequately addressed by single-turn retrieval approaches, motivating the need for structured failure analysis and mitigation architectures.

Method: The authors (1) develop a structured taxonomy of agentic failures in legal information retrieval organized by functional stage; (2) design a four-layer verification architecture covering planning, reasoning, execution, and uncertainty quantification to intercept compounding failures; and (3) conduct a preliminary simulation study on a synthetic e-discovery corpus comparing mandatory Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) escalation thresholds against fully autonomous baselines.

Result: Calibrated uncertainty thresholds reduced privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% compared to fully autonomous deployment, while routing fewer than 25% of documents to attorney review.

Conclusion: A layered verification architecture with HOTL escalation, driven by calibrated uncertainty quantification, significantly mitigates trajectory collapse and privilege-waiver risk in agentic e-discovery workflows without overwhelming human reviewers.

Abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in electronic discovery (e-discovery), where compounding errors across multi-step reasoning chains can constitute legal malpractice. Unlike single-turn retrieval, agentic workflows operating over privileged document corpora exhibit a class of failure we term "trajectory collapse": an early misclassification silently propagates, rendering an entire privilege review invalid. This paper makes three contributions. First, we propose a structured taxonomy of agentic failures in legal information retrieval, organized by functional stage. Second, we introduce a four-layer verification architecture -- spanning planning, reasoning, execution, and uncertainty quantification -- designed to intercept these failures before they compound. Third, we present a preliminary simulation study on a synthetic e-discovery corpus that demonstrates how mandatory Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) escalation thresholds reduce privilege-waiver risk relative to fully autonomous baselines. Our results suggest that calibrated uncertainty thresholds can reduce privilege-waiver risk by up to 61% versus fully autonomous deployment, while routing fewer than one quarter of documents to attorney review.

</details>


### [126] [TelcoAgent: A Scalable 5G Multi-KPM Forecasting With 3GPP-Grounded Explainability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19821)
*Geon Kim,Dara Ron,Sukhdeep Singh,Suyog Moogi,Pranshav Gajjar,V V N K Someswara Rao Koduri,Een Kee Hong,Vijay K. Shah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TelcoAgent is a foundation model-based framework for 5G KPM forecasting that uses a three-agent pipeline to construct a 3GPP knowledge graph, a time-series foundation model for zero-shot prediction, and a reasoning pipeline for explainable diagnostics — achieving high accuracy across 200 cells without site-specific training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ML approaches for KPM forecasting in 5G networks suffer from poor scalability (requiring site-specific training) and lack explainability, limiting real-world deployment. A solution is needed that can forecast multiple KPMs across diverse cells without per-cell retraining while providing actionable, domain-grounded explanations.

Method: TelcoAgent consists of three components: (1) an automated three-agent pipeline that constructs a 3GPP knowledge graph directly from specification documents; (2) a scalable time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline for accurate zero-shot forecasting; and (3) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that produces actionable, domain-grounded diagnostics. Evaluation uses a 3-month real-world city-scale 5G KPM dataset from a U.S. network operator covering 200 cells and 7 KPMs.

Result: TelcoAgent demonstrates high forecasting accuracy across all 7 considered KPMs per cell over 200 cells, delivering both explainable insights and actionable instructions to address network degradations.

Conclusion: Foundation model-based frameworks like TelcoAgent can overcome the scalability and explainability limitations of traditional ML in telecom KPM forecasting, enabling accurate zero-shot prediction with interpretable diagnostics suitable for real-world network operations.

Abstract: Key Performance Measurement (KPM) forecasting is essential for proactive network management of 5G and next-generation telecom networks. However, existing machine learning (ML) approaches face significant limitations in scalability and explainability, restricting their effectiveness in real-world deployments. We propose TelcoAgent, a foundation model-based framework that enables accurate, scalable, and explainable forecasting of multiple KPMs across diverse network cells without the need for site-specific training. Specifically, the framework comprises three key components: (i) an automated three-agent pipeline that constructs a 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) knowledge graph directly from specification documents, (ii) a scalable, time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline to deliver accurate, zero-shot forecasting, and finally (iii) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that provides actionable, domain-grounded diagnostics. Evaluated using a 3-month, real-world, city-scale 5G KPM dataset from a U.S.-based network operator, TelcoAgent demonstrates high forecasting accuracy for all 7 considered KPMs per cell across 200 cells, while delivering explainable insights and actionable instructions to address network degradations.

</details>


### [127] [A Systematic Evaluation of Black-Box Uncertainty Estimation Methods for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19868)
*Jiayi Wang,Xu-Yao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A systematic review and benchmark of black-box uncertainty estimation methods for LLMs, categorizing 24 methods into five families and evaluating them across 4 models and 4 datasets, finding that answer-space reasoning and hybrid methods are generally most effective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucinations and unreliable outputs, making uncertainty estimation critical for trustworthiness. Since many LLMs are only accessible via restricted APIs without access to logits or hidden states, black-box UE is practically essential. However, existing black-box UE research is methodologically fragmented with no unified empirical comparison.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic review organizing black-box UE methods into five categories: (1) verbalization-based, (2) sampling-based, (3) explanation-based, (4) multi-agent, and (5) hybrid methods. They build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings.

Result: No single method consistently dominates across all settings. Methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective. Hybrid methods combining multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions.

Conclusion: The paper provides a structured taxonomy, a reproducible benchmark, and practical guidance for developing future black-box UE methods for LLMs, highlighting the promise of answer-space reasoning and hybrid approaches.

Abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, their outputs often remain unreliable and may contain hallucinations, making uncertainty estimation (UE) essential for building trustworthy LLMs. In practice, many mainstream LLMs are only accessible through restricted APIs, where internal signals such as logits and hidden states are unavailable, making black-box UE especially important. However, existing work on black-box UE for LLMs remains fragmented in methodology and lacks a unified empirical comparison. To address this gap, we present a systematic review of black-box UE methods and organize them into five categories: verbalization-based, sampling-based, explanation-based, multi-agent, and hybrid methods. We further build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings. Our results show that no single method consistently dominates across all settings. Nevertheless, methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective, and hybrid methods that combine multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions. By releasing the benchmark data and a unified evaluation framework, we aim to facilitate reproducible comparisons and support future research, while our empirical findings provide practical guidance for developing future black-box UE methods for LLMs.

</details>


### [128] [MetaResearcher: Scaling Deep Research via Self-Reflective Reinforcement Learning in Adversarial Virtual Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19893)
*Wei Yu,Suxing Liu,Minjie Yu,Jiahao Wang,Zhijian Zheng,Haocheng Deng,Bing Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MetaResearcher scales deep research agent training across four dimensions: an evolving virtual world with temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation, discovery-oriented tasks (hypothesis generation, contradiction resolution), a self-reflective meta-reward mechanism within GRPO that jointly optimizes multiple objectives, and a heterogeneous multi-agent swarm (Scout, Filter, Synthesizer) with coordinated RL — all at zero marginal API training cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep research agent training is limited by three key factors: (1) static simulated environments that fail to capture real-world information dynamics, (2) task designs restricted to fact retrieval rather than genuine research behaviors, and (3) inefficient outcome-based reinforcement learning that leads to repetitive action loops. These constraints prevent agents from developing critical skills like source credibility assessment, temporal reasoning, and collaborative research strategies.

Method: The authors propose MetaResearcher with four synergistic components: (1) An Evolving Virtual World that introduces temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation to force source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution. (2) Discovery-Oriented Tasks including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution, moving beyond fact retrieval. (3) A Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism within the GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) framework that jointly optimizes answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity. (4) A Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm with specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models trained via coordinated reinforcement learning. The framework is built on LiteResearcher infrastructure, requiring zero marginal API cost for training.

Result: This paper presents the framework design and training methodology; experimental validation is planned but not yet reported. The authors target improvements on GAIA and Xbench-DS benchmarks as well as enhanced epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions.

Conclusion: MetaResearcher offers a scalable, cost-efficient approach to training deep research agents that goes beyond fact retrieval toward genuine research capabilities. By integrating environmental dynamics, sophisticated task design, nuanced reward shaping, and multi-agent collaboration, the framework aims to produce agents with greater robustness, reasoning depth, and resistance to misinformation — pending empirical validation.

Abstract: Deep research agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous information gathering and synthesis, yet their training remains constrained by the static nature of simulated environments, the limits of fact-retrieval-only task designs, and the inefficiency of outcome-based reinforcement learning. In this work, we propose MetaResearcher, a novel framework that scales deep research agent training across four synergistic dimensions. First, we introduce an Evolving Virtual World that injects temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation into the training environment, forcing agents to develop source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution skills. Second, we design Discovery-Oriented Tasks -- including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution -- that transcend simple fact retrieval and push agents toward genuine research behaviors. Third, we propose a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism within the GRPO framework that jointly optimizes for answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity, directly addressing the repetitive action loop problem observed in prior work. Fourth, we introduce a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture comprising specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models that learn collaborative research strategies through coordinated reinforcement learning. Built upon the LiteResearcher infrastructure, MetaResearcher requires zero marginal API cost for training while targeting substantial improvements in both benchmark performance (GAIA, Xbench-DS) and epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions. We present the complete framework design, training methodology, and planned experimental validation.

</details>


### [129] [eCNNTO: A Highly Generalizable ConvNet for Accelerating Topology Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19921)
*Shengbiao Lu,Xiaodong Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: eCNNTO is an element-based CNN with residual connections that accelerates density-based topology optimization by predicting near-optimal element densities from final-stage history data, achieving up to 90% (2D) and 97% (3D) iteration reduction while generalizing across diverse boundary conditions, loading cases, geometries, and mesh resolutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Topology optimization requires numerous iterations with FE analysis each time, creating a severe efficiency bottleneck for high-resolution designs. Prior work (Kallioras et al., DBN-based) accelerated TO by skipping iterations but suffered from lack of spatial correlation among neighboring elements, resulting in disconnected structural features.

Method: eCNNTO uses a CNN with residual connections to predict per-element near-optimal densities, capturing spatial correlations missing in prior DBN approaches. A novel training strategy uses final-stage density histories (rather than early-stage) as the training dataset, which reduces data requirements and improves optimization efficiency. The method trains on a small dataset yet generalizes broadly.

Result: eCNNTO achieves up to 90% reduction in iterations for 2D problems and up to 97% reduction for 3D problems. It generalizes successfully to problems with significantly different boundary conditions, loading cases, design domain geometries, mesh resolutions, and non-design domains, all from limited training data.

Conclusion: eCNNTO provides an efficient, generalizable deep-learning-based acceleration for density-based topology optimization, overcoming the spatial disconnection limitations of prior element-wise DBN methods through CNN residual architectures and improved training strategies.

Abstract: This work proposes an element-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to accelerate density-based Topology Optimization (TO), termed eCNNTO. TO generally undergoes a large number of iterations, where finite element analysis is performed in every iteration, leading to the efficiency bottleneck especially when dense meshes are used to achieve high-resolution designs. To address this limitation, eCNNTO is proposed to build upon Kallioras et al. (2020), where a Deep Belief Network (DBN) was trained for every element to predict its near-optimal density from its early history, thereby skipping the great majority of iterations and significantly accelerating the TO procedure. However, the method lacks spatial correlations among neighboring elements and may lead to disconnected features in the final structure. The proposed method employs CNN with residual connections to address this issue. On top of it, a novel training strategy is introduced to further enhance the optimization efficiency, where the training dataset consists of the final stage density histories rather than early ones. This change can also help reduce the required training data size. eCNNTO requires only a small dataset to train and yet it can be generalized to problems with largely different boundary conditions, loading cases, design domain geometries, mesh resolutions, as well as non-design domains. In the end, the generalization capabilities and efficiency of eCNNTO are demonstrated through a variety of examples in two and three dimensions, achieving up to 90% and 97% reduction of iterations, respectively.

</details>


### [130] [QMFOL: Benchmarking Large Language Model Reasoning via Quantifiable Monadic First-Order Logic Test Case Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20227)
*Xinyi Zheng,Ling Shi,Tianlong Yu,Yongxin Zhao,Lorenz Goette,Kailong Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QMFOL is an automated framework that generates monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with quantifiable, controllable complexity, translating formal logical structures into natural language with round-trip verification. The accompanying benchmark QMFOLBench (2880 instances, 960 configurations) reveals that model performance degrades and compute cost increases with logical complexity, with sensitivity to label types and semantic variation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deductive reasoning benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and fail to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency, hindering precise evaluation of LLM reasoning capabilities as models improve.

Method: QMFOL generates formal monadic first-order logic structures using conjunction/disjunction patterns to control reasoning depth, width, label types (True/False/Unknown), and distractors. These structures are translated into natural language via LLMs, with logical consistency verified through round-trip translation using an external automated theorem prover.

Result: Evaluation on six large reasoning models and two LLMs using QMFOLBench (2880 instances) shows: (1) performance degrades and computational overhead increases with logical complexity; (2) models perform better on True-labeled tasks than False or Unknown; (3) models are sensitive to semantic variation.

Conclusion: QMFOL provides a scalable, reliable method for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant progress in reasoning, particularly in deductive reasoning, which is crucial for high-stakes decision-making. As models improve, evaluation benchmarks should evolve to keep pace. However, existing benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and struggle to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency.
  To address these issues, we propose QMFOL, an automated framework for generating monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with quantifiable and controllable complexity. It constructs formal logical structures using conjunction and disjunction patterns, enabling precise control over reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors. These structures are then translated into natural language via LLMs, with logical consistency ensured through round-trip verification using an external prover. Based on our framework, we build QMFOLBench, a benchmark comprising 2880 instances with 960 configurations across diverse logical and semantic dimensions. Evaluations on six large reasoning models (LRMs) and two LLMs show that performance degrades and computational overhead increases with rising logical complexity. Models perform better on True-labeled tasks than on False or Unknown ones, and exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation. Overall, QMFOL offers a scalable and reliable approach for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

</details>


### [131] [The Tao of Agency: Autotelic AI, Embedded Agency and Dissolution of the Self](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19924)
*Aritra Sarkar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper explores autotelic AI—agents that generate their own goals—arguing that the core challenge is not goal generation but self-individuation: how an agent defines and relativizes the boundary between self and environment. It synthesizes intrinsic motivation, homeostasis, causal learning, and embeddedness into a unified framework, then extends it via quantum formulation, non-dual philosophy, and an LLM-based implementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional AI assumes goals are externally specified by designers. The authors aim to investigate what happens when agents autonomously generate their own goals (autotelic AI), identifying that the foundational open problem is not how goals arise, but how the "self" to which goals belong is constituted and made relative.

Method: The paper traces consequences of autotelic agency through five interconnected concepts: intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness. It argues embeddedness is necessary but insufficient—since the agent-environment partition is non-unique—and consolidates these into a unified framework, then extends it along three axes: (1) a quantum formulation making the agent-environment cut physical, (2) a philosophical interpretation drawing on non-dual contemplative traditions, and (3) a concrete LLM-based agentic instantiation.

Result: Embeddedness individuates the agent but reveals non-uniqueness: the same underlying dynamics admit multiple valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self. This makes the central problem one of self-generation and self-relativization rather than goal generation. The agent must simultaneously believe in its boundary (to act) and see through it (to understand).

Conclusion: The deepest problem of autotelic AI is how the agent generates and relativizes the self to which goals are assigned—requiring a dual capacity to both reify and transcend its own boundary. The framework opens novel directions spanning quantum mechanics, non-dual philosophy, and practical LLM agent architectures.

Abstract: Most artificial intelligence systems are built on the assumption that goals are exogenous and specified by the designer. Exploring what happens when an agent begins generating its own goals opens the field of autotelic AI. Agents are expected not merely to pursue objectives but to discover them. In this article, we trace its consequences through intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness; the last of which is found to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Embeddedness individuates the agent at the cost of revealing that the individuation is non-unique, such that the same dynamics admit many valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self.
  The deepest problem with autotelic AI is therefore not how the agent generates goals, but how it generates and relativizes the self to which the goals are assigned. The agent must believe in its own boundary in order to act, and see through that boundary in order to understand. We consolidate these developments into a single framework and extend it along three directions: a quantum formulation in which the agent-environment cut becomes physical, a philosophical reading against non-dual contemplative traditions, and a concrete LLM-based agentic instantiation.

</details>


### [132] [PhysDrift: Bridging the Embodiment Gap in Humanoid Co-Speech Motion Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19935)
*Zhangzhao Liang,Xiaofen Xing,Mingyue Yang,Wenlve Zhou,Xiangmin Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Existing co-speech motion generation pipelines create motions in human-body representations (SMPL-X) then retarget to humanoids, causing an "embodiment gap" that degrades motion diversity and prosody alignment. The authors propose IK-EER for prosody-preserving retargeting to build a robot-native dataset, and PhysDrift, a framework that directly generates executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech, bypassing human representations entirely. This improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, and real-time interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core motivation is the "embodiment gap": human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints are fundamentally mismatched. Standard human-centric pipelines (generate SMPL-X → retarget) disrupt embodiment consistency, compressing motion diversity and weakening prosody-motion synchronization. The authors argue that co-speech motions for humanoids should be generated natively in the robot's joint space to maintain embodiment consistency throughout training and inference.

Method: Two-stage approach: (1) IK-EER — a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during the retargeting process, creating a robot-native motion dataset. (2) PhysDrift — an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework trained on this dataset that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech input without any intermediate human-body representation (e.g., SMPL-X). PhysDrift incorporates physical regularization to stabilize robot motion dynamics and maintains embodiment consistency end-to-end.

Result: Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that the embodiment-aware robot-native generation approach (PhysDrift) substantially outperforms conventional human-centric pipelines across multiple axes: speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability. The IK-EER retargeting framework also shows improved prosody preservation compared to standard retargeting.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that bypassing intermediate human-body representations and directly generating co-speech motions in the robot's native joint space is critical for achieving expressive, physically executable humanoid behaviors. The proposed IK-EER + PhysDrift pipeline effectively bridges the embodiment gap, enabling humanoid robots to perform speech-aligned gestures that are both semantically expressive and physically plausible for real-time interaction.

Abstract: Humanoid robots require co-speech motions that are not only expressive and speech-aligned, but also physically executable under embodiment constraints. Existing co-speech generation pipelines are predominantly human-centric: motions are first generated in human-body representations such as SMPL-X and subsequently retargeted to humanoid robots. In this work, we identify a fundamental embodiment gap in this paradigm, where the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints disrupts embodiment consistency during motion transfer and physical execution. Through extensive analysis, we show that although retargeting can preserve coarse motion semantics, it significantly compresses motion diversity and weakens prosody-motion synchronization, limiting expressive humanoid behaviors. To address this problem, we first propose IK-EER, a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting. Building upon the curated robot-native motion dataset, we further introduce PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech without relying on intermediate human-body representations. Unlike conventional human-centric pipelines, PhysDrift maintains embodiment consistency throughout both training and inference while incorporating physical regularization to stabilize robot motion dynamics. Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that embodiment-aware robot-native generation substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability.

</details>


### [133] [Advancing DialNav through Automatic Embodied Dialog Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19948)
*Leekyeung Han,Sangwon Jung,Hyunji Min,Jinseong Jeong,Minyoung Kim,Paul Hongsuck Seo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAINbow is a large-scale (238K episodes) automatic dialog-navigation dataset built by converting existing VLN data into multi-turn dialogs, combined with Dual-Strategy Training and a VLN-informed localization model, achieving +89% and +100% success rate improvements over the DialNav baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DialNav's performance is bottlenecked by a critical scarcity of training data (only 2K episodes). There is a need for large-scale, cost-efficient training data and complementary methods to unlock its full potential for embodied dialog-based navigation.

Method: (1) An automatic generation pipeline that converts existing Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) datasets into multi-turn dialog episodes, yielding 238K training samples. (2) Dual-Strategy Training to align navigation training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop. (3) A localization model that leverages VLN knowledge to improve spatial understanding.

Result: The proposed model substantially outperforms the DialNav baseline: Val Seen success rate of 58.24 (+89%) and Val Unseen success rate of 29.05 (+100%), establishing a new state of the art on the DialNav benchmark.

Conclusion: Combining large-scale automatic dialog data generation with dual-strategy training and VLN-enhanced localization effectively addresses data scarcity in embodied dialog-navigation, yielding dramatic performance gains and a new SOTA.

Abstract: For embodied agents capable of physical interaction, the capability to create and understand dialog is crucial to ensure both safety and effectiveness. While DialNav~\cite{han2025dialnav} provides a framework for holistic evaluation of the dialog--execution loop in photorealistic indoor navigation, its performance remains limited by a critical scarcity of training data (2K episodes). To address this, we propose an automatic generation pipeline, and construct the \textbf{RAINbow} dataset, a large-scale training dataset with 238K episodes for DialNav. Our pipeline converts existing VLN datasets into multi-turn dialog and creates cost-efficient and high-quality dataset. Then, we introduce two additional complementary advances to unlock the data's full potential: (1) Dual-Strategy Training, a navigation training scheme to align the navigation training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop, and (2) a localization model that leverages VLN knowledge. By combining these complementary solutions, our model substantially outperforms the baseline in success rate on both \textbf{Val Seen} (58.24, \textbf{+89\%}) and \textbf{Val Unseen} (29.05, \textbf{+100\%}) splits, establishing a new state of the art.

</details>


### [134] [ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19980)
*Wenli Xiao,Jia Xie,Tonghe Zhang,Haotian Lin,Letian "Max" Fu,Haoru Xue,Jalen Lu,Yi Yang,Cunxi Dai,Zi Wang,Jimmy Wu,Guanzhi Wang,S. Shankar Sastry,Ken Goldberg,Linxi "Jim" Fan,Yuke Zhu,Guanya Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ENPIRE is a closed-loop harness framework that enables coding agents to autonomously improve real-world robotic manipulation policies by formalizing a physical feedback loop: reset, execute, verify, and refine — achieving 99% success on dexterous tasks like pin box organization, zip tie fastening, and tool use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world dexterous robotic manipulation research is bottlenecked by heavy reliance on human supervision and manual algorithm engineering. While coding agents can automate algorithm search in digital domains, they lack the physical-world feedback loop necessary for robotics research automation.

Method: ENPIRE consists of four core modules: (1) Environment (EN) for automatic scene reset and outcome verification; (2) Policy Improvement (PI) for launching policy refinement; (3) Rollout (R) for parallel policy evaluation across one or multiple physical robots; and (4) Evolution (E) where coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, and improve both training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes.

Result: Frontier coding agents powered by ENPIRE autonomously trained policies achieving 99% success on dexterous manipulation tasks (organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, tool use). Performance further accelerated when deploying agent teams across a robot fleet.

Conclusion: ENPIRE offers a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advance robotics in the physical world, minimizing human effort while enabling fair ablation studies.

Abstract: Achieving dexterous robotic manipulation in the real world heavily relies on human supervision and algorithm engineering, which becomes a central bottleneck in the pursuit of general physical intelligence. Although emerging coding agents can generate code to automate algorithm search, their successes remain largely confined in digital environments. We conjecture that the missing abstraction to automate robotics research is a repeatable feedback loop for real-world policy improvement: reset the scene, execute a policy, verify the outcome, and refine the next iteration. To bridge this gap, we introduce ENPIRE, a harness framework for coding agents that instantiates this physical feedback routine with four core modules: an Environment module (EN) for automatic reset and verification, a Policy Improvement module (PI) that launches policy refinement, a Rollout module (R) to evaluate policies with one or multiple physical robots operating in parallel, and an Evolution module (E) in which coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This closed-loop system transforms real-world manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure, minimizing human effort while allowing fair ablations across training recipe and agent variants. Powered by ENPIRE, frontier coding agents can autonomously train a policy to achieve a 99% success rate on challenging, dexterous manipulation tasks, such as organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use, a process that further accelerates when we dispatch an agent team on a robot fleet. Our results suggest a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advancing robotics in the physical world.

</details>


### [135] [Reward as An Agent for Embodied World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19990)
*Pu Li,Zhigang Lin,Qiang Wu,Yongxuan Lv,Fei Wang,Shan You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper challenges the conservative exploration paradigm in RL-based world model refinement by introducing (1) Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework for robust verification, and (2) DynDiff-GRPO, a diversification method for broader embodied exploration. Together, they mitigate reward hacking and achieve significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for refining world models rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, which limits exploration, behavioral diversity, and discovery of richer dynamics. The authors argue the core bottleneck is not exploration per se, but the absence of reliable verification strategies that can support broader exploration without succumbing to reward hacking — where policies exploit imperfect reward signals without genuine improvement.

Method: The paper proposes two complementary components: (1) Reward as an Agent — an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to produce robust reward signals resilient to distribution shift, and (2) Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification via DynDiff-GRPO — which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories and broaden state-action coverage. These are unified in embodied world model settings where physical plausibility and task completion serve as rigorous evaluation criteria.

Result: The unified approach yields significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, demonstrating that broader exploration scales successfully when grounded in robust verification, effectively mitigating reward hacking.

Conclusion: Broader exploration in RL-based world model refinement is viable and beneficial when paired with reliable verification. The combination of agentic reward verification and rollout diversification overcomes the reward hacking problem that previously necessitated conservative exploration regimes.

Abstract: While RL has become a promising tool for refining world models, existing methods largely rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, limiting exploration, behavioral diversity, and richer dynamic discovery. In this work, we challenge this conservative paradigm. We argue that the core limitation is not exploration itself, but the lack of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration. Without reliable verification, expanded exploration becomes highly susceptible to reward hacking, where policies exploit imperfect rewards without achieving genuine improvement. To evaluate this motivation, we instantiate our method in embodied world models, where physical plausibility, and task completion provide a rigorous testbed for scalable RL under complex dynamics. On the verification side, we introduce Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts. On the exploration side, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification through DynDiff-GRPO, which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors beyond conservative rollout regimes. By unifying Reward as an Agent with DynDiff-GRPO, we enable RL on a more reliable reward foundation with substantially diversified sampling, effectively mitigating reward hacking while yielding significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, thereby demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.

</details>


### [136] [Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20058)
*Harsh Rao Dhanyamraju,Leonidas Raghav,Aaron Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A study evaluating multi-agent orchestration architectures (DAG Plan & Execute vs. ReAct) across 208 enterprise scenarios at three scales finds that scale—not task complexity—dominates performance degradation, with agent discovery noise as the primary bottleneck. A Task Manager with priority inference, event merging, and preemption improves latency and correctness at enterprise scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI requires continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across many specialist agents, but existing multi-agent systems are designed for discrete request-response workflows and have not been rigorously evaluated at enterprise scale (hundreds of agents). The gap between current architectures and real enterprise demands motivates this work.

Method: The authors evaluate two multi-agent orchestration architectures—DAG-based Plan and Execute and ReAct—across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20–80 agents), and Enterprise (~200 agents). They also introduce a Task Manager component that adds continuous operation capabilities: priority inference, related-event merging, and task preemption. Performance is measured along dimensions of orchestration quality, latency, and correctness.

Result: Both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade significantly at enterprise scale, with agent discovery noise emerging as the primary bottleneck. Simple tasks degrade more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan & Execute offers higher precision and better structured parallelization at smaller scales but suffers from overhead at enterprise scale; ReAct proves more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

Conclusion: Scale is the dominant factor in multi-agent orchestration performance, outweighing task complexity. The choice of architecture should consider scale-dependent trade-offs: DAG suits smaller, structured deployments while ReAct scales more gracefully. Continuous operation mechanisms like the proposed Task Manager are critical for viable enterprise-scale multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

</details>


### [137] [Process-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Theorem Proving via Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20068)
*Minsu Kim,Se-Young Yun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes using the Lean proof assistant as a process-level reward oracle during RL training for formal theorem proving. By extracting both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level feedback from Lean's elaboration process, and incorporating these structured rewards into a GRPO-style RL objective, the method outperforms outcome-only baselines on MiniF2F and ProofNet benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
