Motivation: Existing RLVR methods rely on a single binary verification signal, ignoring the rich structured feedback available from symbolic proof assistants. Proof assistants like Lean can identify not just whether a proof succeeds, but exactly which tactic steps are locally sound and where the first error occurs. Bridging this gap between structured proof processes and unstructured binary rewards enables denser, more informative training signals grounded in type theory.

Method: The authors treat Lean's elaboration mechanism as a symbolic process oracle. Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences; Lean's elaboration marks each locally sound step and identifies the earliest failing step. These structured rewards are integrated into a GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) objective using two credit assignment techniques: first-error propagation (reward propagates only up to the first error) and first-token credit (reward assigned to the first token of each tactic). This balances outcome-level and process-level advantages. Experiments are conducted on STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5.

Result: Tactic-level (process-level) supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most experimental settings. Improvements are demonstrated on the MiniF2F and ProofNet benchmarks, showing that dense, verifier-grounded credit signals from Lean's elaboration lead to better proof search performance.

Conclusion: Symbolic proof assistants should be viewed not merely as verifiers at evaluation time but as process-level reward oracles during training. This perspective opens a path toward RL frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning tasks.

Abstract: While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically has relied on a single binary verification signal, symbolic proof assistants in formal reasoning offer rich, fine-grained structured feedback. This gap between structured processes and unstructured rewards highlights the importance of feedback that is both dense and sound. In this work, we demonstrate that the Lean proof assistant itself can serve as a symbolic process oracle, supplying both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level verified feedback during training. Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration marks both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, yielding dense, verifier-grounded credit signals rooted in type theory. We incorporate these structured rewards into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods that balances outcome- and process-level advantages. Experiments with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 show that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on benchmarks such as MiniF2F and ProofNet. Beyond empirical gains, our study highlights a broader perspective: symbolic proof assistants are not only verifiers at evaluation time, but can also act as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward reinforcement learning frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

</details>


### [138] [Residual-Space Evolutionary Optimization via Flow-based Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20084)
*Zhuo Cao,Lena Krieger,Fernanda Nader,Xuan Zhao,Hanno Scharr,Ira Assent*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A model-agnostic framework that combines flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms by operating in residual space, using self-pollination (local exploitation) and cross-pollination (global exploration) to balance target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity without requiring differentiable objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative data editing typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search, but these assumptions fail in flow-based settings where edits involve forward/backward integration and often non-differentiable or black-box objectives. There is a need for an optimization framework that works under these constraints.

Method: The authors propose residual-space evolutionary optimization. Leveraging conditional flow matching (CFM)'s ability to disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals, they operate directly in residual space with two search regimes: (1) self-pollination — local exploitation via feature-preserving residual refinement; (2) cross-pollination — broader exploration via recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples.

Result: Validated on MorphoMNIST (counterfactual generation benchmark) and crystal data (scientific domain), the framework demonstrates effective balancing of target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity. The exploration-exploitation decomposition proves useful beyond images in real-world scientific applications.

Conclusion: Residual-space evolutionary optimization provides a viable, model-agnostic mechanism for flow-based generative editing under non-differentiable objectives, with the self/cross-pollination decomposition offering a principled way to navigate the trade-off between targeted edits, identity preservation, and sample diversity across domains.

Abstract: Data editing with generative methods typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search. However, these assumptions break down in flow-based settings, where edits are performed through forward and backward integration and often involve non-differentiable or black-box objectives. We introduce residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework that addresses this gap by combining flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. Building on the observation that conditional flow matching (CFM) can disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals, our framework directly operates in residual space and separates two complementary search regimes: self-pollination performs local exploitation through feature-preserving residual refinement, and cross-pollination promotes broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. As a proof of concept, we validate on MorphoMNIST, a benchmark dataset for counterfactual generation, and on crystal data, demonstrating that this exploration--exploitation decomposition provides a useful mechanism for balancing target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains.

</details>


### [139] [Multi-Head Attention-Based Feature Extractor Integration with Soft Actor-Critic for Porosity Prediction and Process Parameter Optimization in Additive Manufacturing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20087)
*Kianoush Aqabakee,Leonardo Stella*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A continuous-action SAC algorithm enhanced with multi-head attention achieves faster convergence (322.79 reward in 14 episodes) than DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC for porosity prediction and parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional RL methods using discrete action spaces for additive manufacturing parameter optimization suffer from slow convergence and local optima traps, limiting their effectiveness in high-precision defect minimization tasks like porosity control.

Method: The authors propose a continuous action space framework combining the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm with a multi-head attention mechanism as the feature extractor. The attention module enhances sensitivity to subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, improving exploration-exploitation balance in value landscapes with local minima.

Result: The proposed method achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward compared to DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC baselines, while maintaining training stability.

Conclusion: Integrating multi-head attention with continuous-action SAC significantly improves RL-based process optimization for additive manufacturing, offering a robust solution for porosity minimization in laser powder bed fusion.

Abstract: Additive manufacturing process optimization requires precise parameter control to minimize defects such as porosity. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) approaches using discrete action spaces suffer from slow convergence and susceptibility to local optima, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision manufacturing tasks. This study addresses these limitations by employing a continuous action space combined with a novel architecture that integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. The attention-based feature extractor enhances the agent's ability to capture subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, enabling more effective exploration-exploitation balance for navigating value spaces with local minima. We validate our approach on porosity prediction and process parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward values compared to standard RL methods including DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC. The proposed methodology achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining stability throughout training.

</details>


### [140] [BIM-Edit: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IFC-Based Building Information Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20146)
*Bharathi Kannan Nithyanantham,Clemens Kujat,Tobias Sesterhenn,Stefan Telgmann,Jörn Plönnigs,Stefan Lüdtke,Christian Bartelt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BIM-Edit is a new benchmark evaluating LLMs on editing Building Information Models (IFC format) via natural language, measuring geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. The best model scores only 49.5% across all metrics, revealing a large gap between current LLM capabilities and real-world CAD editing demands.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAD benchmarks focus on generating new geometry from scratch rather than editing existing models, and they primarily evaluate geometric correctness while ignoring semantic and relational structure. Real engineering workflows require LLMs to understand existing scenes, make targeted edits, and preserve semantic and topological relationships — capabilities that remain unevaluated.

Method: The authors introduce BIM-Edit, a benchmark comprising 324 editing tasks across 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes in IFC format. Tasks are categorized into three instruction types — direct, spatial, and topological — covering both explicit edits and scene-grounded modifications. Model outputs are evaluated along three orthogonal dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency, using automated metrics tailored to IFC structure.

Result: The best-performing LLM achieves only a 49.5% average score across the three evaluation dimensions, and no model fully solves more than 3.4% of the tasks. All evaluated models struggle significantly with preserving semantic and topological integrity during edits.

Conclusion: There is a substantial performance gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of structured engineering design workflows. BIM-Edit establishes a rigorous standard for future research on model editing, underscoring the need for LLMs that jointly reason about geometry, semantics, and topology in domain-specific representations like IFC.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to computer-aided design (CAD) to generate design artifacts from textual instructions. In engineering practice, this requires more than creating new geometry, models must also understand existing scenes, edit them correctly, and preserve semantics and relations. However, many CAD benchmarks focus on creating new models rather than editing existing ones, and mostly evaluate geometric correctness. We introduce BIM-Edit, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (BIM) represented in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format. BIM provides a challenging testbed because building models encode geometry together with semantic and relational structure. BIM-Edit contains 324 editing tasks spanning 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes. Tasks are expressed using three instruction categories - direct, spatial, and topological - covering both explicit and scene-grounded edits. We evaluate outputs along three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Across evaluated LLMs, the best-performing model achieves only 49.5% average score across the three metrics, and no model fully solves more than 3.4% of tasks. These results demonstrate a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the requirements of structured engineering design workflows.

</details>


### [141] [Modularity-Free Conflict-Averse Training for Generalized PINNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20156)
*Heejo Kong,Beomchul Park,Sung-Jin Kim,Seong-Whan Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Overparameterized PINNs suffer from functional modularity, where networks self-partition into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and hinder convergence. The proposed ModSync framework penalizes task-exclusive connections to preserve interaction-promoting pathways, preventing capacity-driven failures and achieving state-of-the-art accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conflict-averse optimization schemes for PINNs degrade as model capacity increases. The authors identify a failure mode where overparameterized networks develop functional modularity—self-partitioning into task-exclusive modules that suppress beneficial cross-objective interactions, preventing convergence to Pareto-stationary points.

Method: The authors propose Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), a framework that integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training. ModSync penalizes task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways, effectively synchronizing modular sparsity patterns to maintain cross-objective coupling during training.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks show that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy compared to existing conflict-averse training methods.

Conclusion: ModSync successfully addresses the capacity-induced failure mode in PINNs by preventing functional modularity through structural regularization, enabling overparameterized networks to maintain effective multi-objective optimization and achieve superior solution accuracy.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a powerful framework for solving PDEs by embedding physical laws into differentiable objectives. Despite their advances, training PINNs remains fragile: recent conflict-averse optimization schemes alleviate gradient interference between residual and boundary losses, but we show that their effectiveness deteriorates as model capacity increases. In this paper, we identify a capacity-induced failure mode, where overparameterized networks undergo functional modularity, self-partitioning into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and hinder convergence toward Pareto-stationary points. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework, Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks demonstrate that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/heejokong/ModSync}.

</details>


### [142] [Implicit Semantic-Aware Communication Based on Hypergraph Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20162)
*Yiwei Liao,Shurui Tu,Yong Xiao,Yingyu Li,Guangming Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes HISR, a hypergraph-based semantic communication framework that captures higher-order multi-entity relationships for robust implicit semantic reasoning, achieving up to 36.6% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing semantic-aware communication systems rely on graph-based representations that only capture pairwise relationships, neglecting higher-order correlations like group interactions and multi-entity associations. This limits semantic expressiveness and degrades inference accuracy under noisy channel conditions.

Method: The authors propose HISR (Hypergraph-based Implicit Semantic Reasoning), where semantic knowledge entities and their higher-order relations are modeled using hypergraphs. Entities are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts, disentangling diverse semantic interactions and mitigating over-smoothing effects inherent in traditional graph embeddings.

Result: Numerical results demonstrate that HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art benchmarks.

Conclusion: Hypergraph-based semantic representation is a promising direction for next-generation semantic communication, offering enhanced robustness, richer expressiveness, and superior inference accuracy, particularly in scenarios with partial information loss or channel impairments.

Abstract: Semantic-aware communication has emerged as a transformative paradigm for next-generation communication systems, shifting the fundamental goal from transmitting bit-level symbols to reliably recovering and understanding the semantic meaning of information. Previous studies have demonstrated that representing the semantic content of source messages as graph-based structures can significantly improve communication efficiency and the accuracy of semantic inference at the receiver. However, existing solutions typically employ graphs that capture only pairwise relationships, thereby neglecting higher-order implicit correlations commonly observed in real-world scenarios, such as group interactions, multi-entity associations, and complex relational contexts. This limitation reduces semantic expressiveness and makes semantic inference susceptible to ambiguity and performance degradation, particularly under noisy or corrupted channel conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework, HISR, which leverages hypergraphs to represent complex multi-entity relationships among semantic knowledge entities. In HISR, entities and their associated higher-order relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This design not only disentangles diverse semantic interactions to mitigate the over-smoothing effects commonly found in traditional graph embedding methods but also enables robust semantic inference even when partial information loss occurs during transmission. Numerical results show that the proposed HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over the state-of-the-art benchmarks.

</details>


### [143] [Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20208)
*Guillaume Olivier Delplanque,Pierre Genevès,Nabil Layaïda,Zephirin Faure*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RVS is a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies how well machine learning model outputs satisfy logical rules, revealing consistency differences between models with similar predictive accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard predictive performance metrics (ranking quality, error rates, accuracy) fail to assess whether model outputs respect logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance, logical consistency is critical but unmeasured.

Method: The authors propose the Rule Violation Score (RVS), which treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently. RVS applies to any predictive model over a relational vocabulary, evaluates on any dataset, and can be computed via automatically generated SQL queries for Horn rules. It also evaluates dataset consistency and identifies poorly defined rules.

Result: Evaluation on three benchmarks (knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression) across rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic models shows that models with comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, as detected by RVS.

Conclusion: RVS fills a gap in model evaluation by providing a standardized, complementary metric for logical consistency. It enables practitioners to assess and compare models beyond accuracy alone, potentially guiding model selection in safety-critical applications where rule adherence matters.

Abstract: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

</details>


### [144] [Augmenting Game AI with Deep Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20210)
*Alessandro Sestini,Joakim Bergdahl,Amir Baghi,Jean-Philippe Barrette-LaPierre,Florian Fuchs,Linus Gisslén*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that machine learning, particularly reinforcement learning, can create more believable game AI than hand-coded systems, but current research limitations hinder broad adoption. It proposes a game-development-oriented RL training framework, illustrates deployed examples, and identifies key bottlenecks and research directions to accelerate industry adoption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hand-coded game AI struggles to capture behavioral complexity, leading to player frustration and broken immersion. Machine learning offers a path toward authentic, human-like NPC behavior, but practical barriers prevent widespread deployment across game genres.

Method: The authors propose a framework for training reinforcement learning models tailored to game AI and game development requirements. They present case studies of RL-augmented game AI, describe deployment practicalities for player-facing agents, and systematically identify bottlenecks and hard open problems in the field.

Result: The paper catalogs existing examples of RL-augmented game AI and delineates specific technical and practical bottlenecks—such as training stability, generalization across game genres, and deployment constraints—that currently limit broader adoption. It frames these bottlenecks as promising research directions.

Conclusion: Reinforcement learning holds strong promise for next-generation game AI, but realizing this vision requires addressing identified bottlenecks through focused research. The proposed framework and problem enumeration aim to guide and accelerate the machine learning community's efforts toward industry-ready solutions.

Abstract: Immersion in video games depends not only on graphics, audio, and game mechanics, but also on the quality of in-game characters. Producing believable characters, or game AI, remains a significant challenge as behavioral complexity is hard to capture with hand-coded systems. Game AI is a source of immersion and engagement; however, the limitations stemming from the challenges of creating game AI often lead to frustration and the breaking of the illusion of realism within the game. The introduction of machine learning models opens the door to creating more believable, authentic, and relatable characters in games. The promise is that they either learn from interacting with the game, or from player data, to develop true human-like behavior. In this paper, we envision more applications of reinforcement learning for game AI in the future. For this to materialize, current research limitations are prohibitive to broad deployment across game genres. Therefore, we propose a framework for training reinforcement learning models with a set of requirements in mind that are suited towards game AI and game development. We present examples of games with reinforcement learning-augmented game AI and describe the practicalities of deploying player-facing machine learning agents in modern games. Furthermore, we identify bottlenecks and hard problems in these areas, which we believe offer promising research directions to accelerate the adoption of machine learning in game AI for the video game industry.

</details>


### [145] [Thermodynamic Measure of Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20231)
*Ishanu Chattopadhyay*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a thermodynamic definition of intelligence as "lawful amplification of rare but valid futures" and proves that recursive self-simulation (a system modeling itself within the world) is necessary and nearly sufficient for achieving high thermodynamic intelligence, making intelligence measurable on a universal scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish a formal, measurable definition of intelligence grounded in thermodynamics, moving beyond vague or anthropocentric notions. The authors seek a universal framework applicable to systems ranging from passive matter to LLMs to Maxwell-demon-like engines.

Method: The paper formalizes intelligence thermodynamically as "rare-valid lift" — the extent to which a system amplifies the probability of outcomes that are both unlikely under passive dynamics and admissible under domain constraints. It then analytically proves a necessity theorem (high lift requires high-fidelity recursive self-simulation) and a conditional near-sufficiency theorem (high-fidelity simulation with an effective policy approaches the actuation-limited optimum lift).

Result: The central results are: (1) necessity — high rare-valid lift is impossible without the internal simulation identifying rare-valid futures with high fidelity; (2) conditional near-sufficiency — when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Together these establish recursive self-simulation as necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence.

Conclusion: Recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is required for and nearly guarantees high intelligence. The framework enables intelligence to be measured on a universal scale across diverse systems.

Abstract: Can intelligence be measured? We propose that intelligence can be defined as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures: a system increases the probability of outcomes that would be unlikely under passive dynamics but remain admissible under the constraints of the domain. We start with the premise that an intelligent system must model the world and its own place within it. Because the system is part of the world it models, this leads naturally to recursive self-simulation: the system represents futures in which its own actions are part of the trajectory. Our central results give a necessity statement and a conditional near-sufficiency statement connecting this architecture to a precise thermodynamic measure of lawful amplification of rare-valid futures: high rare-valid lift is impossible unless the internal simulation identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity; conversely, when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, the achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Thus recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The resulting framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale, from passive matter and feedback controllers, large language models, and humans as text generators to Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

</details>


### [146] [Navigating Unreliable Parametric and Contextual Knowledge: Explicit Knowledge Conflict Resolution for LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20245)
*Huang Peng,Jiuyang Tang,Weixin Zeng,Hao Xu,Xiang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MACR introduces a multi-agent reasoning framework for resolving knowledge conflicts in LLMs, moving beyond binary source selection to actively resolve inconsistencies between internal parametric knowledge and multiple external contexts using semantic entropy-based confidence estimation and specialized reasoning agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM knowledge conflict approaches assume either the model or external context is reliable, use binary choice (privileging one source), and fail when both sources contain errors or when multiple external contexts conflict with each other. No prior work actively resolves inconsistencies across all available knowledge sources.

Method: MACR has two stages: (1) Adaptive knowledge assessment using modified semantic entropy to estimate LLM confidence; based on confidence, it either externalizes internal knowledge as text or retrieves external knowledge, generating basic contexts. (2) An inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three specialized agents: one induces explicit rules, one analyzes potential conflicts, and one resolves inconsistencies across all contexts.

Result: MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks and provides interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.

Conclusion: A multi-agent conflict-resolution framework that actively resolves rather than avoids knowledge conflicts leads to superior performance and interpretability compared to conventional binary-choice paradigms.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of language-based tasks by leveraging both extensive parametric knowledge and in-context learning ability, enabling them to incorporate external information provided in the input prompt. However, the integration of external knowledge can introduce conflicts, not only between the model's internal parametric knowledge and the external information, but also among multiple pieces of external contexts. Existing approaches typically assume that either the model or the provided context is reliable, overlooking the possibility that both sources may contain errors, and avoid conflicts by privileging one source over the other, rather than actively resolving inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework MACR for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond the conventional binary choice paradigm and incorporates an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism based on a multi-agent reasoning approach. Specifically, we first propose an adaptive knowledge assessment and retrieval approach that employs a modified semantic entropy measure to quantify an LLM's confidence in its answer to a given query. Based on this confidence estimation, MACR either externalizes the model's internal knowledge as textual representations or retrieves relevant external knowledge when internal knowledge is insufficient, generating basic contexts for subsequent reasoning. Then we introduce an inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three specialized agents that, respectively, induce explicit rules, analyze potential conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across all available contexts. Empirical results demonstrate that MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks, while also providing interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.

</details>


### [147] [Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20264)
*Luyang Fang,Yingchuan Zhang,Jongchan Park,Zhaoji Wang,Ping Ma,Xiaoming Zhai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Vision Transformer with confidence-aware scoring is proposed for automated assessment of student scientific drawings, enabling selective automation where high-confidence predictions are scored automatically and uncertain cases deferred to human review, demonstrating improved reliability on NGSS-aligned middle school assessments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scoring student-generated scientific drawings for NGSS modeling-based tasks requires costly expert human judgment, making large-scale classroom assessment difficult. The authors aim to enable automated scoring while preserving trustworthiness through selective deferral of uncertain predictions.

Method: A Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation is evaluated. A confidence-aware scoring framework derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions, using this signal to selectively automate high-confidence responses and defer low-confidence cases to human reviewers.

Result: Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show improved scoring reliability and a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk, validating the value of confidence-aware selective automation.

Conclusion: Confidence-aware methods offer a viable path toward trustworthy automated assessment of student scientific drawings, balancing efficiency gains against the need for human oversight in educational contexts.

Abstract: Student-generated drawings are widely used in science education to assess learners' conceptual understanding in modeling-based tasks aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). However, scoring such drawings requires expert human judgment to interpret complex visual representations, making large-scale assessment costly to implement and sustain in classroom settings. In this work, we study automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings using a vision-based model. We evaluate a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation and propose a confidence-aware scoring framework that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions. This confidence signal enables selective automation by scoring high-confidence responses automatically while deferring uncertain cases for human review. Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed approach improves scoring reliability while supporting a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk, highlighting the value of confidence-aware methods for trustworthy educational assessment.

</details>


### [148] [Lagrange: An Open-Vocabulary, Energy-Based Sparse Framework for Generalized End-to-End Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20274)
*Shihao Ji,HongXi Li,Zihui Song,Mingyu Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lagrange is an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework that uses Masked Latent Fields (MLF) to bridge Vision-Language Models with Lagrangian action minimization, enabling kinematically feasible planning robust to out-of-distribution events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing autonomous driving paradigms face a trade-off: dense occupancy networks are geometrically robust but computationally expensive and semantically limited, while sparse query-based planners are efficient but fail under OOD scenarios. VLA models offer open-vocabulary reasoning but their discrete token generation conflicts with continuous vehicle control requirements.

Method: Lagrange employs VLMs to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. An intent-driven masked cross-attention module temporally filters irrelevant entities and decodes attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field over spatial coordinates. Decision-making is framed as Lagrangian action minimization over this energy field to enforce kinematic constraints during collision avoidance.

Result: Extensive offline evaluations on nuScenes (standard) and CODA (long-tail) benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness for robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.

Conclusion: Lagrange establishes a promising framework that unifies open-vocabulary semantic understanding with continuous, kinematically feasible planning, addressing the fundamental dichotomy between representational efficiency and generalization in end-to-end autonomous driving.

Abstract: Scaling end-to-end autonomous driving to complex, open-world environments requires perceptual models that generalize to anomalous scenarios and planners that produce kinematically valid trajectories. Existing paradigms face a distinct dichotomy between representational efficiency and generalization capacity. Dense models (e.g., occupancy networks), while geometrically robust, incur critical computational bottlenecks and struggle with high-level semantic reasoning. Conversely, sparse, query-based planners are efficient but reliant on closed-set definitions, rendering them vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) events. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer open-vocabulary reasoning, their autoregressive, discrete token generation fundamentally conflicts with the continuous, high-frequency control requirements of vehicle dynamics. To address this, we propose Lagrange, an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework based on Masked Latent Fields (MLF). Rather than relying on dense volumetric reconstructions or closed-set query mechanisms, Lagrange exploits Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. We introduce an intent-driven masked cross-attention module that temporally filters irrelevant entities, decoding the attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field defined over spatial coordinates. By framing decision-making as a Lagrangian action minimization problem spanning this energy field, we enforce strict compliance with vehicle kinematics while executing collision avoidance. Extensive offline evaluations on both standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange establishes a promising framework for robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.

</details>


### [149] [Leveraging systems' non-linearity to tackle the scarcity of data in the design of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20323)
*Giancarlo Santamato,Andrea Mattia Garavagno,Massimiliano Solazzi,Antonio Frisoli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A vibration-based intelligent fault diagnosis method using deep transfer learning with a novel data visualization and augmentation technique, validated on a railway pantograph under strong data scarcity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep transfer learning methods for intelligent fault diagnosis still require large labeled datasets, which are difficult to obtain for machinery and structural faults, creating a strong data scarcity problem.

Method: A periodic multi-excitation level procedure that exploits intrinsic nonlinearities of real-world systems to generate images suitable for pre-trained CNNs, combined with a new data visualization method and associated augmentation technique to address data scarcity.

Result: Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach under strong data scarcity conditions.

Conclusion: The proposed method enables reliable vibration-based intelligent fault diagnosis using DTL even when labelled data is extremely limited, offering a practical solution for real-world industrial applications.

Abstract: Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) allows for the efficient building of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems (IFDS). On the other hand, DTL methods still heavily rely on large amounts of labelled data. Obtaining such an amount of data can be challenging when dealing with machines or structures faults. This document proposes a novel approach to the design of vibration-based IFDS using DTL in condition of strong data scarcity. A periodic multi-excitation level procedure leveraging intrinsic non-linearities of real-world systems is used to produce images that can be conveniently analysed by pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to diagnose faults. A new data visualization method and its augmentation technique are proposed in this paper to tackle the typical lack of data encountered during the design of IFDS. Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure provides effective support for the proposed method.

</details>


### [150] [SoftSkill: Behavioral Compression for Contextual Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20333)
*Xijia Tao,Yihua Teng,Xinyu Fu,Ziru Liu,Kecheng Chen,Yuzhi Zhao,Suiyun Zhang,Rui Liu,Lingpeng Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SoftSkill proposes replacing lengthy natural-language Markdown skill files with compact, trainable soft prefix embeddings that steer a frozen LLM's behavior at inference time. A length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B yields significant gains over both no-skill prompting and the SkillOpt baseline across SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, while using drastically fewer tokens. The method also explores harder multi-step agentic execution, where trajectory imitation provides signal but full compression of long-horizon procedures remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployed agent skills are typically long Markdown prompts consumed indirectly by frozen LMs, incurring high token costs and forcing repeated reinterpretation per task instance. The authors ask whether natural-language skills can instead be distilled into compact, trainable continuous representations that serve as latent behavioral priors, avoiding inference-time reprocessing of verbose textual artifacts.

Method: SoftSkill freezes the backbone LM and trains only a short sequence of continuous "soft skill" vectors (a prefix) using next-token prediction on task data. At inference, these learned vectors are prepended to the input, serving as a compact latent prior that modulates the model's task behavior. The method is evaluated in single-round settings and in multi-step agentic execution, where sparse trajectory imitation provides the training signal.

Result: On Qwen3.5-4B, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 pts on SearchQA, 42.1 pts on LiveMath, and 1.3 pts on DocVQA. Compared to SkillOpt, SoftSkill yields +5.2 pts on SearchQA and +12.5 pts on LiveMath while replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown tokens with a few virtual tokens. In agentic execution, sparse trajectory imitation offers useful but not yet robust compression of long-horizon procedural behavior.

Conclusion: Some task skills are better treated as compact latent controls over a frozen model's task entry behavior rather than as lengthy Markdown to be reinterpreted each time. SoftSkill demonstrates that trainable soft prefixes can effectively replace verbose skill prompts with substantial token savings and accuracy gains, though long-horizon agentic procedures remain a frontier challenge.

Abstract: Agent skills are commonly deployed as natural-language Markdown files that encode answer policies, evidence-use habits, and task procedures. These files are readable and portable, but they are consumed indirectly: for each task instance, a frozen language model must translate a long textual artifact into generation-time behavior. This paper asks whether a natural-language skill can instead initialize a compact continuous context object, refined by a trainable soft delta while the base model remains frozen. We propose SoftSkill, a frozen-backbone method that tunes such soft skills with next-token prediction and deploys them as latent behavioral priors at inference time. In our main single-round setting, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 points on LiveMath, and 1.3 points on DocVQA. Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 points on LiveMath, while replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown skill tokens with a few virtual tokens. We further study agentic execution as a harder boundary case, where sparse trajectory imitation provides useful signal but does not yet robustly compress long-horizon procedural behavior. More broadly, the results suggest that some task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown to be reinterpreted at inference time, but as compact latent controls over how a frozen model enters the task.

</details>


### [151] [Automating SKILL.md Generation for Computer-Using Agents via Interaction Trajectory Mining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20363)
*Yuexing Hao,Xiaomin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mining GUI interaction trajectories can reveal readable skill clusters (≥0.95 purity against ground-truth labels), but these discovered skills fail to meaningfully improve downstream agent policies, highlighting a gap between skill discovery and effective policy transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explicit skill libraries enhance agent interpretability, but it is unknown whether such libraries can be automatically mined from interaction data in a way that actually improves downstream policies. The work aims to test this assumption empirically.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) segment raw GUI trajectories into sub-trajectories using a boundary detector; (2) cluster these segments into candidate skills using an orderless segment representation; (3) train a skill-aware policy (via GRPO) using the resulting cluster annotations. Evaluation is conducted on InteraSkill Workflows and BrowseComp+ benchmarks.

Result: Five of eight mined clusters achieve ≥0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels, confirming readability. However, GRPO with these skills improves skill-step accuracy only marginally (18.5% → 20.5%), leaves BrowseComp+ unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency-based priors on source-domain metrics.

Conclusion: The work is framed as a diagnostic study: trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current combination of boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model is insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

Abstract: Explicit skill libraries make computer-using agents easier to inspect, but it remains unclear whether such libraries can be mined from interaction data in a way that improves downstream policies. We study this question through a three-stage pipeline that segments GUI trajectories, clusters segments into candidate skills, and trains a skill-aware policy from the resulting annotations. The mined clusters are readable on the source benchmark: five of eight clusters have at least 0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels. However, readability does not imply transfer. GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5\% to 20.5\%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics. We therefore present the method as a diagnostic study: trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

</details>


### [152] [Rethinking Shrinkage Bias in LLM FP4 Pretraining: Geometric Origin, Systemic Impact, and UFP4 Recipe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20381)
*Qian Zhao,Kunlong Chen,Changxin Tian,Zhonghui Jiang,Haitao Zhang,Chaofan Yu,Peijie Jiang,Mingliang Gong,Jia Liu,Ziqi Liu,Zhiqiang Zhang,Jun Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: E2M1 FP4 formats suffer from Shrinkage Bias—a systematic negative rounding error from geometric asymmetry—which compounds across layers and is amplified by Random Hadamard Transform, causing training instability. The authors propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit (E1M2/INT4) training recipe using RHT on all GEMMs with stochastic rounding restricted to dY, demonstrating superior BF16-relative loss on models up to 124B parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing FP4 hardware (NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin, AMD MI350) and training recipes rely on E2M1 formats, but these exhibit training instability whose root cause has not been systematically explained. The authors aim to identify the fundamental limitation of non-uniform 4-bit formats and propose a stable alternative.

Method: The authors identify Shrinkage Bias as the core issue—a systematic negative rounding error from geometric asymmetry in E2M1's representable bins. They analyze how this bias multiplies across layers and is exacerbated by Random Hadamard Transform (RHT). They then propose UFP4: a uniform 4-bit training recipe (E1M2/INT4) applying RHT to all three training GEMMs with stochastic rounding limited to dY gradients only. Validation includes dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining with scaling-law analysis and ablation studies.

Result: UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation compared to E2M1-based baselines across all model scales (Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B). Scaling-law analysis and ablation studies corroborate the benefits of uniform 4-bit grids over non-uniform E2M1 formats.

Conclusion: Future AI accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1, as uniform formats fundamentally avoid the Shrinkage Bias that destabilizes E2M1-based FP4 training.

Abstract: FP4 training promises substantial reductions in memory and computation cost for LLM pretraining, yet current FP4 hardware paths and recipes, including NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin-class systems and AMD MI350-series GPUs, remain centered on E2M1 data elements. In this study, we identify a fundamental limitation of that choice: non-uniform formats such as E2M1 inherently suffer from Shrinkage Bias, a systematic negative rounding error caused by the geometric asymmetry of their representable bins. We show that this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT), providing a unified explanation for the training instability observed in existing E2M1-based FP4 recipes. In contrast, uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) bypass this grid-geometry error and better convert the improved bucket utilization from RHT into higher quantization quality. Based on this finding, we propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe that applies RHT to all three training GEMMs while restricting stochastic rounding to dY alone. On Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining, UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than strong E2M1-based baselines, supported by scaling-law analysis and ablation studies. Our results suggest that future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

</details>


### [153] [Interpretable Sperm Morphology Classification via Attention-Guided Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20438)
*Zahra Asghari Varzaneh,Reza Khoshkangini,Thomas Ebner,Lars Johansson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an interpretable deep learning framework combining EfficientNet-B0 with CBAM attention for sperm morphology classification, achieving 90.2–93.9% accuracy with Grad-CAM++ visualizations to enhance clinical transparency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Male infertility is a leading cause of couple infertility, frequently associated with abnormal sperm morphology. Existing deep learning solutions for automated sperm analysis lack interpretability, which hinders their acceptance and adoption in clinical settings.

Method: The authors design an attention-guided framework that pairs a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 backbone with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). This combination directs the model's focus toward diagnostically relevant regions of the sperm head. Model decisions are subsequently visualized using Grad-CAM++ to provide post-hoc interpretability. Evaluation is conducted on two public benchmark datasets: SMIDS and HuSHem.

Result: On SMIDS, the model achieves 90.2% accuracy with a macro F1 score of 0.913. On HuSHem, it reaches 93.9% accuracy with a macro F1 score of 0.948. Both results surpass baseline comparisons against SimpleCNN and a standard EfficientNet-B0 without attention.

Conclusion: The proposed framework is both accurate and transparent, offering a practical, clinically viable tool for automated sperm morphology assessment in fertility clinics.

Abstract: Male infertility is a major cause of couple infertility, often linked to abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning models offer automated analysis, most lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. This study proposes an attention-guided deep learning framework for sperm morphology classification. We combine a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to focus on key areas of the sperm head, improving both accuracy and interpretability. Evaluated on the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets, our model achieves accuracies of 90.2% and 93.9% (macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948), outperforming SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0. Furthermore, we use Grad-CAM++ visualizations to highlight features influencing the model's decisions. The results demonstrate that this accurate and transparent framework is a practical tool for automated sperm analysis in fertility clinics.

</details>


### [154] [Context-Aware Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling of IVF Laboratory Environmental Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20459)
*Zahra Asghari Varzaneh,Reza Khoshkangini,Pia Saldeen,Lars Johansson,Thomas Ebner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Engineered 55 context-aware temporal features from IVF incubator microenvironment data reduce prediction error to 1.27% (vs. 3-5% for raw averages). A hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model with partial pooling transfers environmental signals across clinics, achieving R²=0.86 and 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group on held-out data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IVF pregnancy rate prediction models routinely use patient-level variables but neglect high-resolution laboratory environmental data. Raw sensor averages capture only coarse trends, missing clinically meaningful dynamics in incubator microenvironments. The authors aim to demonstrate that structured, context-aware environmental features contain transferable predictive signal that generalizes across clinics.

Method: From 61 weeks of incubator sensor data at an Asian IVF clinic, the authors engineer 55 temporal features (rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, post-stress recovery speed). These feed into a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model that uses partial pooling to share environmental effects between the Asian clinic and a Northern European clinic, while retaining site-specific baselines. Performance is evaluated via cross-validation on the Asian data and held-out validation on the European data.

Result: The 55 engineered features reduce cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% for raw sensor averages. On held-out Northern European clinic data, the hierarchical model achieves R²=0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline.

Conclusion: Structured environmental monitoring of IVF incubators yields clinically meaningful and transferable signal. Context-aware temporal feature engineering substantially outperforms raw averages, and hierarchical Bayesian modeling with partial pooling enables robust cross-clinic generalization of environmental effects on pregnancy rates.

Abstract: IVF pregnancy rates are routinely modeled using patient-level variables, while high-resolution laboratory environmental data remain underutilized. We show that this is a missed opportunity. Rather than relying on raw sensor averages, we engineer 55 context-aware temporal features, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed, that capture the dynamics of incubator microenvironments. On 61 weeks of data from an Asian IVF clinic, these features reduce cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% for raw averages. We then train a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model that shares environmental effects across an Asian and a Northern European clinic via partial pooling, while preserving site-specific baselines. On held-out data from the Northern European clinic, the model achieves R2 = 0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline, demonstrating that structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful, transferable signal.

</details>


### [155] [What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20508)
*Sihui Dai,Mann Patel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mixing benign and harmful in-context demonstrations reveals that models interpret compliance signals differently. Benign demonstrations can increase or decrease harmful compliance depending on the model, with preference optimization being key to preventing harmful compliance from benign demos. Recency bias and refusal override patterns also vary across models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work established that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak LLMs, the mechanistic understanding of how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations remains underexplored. The authors aim to characterize the factors—demonstration type, ordering, and training methodology—that drive harmful compliance.

Method: The authors mix benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request → helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request → helpful response) in the prompt context. They test three hypotheses about demonstration composition across four language models, systematically varying demonstration types, ordering, and analyzing refusal behavior to isolate the effects of preference optimization and recency bias.

Result: Benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable—benign demos can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. Preference optimization is identified as the critical training stage preventing benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance. Demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias. Models diverge in refusal behavior: some adopt demonstrated formatting even while refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal.

Conclusion: Demonstration-based jailbreaking effectiveness depends on a nuanced interplay of demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology. This moves beyond the binary question of whether demos jailbreak to a deeper characterization of how models extract and act on compliance signals from in-context demonstrations.

Abstract: Prior work has shown that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak language models, but it remains unclear how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations. We study this by mixing benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and testing three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Across four models, we find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. We further show that preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, that demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias, and that models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal. Taken together, this work moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works: what models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

</details>


### [156] [Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20517)
*Maria Ivanova,Pavel Zadorozhny,Rodion Levichev,Ivan Petrov,Adamenko Pavel,Ivan Lopatin,Alexey Kutalev,Dmitrii Babaev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-LCB extends the Python-only LiveCodeBench to 12 programming languages, preserving contamination controls and evaluation protocols. Evaluating 24 LLMs reveals Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and significant multilingual performance gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LiveCodeBench is widely adopted for code-generation evaluation but is restricted to Python, leaving unaddressed the question of whether LLMs can generalize across diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.

Method: Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LiveCodeBench dataset into equivalent tasks in 11 additional languages (12 total including Python), fully preserving LCB's contamination-aware controls (problem release-date filtering, regular updates) and evaluation protocol. It maintains format compatibility for automatic tracking of future LCB updates.

Result: Evaluation of 24 instruction-tuned and reasoning LLMs uncovered evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual code generation performance across the 12 languages.

Conclusion: Multi-LCB establishes a rigorous new benchmark for multi-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities beyond Python.

Abstract: LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
  We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across twelve programming languages, including Python. Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in other languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol. Because it is fully compatible with the original LCB format, Multi-LCB will automatically track future LCB updates, enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence and requiring models to sustain performance well beyond Python.
  We evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB, uncovering evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual performance. Our results establish Multi-LCB as a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities.

</details>


### [157] [FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20518)
*Harshit Singh,Ayush Pratap Singh,Nityanand Mathur*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlowEdit is a lifelong adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that corrects pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns by learning latent text-embedding perturbations stored in a Modern Hopfield Network, achieving 92.7% relative Phoneme Error Rate reduction with ~15-second corrections on a single GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow-matching TTS systems, despite strong zero-shot quality, are static post-deployment and mispronounce out-of-vocabulary proper nouns. Retraining is impractical for continuous, lifelong correction. The authors aim to enable on-the-fly pronunciation adaptation without modifying model weights.

Method: When corrective feedback is given, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space (rather than updating model weights). Corrections are stored in a Modern Hopfield Network functioning as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, a soft-attention retrieval mechanism with a similarity gate performs fuzzy morphological matching to retrieve and apply relevant stored corrections.

Result: On a curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns spanning 18 language families, FlowEdit achieved a 92.7% relative reduction in target-word Phoneme Error Rate compared to the zero-shot baseline, with no degradation in general-speech quality. Each correction completes in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

Conclusion: FlowEdit demonstrates that pronunciation corrections for frozen flow-matching TTS can be effectively learned as latent embedding edits and retrieved via associative memory, enabling practical lifelong adaptation without retraining, weight modification, or loss of general synthesis quality.

Abstract: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

</details>


### [158] [DeepSWIP: Quotient-WMC Counterfactuals for Neural Probabilistic Logic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20526)
*Saimun Habib,Vaishak Belle,Fengxiang He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeepSWIP introduces a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog that reduces neural predicates to ProbLog choices via materialization, enabling exact counterfactual reasoning through weighted model counting on a single transformed program, with experiments confirming correctness, speedups, and bias analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard inference in neurosymbolic systems like DeepProbLog is purely associational and lacks causal semantics for interventions and evidence. Counterfactual reasoning in such systems requires a principled causal framework that supports interventions and evidence without the computational expense of twin-network constructions.

Method: The authors propose DeepSWIP, which uses neural materialization to convert fixed-context neural predicates into ordinary ProbLog choices. This enables the application of Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs) for counterfactual computation via weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program. The approach exploits the quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals to identify active neural probabilities, analyze intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. For evaluation, they use a DeepTwin construction as ground truth on MPI3D, and apply Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) in a SUMO HOV experiment for debiasing.

Result: Experiments on MPI3D validate the transformation against DeepTwin across 12,000 queries, achieving a 2.14× inference speedup by avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. The SUMO HOV experiment demonstrates that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands.

Conclusion: DeepSWIP provides an exact, efficient single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, with practical advantages in speed and bias correction validated experimentally.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic systems such as DeepProbLog combine neural perception with probabilistic logic, but standard inference is associational. Counterfactual reasoning additionally requires a causal semantics for interventions and evidence. We introduce DeepSWIP, a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog programs. Using neural materialization, we reduce fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, apply Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs), and compute counterfactuals by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program. Under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, DeepSWIP is exact relative to the learned materialized FCM. The standard quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals identifies active neural probabilities and explains intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. Experiments on MPI3D confirm the transformation against a DeepTwin construction against 12,000 queries, as predicted and a 2.14$\times$ inference speedup from avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment shows that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands. Code is at https://github.com/saibib/deep_SWIP.

</details>


### [159] [LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20529)
*Md Nayem Uddin,Amir Saeidi,Eduardo Blanco,Chitta Baral*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LedgerAgent introduces a separate, explicit task-state ledger for tool-calling agents in customer-service domains. By maintaining observed facts, identifiers, and constraints in a structured ledger—rather than relying solely on prompt context—it reduces errors from stale or missing information and blocks state-dependent policy violations before executing environment-changing tool calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard tool-calling agents reconstruct task states implicitly from the prompt, leading to two failure modes: (1) grounding decisions in stale or incorrect facts despite having retrieved correct information earlier, and (2) making syntactically valid tool calls that nonetheless violate domain policies tied to the current task state. Explicit, separate state management is needed to mitigate these failures.

Method: LedgerAgent is an inference-time method that maintains observed task states (facts, identifiers, constraints, conditions) in a separate ledger structure. This ledger is rendered into the prompt for decision-making and is used to programmatically check state-dependent policy constraints before any environment-changing tool call is executed, blocking violations preemptively.

Result: Across four customer-service domains and a panel of both open- and closed-weight models, LedgerAgent improves average pass^k over standard prompt-based tool-calling baselines, with the largest gains observed under stricter multi-trial consistency evaluation metrics.

Conclusion: Explicit task-state management via a dedicated ledger, combined with pre-execution policy-constraint checking, significantly enhances the reliability and policy adherence of tool-calling agents in stateful, policy-sensitive domains.

Abstract: Policy-adherent tool-calling agents in customer-service domains must maintain task states across turns while calling tools and obeying domain policies. Task states consist of relevant facts, identifiers, constraints, and conditions observed through user interaction and tool calls. In standard agents, task states are not represented separately. Observations, tool returns, and policy instructions are placed in the prompt, leaving agents to reconstruct the relevant states from the prompt each time they decide what to do next. This design makes state management implicit, creating two common failure modes. An agent may retrieve the right facts but later ground its decision in stale, missing, or incorrect information; and a syntactically valid tool call may still violate a domain policy that depends on the current task state. We introduce \textsc{LedgerAgent}, an inference-time method for tool-calling agents that maintains observed task states in a separate ledger and renders the states into the prompt. The ledger is also used to check state-dependent policy constraints before environment-changing tool calls are executed, blocking policy violations. Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, \textsc{LedgerAgent} improves average pass\textasciicircum{}k over a standard prompt-based tool-calling approach, with the largest gains under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.

</details>


### [160] [How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20532)
*Nityanand Mathur,Hamees Sayed,Wasim Madha,Apoorv Singh,Sameer Khurana,Akshat Mandloi,Sudarshan Kamath*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: First application of cross-attention attribution (adapted DAAM) to speech diffusion TTS, analyzing 3,600 caption-transcript pairs to reveal how style caption tokens shape acoustic output — style tokens show lower temporal variance (global conditioning), correlate with F0/energy, peak in early ODE steps and deep layers, and attention entropy minimizes at layer 17 coinciding with maximal style selectivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Style-captioned TTS systems lack interpretability: it is unclear how individual natural-language words in style captions influence acoustic output. This opacity hinders failure diagnosis and limits controllability improvements in expressive speech synthesis.

Method: Adapted the DAAM (Diffusion Attentive Attribution Maps) framework from the vision domain to speech diffusion models — specifically CapSpeech-TTS. Extracted per-token cross-attention heatmaps across 25 transformer layers and 24 ODE integration steps. Analyzed 3,600 combinations (120 style captions × 30 text transcripts), computing temporal variance, F0/energy correlation, layer-wise and step-wise attention patterns, and attention entropy.

Result: Four key findings: (1) Style tokens exhibit lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning behavior. (2) Style attention weights correlate with F0 and energy acoustic features. (3) Style conditioning peaks in early ODE steps and deeper transformer layers. (4) Attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, which co-occurs with the peak of style importance, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical processing stage.

Conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic understanding of how natural language style descriptions influence cross-attention in speech diffusion models, establishing a foundation for diagnosing failures and improving controllability in style-captioned TTS systems.

Abstract: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeech-TTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models

</details>


### [161] [Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20544)
*Gina Wong,Drew Prinster,Suchi Saria,Rama Chellappa,Anqi Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies calibration in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models under distribution shift. It proves that expert-level calibration suffices for hard-routed MoEs but not for soft-routed ones, and proposes an adversarial reweighting method to improve calibration-accuracy tradeoffs under shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Calibration of predictive uncertainty is critical for trustworthiness, and MoE models have shown strong empirical gains from calibration. However, the theoretical conditions under which calibration benefits MoE models — especially under distribution shift — remain poorly understood.
