Method: The authors formally analyze how routing mechanisms (hard vs. soft) interact with expert-level calibration under distribution shift. They prove sufficiency of expert calibration for hard-routed MoEs and show a counterexample for soft-routing. They then propose an adversarial reweighting scheme that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift.

Result: Expert calibration is sufficient for overall model calibration under broad distribution shifts in hard-routed MoEs, but insufficient for soft-routed ones. The proposed adversarial reweighting method improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult data subsets, across model classes, tasks, and shifts.

Conclusion: Routing mechanism choice critically affects calibration guarantees under distribution shift. Hard routing preserves expert calibration, while soft routing requires explicit intervention. Adversarial reweighting effectively addresses the gap for soft-routed MoEs.

Abstract: Calibration aligns a model's predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how MoE models behave under distribution shift, focusing on how routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration. We show that expert calibration is sufficient to ensure calibration of the overall model under a broad class of distribution shifts in hard-routed models, but is insufficient for calibrating soft-routed models. To address this, we propose an adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift, and we demonstrate that it improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult subsets of the data, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.

</details>


<div id='cs.HC'></div>

# cs.HC [[Back]](#toc)

### [162] [LLM-Mediated Human-AI Interaction in Search and Rescue: Impact of Expertise on Attentional Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19514)
*Elahe Oveisi,Hemanth Manjunatha*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: LLM guidance in a simulated search-and-rescue task improved efficiency but not overall success. Eye-tracking revealed an attention-guidance trade-off where visual resources shifted toward the chat interface, and expertise moderated reliance: novices passively relied on AI while experts maintained environmental scanning for verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how real-time LLM-based AI guidance shapes human cognition, attention, and behavior in complex human-AI teaming tasks, and how these effects differ across levels of operator expertise.

Method: A simulated search-and-rescue (SAR) experiment comparing two LLM-guided conditions against a no-LLM baseline. Multi-level analysis was conducted using task performance metrics, eye-tracking (attention allocation, pupil size variability), and behavioral measures of planning and decision-making, with expertise as a moderating variable.

Result: LLM guidance improved task efficiency (higher rewards and victims-per-step) but not total victims saved. Eye-tracking showed an attention-guidance trade-off: increased dwell on the chat interface and greater pupil size variability. Novices exhibited passive AI reliance, while experts maintained a "verification loop" through persistent environmental scanning.

Conclusion: LLM-mediated teaming efficacy hinges on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth to preserve situational awareness. Expertise is a critical moderating factor in human-AI teaming outcomes.

Abstract: Human-AI teaming (HAT) increasingly involves AI systems that provide real-time, context-aware guidance in complex tasks. While such systems can improve performance, their effectiveness depends on how they shape human cognition and behavior. In particular, AI assistance can introduce cognitive demands and influence attention, planning, and interaction with the task environment, with effects that can vary across levels of expertise. This work investigates these mechanisms in a simulated search and rescue (SAR) environment. We compare human performance under two LLM (Large Language Model)-guided conditions and a no-LLM baseline, and analyze interaction at multiple levels, including task performance, eye-tracking measures, and planning behavior. Eye tracking provides fine-grained insight into attention allocation and interaction with AI guidance, while behavioral measures capture how users structure and adapt their decisions over time. Results indicate that LLM guidance enhanced task efficiency (higher rewards and victims-per-step) but did not increase total victims saved. Eye-tracking data revealed an attention-guidance trade-off, with visual resources shifting to the chat interface alongside increased pupil size variability. Expertise moderated this effect: novices exhibited passive AI reliance, whereas experts maintained a "verification loop" through persistent environmental scanning. These findings suggest that LLM-mediated teaming efficacy depends on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth to maintain situational awareness.

</details>


### [163] [Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19570)
*Naaz Sibia,Jessica Wen,Amber Richardson,Yashika Jain,Khushi Malik,Bogdan Simion,Carolina Nobre,Angela Zavaleta Bernuy,Andrew Petersen,Michael Liut*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A gaze-tracking study of 19 post-CS2 undergraduates found that despite well-designed visual scaffolds, students spent ~50% of time on code and often ignored metaphor views. Three non-cognitive factors explain this: agency (desire for control over cognitive effort), representational fit (subjective experience of helpfulness vs. overload), and legitimacy (perception of visualizations as "childish" or academically unserious). These affective/social factors help explain why cognitively sound visualization tools fail to engage learners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Program visualizations are widely used but often ignored or resisted by students. While MER research provides cognitive design principles for coordinating views, there is limited understanding of what actually shapes learners' engagement with available representations. The authors aim to uncover the non-cognitive factors driving selective engagement, explaining the gap between well-designed tools and actual student uptake.

Method: Within-subjects study with 19 undergraduates who completed CS1 and CS2. Participants used two multi-representational tools (a custom probe with synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views, plus Python Tutor) across three topics (scope, while loops, linked lists). Data collected through think-aloud task protocols, reflective interviews, and webcam-based gaze tracking to quantify visual attention allocation and qualitative reasoning.

Result: Gaze analysis: students spent nearly half their time on code despite available visual scaffolds; those without prior experience anchored more heavily in code and engaged minimally with metaphor views. Interviews revealed three factors: (1) agency — students sought control over cognitive effort rather than passive reduction; (2) representational fit — identical designs were experienced as helpful by some and overwhelming by others; (3) legitimacy — metaphorical scaffolds were avoided when perceived as "childish" or lacking university-level rigor.

Conclusion: Multi-representational computing tools must address affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical recommendations include positioning visualizations as verification instruments, offering toggleable abstraction levels, and framing tools to signal disciplinary legitimacy. The three themes (agency, representational fit, legitimacy) provide a broader framework for understanding why cognitively sound tools may fail to engage target students.

Abstract: Program visualizations are widely used to support novice programmers, yet students often ignore or resist well-designed visual scaffolds. Research on multiple external representations (MERs) offers cognitive design principles for coordinating views, but less is known about what shapes learners' engagement with available representations.
  We conducted a within-subjects study with 19 undergraduates who had completed CS1 and CS2. Students completed think-aloud tasks, reflective interviews, and webcam-based gaze tracking while using a multi-representational probe with synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views, and Python Tutor, across scope, while loops, and linked lists.
  Gaze analysis showed that students spent nearly half their time focused on code despite available visual scaffolds. Students without prior experience anchored even more heavily in code and engaged minimally with metaphor views. Interviews identified three factors shaping selective engagement: agency, as students sought control over cognitive effort rather than simply having it reduced; representational fit, as identical designs differed in whether they felt helpful or overwhelming; and legitimacy, as some students avoided metaphorical scaffolds they perceived as childish or insufficiently rigorous for university-level work.
  These findings suggest that multi-representational tools in computing education require attention to affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical considerations include positioning visualizations as verification instruments, offering toggleable abstraction levels, and framing tools to signal disciplinary legitimacy. More broadly, the themes help explain why cognitively sound visualization tools may fail to engage the students they are designed to help.

</details>


### [164] [Building Drift: Documenting On-Site Construction Adaptations Across Material Lifecycles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19609)
*Ritik Batra,Martin Tamke,Tom Svilans,Jan Hüls,Amritansh Kwatra,Steven J. Jackson,Thijs Roumen,Mette Ramsgaard Thomsen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper introduces "building drift"—the deviation between physical construction and digital models due to on-site adaptations when using reclaimed materials—and presents a taxonomy characterizing this drift alongside Pentimento, a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based documentation tool that spatially, temporally, and semantically captures these adaptations to support material reuse across building lifetimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reclaimed materials in circular construction carry prior histories and introduce unpredictability that necessitates on-site improvisation. These ad-hoc adaptations are rarely documented, leaving future collaborators, evaluators, and inheritors without the information needed to continue, assess, and reuse materials across building lifetimes. This documentation gap hinders scaling sustainable material reuse practices.

Method: The authors conduct a case study of ReShelter, a reclaimed timber pavilion built in the forest, to develop a five-category taxonomy of building drift: Tending the Site, Foraging for Fit, Interpreting the Material, Marking Measurements, and Coordinating Across Communities. They then design and implement Pentimento, a documentation tool using video capture and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to represent on-site adaptations spatially, temporally, and semantically in relation to the original digital model.

Result: The taxonomy provides a structured characterization of how and why physical-digital deviations occur during reclaimed material construction. Pentimento demonstrates a practical computational approach for capturing these deviations, enabling stakeholders to navigate material histories and reducing barriers to reuse.

Conclusion: Computational tools like Pentimento that support and document on-site improvisation are essential for scaling circular construction with reclaimed materials. The building drift taxonomy and Pentimento open pathways toward more sustainable cycles of recovery, repair, and reuse in the built environment.

Abstract: In a circular economy for construction, reclaimed materials carry prior lives of use and go on to have post-lives in future buildings. Yet working with such materials introduces unpredictability that requires on-site improvisation, making their reuse challenging to document and scale across building lifetimes. Without documentation, the on-site adaptations that make construction with reclaimed materials possible leave collaborators, evaluators, and inheritors without the information they need to continue, assess, and reuse materials. We call the collective deviation of the physical state from the digital model through these adaptations "building drift." Through a case study, ReShelter, a reclaimed timber pavilion constructed in the forest, we develop a taxonomy for building drift that characterizes the collective deviation across building lifetimes: Tending the Site, Foraging for Fit, Interpreting the Material, Marking Measurements, and Coordinating Across Communities.
  To put our taxonomy for building drift into practice, we present Pentimento, a documentation tool that leverages video documentation and 3D Gaussian Splatting to spatially, temporally, and semantically represent on-site adaptations in relation to the designed model. Pentimento enables each stakeholder to navigate material histories in ways that reduce barriers to material reuse. Together, these contributions open pathways towards computational tools that support the on-site improvisation essential to construction with reclaimed materials, enabling more sustainable cycles of recovery, repair, and reuse.

</details>


### [165] [Syndesmoscope: The Power of Invariant Plots\\Linked to Traditional Network Views](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19689)
*Matt Oddo,Indira Sowy,Stephen Kobourov,Tamara Munzner*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Syndesmoscope is an interactive network exploration system that juxtaposes traditional force-directed layouts with interpretable invariant plots (dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, spectral bisection, and the novel kSnakes), enabling two key interactions—leapfrogging and hopscotching—to reveal network patterns invisible through any single view.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional network visualizations (node-link, adjacency matrices) produce inconsistent visual patterns depending on layout/seriation algorithms, while invariant plots—which consistently surface the same pattern for a given topology—remain underexplored and unintegrated into interactive visualization systems. The authors aim to bridge this gap.

Method: The authors built Syndesmoscope, a multi-pane interactive system displaying one force-directed view and three invariant geometric layouts (dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, spectral bisection). They also contribute kSnakes, a novel invariant plot using density decomposition. The system supports two novel interaction techniques: leapfrogging (linked highlighting across interpretable views) and hopscotching (hop-based traversal extending selections through topology). The system was evaluated through usage scenarios on a corpus of 72 diverse networks.

Result: Usage scenarios across 72 diverse networks demonstrated that the combination of multiple juxtaposed views—both traditional and invariant—along with leapfrogging and hopscotching interactions reveals network patterns that are inaccessible through any single view alone.

Conclusion: Invariant plots, when integrated into interactive multi-view systems like Syndesmoscope with tailored interactions (leapfrogging, hopscotching), significantly enhance network exploration and pattern discovery beyond what conventional single-view approaches can offer.

Abstract: Traditional network representations, such as node-link views and adjacency matrices, can show dramatically different visual patterns, depending on the underlying layout or seriation algorithm. In contrast, invariant plots consistently surface the same visual pattern for the same input topology; yet researchers have underexplored them and have not integrated them into visualization systems. We present Syndesmoscope, an interactive system for network exploration that juxtaposes multiple views of the same network. Panes show a familiar a force-directed view alongside three panes with interpretable geometric layouts based on graph-theoretic properties: dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, and spectral bisection. As a secondary contribution, we introduce kSnakes, a new invariant plot based on density decomposition. Syndesmoscope supports two key interactions: leapfrogging, or linked highlighting between different and interpretable visual patterns; and hopscotching, or hop-based traversal that extends data selections through the underlying topology. Through usage scenarios across a corpus of 72 diverse networks, we demonstrate how these interactions reveal network patterns inaccessible through any single view alone. Live demo available at https://syndesmoscope.vercel.app/.

</details>


### [166] [Vibe Coding for Visualization Implementation: An Empirical Study of Practices and Challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19703)
*Zhengyu Sun,Xiaolin Wen,Fengjie Wang,Can Liu,Yi Lai,Christophe Hurter,Yong Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: An empirical study with 16 participants investigating how users with varying expertise employ "vibe coding" (AI-driven natural language) tools for data visualization implementation, characterizing practices in prompting, evaluation, and iteration, and identifying key challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data visualization creation remains labor-intensive despite its importance. While AI-driven "vibe coding" tools lower barriers by enabling natural language interaction, visualization implementation demands precise alignment between user intent and visual representation — a requirement that may diverge from general software development. Understanding how users actually employ these tools for visualization is needed.

Method: An empirical study with 16 participants of varying expertise levels. Each participant completed two visualization tasks using vibe coding tools, followed by a semi-structured interview. The study examined user practices across three phases: prompting, evaluation, and iteration.

Result: The study characterized diverse user practices across prompting, evaluation, and iteration phases. It also surfaced multiple challenges users encounter throughout the visualization implementation process when using vibe coding tools.

Conclusion: Vibe coding tools offer promise for democratizing visualization creation, but the mismatch between natural language expression and precise visual specification creates distinct challenges. The findings provide empirical grounding for improving AI-assisted visualization tools and workflows.

Abstract: Data visualization is essential for data analysis and communication, yet creating expressive visualizations remains labor-intensive. Recent AI-driven ``vibe coding'' tools enable users to generate visualizations through natural language interaction, lowering the barrier to entry. However, visualization implementation requires precise alignment between user intent and visual representation, which may differ from general software development practices. We present an empirical study with 16 participants of varying expertise to examine how users employ vibe coding tools for visualization implementation. Participants completed two visualization tasks and a semi-structured interview. Our findings characterize the diverse practices users adopt across prompting, evaluation, and iteration, and surface the challenges they encounter throughout the process.

</details>


### [167] [Designing for Interconnected Islamic Learning: A Qualitative Study of Muslim Women's Experiences with Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah Apps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19745)
*Ishrat Jahan Easha,Nabil Mosharraf Hossain,Araf Mohammad Mahbub,Fairoze Bint Abu Hassan,Zunaid Aslam,Yemin Sajid,Riasat Islam*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Islamic learners need Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah context integrated at the point of reading, but only when trustworthy, optional, and non-disruptive. The paper introduces "layered contextuality" to balance contextual expansion with interpretive accountability and devotional flow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Islamic learning interweaves Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah, but digital tools fragment these sources across separate apps and interfaces. This fragmentation creates a human-computer interaction problem that has not been systematically examined from the perspective of learners, particularly Muslim women in online learning communities.

Method: Semi-structured interviews (n=5) with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community, analyzed through three theoretical lenses: gendered digital religion, epistemic trust, and seamless learning.

Result: Five themes emerged: (1) need for contextual understanding at the point of reading, (2) concerns about authenticity and epistemic trustworthiness of contextual sources, (3) tension between interface clutter and contextual richness, (4) distinct study modes requiring different levels of contextual support, and (5) desire for guidance features. The core tension: learners want Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah context available but only when trustworthy, optional, and non-interrupting.

Conclusion: The paper proposes "layered contextuality" as a novel HCI construct: contextual expansion must be balanced with interpretive accountability, devotional flow, and continuity across devices and study intensities. This framework offers design implications for digital Islamic learning tools.

Abstract: Islamic learning often depends on reading the Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah together, yet digital tools typically separate these sources across apps, screens, and search pathways. We examine this as a human-computer interaction problem through five semi-structured interviews with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community. Participants described a recurring tension: they wanted Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah context at the point of reading, but only when contextual expansion remained trustworthy, optional, and did not interrupt reading. Interpreting the interviews through gendered digital religion, epistemic trust, and seamless learning, we identify five themes concerning contextual understanding, authenticity, interface clutter, study modes, and guidance features. We introduce layered contextuality as an HCI account of this domain: contextual expansion must be balanced with interpretive accountability, devotional flow, and continuity across devices and study intensities.

</details>


### [168] [MemGUI-Agent: An End-to-End Long-Horizon Mobile GUI Agent with Proactive Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19926)
*Guangyi Liu,Gao Wu,Congxiao Liu,Pengxiang Zhao,Liang Liu,Mading Li,Qi Zhang,Mengyan Wang,Liang Guo,Yong Liu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: MemGUI-Agent introduces Context-as-Action (ConAct), which treats context management as first-class actions for long-horizon mobile GUI tasks. Using structured context fields (folded action history, folded UI state, recent step record) instead of passive history accumulation, it prevents prompt explosion and fact dilution. Trained on MemGUI-3K (2,956 trajectories), the 8B model achieves state-of-the-art open-data performance on MemGUI-Bench and generalizes to MobileWorld.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM-based mobile GUI agents using ReAct-style prompting passively accumulate per-step records, which causes prompt explosion and dilution of critical cross-app facts during long-horizon tasks. This makes them unreliable for tasks requiring retention of intermediate facts across many steps and app transitions.

Method: The authors propose MemGUI-Agent with Context-as-Action (ConAct), where context management is emitted as first-class actions alongside UI actions. ConAct maintains three structured context fields: (1) folded action history, (2) folded UI state, and (3) recent step record. This preserves critical UI facts while keeping context compact. The policy jointly selects both UI actions and context management actions. To enable training, they construct MemGUI-3K, a dataset of 2,956 trajectories with full ConAct annotations, and train an 8B model via supervised fine-tuning.

Result: The resulting MemGUI-8B-SFT model achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and successfully generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark.

Conclusion: Proactive context management via ConAct, where context operations are treated as learnable first-class actions, effectively addresses the long-horizon reliability problem in mobile GUI agents without prompt explosion, and the approach generalizes beyond its training distribution.

Abstract: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress on short-horizon tasks, yet remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks that require retaining intermediate facts across many steps and app transitions. We attribute this limitation to ReAct-style prompting, which passively accumulates per-step records, leading to prompt explosion and dilution of critical cross-app facts. To address this, we introduce MemGUI-Agent, an end-to-end long-horizon mobile GUI agent with proactive context management. MemGUI-Agent is built on Context-as-Action (ConAct), which casts context management as first-class actions emitted by the same policy that selects UI actions. Instead of passively appending history, ConAct maintains three structured context fields: folded action history, folded UI state, and recent step record, preserving critical UI facts while keeping context compact. To make proactive context management learnable across model scales, we construct MemGUI-3K, a 2,956-trajectory dataset with full ConAct annotations for supervised training and offline analysis. Training an 8B model on MemGUI-3K produces MemGUI-8B-SFT, an 8B MemGUI-Agent that achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://memgui-agent.github.io/.

</details>


### [169] [MobileForge: Annotation-Free Adaptation for Mobile GUI Agents with Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19930)
*Guangyi Liu,Pengxiang Zhao,Gao Wu,Yiwen Yin,Mading Li,Liang Liu,Congxiao Liu,Zhang Qi,Mengyan Wang,Liang Guo,Yong Liu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: MobileForge is an annotation-free adaptation system that enables MLLM-based mobile GUI agents to adapt to real target apps without manual supervision. It combines MobileGym (for task generation and rollout evaluation in real app environments) with HiFPO (a hierarchical feedback-guided policy optimization method using step-level GRPO updates informed by trajectory outcomes, process feedback, and corrective hints). The adapted model, ForgeOwl-8B, achieves state-of-the-art results among open-data mobile GUI agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adapting MLLM-based GUI agents to real target apps is prohibitively expensive due to the vast number of frequently updated mobile apps, making it impractical to create human-written tasks, demonstrations, or reward labels. Existing annotation-free methods lack a unified framework that integrates target-app exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and feedback, while policy optimization tends to rely on isolated rollouts and coarse rewards that provide unreliable improvement signals.

Method: MobileForge comprises two components: (1) MobileGym, which grounds task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interactions, providing a substrate for exploration and curriculum mining; and (2) Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization (HiFPO), which converts trajectory outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints into hint-contextualized step-level GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) updates for reliable policy improvement.

Result: Using only automatically generated annotation-free data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to achieve 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld, approaching the closed-data GUI-specialized GUI-Owl-1.5-8B (69.0%). The adapted ForgeOwl-8B model further reaches 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, establishing it as the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent in the evaluation.

Conclusion: MobileForge demonstrates that annotation-free adaptation can produce mobile GUI agents competitive with or surpassing closed-data specialized models. The combination of grounded task generation via MobileGym and hierarchical feedback-driven policy optimization via HiFPO provides a unified and effective pipeline for adapting GUI agents to real-world apps without manual supervision. Code, data, and models are publicly released.

Abstract: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress in UI understanding and action execution, but adapting them to real target apps remains costly because mobile apps are numerous, frequently updated, and hard to cover with human-written tasks, demonstrations, or reward labels. Existing annotation-free GUI learning reduces manual supervision, yet lacks a unified substrate connecting target-app exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and feedback, while policy optimization often relies on isolated rollouts and coarse rewards that are hard to convert into reliable improvement signals. We present MobileForge, an annotation-free adaptation system for mobile GUI agents. MobileForge consists of MobileGym, which grounds task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interaction, and Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization (HiFPO), which turns trajectory outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints into hint-contextualized step-level GRPO updates. Using only automatically generated annotation-free adaptation data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld, close to the closed-data GUI-specialized GUI-Owl-1.5-8B base model at 69.0%. The MobileForge-adapted ForgeOwl-8B further reaches 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, establishing the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent in our evaluation. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://mobile-forge.github.io/.

</details>


### [170] [AI Conversational Interviewing: Scaling Up Semi-Structured and In-depth Interviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20064)
*Alexander Wuttke,Max Melchior Lang,Christopher Klamm,Quirin Würschinger,Frauke Kreuter*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces "AI Conversational Interviewing," a scalable method for collecting open-ended public opinion data using AI-led interviews. Tested across voice, chat, and free-choice modes with 571 respondents on migration policy, the method surfaces considerations missed by standardized surveys. Participants rated the AI interview as favorably as traditional surveys, though completion rates varied by mode. Open data and pipelines are released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public opinion research faces a persistent trade-off: standardized surveys achieve scale but force responses into researcher-defined categories, missing the diverse, unexpected considerations underlying public sentiment. Conversational interviews capture this richness but are prohibitively expensive and difficult to scale due to reliance on trained human interviewers. The authors aim to resolve this depth-versus-scale dilemma by leveraging AI to conduct open-ended interviews at scale.

Method: The study developed an AI-led conversational interview system and tested it alongside a standardized survey on migration policy with 571 respondents from Prolific and Payback Panel. It pursued three objectives: (1) demonstrating analytical value of conversational data beyond closed-ended items, (2) assessing practical viability through participant evaluations, and (3) experimentally comparing voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice interview modes to inform implementation.

Result: AI conversational transcripts revealed considerations and mental models of migration that the standardized battery missed — including markedly different reasoning patterns among subgroups with similar attitude levels. Participants rated the AI interview at or above the standardized survey across all modes. However, interview completion rates varied significantly by condition (voice vs. chat vs. free-choice).

Conclusion: AI Conversational Interviewing is a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit, successfully combining the depth of conversational methods with the scalability of automated administration. The authors contribute open data and open-source pipeline materials to support the growing literature on using AI to expand public opinion measurement methods.

Abstract: Public opinion research has long faced a trade-off between depth and scale: standardized surveys enable large-scale measurement but restrict respondents to researcher-defined categories, obscuring the diversity of unexpected considerations that underlie public sentiment. More conversational interviews provide richer insights through open-ended probing, but their reliance on trained human interviewers has kept them difficult to scale. This study introduces AI Conversational Interviewing as a method for collecting open-ended public opinion data at scale, pursuing three objectives: to demonstrate the analytical value of conversational text data for questions beyond the reach of closed-ended items; to assess the method's practical viability through participants' own evaluations; and to inform implementation by experimentally comparing voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice interview modes. We conducted a study combining an AI-led interview with a standardized survey on migration policy among 571 respondents recruited via Prolific and Payback Panel. The findings establish AI Conversational Interviewing as a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit. The conversational transcripts surface considerations and reasoning that a comprehensive standardized battery does not capture such as markedly different mental models of migration among subgroups with similar attitudes levels. Among respondents who completed the interview, evaluations of the AI interview were at or above those of the standardized survey across modes, although completion itself varied by condition. By releasing open data and open-source pipeline materials, the study contributes to a growing literature on harnessing artificial intelligence to expand the methods of public opinion measurement.

</details>


### [171] [Editorial Alignment: A Participatory Approach to Engaging Editorial Expertise in LLM-mediated Knowledge Dissemination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20258)
*Simon Aagaard Enni,Malthe Stavning Erslev,Karl-Emil Kjær Bilstrup,Kristoffer Laigaard Nielbo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces "editorial alignment" as a Participatory AI design practice, demonstrated through a case study with a Nordic public knowledge institution where editors co-designed an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface to realign pretrained models with editorial standards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-driven information services threaten to absorb the editorial function of public knowledge institutions. Pretrained LLMs arrive pre-aligned with commercial developers' values and dissemination strategies, undermining institutional editorial authority. The paper seeks to explore how editors can participate in re-aligning LLM interfaces to their own editorial standards.

Method: The authors conducted design workshops with editors from a Nordic public knowledge institution in a case study format. Through these participatory workshops, they co-designed and implemented an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface. The process involved translating editorial practices and values into concrete alignment objectives for technical implementation.

Result: The study produced the concept of "editorial alignment" — framing AI alignment as a participatory design process where the editorial standard functions as a design artefact bridging editorial values and technical alignment objectives. The implemented interface demonstrated how editors could regain agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination.

Conclusion: Editorial alignment creates space for ongoing participation and gives editors meaningful agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination. The approach positions alignment not as a one-time technical fix but as a sustained, participatory design practice that enables public knowledge institutions to maintain their editorial function in the age of LLMs.

Abstract: The emergence of LLM-driven information services is reshaping the conditions under which public knowledge institutions operate, threatening to absorb the editorial function these institutions exist to exercise. While LLMs offer powerful new affordances for knowledge dissemination, editorial authority is challenged by pretrained LLMs that arrive already aligned with the values and dissemination strategies of their commercial developers. This paper investigates editor participation in re-aligning LLM interfaces to editorial standards through design workshops, in a case study where we design and implement an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface with a Nordic public knowledge institution. We introduce editorial alignment as a design practice within Participatory AI, framing AI alignment as a design process and positioning the editorial standard as a design artefact that translates editorial practice and values into alignment objectives for technical implementation. Last, we discuss how editorial alignment can create space for ongoing participation and give editors agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination.

</details>


### [172] [Organizing in the Digital Age: Understanding Community, Challenges, and Consequences in Digitally-facilitated Labor Organizing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20375)
*Frederick Reiber,Alishah Chator,Dana Calacci,Allison McDonald*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This qualitative interview study (n=17) examines how American labor unions use text-based digital platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing, revealing that while these tools are essential for bridging spatial/temporal gaps, they introduce challenges around security, information overload, and trust-building.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The contemporary American workforce is highly geographically dispersed, creating significant spatial and temporal gaps that hinder traditional face-to-face union organizing. Digital communication tools have become necessary to bridge these gaps, yet their role, affordances, and limitations in labor organizing remain underexplored.

Method: The study employed 17 qualitative, semi-structured interviews with workers from various labor unions who use digital, text-based communication platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing purposes. Thematic analysis was conducted to identify challenges and opportunities.

Result: Digital tools were found to be integral to contemporary labor organizing successes, enabling communication across dispersed workforces. However, three key problem areas emerged: (1) navigating technical security concerns, (2) managing information overload, and (3) building trust and consensus in text-based environments. These factors introduce novel complexities into union organizing practices.

Conclusion: Digital communication platforms are now indispensable for labor organizing in a dispersed workforce, but they are double-edged — enabling coordination while simultaneously introducing socio-technical friction. The findings contribute to broader understandings of digital organizing and highlight the need for unions to strategically address security, information management, and trust dynamics when adopting these tools.

Abstract: The contemporary American labor force is highly dispersed, necessitating the use of digital communication tools to bridge spatial and temporal gaps in union organizing. This study provides an in-depth analysis of how workers within various labor unions utilize digital, text-based communication platforms -- including Discord, WhatsApp, and Slack -- for labor organizing. Through 17 qualitative interviews, we examine the challenges and opportunities presented by digital organizing, identifying both technical and social obstacles. Our findings reveal that although digital tools are integral to contemporary labor successes, they also introduce new complexities, such as navigating technical security, managing information overload, and building trust and consensus. Based on these insights, we draw connections to broader understandings of digital organizing and the role of digital tools in unions.

</details>


### [173] [DataMagic: Transforming Tabular Data into Data Insight Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20388)
*Yupeng Xie,Chen Ma,Zhenyang Wang,Liangwei Wang,Jiayi Zhu,Chuxuan Zeng,Zhouan Shen,Boyan Li,Yuyu Luo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: DataMagic is an end-to-end system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos, using a declarative specification (DVSpec) for data fidelity and a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture for narrative coherence, while supporting interactive exploration modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Producing high-quality data videos requires multidisciplinary expertise (data analysis, narrative design, video production). Existing tools fall short: BI dashboards lack narrative and animation; authoring tools require pre-prepared visualizations, not raw data; generative video models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance. An integrated solution is needed.

Method: The system introduces: (1) DVSpec, a declarative specification binding visual/animation elements to data fields via semantic references for data fidelity; (2) a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that parallel-generates candidate scenes and globally optimizes narrative coherence to manage design-space combinatorics; (3) three interaction modes and provenance-based structured Q&A enabled by DVSpec's logic-rendering decoupling.

Result: Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of DataMagic in generating narrative data-insight videos from raw tabular data.

Conclusion: DataMagic demonstrates a viable end-to-end approach for automatically producing high-fidelity, interactive narrative data videos directly from raw data, bridging the gap between static visualization and manual video production.

Abstract: Data videos integrate dynamic charts, voice narration, and synchronized animations to communicate data insights as temporal narratives, making them an effective medium for improving data consumption efficiency in the data management lifecycle. However, producing high-quality data videos requires expertise spanning data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing approaches fall short: static visualization tools (e.g., BI dashboards) lack narrative logic and animation; authoring tools require users to pre-prepare visualizations rather than working from raw data; pixel-level video generation models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance. We demonstrate DataMagic, an end-to-end interactive system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos. To ensure data fidelity, DataMagic introduces the declarative specification DVSpec, which binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields through data-driven semantic references. To address the combinatorial explosion of the design space, DataMagic adopts a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that generates candidate scenes in parallel and then optimizes narrative coherence through global orchestration. Leveraging DVSpec's decoupling of logic and rendering, the system further supports three interaction modes and structured provenance-based data Q&A, transforming one-way videos into explorable interactive data interfaces. Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of the DataMagic. Homepage: https://datamagic-home.github.io/

</details>


### [174] [Human-AI Agent Interaction in a Business Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18716)
*Kathrin Paimann,Elizangela Valarini,Sebastian Juhl*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study explores principles, criteria, and measurement methods for positive user experience (UX) in human-AI agent interactions within business contexts. Using a mixed-methods approach, it identifies user expectations to foster adoption, trust, and user-centered design decisions, culminating in a survey experiment to evaluate design element effectiveness at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents become embedded in core business processes, there is a pressing need to understand how to design interaction patterns that create value. The study is motivated by the goal of facilitating user adoption, building trust, and enabling user-centered decision-making by development teams through identification of UX principles and user expectations.

Method: A mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative techniques is employed. Initial exploratory research identifies interaction patterns between humans and AI agents. These findings then inform the development of a survey experiment designed to evaluate the effectiveness of specific design elements at a larger scale.

Result: The paper reports exploratory findings on human-AI agent interaction patterns, which serve as the foundational basis for constructing a larger-scale survey experiment. Specific empirical results from the survey experiment are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: This foundational research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings, providing a basis for future design and evaluation of UX principles for AI agents.

Abstract: As AI agents are increasingly integrated into core business processes, understanding and designing effective interaction patterns between humans and AI agents becomes crucial for value creation. This study identifies and evaluates principles and criteria for a positive User Experience (UX) with AI agents, along with methods for its measurement. We identify user expectations and needs to facilitate adoption, build trust, and support user-centered decision-making by development teams. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative techniques, we explore interaction patterns between humans and AI agents. The findings from this exploratory research serve as the basis to develop a survey experiment which evaluates the effectiveness of specific design elements on a larger scale. This foundational research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings.

</details>

### [175] [Secure Coding Drift in LLM-Assisted Post-Quantum Cryptography Development: A Gamified Fix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19474)
*R. D. N. Shakya,C. P. Wijesiriwardana,S. M. Vidanagamachchi,Nalin A. G. Arachchilage*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Introduces "Secure Coding Drift in PQC," a model describing how sustained reliance on LLM-generated code gradually erodes secure coding practices in post-quantum cryptography implementations, and proposes a gamified, LLM-augmented framework with adversarial evaluation and behavioral feedback to mitigate this risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PQC transition demands rigorous constant-time execution, side-channel resistance, and precise parametrization, yet LLMs increasingly used in cryptographic engineering are known to produce insecure code. Prior work only addresses static vulnerabilities, missing the longitudinal behavioral degradation arising from human-AI interaction during development.

Method: The authors conceptualize security risk as a socio-technical, longitudinal behavioral phenomenon (Secure Coding Drift). They then propose a gamified, LLM-augmented secure coding framework integrating adversarial evaluation, behavioral feedback loops, and security scoring directly into development workflows, repositioning LLMs as active security co-pilots.

Result: The paper presents a novel vulnerability model and a mitigation framework; specific empirical results or quantitative evaluations are not described in the abstract.

Conclusion: Reframing LLMs from passive assistants to active security co-pilots via gamified, feedback-driven frameworks can contribute to safer PQC implementations in AI-mediated environments, counteracting the gradual erosion of secure coding practices.

Abstract: The transition to Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) introduces considerable implementation complexity, requiring strict adherence to constant-time execution, side channel resistance, and precise parametrisation. Simultaneously, large language models (LLMs) are heavily embedded in software development workflows, including cryptographic engineering. While LLMs improve productivity, evidence shows that they frequently generate insecure or suboptimal code, particularly in security critical domains. This paper introduces Secure Coding Drift in PQC, a novel socio technical vulnerability model capturing the gradual degradation of secure coding practices due to sustained reliance on LLM-generated code. Unlike prior work that focuses on static vulnerabilities, we conceptualise security risk as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon rising from human AI interaction. To mitigate this, we propose a gamified, LLM augmented secure coding framework that embeds adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into development workflows. Our approach reframes LLMs from passive assistants into active security co-pilots, contributing toward safer PQC implementation in AI mediated environments.

</details>


### [176] [FloatDoor: Platform-Triggered Backdoors in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19535)
*Nils Loose,Jonas Sander,Felix Mächtle,Thomas Eisenbarth*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FloatDoor introduces the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack on LLMs. By exploiting floating-point non-associativity and platform-specific numerical divergence, two lightweight LoRA adapters cause a model to behave maliciously only on a target platform (e.g., specific GPU/TPU) while remaining benign elsewhere, creating a time-of-check/time-of-use gap in model auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in safety-critical settings like software engineering, yet identical models produce measurably different outputs across deployment platforms due to non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. This platform-dependent variability represents an underexplored attack surface. The authors aim to demonstrate that adversaries can exploit this to create backdoors that evade pre-deployment auditing.

Method: FloatDoor uses two lightweight LoRA adapters: (1) a "divergence amplifier" adapter that exaggerates inter-platform numerical differences to create a stable platform-specific signature, and (2) a "binding" adapter that ties this signature to a malicious downstream behavior. The approach is input-independent — the backdoor triggers solely based on the deployment platform's floating-point computation characteristics, not on input patterns. The method preserves aggregate model utility so the backdoor remains stealthy during evaluation.

Result: FloatDoor was demonstrated on Qwen3-4B across multiple deployment targets including NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. The attack reliably induced exploitable code vulnerabilities (e.g., in software engineering tasks) selectively on the target platform while maintaining benign behavior on all other platforms.

Conclusion: FloatDoor establishes a new class of LLM deployment attacks that exploit platform-dependent numerical variability. The work highlights a critical vulnerability in model supply chains: a model passing security audits on one platform may behave maliciously when served on another. This underscores the urgent need for trusted, verifiable model supply chains in sensitive LLM-powered applications.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in sensitive settings such as software engineering, where their outputs directly shape downstream artifacts. Recent work has shown that an identical model can produce measurably different outputs depending on the deployment platform, a consequence of non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. We study the security implications of this platform-dependent variability and uncover a novel attack surface on LLM deployments. We introduce FloatDoor, the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack against generative LLMs. The compromised model exhibits adversary-chosen behavior when served on a target platform and is otherwise benign. FloatDoor is realized through two lightweight LoRA adapters, one that amplifies inter-platform numerical divergence and one that binds the resulting platform signature to a malicious downstream task, while leaving aggregate model utility largely intact. FloatDoor exploits a pronounced time-of-check, time-of-use gap between model auditing and serving. We demonstrate FloatDoor on Qwen3-4B across a broad range of deployment targets, including NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. As a final case study, we show that FloatDoor reliably induces exploitable code vulnerabilities on a chosen target platform. Our results establish a new class of attacks on LLM deployments and underscore the pressing need for trusted model supply chains in sensitive, LLM-powered applications.

</details>


### [177] [G-Lox: Group-Adaptive, Privacy-Preserving Bridge Distribution with Two-Party Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19620)
*Baigang Chen,Nicholas Hopper*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: G-Lox extends the Lox anonymity system with group-adaptive bridge distribution, using two-server secure computation to enable stateful group-level policies (blockage reporting, reassignment, splitting) while preserving distributor blindness—achieving low overhead (~0.25s per iteration, ~3KB communication) and improved robustness against Sybil attacks and group-specific blocking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing bridge distribution systems like Lox offer distributor blindness but treat all users uniformly, lacking the ability to adapt distribution policies per group. Meanwhile, systems like rBridge provide group-level adaptation but sacrifice distributor blindness. The motivation is to simultaneously achieve both properties: hidden group-level stateful adaptation without any single server learning group identifiers or group-to-bridge assignments.

Method: G-Lox places adaptive assignment logic behind a two-server privacy wall. It uses distributed point functions (DPF) / function secret sharing (FSS) protocols and secure two-party computation (2PC) for private state access and state-dependent updates. This enables three key operations: (1) blockage reporting, (2) transport-aware reassignment, and (3) privacy-preserving group splitting. The system never reveals group identifiers or assignments to any single server. Implementation is in C++ using the EMP framework over real TCP sockets.

Result: System measurements show low client-visible overhead: communication stays in low-KiB range across state sizes up to 2^16. At M=1024, the client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in ~0.25s. Policy simulations with group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration demonstrate that G-Lox improves robustness over Lox- and rBridge-like baselines while maintaining broad issuance.

Conclusion: G-Lox demonstrates that group-adaptive, stateful bridge distribution can be achieved with strong privacy guarantees and practical performance, offering a superior trade-off between anonymity (distributor blindness) and robustness (group-level adaptation) compared to prior systems.

Abstract: We present G-Lox (group-adaptive Lox), a bridge-distribution system that preserves Lox-style distributor blindness while enabling hidden, stateful group-level adaptation. G-Lox places adaptive assignment logic behind a two-server privacy wall, so no single server learns group identifiers or group-to-bridge assignments. Private state access and state-dependent updates use two-server DPF/FSS protocols and secure two-party computation, supporting blockage reporting, transport-aware reassignment, and privacy-preserving group splitting.
  We evaluate G-Lox through system measurements and policy simulation. In our C++/EMP implementation over real TCP sockets, private state access has low client-visible overhead: across state sizes up to 2^16, communication remains in the low-KiB range per iteration. At M=1024, the client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in about 0.25 s. Simulations with group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration show that G-Lox improves robustness over Lox- and rBridge-like baselines among systems that maintain broad issuance.

</details>


### [178] [PUFFERDOS: Efficient and Effective Attack String Generation for Regular Expression Denial of Service Vulnerabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19654)
*Shangzhi Xu,Ziqi Ding,Xiao Cheng,Yuekang Li,Nan Sun,Benjamin Turnbull,Shuangxiang Kan,Siqi Ma*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PUFFERDOS is an attack string generator that synthesizes realistic-length, program-level validated inputs to effectively exploit ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs, overcoming limitations of prior static and dynamic approaches that generate impractical attack strings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ReDoS detection tools generate attack strings that are impractical for real-world exploitation because they assume unrealistic input-length budgets and lack program-level validation of attack effectiveness. This renders many generated attack strings useless against real programs.

Method: PUFFERDOS defines three vulnerable regex patterns via formal verification, synthesizes attack strings matching these patterns, then refines and validates them using ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution to ensure real-world exploitability within realistic length budgets.

Result: The paper claims PUFFERDOS can generate attack strings that are both feasible within realistic length constraints and validated at the program level, enabling effective exploitation of ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs where prior techniques fail.

Conclusion: Combining pattern-based synthesis with compositional concolic execution yields a practical and effective approach for generating real-world-exploitable ReDoS attack strings, significantly improving over purely static or dynamic methods that ignore length budgets and program-level validation.

Abstract: ReDoS attacks constitute a critical class of resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities. In such attacks, adversaries exploit the pathological worst-case execution behavior of regular expression (regex) engines to induce highly asymmetric computational workloads, ultimately exhausting system resources and degrading service availability. To protect systems against ReDoS attacks, numerous detection techniques have been proposed that simulate the attack process by generating attack strings to proactively exploit ReDoS vulnerabilities at the early development stage and facilitate remediation. Existing techniques broadly fall into two classes: static analyses that search for pathological regex structures, and dynamic exploration methods that synthesize candidate attack strings. However, the generated attack strings are often impractical for real-world exploitation because they usually assume unrealistic input-length budgets and do not validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the attack at the program level. Therefore, many generated strings fail to trigger vulnerable regexes when applied to real-world programs, further limiting the practical utility. To address these shortcomings, we introduce an effective and efficient attack string generator, PUFFERDOS, designed to synthesize attack inputs that are both feasible within realistic length budgets and validated at the program level, enabling effective exploitation of ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs. Specifically, we first define three vulnerable patterns based on our observation and formal verification. According to the patterns, PUFFERDOS conducts a synthesis technique to generate attack strings, and then refines and validates the strings with ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution to guarantee real-world exploitability.

</details>


### [179] [A Layered Security Framework Against Prompt Injection in RAG-Based Chatbots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19660)
*Gulshan Saleem,Nisar Ahmed,Muhammad Imran Zaman,Ali Hassan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A three-layer middleware framework for defending LLM-based RAG systems against both direct and indirect prompt injection attacks, achieving a reduction in Attack Success Rate from 71.4% to 11.3% with minimal latency overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing prompt injection defenses operate at isolated pipeline stages (input filters miss retrieved documents; output monitors miss malicious payloads reaching the model), leaving RAG chatbots vulnerable to indirect injection where poisoned knowledge-base documents compromise all queries that retrieve them. A comprehensive, multi-stage defense is needed.

Method: A three-layer model-agnostic middleware framework: Layer 1 screens user input via rule-based pattern matching and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier; Layer 2 enforces provenance-based instruction hierarchy during context assembly to prevent retrieved content from overriding operator policy; Layer 3 audits model output using a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector. A continuous audit loop aggregates logs and supports classifier retraining against emerging attacks.

Result: Evaluated on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B: ASR reduced from 71.4% to 11.3%, outperforming the best single-layer baseline by 27.3 pp and a published guardrail system by 23.8 pp, with a 4.8% false positive rate and 61.2 ms median latency overhead. Ablation studies confirmed complementary protection across all three layers with synergistic combined effects.

Conclusion: The three-layer framework provides effective, complementary defense against both direct and indirect prompt injection in RAG pipelines, is model-agnostic, deploys as middleware, and adapts to emerging threats through continuous audit and retraining.

Abstract: Prompt injection is ranked as the most critical vulnerability in large language model (LLM) deployments by the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, yet existing defenses operate at isolated pipeline stages and remain incomplete. Input filters cannot inspect retrieved documents, while output monitors cannot prevent malicious payloads from reaching the model. Consequently, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbots remain vulnerable to indirect injection, where a poisoned knowledge-base document compromises every user whose query retrieves it. We present a three-layer framework that intercepts both direct and indirect prompt injection throughout the inference pipeline. Layer 1 screens user input using a rule-based pattern library and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier. Layer 2 enforces a provenance-based instruction hierarchy during context assembly, preventing retrieved content from overriding operator policy. Layer 3 audits model output using a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector before delivery. A continuous audit loop aggregates structured logs and supports retraining to adapt the classifier to emerging attack patterns. The framework is model-agnostic and deploys as middleware without modifying the underlying LLM. Evaluation on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B shows that the framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 71.4\% to 11.3\%, outperforming the best single-layer baseline by 27.3 percentage points and a published guardrail system by 23.8 percentage points, while maintaining a 4.8\% false positive rate and a median latency overhead of 61.2 ms. Ablation studies confirm that all three layers provide complementary protection and that their combined effect exceeds the sum of individual contributions.

</details>


### [180] [When Global Gating Is Enough: Admission-Time Hubness Control in Anisotropic Vector Retrieval Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19692)
*Prashant Kumar Pathak,Tarun Kumar Sharma*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes an admission-time gating mechanism to mitigate vector hubness poisoning attacks in RAG systems. Instead of periodic reverse-kNN scans, the method scores each candidate document against sentinel queries before insertion, quarantining hub-like documents. The global gate achieves near-perfect recall (1.0) at the critical embedding-space threshold, with ~1% false positive rate and negligible latency overhead (~3.1% on HNSW).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing defenses against hubness-based poisoning in RAG rely on periodic reverse-kNN scans, which leave a vulnerability window between scans and impose repeated corpus-wide computational work. The authors aim to shift defense to admission time — intercepting poisoned documents before they enter the vector index — thereby eliminating the exposure window and reducing recurring costs.

Method: The core approach is an admission-time gate that scores each candidate document against a fixed set of sentinel queries. If a document acts as a hub (nearest neighbor to many sentinel queries), it is quarantined before index insertion. The paper evaluates: (1) a global gate with shared thresholds, (2) a per-topic gate with topic-specific thresholds. Key technical features include incremental threshold maintenance, corpus-size-independent insertion cost, and amortized deletion cost. Experiments span two 100K-document corpora, five encoders, disjoint attacker/defender query sets, and HotFlip adversarial attacks. Approximate indexing effects are also tested on HNSW.

Result: The global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point (≥0.92 across the effective range) and 0.91 ± 0.07 on HotFlip attacks, with 1% false positives on general documents. Per-topic gating provides no reliable benefit, which the authors attribute to anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Threshold maintenance is incremental and efficient. On HNSW, admission adds ~3.1% to ingestion latency; scoring remains flat up to 10^6 vectors. Only 1.2% of decisions flip under approximate indexing, and none involve attack documents. Provenance is identified as a complementary mechanism for natural or tight-domain hubs.

Conclusion: Admission-time gating with sentinel queries is a practical, low-overhead defense against vector hubness poisoning in RAG. The approach eliminates the exposure window inherent to periodic scanning, scales independently of corpus size for insertion, and maintains high recall with few false positives. Per-topic gating offers no advantage due to embedding anisotropy. The method integrates well with approximate indexing and can be complemented by provenance-based checks for edge cases.

Abstract: Vector hubness, where a few points become nearest neighbors of many queries, creates a poisoning risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): one injected document can influence unrelated requests. Existing defenses use periodic reverse-kNN scans, leaving an exposure window and repeated corpus-wide work. We study admission-time control, scoring each candidate against sentinel queries and quarantining hub-like documents before insertion. Across two 100,000-document corpora, five encoders, and disjoint attacker and defender query sets, a global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point (>=0.92 across the effective range) and 0.91 +/- 0.07 on HotFlip attacks, with 1% false positives on general documents. A per-topic gate provides no reliable benefit, consistent with anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, with corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion cost. On HNSW, admission adds about 3.1% to ingestion latency, scoring remains flat to 10^6 vectors, and 1.2% of decisions flip under approximate indexing, none involving attacks. Provenance complements the gate for natural or tight-domain hubs.

</details>


### [181] [SafeSpec: Fast and Safe LLM via Dynamic Reflective Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19755)
*Haotian Xu,Zeyang Zhang,Linbao Li,Huadi Zheng,Yu Li,Cheng Zhuo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SafeSpec integrates safety evaluation into speculative decoding by attaching a lightweight safety head to the target model, enabling joint semantic and safety verification in a single forward pass. When unsafe content is detected, it applies rollback and safety-guided multi-sampling to recover safe continuations rather than terminating generation, achieving a 15% attack success rate reduction while preserving 2.06× inference speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM safety defenses are fundamentally incompatible with speculative inference: they either add computational overhead that negates acceleration benefits or disrupt the draft-verify mechanism. No existing framework jointly optimizes inference-time safety and speculative decoding speed, creating a critical gap for deploying safe, efficient LLMs.

Method: SafeSpec introduces three key components: (1) a lightweight latent safety head attached to the target model that jointly evaluates semantic validity and safety in one forward pass during the verification stage; (2) a rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling mechanism that recovers safe continuations when unsafe generations are detected, rather than terminating abruptly; (3) a formal model of jailbreak attacks as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase harmful continuation probability without eliminating safe ones, enabling risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process.

Result: On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06× inference speedup on benign workloads. The framework demonstrates a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks.

Conclusion: Speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized rather than treated as conflicting objectives. SafeSpec demonstrates that integrating safety verification into the speculative decoding workflow — with lightweight risk estimation and recovery mechanisms — achieves both strong defense against jailbreak attacks and maintained speedup, establishing a new paradigm for safe, efficient LLM deployment.

Abstract: Speculative inference accelerates large language model (LLM) decoding but provides no inherent safety guarantees. Existing safety defenses are largely incompatible with speculative inference: they either introduce additional computation or disrupt the draft-verify mechanism, negating acceleration benefits. This reveals a fundamental incompatibility between current safety methods and speculative decoding. We propose SafeSpec, a safety-aware speculative inference framework that integrates risk estimation directly into the verification process. SafeSpec attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model to jointly evaluate semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass. When unsafe generations are detected, SafeSpec applies rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations rather than terminating generation. We model jailbreak attacks as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase the probability of harmful continuations without eliminating safe ones. Under this model, SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process. Across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks, SafeSpec achieves a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off. On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06x inference speedup on benign workloads, demonstrating that speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized.

</details>


### [182] [DISARM: Target Electronic Device Informed Mitigation of Software Runtime Side-Channel Vulnerabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19807)
*Tasneem Suha,Tanzim Mahfuz,Rima Asmar Awad,Prabuddha Chakraborty*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DISARM is a joint hardware-software methodology that uses real device timing measurements to generate targeted software mitigations for runtime side-channel attacks, outperforming existing solutions across multiple embedded devices in terms of overhead and correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing runtime side-channel mitigation techniques fail to account for the underlying hardware/device characteristics, leading to over-fixing, under-fixing, or outright failures. A hardware-aware approach is needed to produce effective, efficient mitigations.

Method: DISARM employs a joint hardware-software methodology that collects timing values from real embedded devices and uses them to generate targeted software fixes. It supports C, C++, and Java source code and was validated across 22 standard benchmarks on five different embedded/edge devices.

Result: DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions (PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR) across three metrics: execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness, evaluated on five different embedded/edge devices.

Conclusion: A hardware-aware, joint hardware-software approach to runtime side-channel mitigation is essential for producing correct and efficient fixes. DISARM demonstrates that leveraging real device timing data significantly improves mitigation quality over hardware-agnostic techniques.

Abstract: Program runtime or timing attacks exploit variations in a program's execution times to extract sensitive information from the program (e.g. encryption keys, sensitive variable data, intellectual property). State-of-the-art solutions to runtime side-channel attacks attempt to balance the execution time of the sensitive code for different control flow paths to eliminate the timing leakage. However, during the mitigation process, most techniques do not consider the underlying hardware or device on which the target program is supposed to run on. This can lead to over-fixing (unnecessary extra operations), under-fixing (not solving the imbalance properly), and even failures. We propose DISARM, a joint hardware-software methodology (unlike any existing solution) for mitigating runtime side-channel vulnerabilities that utilizes timing values from real embedded devices to generate targeted software fixes. We implement DISARM to support C, C++, and Java source codes and validate it across 22 standard benchmarks. DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions such as PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR in terms of execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness on five different embedded or edge devices.

</details>


### [183] [Heterogeneous LLM Debate Under Adversarial Peers: Honest Gains, Replacement Costs, and Resilience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19826)
*Prashanti Nilayam,Kiran Kumar Ramanna,Prashil Tumbade,Sankalp Nayak*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether heterogeneous LLM debate (using diverse model families as peers) leads to net correction or net harm. By tracking revision behavior across controlled panel configurations, the authors find that an honest heterogeneous peer significantly reduces harmful revisions, while an adversarial one reverses this benefit. Notably, when a malicious same-family peer is already present, adding an honest heterogeneous peer acts as a defense, substantially reducing the loss of initially correct answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent LLM debate has been proposed as a way for diverse models to correct each other's errors. However, the same diversity that enables correction also introduces an attack surface for adversarial influence. The key open question is which effect — correction or adversarial contamination — dominates when heterogeneous peers are introduced into a debate. Prior work has not systematically disentangled these opposing forces.

Method: The authors design a controlled experimental framework with matched panels: (1) homogeneous baseline (same-family agents only), (2) honest-mixed (adding an honest heterogeneous peer), (3) adversarial-mixed (adding an adversarial heterogeneous peer), and (4) contaminated panels where a malicious same-family peer already exists and an honest heterogeneous peer is added. They measure two key metrics: the harmful revision rate (how often correct answers change to incorrect) and the flip rate on initially-correct answers. Experiments span four model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral) and three reasoning benchmarks (MATH-hard, GPQA, MMLU-Pro).

Result: For Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard, the harmful revision rate drops from 89% (homogeneous) to 35% with an honest heterogeneous peer, and rises back to 90% with an adversarial heterogeneous peer. Adversarial effects can be masked on weak defenders when using conditional rates, but end-of-debate flip rates expose the damage. In already-contaminated panels: adding an honest heterogeneous peer cuts the flip rate on initially-correct items from 31% (under a same-family adversary) to 6% for Llama-3.1-70B defenders. The sign of these effects is consistent across model families and benchmarks, though magnitude varies by defender-benchmark regime.

Conclusion: Heterogeneity in LLM debate is a double-edged sword: it is both an attack surface (adversarial peers can cause harm) and, crucially, a defense mechanism. When a malicious agent is already present, introducing an honest heterogeneous peer provides substantial protection, reducing harmful revisions and preserving initially-correct answers. This reframes heterogeneity not merely as a vulnerability but as a practical mitigation strategy in multi-agent LLM systems.
