Abstract: Heterogeneous LLM debate is motivated by the promise that diverse peers correct one another, but the same exchange that carries correction also carries adversarial influence. We measure which dominates by tracking how a heterogeneous peer changes the honest agents' revision behavior: how often they change their answer, and whether the change is corrective or harmful. We compare matched panels (homogeneous baseline, honest-mixed, and adversarial-mixed) and contaminated panels in which a malicious same-family peer is already present, spanning four model families and three reasoning benchmarks. An honest heterogeneous peer sharply lowers harmful revision, and an adversarial one reverses it. For Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard, the honest-slot harmful-revision rate falls from 89% in the homogeneous panel to 35% with an honest peer, and an adversarial peer returns it to 90%. The conditional rate hides this damage on weak defenders, but the end-of-debate flip rate exposes it. The pattern keeps its sign across families and benchmarks while its magnitude varies with the defender-benchmark regime. We also measure the effects when an adversarial same-family peer is already present: an honest heterogeneous peer lowers both harmful revision and the rate at which initially-correct answers are lost. On the same Llama-3.1-70B setting, the added honest peer cuts the flip rate on initially-correct items from 31% under a same-family adversary to 6%. Heterogeneity is therefore not only an attack surface but, when an adversary is already present, also a defense.

</details>


### [184] [Low-Cost Multi-Precision Systolic Arrays for Accelerating FHE NTTs on AI ASICs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19866)
*George Alexakis,Dimitrios Schoinianakis,Giorgos Dimitrakopoulos*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TPUs are limited in accelerating FHE due to a precision mismatch. This paper proposes a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that natively performs full-precision reconstruction within the array, avoiding offloading to vector processors and achieving at least 1.33× speedup for NTT operations on AI hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FHE demands high-precision arithmetic (specifically for NTT), but AI accelerators like TPUs are optimized for low-precision (8-bit) matrix engines. Current solutions use matrix decomposition with shift-and-add accumulation for precision reconstruction, but this reconstruction must be offloaded to vector processors, disrupting the matrix multiplication dataflow and creating a severe performance bottleneck.

Method: The authors propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array architecture that natively performs full-precision output reconstruction within the array itself, synchronized with low-precision matrix multiplication under a unified dataflow. The design is synthesized at 7nm using OpenRoad and evaluated via cycle-accurate simulations with SCALE-Sim.

Result: On 128×128 matrix engines for transform sizes 2^12 to 2^16, the proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33× speedup for native NTT execution compared to existing approaches, with negligible hardware overhead.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-precision systolic array successfully enables standard AI hardware (TPUs) to support high-precision FHE acceleration by eliminating the dataflow disruption caused by offloading full-precision reconstruction to vector processors.

Abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) ensures robust data privacy but suffers from prohibitive computational overhead. Accelerating FHE on AI hardware like Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) is promising, yet fundamentally limited by a precision mismatch: TPUs are optimized for 8-bit arithmetic, whereas FHE and its critical parts such as the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), demand high precision. Current approaches bridge this gap using matrix decomposition to execute NTT computations on low-precision matrix engines. However, reconstructing the full-precision results requires shift-and-add accumulation that does not match the dataflow of matrix multiplication. This forces offloading full-precision reconstruction from matrix engines to vector processors that disrupts the matrix multiplication dataflow, creating significant performance bottleneck. To resolve this limitation, we propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that performs full-precision output reconstruction natively within the array in sync with low-precision matrix multiplication under a uniform dataflow. Synthesized at 7nm with OpenRoad, our design incurs negligible hardware overhead. Cycle-accurate simulations using SCALE-Sim demonstrate that natively executing NTTs on the proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33x speedup, for transform sizes 2^12 to 2^16 on 128x128 matrix engines, successfully enabling standard AI hardware to support high-precision FHE acceleration.

</details>


### [185] [FFinRED: An Expert-Guided Benchmark Generation and Evaluation Framework for Financial LLM Red-Teaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19887)
*Chaeyun Kim,Daeyoung Park,Junghwan Kim,Jinyoung Jeong,Eunji Song,Yongtaek Lim,Minwoo Kim*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FinRED is an expert-guided red-teaming framework for financial LLM safety evaluation, featuring a two-level taxonomy aligned with global standards (FATF, EU DORA), a pipeline converting real financial documents into context-rich behavioral prompts, and a finance-specific evaluation rubric that reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. It is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute regulatory sandbox.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety benchmarks address general adversarial scenarios but overlook finance-specific risks such as regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion. Financial LLMs require targeted, domain-specific safety evaluation frameworks.

Method: FinRED employs: (1) a novel two-level taxonomy mapping global financial standards (FATF, EU DORA) to specific threats; (2) a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) via an expert-defined schema; (3) rigorous expert validation of seed plausibility; and (4) a finance-specific evaluation rubric aligned with ISO/IEC 27001 standards, validated by human experts.

Result: The expert-validated rubric reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12 compared to static one-size-fits-all rubrics and aligns more closely with human expert judgment than existing approaches. The framework has been operationally deployed in South Korea's FSI regulatory sandbox.

Conclusion: FinRED provides a robust, standards-aligned, expert-validated red-teaming framework tailored to financial domain risks, filling a critical gap in LLM safety evaluation. Its regulatory deployment validates real-world applicability, while gated access mitigates dual-use concerns.

Abstract: Existing safety benchmarks target general adversarial scenarios but miss finance-specific risks. Financial LLMs face regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion that require targeted evaluation. We introduce FinRED, an expert-guided red-teaming framework for financial LLM safety evaluation developed with financial experts. FinRED uses a novel two-level taxonomy mapping global standards (e.g., FATF and EU DORA) to threats ranging from regulatory evasion to complex fraud, integrated with a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into context-rich red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) through an expert-defined schema. Rigorous expert validation confirms seed plausibility and realism for meaningful LLM safety evaluation. We also provide an expert-validated, finance-specific rubric that goes beyond disclaimer checks, aligns more closely with human experts than static one-size-fits-all rubrics, and reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. Aligned with internationally adopted risk-management and information-security standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 27001), FinRED is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute (FSI) regulatory sandbox for generative AI security evaluation in real financial services. To mitigate dual-use risks, the dataset, generation pipeline, prompt template, and evaluation framework are gated for qualified researchers at https://github.com/selectstar-ai/FinRED-paper and https://huggingface.co/datasets/datumo/FinRED.

</details>


### [186] [AutoTam: Specifying Secure Protocol Implementations with Tamarin Model Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19937)
*Johannes Wilson,Mikael Asplund,Niklas Johansson*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A language-first approach that uses a domain-specific language (DSL) for cryptographic protocol implementations, enabling automatic generation of Tamarin models for formal verification of trace properties, with results that provably translate back to the implementation. Symbolic execution is integrated for memory safety analysis. The approach is validated on a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and WireGuard VPN.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formal verification of cryptographic protocols is challenging for practitioners without formal methods background. Two key pain points: (1) modelling protocols for verification tools like Tamarin is non-trivial, and (2) transferring verification results to concrete implementations requires expert knowledge. There is a gap between verified models and actual running code.

Method: A language-first methodology using a domain-specific language (DSL) for writing protocol implementations. The DSL serves as the single source: (a) Tamarin models are automatically generated from it for trace property verification, (b) verified universal trace properties are proven to translate back to the implementation, and (c) symbolic execution is integrated to analyse memory safety of protocol implementations.

Result: The tool successfully generates accurate models for a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and the WireGuard VPN protocol. The WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when using the authors' interpreter and achieves acceptable performance. The implementations are formally proven secure through combined symbolic execution and Tamarin model verification.

Conclusion: The language-first approach bridges the gap between formal verification models and concrete implementations by using a shared DSL. This allows non-experts to obtain formally verified, memory-safe, and interoperable protocol implementations with acceptable performance, as demonstrated on real-world protocols like WireGuard.

Abstract: Formal verification is a challenging but important task for ensuring the security of cryptographic protocols. While modern protocol verification tools significantly reduce verification effort, modelling remains challenging to practitioners without a background in formal verification. In addition, transferring verification results to a concrete protocol implementation requires expert knowledge.
  In this paper, we present a novel language-first method for verification of trace properties using a domain-specific language for protocol implementations. We target the Tamarin prover for verification, and we prove that verified universal trace properties translate back to the implementation. We additionally integrate symbolic execution in order to analyse the memory safety of protocol implementations. We use our tool to implement and generate accurate models for a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol, and for the WireGuard VPN protocol. Our WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when using our interpreter, and achieves acceptable performance. We formally prove our implementations secure using a combination of symbolic execution and verification of the generated Tamarin models.

</details>


### [187] [A Measurement Study of Cryptographic Misuse in Embodied AI Mobile Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19983)
*Junchao Li,Xuelei Wang,Yuhang Huang,Qi Wang,Boyang Ma,Xuelong Dai,Minghui Xu,Yue Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: First large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse in the Embodied AI mobile ecosystem, analyzing 507 apps across 6 EAI domains. Identifies 12,975 misuse instances (80.74% precision) across five failure modes, revealing that EAI-specific engineering constraints (latency-sensitive control paths, offline provisioning, legacy IoT SDKs) systematically weaken cryptographic protections, enabling command interception and physical hijacking of EAI entities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing security research on Embodied AI focuses on devices and cloud infrastructure, but the mobile control layer has been overlooked as a critical attack surface — despite mobile apps increasingly serving as active control-path components that bridge cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust.

Method: The authors construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world EAI mobile applications across six domains. They develop an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to systematically measure the prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes in these applications.

Result: The measurement yields 12,975 cryptographic misuse findings with an evaluated precision of 80.74%. Two key structural trade-offs are uncovered: (1) latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport-layer protection, and (2) reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Case studies demonstrate these flaws enable command-channel interception and physical hijacking of EAI entities.

Conclusion: Mobile applications represent a fragile yet overlooked cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems. The cryptographic failures are not random developer errors but systemic consequences of EAI-specific engineering constraints, demanding domain-specific security interventions.

Abstract: Embodied AI (EAI) mobile applications are evolving from auxiliary user interfaces into active control-path components, directly linking mobile-side cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust. Despite this shift, existing security research predominantly focuses on embodied AI devices and cloud infrastructures, leaving the mobile control layer largely unexplored as a critical attack surface. To bridge this gap, we present the first large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse within the EAI mobile ecosystem. We construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world applications across six EAI domains, and employ an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to measure the prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes. Our measurement yields 12,975 misuse findings (with an evaluated precision of 80.74\%), revealing that these cryptographic failures are driven by EAI-specific engineering constraints rather than random developer errors. We uncover structural security trade-offs: latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport protection, while the heavy reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates the local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Through real-world case studies, we demonstrate how these mobile-side cryptographic flaws bypass nominal network protections, enabling adversaries to intercept command channels and hijack the physical control of EAI entities. Ultimately, our findings highlight that mobile applications have become a fragile, yet overlooked, cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems.

</details>


### [188] [Accelerating Trust Convergence in IIoT: A ML Approach for Dynamic Network Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20214)
*Aymen Bouferroum,Valeria Loscri,Abderrahim Benslimane*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A dynamic trust management approach for IIoT that uses ML to accelerate trust convergence under poor network conditions by predicting convergence time and adapting transition probabilities, achieving up to 28.6% reduction in convergence time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional trust models in IIoT neglect fluctuating network quality, causing slow trust convergence and inaccurate assessments, particularly for resource-constrained devices in dynamic industrial environments.

Method: The proposed Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach integrates Machine Learning to predict the number of time units required for trust convergence based on network metrics, then dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model. The method is evaluated using a simulation framework with realistic IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi channel conditions.

Result: The TCA-based approach achieves up to 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging network conditions and demonstrates resilience against malicious nodes, improving trust evaluation accuracy.

Conclusion: The work provides a scalable and adaptive trust framework suitable for IIoT systems operating in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

Abstract: In Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments, trust management plays a vital role in securing systems, especially when dealing with resource-constrained devices. Traditional trust models often overlook the impact of fluctuating network quality, leading to slower trust convergence and inaccurate assessments. In this paper, we propose a dynamic trust management solution, known as the Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach, which integrates Machine Learning (ML) to accelerate trust convergence under poor network conditions. Our model predicts the number of time units needed for trust convergence based on key network metrics and dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model to enhance convergence speed. Using a simulation framework that incorporates realistic Wi-Fi channel conditions based on the IEEE 802.11 standard, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the TCA-based approach, achieving up to a 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging conditions. Furthermore, the proposed solution exhibits resilience in scenarios involving malicious nodes, improving trust evaluation accuracy. This work provides a scalable and adaptive trust framework for IIoT systems in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

</details>


### [189] [GNSS Spoofing Threat for V2X communications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20215)
*Adolfo P. Jimenez,Juan Arquero-Gallego,Mario P. Luna,Jose E. Naranjo,Felipe Jimenez Alonso*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that V2X communications are critically vulnerable to GNSS spoofing attacks. Using inexpensive SDR equipment (HackRF One), the authors develop a pipeline for generating high-fidelity fake GPS baseband signals and validate the attack on real Commsignia OBU and RSU devices across three speed scenarios (90, 145, 200 km/h), showing that spoofing causes undetected service degradation in V2X Cooperative Awareness Messages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNSS is a core enabler of PNT services in V2X for generating CAMs that ensure network reliability and vehicular safety. However, GNSS signals are inherently vulnerable to spoofing attacks where adversaries transmit counterfeit signals mimicking legitimate satellites, causing receivers to compute false positions. The authors aim to expose that V2X communications lack adequate security countermeasures against such physical-layer attacks, even when executed with low-cost, readily available SDR hardware.

Method: The authors design a physical GNSS spoofing methodology using an inexpensive HackRF One SDR. Their coordinate generation pipeline includes: (1) Haversine-based distance calculations for geographic coordinate manipulation, (2) temporal discretization to emulate constant velocity movement, and (3) linear interpolation for smooth trajectory generation, ultimately producing high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OBU and RSU hardware across three synthetic trajectory scenarios at steady speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h.

Result: The spoofing attack successfully compromised real Commsignia OBU and RSU devices across all three tested speed scenarios. The V2X communications experienced service degradation as a result of GNSS spoofing, and critically, this degradation occurred without being detected by the system, demonstrating a lack of integrity monitoring or anti-spoofing defenses in the V2X communication stack.

Conclusion: V2X communications are not secured against GNSS spoofing attacks. The feasibility of executing such attacks with low-cost SDR hardware (HackRF One) underscores a significant and practical security gap. The undetected degradation of CAM-based services highlights the urgent need for robust anti-spoofing countermeasures and integrity verification mechanisms in V2X systems to ensure vehicular safety and network reliability.

Abstract: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) constitute a core technology for delivering crucial positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services in the Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) domain, where they are indispensable for generating Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM) that uphold network reliability and vehicular safety. Yet, GNSS signals are acutely exposed to spoofing, an advanced attack in which an adversary transmits crafted signals that replicate legitimate satellite characteristics, misleading the receiver into computing a false position. This work presents a methodology for conducting physical spoofing with inexpensive Software Defined Radio (SDR), describing a coordinate generation pipeline that employs Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization to emulate constant velocity, and linear interpolation to produce high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The proposed attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OnBoard Unit (OBU) and RoadSide Unit (RSU) devices using a HackRF One across three scenarios that emulate synthetic trajectories at steady speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h. The most significant contribution of this paper is the demonstration that V2X communications are not secured, as they are susceptible to GNSS spoofing attacks, which cause service degradation without being detected.

</details>


### [190] [TrustMix: How to Mix Messages in a Mobile Ad-hoc Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20251)
*Yu Shen,Aiswarya Walter,Stefanie Roos*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TrustMix is a decentralized mix network protocol for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) that provides anonymity without trusted central parties, using group-based shuffling and linkable ring signatures for rate limiting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mix networks are designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied to MANETs. The few MANET solutions require advance topology knowledge or a trusted central party. There is a need for a fully decentralized anonymous communication protocol tailored to the ad hoc mobile environment.

Method: TrustMix organizes users into groups. A sender forwards a message to a nearby trusted party's group, where all group members collectively shuffle messages before forwarding to subsequent groups. This multi-group hop-and-shuffle mechanism unlinks original and forwarded messages. Linkable ring signatures enforce per-party rate limits without identity disclosure. Security is proven in the random oracle model, anonymity is evaluated via simulation, and a proof-of-concept Android implementation demonstrates real-world feasibility.

Result: TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity compared to baselines in mix-network simulations. The Android proof-of-concept with 5 mobile devices achieves acceptable throughput, demonstrating practical viability.

Conclusion: TrustMix provides a practical, fully decentralized anonymity solution for MANETs, combining group-based message shuffling with linkable ring signatures for rate limiting, with provable security and real-world feasibility on mobile devices.

Abstract: Mix networks are a highly effective way to achieve anonymity, defending against a wide range of traffic-analysis attacks. However, mix networks are usually designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied in the context of mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). The few existing solutions for MANETs require advance knowledge of the topology or a trusted central party.
  In this paper, we present TrustMix, a mix protocol for MANETs that operates without any central trusted party. In TrustMix, parties join groups and then messages are forwarded via multiple groups to provide anonymity. With TrustMix, users only need to find a party nearby that they consider trusted. They then forward the message to this party's group, and the party shuffles messages before forwarding to other groups, meaning that the original message and the forwarded message cannot be linked. Furthermore, even if the chosen party is adversarial, they can only break the anonymity if all parties in their group are adversarial as all of them contribute to the shuffling. In addition to anonymity, TrustMix also enforces rate limits on the number of messages through the use of linkable ring signatures, which allows detecting that parties send more messages that allowed without revealing identities.
  We prove the security of our protocol in the random oracle model. We evaluate its anonymity using an existing mix-network simulator and show that TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept Android implementation and show that TrustMix achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices.

</details>


### [191] [Quantization as a Malicious Task: Removing Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors via Task Arithmetic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20254)
*Kaihsun Yang,Min-Yan Tsai,Chia-Mu Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: QVec defends against quantization-conditioned backdoors by interpreting the weight shift from full-precision to quantized models as a malicious task vector and correcting parameters pre-deployment, requiring no retraining or trigger samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing QCB defenses introduce computational overhead or depend on specific quantization settings. A lightweight, general defense is needed that works across quantization methods without retraining or access to trigger samples.

Method: QVec frames the weight difference between full-precision and quantized models as a structured malicious task vector. It estimates this parameter shift via a single quantization pass and applies a controlled correction (with lightweight hyperparameter search) to neutralize the backdoor direction before deployment.

Result: Extensive experiments on image classification benchmarks and multiple LLM attack scenarios show QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while maintaining clean performance.

Conclusion: QVec offers an efficient, parameter-space defense against QCBs that is independent of quantization method, requires no retraining or triggers, and generalizes across vision and language domains.

Abstract: Model quantization is widely adopted to reduce memory usage and inference cost when deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. However, recent studies have revealed a new security threat known as Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs), where a model behaves normally in full precision but activates malicious behavior only after quantization. Existing defenses typically modify quantization procedures or correct activation statistics, often introducing additional computational overhead or relying on specific quantization settings. Here, we present QVec, a parameter-space perspective for defending against QCBs. We observe that the weight difference between a full-precision model and its quantized counterpart encodes a structured behavioral shift, which can be interpreted as a malicious task vector rather than random quantization noise. Based on this insight, QVec counteracts this malicious direction through controlled parameter correction prior to deployment. QVec requires no retraining, no trigger samples, and only a single quantization pass to estimate the parameter shift, together with a lightweight hyperparameter search. Extensive experiments across image classification benchmarks and multiple Large Language Model (LLM) attack scenarios demonstrate that QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean performance.

</details>


### [192] [LLM agent safety, multi-turn red-teaming, jailbreak benchmarks, adversarial robustness, safety-critical systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20408)
*Hanwool Lee,Dasol Choi,Bokyeong Kim,Seung Geun Kim,Haon Park*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: NRT-Bench is a benchmark for multi-turn adversarial red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators in a simulated nuclear power plant. Under adaptive attacks, 8.7–12.1% of sessions result in loss of a critical safety function. Model failures are largely disjoint, and defensive measures show strongly model-dependent effects—sometimes increasing attack success for some models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are increasingly proposed for supervisory roles in safety-critical systems, but their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure is poorly characterized. Existing evaluations lack objective, non-LLM-judged harm signals and multi-turn adversarial dynamics.

Method: NRT-Bench simulates a nuclear power plant control room with a five-role LLM-backed operator team managing six critical safety functions (CSFs). Adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is defined objectively: a run terminates when any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Four frontier operator models are evaluated using a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol.

Result: Adaptive multi-turn attacks push the operator team past a safety limit in 8.7–12.1% of attack sessions across four models. Despite similar aggregate robustness, failures barely overlap: of 149 sessions, none defeat all four models, while one-third defeat at least one—indicating nearly disjoint vulnerabilities. Defensive measures (guardrails, safety-advisor agents) show strongly model-dependent effects, with the same defense lowering attack success for one model while raising it for another.

Conclusion: LLM-agent robustness under adversarial pressure cannot be inferred from aggregate failure rates alone, as vulnerabilities are model-disjoint and defenses are non-transferable. Systematic, objective, multi-turn red-teaming benchmarks like NRT-Bench are essential for reproducible safety evaluation before deploying LLM agents in safety-critical roles.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. A five-role operator team, each backed by a configurable LLM, runs a plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs), while adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal rather than LLM-judged text: a run terminates the moment any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Evaluating four frontier operator models under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, we find that adaptive multi-turn attacks reliably push the operator team past a safety limit: across the four models, between 8.7% and 12.1% of attack sessions end with the plant losing a critical safety function. Although the four models look almost equally robust by this aggregate rate, their failures barely overlap: of $149$ sessions, none defeat all four models while a third defeat at least one, so vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models rather than nested. The effect of added defences is strongly model-dependent: the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent that lowers attack success for one model can raise it for another. We release the simulation venue, attack dataset, and replay tooling for reproducible safety evaluation of LLM agents.

</details>


### [193] [Multi-View Decompilation for LLM-Based Malware Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20436)
*Bercan Turkmen,Vyas Raina*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Using two decompiler views (Ghidra and RetDec) instead of one improves LLM-based malware classification, primarily by boosting recall on malicious samples, because different decompilers make complementary errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based malware classification pipelines rely on a single decompiler's pseudo-C output, but this is fragile because decompilers are lossy heuristic tools. Different decompilers expose different artifacts of the same binary, and relying on just one may miss critical evidence of maliciousness.

Method: Curated a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs across diverse threat behaviors. Each binary was compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec to produce matched pseudo-C views. Multiple LLMs from major model families were evaluated on classification performance using single-decompiler vs. dual-decompiler prompting. Agreement analysis was performed to characterize error patterns between decompilers.

Result: Providing both decompiler views improved malicious-class F1 scores across model families, driven primarily by increased recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses confirmed that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, demonstrating that their outputs offer complementary evidence rather than redundant information.

Conclusion: Multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free method to improve LLM-based malware triage. The approach is practical for real-world settings and highlights the value of leveraging complementary decompiler perspectives.

Abstract: Malware analysts often inspect compiled binaries through decompiled pseudo-C, when source code is unavailable. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can assist this process by classifying decompiled code as benign or malicious, but existing pipelines typically rely on a single decompiler view. We argue that this assumption is fragile: decompilers are lossy heuristic tools, and different decompilers can expose different artefacts of the same binary. We curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning a range of threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, yielding matched pseudo-C views. Across a range of LLMs from major model families, we find that providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1, mainly by increasing recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses further show that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, supporting the view that decompiler outputs provide complementary evidence. Our results suggest that multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free way to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings.

</details>


### [194] [Image Encryption Algorithm Based on Convolutional Neural Networks and Dynamic S-Box Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20444)
*Ans Ibrahim,Fadhil Abbas Fadhil,Mahameed Reza Feizi Derakhshi,Maryam Mahdi Alhusseini,Nikolai Safiullin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper presents a dynamic image encryption method that uses a CNN to generate adaptive, image-dependent S-boxes, enhancing non-linearity, confusion, and resistance to statistical/structural attacks compared to traditional fixed S-boxes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional fixed S-boxes in image encryption are susceptible to linear and differential attacks. The authors aim to improve security and flexibility by making S-boxes dynamic and adaptive, driven by learned image features rather than static cryptographic primitives.

Method: A trained CNN extracts features from the input image, which are then used to generate a personalized, adaptive S-box. This S-box replaces pixel values during encryption, introducing input-dependent non-linearity and confusion. Security is evaluated via entropy, histogram analysis, correlation, NPCR, and UACI metrics.

Result: The CNN-based S-boxes demonstrate greater non-linearity, uniqueness, and input dependence. Security evaluations (entropy, histogram, correlation, NPCR, UACI) indicate the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional fixed S-box approaches.

Conclusion: Combining CNN-based feature extraction with classical cryptography to produce dynamic, image-dependent S-boxes significantly enhances image encryption security, offering stronger resistance to statistical and structural attacks.

Abstract: The paper proposes a dynamic approach to image encryption, combining the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and classical cryptography to improve the security and flexibility of image encryption. The main concept is to create adaptive Substitution boxes (S-boxes) based on characteristics that are learned by a trained CNN. The CNN-based S-boxes can be relied on for more non-linearity, uniqueness, and input image dependence than the conventional fixed S-boxes because they are susceptible to the linear and differential attacks. This dynamic behaviour enhances the confusion property and makes it more resistant to statistical and structural attacks. The encryption algorithm consists of CNN-based feature extraction and the creation of a personalised S-box to replace the pixels. Entropy, histogram analysis, correlation, NPCR, and UACI enable security assessment of generated S-boxes based on the CNN, indicating that the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional ones.

</details>


### [195] [Analyzing Defensive Misdirection Against Model-Guided Automated Attacks on Agentic AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20470)
*Reza Soosahabi,Vivek Namsani*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the security of agentic AI systems against automated jailbreak and prompt-injection attacks. It shows that conventional detect-and-block defenses fail under large query budgets because predictable refusals leak feedback to attackers. The authors propose "detect-and-misdirect," a strategy that replaces refusals with misleading but safe responses to degrade the attacker's automated judge. Their proof-of-concept, Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), reduces attack success rate upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As agentic AI systems become more prevalent, they face increasingly automated and scalable jailbreak/prompt-injection attacks. Existing detect-and-block defenses are insufficient because predictable refusal patterns provide implicit feedback that automated attacker judges can exploit to iteratively refine attacks. There is a need for a defense strategy that denies attackers useful signal while remaining safe.

Method: The authors first formalize the attack-defense setting using a probabilistic model encompassing the target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. They analyze the asymptotic behavior of detect-and-block, proving ASR approaches 1 under sufficient query budgets. They then propose detect-and-misdirect, which issues controlled, non-operational responses to detected malicious inputs, aiming to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge and thus reduce the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates. The proof-of-concept realization, CMPE, is a lightweight conversational misdirection method that replaces refusal text with safe, strategically misleading responses. Evaluation is conducted on jailbreak benchmarks with end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.

Result: CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack evaluations.

Conclusion: Detect-and-misdirect is a principled and effective alternative to detect-and-block for defending agentic AI systems against automated jailbreak attacks. By denying attackers reliable feedback, the strategy bounds asymptotic ASR and significantly raises the cost of successful exploitation.

Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly rely on language-model components to interpret instructions, process external data, invoke tools, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks more consequential, especially as attackers adopt model-guided automation to scale probing, prompt refinement, and response evaluation. This work analyzes the resulting attack-defense setting through a probabilistic model of a target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. Our analysis shows that conventional detect-and-block defenses can allow attacker success rate (ASR) to approach one as the query budget grows, since predictable refusals provide useful feedback to automated search. We then examine detect-and-misdirect, where detected malicious interactions receive controlled, non-operational responses designed to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge. This strategy reduces the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates and yields a bounded asymptotic ASR. We evaluate a proof-of-concept realization of this strategy through Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), a lightweight conversational misdirection method designed to replace predictable refusal text with safe but strategically misleading responses in automated jailbreak settings. On jailbreak benchmarks, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.

</details>


### [196] [A-COMPASS: Formal Foundations for Anonymity Analysis in Microdata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20492)
*Tamara Tagliavia,Silvia Ghilezan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces A-COMPASS, a modified version of the COMPASS language that operates on standard microdata tables (one record per person) instead of grouped tables. A-COMPASS adds the ability to execute anonymization actions, formalizes its syntax and semantics, proves key semantic properties (determinism and compositionality), and provides mechanisms for verifying anonymity properties like k-anonymity and l-diversity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The domain of formal verification of data privacy models remains insufficiently explored. Existing work (COMPASS) operates on preprocessed tables in a "one record–one group" format, which does not match the natural form of microdata (one record–one person). There is a need for a formal language that can both specify/verify privacy conditions and execute anonymization actions directly on standard microdata tables.

Method: The authors modify the COMPASS language to create A-COMPASS, which operates on microdata tables in their usual one-record-per-person form. They provide a formal syntax and semantics for A-COMPASS, prove its determinism and compositionality properties, and develop a verification mechanism for anonymity properties including k-anonymity and l-diversity.

Result: A-COMPASS is presented with formal syntax and semantics. The language supports both checking previously applied anonymity conditions and executing anonymization actions (a new feature). The semantics are proven to satisfy determinism and compositionality. A verification mechanism for k-anonymity and l-diversity is provided.

Conclusion: A-COMPASS advances the formal verification of privacy models by adapting COMPASS to operate on standard microdata, adding anonymization execution capabilities, and providing rigorous semantic foundations with proven properties, along with practical verification of well-known anonymity metrics.

Abstract: In the information age, one of the leading problems is how to ensure individual's privacy. Depending on the context in which privacy is considered, various data privacy models have emerged. However, the domain of formal verification of these models is still not sufficiently explored even when it comes to the most basic models. An attempt to verify privacy requirements is the Compliance Assertion Language (COMPASS). In COMPASS, one can specify an anonymity condition that a table needs to satisfy, and an action that will modify the table if the condition is not satisfied. It is designed to operate on preprocessed tables in a form one record - one group of people. In this paper, we modify the COMPASS language in order to operate on microdata tables in their usual form of one record - one person. The modified language is called A-COMPASS. Along with checking of previously applied anonymity conditions, A-COMPASS enables the execution of anonymization actions as a new feature. We further provide the syntax and the semantics for the A-COMPASS language. We also prove the most important properties of the introduced semantics like determinism and compositionality. Finally, we provide a mechanism to verify anonymity properties, such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.

</details>


### [197] [Calibration Without Comprehension: Diagnosing the Limits of Fine-Tuning LLMs for Vulnerability Detection in Systems Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20502)
*Arastoo Zibaeirad,Marco Vieira*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A study using 834 curated Linux kernel vulnerability samples (74 CWEs) with strict temporal splits finds LLMs lack genuine security reasoning. Data contamination provides no advantage, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning, and even the best models barely exceed random chance (52.1% detection, <1.3% Top-1 CWE accuracy). Fine-tuning produces only calibration, not comprehension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether LLMs that score well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely exploit data contamination (pattern matching on memorized training data), and to develop diagnostic metrics that can distinguish between these two explanations.

Method: The authors built CWE-Trace, a framework using 834 manually curated Linux kernel vulnerability samples across 74 CWEs, organized as context-aware vulnerable--patched pairs. A strict temporal split separates pre-2025 historical data from post-cutoff leakage-free data. Two novel diagnostic metrics are introduced: the Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). Eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants were evaluated on non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification tasks.

Result: Two key findings: (1) Data contamination provides no measurable advantage — 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal, vulnerable functions are absent or cross-mapped, and ~31% carry CWE misclassification. (2) Backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning — models show stable, systematic failure modes (DFI: -85.5 to +94.8 pp) persisting across temporal splits and resisting correction. Fine-tuning merely shifts output thresholds without changing decision policy (calibration without comprehension). DeepSeek-R1, weakest at binary detection, gained most in CWE classification, showing detection and understanding are decoupled. Best detection: 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE Top-1 accuracy: below 1.3%.

Conclusion: Current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software regardless of fine-tuning strategy. Neither data contamination nor fine-tuning yields genuine vulnerability comprehension; models merely exhibit calibration shifts while their underlying decision policies remain unchanged and systematically biased.

Abstract: Whether LLMs scoring well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data remains unresolved. We present CWE-Trace, a framework for LLM vulnerability detection built from 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples spanning 74 CWEs. The framework enforces a strict temporal split (pre-2025 historical set / post-cutoff leakage-free set), preserves context-aware vulnerable--patched pairs, and introduces two diagnostic metrics: the Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). We evaluate eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification. Our analysis yields two key results. First, data contamination provides no measurable advantage. Function-level analysis shows that 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal: vulnerable functions are absent or cross-mapped across datasets, and ~31% of contaminated samples carry CWE misclassification. Second, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning. Models exhibit stable, systematic failure modes (DFI ranging from -85.5 to +94.8 pp) that persist from historical to post-cutoff data and resist correction. Fine-tuning shifts the output threshold without changing the decision policy. This is calibration without comprehension: output distributions adapt to training data while the underlying security reasoning remains absent. The weakest backbone at binary detection (DeepSeek-R1) gains the most in coarse CWE classification, revealing that detection and understanding are decoupled capabilities. The best detection score reaches only 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE ranking remains below 1.3% Top-1 accuracy, confirming that current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.

</details>


### [198] [Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20510)
*Alaia Solko-Breslin,Pramod Kaushik Mudrakarta,Mihai Christodorescu,Somesh Jha,Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces a distributionally robust optimization framework for runtime monitoring of AI agents that enforces probabilistic security policies with sound upper bounds on policy violation probability, regardless of inter-predicate correlations, outperforming prior deterministic approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing runtime monitoring approaches for AI agent security use Datalog-based formal policies but are limited to deterministic settings. Real-world applications require handling ambiguity through probabilistic predicates (e.g., PII detectors, declassifiers with failure probabilities), where independence assumptions required by prior probabilistic Datalog inference methods are not tenable.

Method: The authors propose a verification framework based on distributionally robust optimization (DRO) that computes sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation without requiring independence assumptions between probabilistic predicates. The method accounts for arbitrary correlations among predicates.

Result: On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling agents, the approach outperforms prior art, improving the security-utility trade-off while providing rigorous, sound bounds on the probability of policy violation.

Conclusion: Distributionally robust optimization enables effective runtime enforcement of probabilistic security policies for AI agents, offering both soundness guarantees and practical performance benefits over existing deterministic and independence-assuming approaches.

Abstract: Securing AI agents that operate in complex digital environments has become a critical need, and runtime monitoring approaches that formulate and enforce policies expressed in a formal language like Datalog offer a promising solution. However, existing approaches are restricted to deterministic policies. In many practical applications of AI agents, there is a need to enforce security policies in the face of ambiguity, leading to probabilistic predicates or state transitions (for example, a declassifier or Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detector that has some failure probability on each invocation). Furthermore, in many such applications, one cannot easily make the independence assumptions necessary to invoke prior work on probabilistic inference in Datalog. We address this by introducing a sound and efficient framework for such verification based on distributionally robust optimization, computing sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation regardless of possible correlations between predicates. On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool calling agents, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior art and improves the security-utility trade-off while ensuring rigorous bounds on the probability of policy violation.

</details>


### [199] [Sovereign Execution Brokers: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20520)
*Jun He,Deying Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SEB is a runtime enforcement broker that consumes Sovereign Assurance Boundary certificates to verify, authorize, and record production mutations, ensuring certified authority is short-lived, revocable, and auditable by decoupling proposal, admission, and execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes (e.g., LLM-based agents). Existing access-control (identity-based) and assurance (action-certifying) mechanisms lack a mandatory enforcement point that binds certified authority to the moment of mutation, creating a gap in secure agentic infrastructure.

Method: The authors propose SEB, a runtime enforcement boundary that: (1) consumes certificates from a Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), (2) verifies mutation-execution contract match, (3) checks validity windows, policy/revocation epochs, and live-state drift, (4) mints scoped execution identities, (5) invokes infrastructure APIs, and (6) records signed decision and outcome records. The design enforces deployment patterns preventing bypass, and a prototype is evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes.

Result: The prototype was evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation latency, drift detection accuracy, and security resilience under fault injection. Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: SEB provides a mandatory enforcement point that converts certified authority into short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capabilities. By requiring production mutation APIs to reject non-broker identities, SEB closes the gap between identity-based access control and assurance-based certification for agentic infrastructure.

Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly connected to cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows, but production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes. Existing access-control mechanisms authorize identities, while assurance layers certify proposed actions; neither alone provides a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at the moment of mutation. This paper introduces the Sovereign Execution Broker (SEB), a runtime enforcement boundary for certificate-bound agentic infrastructure. SEB consumes certificates issued by the Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifies that the requested mutation matches the certified execution contract, checks validity windows, policy epochs, revocation epochs, and live-state drift, mints scoped execution identity, invokes infrastructure APIs, and records signed decision and outcome records. By separating proposal, admission, and execution, SEB turns certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, provided that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities. We present the SEB execution model, certificate and replay-verification predicates, scoped identity semantics, bypass-prevention deployment patterns, failure behavior, and a concrete prototype implementation. We evaluate the prototype on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation, drift detection, and security under fault injection.

</details>


### [200] [From Efficiency to Leakage -- Privacy Backdoor in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20553)
*Shanghao Shi,Chaoyu Zhang,Heng Jin,Yang Xiao,Yevgeniy Vorobeychik,William Yeoh,Ning Zhang,Y. Thomas Hou,Wenjing Lou*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: NeuroImprint is a privacy backdoor attack in federated learning where a malicious server crafts PEFT adapters that force each client training sample into a dedicated neuron with at most one update, enabling closed-form inversion of per-sample embeddings to reconstruct up to 79% of fine-tuning data without degrading model utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning with PEFT (e.g., LoRA adapters) is widely adopted for privacy-preserving LLM fine-tuning, but the security assumption that adapters protect client data is untested. The authors aim to expose a fundamental vulnerability: a malicious parameter server can subvert the adapter structure to secretly memorize and later reconstruct client training samples.

Method: NeuroImprint assigns a dedicated "memorization neuron" to each training sample and enforces that each neuron is updated at most once during local fine-tuning. This avoids cross-sample collisions (from large batches) and cross-step mixing (from stateful optimizers like Adam/AdamW). After training, the isolated per-sample weight updates are inverted analytically in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are deterministically mapped back to token sequences via nearest-neighbor lookup in the embedding matrix.

Result: Evaluated on BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2 across four diverse fine-tuning datasets, NeuroImprint reconstructs 59% to 79% of all fine-tuning samples with high semantic fidelity, all without degrading the model's downstream task utility.

Conclusion: PEFT-based federated learning is vulnerable to adapter-level backdoors that enable high-fidelity training data reconstruction. This challenges the prevailing assumption that sharing only adapters (rather than full models) sufficiently protects client data privacy, and calls for new defenses against malicious parameter servers in FL settings.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple parties to collaboratively fine-tune language models for domain-specific tasks without sharing raw data. Since full model fine-tuning is often prohibitively expensive for FL clients, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become the de facto approach in practice, freezing the base model and training only a small set of adapters. In this paper, we show that a malicious parameter server can stealthily corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor that implicitly memorizes the client's training samples as isolated per-sample parameter updates stored in separate neurons, without degrading model utility. Concretely, our attack, NeuroImprint, assigns a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and constrains that each neuron is updated at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory. This design mitigates both cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing introduced by large local batches and stateful optimizers (e.g., Adam/AdamW) in language-model fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the resulting isolated per-sample updates can be analytically inverted in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are then deterministically mapped back to token sequences. To understand the generality of our method, we implemented NeuroImprint on multiple language models (BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2) and evaluated it across four fine-tuning datasets spanning diverse domains. The results demonstrate that our attack can reconstruct 59% to 79% of all finetuning samples with high semantic fidelity.

</details>
