### [201] [MonaVec: A Training-Free Embedded Vector Search Kernel for Edge and Offline AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19458)
*Oğuzhan Yenen*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: MonaVec is a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel (akin to "SQLite for vectors") that uses a training-free, data-oblivious quantization pipeline (Randomized Hadamard Transform + precomputed Lloyd-Max tables) to compress embeddings to 4 bits, achieving strong recall with minimal memory and byte-identical reproducibility across architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vector-search systems require persistent servers, large RAM, or a training pass over the corpus. The authors identify a gap for an embedded, offline-first vector search solution — the same niche SQLite fills for relational databases. Target use cases include on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval where server infrastructure and training data are unavailable.

Method: The core innovation is a training-free, data-oblivious quantization pipeline: (1) a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions any input distribution toward N(0,1); (2) precomputed Lloyd-Max tables quantize the normalized vectors to 4 bits (8× compression) without learning a codebook or scanning the corpus. The index persists as a single .mvec file with an embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed, guaranteeing byte-identical results across architectures. A single-pass global standardization (`fit()`) extends the pipeline to L2 distance. Optional IvfFlat and HNSW backends support million-vector corpora. Implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar).

Result: On AG News (45K × 1024-dim BGE-M3 embeddings, cosine similarity), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce achieves 0.960 Recall@10 in only 27 MB, outperforming float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall, while trading peak throughput for deterministic, byte-identical results across builds.

Conclusion: MonaVec successfully fills the embedded vector-search niche — delivering competitive recall with extreme compression, full determinism, and zero training requirements — positioning it as the "SQLite for vector data" suitable for on-device and offline AI applications.

Abstract: We present MonaVec, a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel for edge and offline AI -- settings where server infrastructure, network connectivity, and training data are all unavailable. Existing vector-search systems assume a persistent server, gigabytes of RAM, or a training pass over the corpus; MonaVec instead targets the deployment profile of SQLite: one file, one function call, runs anywhere. Its quantization core is training-free by default and data-oblivious: a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions any input distribution toward N(0,1), so precomputed Lloyd-Max tables quantize to 4 bits (8x smaller) with no learned codebook and no data pass. The index persists as a single .mvec file whose embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed makes results reproducible across architectures and byte-identical within a build -- a determinism guarantee that parallel-build graph libraries cannot offer.
  On semantic embeddings (AG News, 45K x 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce reaches 0.960 Recall@10 in 27 MB -- leading float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall -- while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism. A single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends the same data-oblivious pipeline to magnitude-sensitive L2 data, and optional IvfFlat and HNSW backends carry it to million-vector corpora.
  MonaVec is implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar). It targets on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval -- the niche SQLite occupies for relational data: one file, one call, runs anywhere.

</details>


### [202] [VCG: A Multimodal Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Video Feeds under Extreme Cold-Start Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19627)
*Katya Mirylenka,Egor Malykh,Mahdyar Ravanbakhsh,Michael Gygli,Marco-Andrea Buchmann,Andrew Dzhoha,Svitlana Borzenko,Francesca Catino,Mohamed Gaafar,Maarten Versteegh,Thomas Kober,Dario d'Andrea,Ellie Langhans*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A multimodal retrieval system (VCG) using domain-adapted CLIP embeddings solves the extreme cold-start problem for short-form video feeds in e-commerce, outperforming generative LLM embeddings which suffer from embedding space collapse. Online A/B testing shows a 50% uplift in deep video completion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from static catalogs to dynamic immersive video feeds creates an "extreme cold-start" problem: new short-form videos lack interaction history for collaborative filtering, and immersive feeds introduce strong position and duration biases that distort engagement signals. A solution is needed for zero-shot retrieval based on visual content.

Method: The VCG system uses a domain-adapted CLIP-based vision-language model to map users and videos into a shared semantic embedding space, enabling zero-shot multimodal retrieval without behavioral history. The authors compare discriminative (CLIP) vs. generative (LLM) embeddings and conduct online A/B testing, plus an interactive demo for three retrieval scenarios: Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search.

Result: Discriminative CLIP embeddings outperform generative LLM embeddings for retrieval; LLMs suffer from embedding space collapse despite excelling at attribute prediction. Online A/B testing shows VCG yields a 50% uplift in deep video completion and effectively mitigates engagement biases.

Conclusion: Domain-adapted discriminative vision-language embeddings are superior to generative LLM embeddings for multimodal video retrieval in e-commerce cold-start settings. The VCG system demonstrates practical scalability and significant engagement gains in production.

Abstract: The digital commerce landscape is shifting from static, search-driven catalogs to dynamic, immersive video feeds. This transition introduces an ``extreme cold-start'' problem: unlike traditional items, new short-form videos lack the dense interaction history required for collaborative filtering. Furthermore, immersive feeds introduce strong position and duration biases that distort standard engagement signals. In this paper, we demonstrate the Video Candidate Generation (VCG) system, a scalable multimodal retrieval engine designed to solve these challenges in a large-scale e-commerce environment. By leveraging a domain-adapted vision-language model (based on CLIP), we map users and videos into a shared semantic space, enabling zero-shot retrieval based on visual content rather than behavioral history. We detail the system's architecture and present a rigorous evaluation comparing generative (LLM) vs. discriminative (CLIP) embeddings. Our results show that while generative models excel at attribute prediction, they suffer from embedding space collapse in retrieval tasks. Online A/B testing demonstrates that VCG effectively mitigates engagement biases, yielding a 50\% uplift in deep video completion. To showcase the system's capabilities, we present an interactive demonstration featuring three bi-directional retrieval scenarios: Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search.

</details>


### [203] [Token Factory: Efficiently Integrating Diverse Signals into Large Recommendation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19635)
*Xilun Chen,Shao-Chuan Wang,Baykal Cakici,Lukasz Heldt,Lichan Hong,Raghu Keshavan,Aniruddh Nath,Li Wei,Xinyang Xi*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Token Factory transforms traditional recommendation signals into compressed "soft tokens" for efficient integration with Large Recommendation Models (LRMs), avoiding prompt length explosion and reducing memory/computational overhead while improving performance in production-scale environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for integrating traditional signals into transformer-based LRMs—either by textualizing signals (causing excessively long prompts) or creating discrete item representations—result in substantial memory footprints and high computational overhead. There is a need for a more efficient method to holistically incorporate heterogeneous input features into LRMs without these drawbacks.

Method: The authors propose "Token Factory," a framework that transforms traditional recommendation signals into "soft tokens"—continuous, compressed vector representations that can be directly consumed by LRMs. This approach compresses heterogeneous input features into a fixed, compact set of tokens rather than expanding them into lengthy textual or discrete representations.

Result: Experimental results in a production-scale recommendation environment validate that Token Factory effectively integrates and compresses heterogeneous input features, prevents prompt length explosion, and enhances model performance compared to conventional approaches.

Conclusion: Token Factory provides an efficient and effective solution for integrating traditional signals into LRMs, addressing key scalability challenges in industry-scale recommendation systems through soft token-based feature compression.

Abstract: Large Recommendation Models (LRMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in industry-scale recommendation tasks. However, holistically integrating traditional signals into these transformer-based architectures effectively and efficiently remains a major challenge. Conventional approaches that "textualize" these signals directly or create discrete item representations often lead to excessively long prompts, substantial memory footprints, and high computational overhead. To overcome these limitations, we propose "Token Factory", a framework designed to transform traditional signals into "soft tokens" that can be directly processed by LRMs. This approach enables efficient integration and compression of heterogeneous input features, preventing prompt length explosion while enhancing model performance. We detail the architecture of Token Factory and present experimental results validating its effectiveness in a production-scale recommendation environment.

</details>


### [204] [SAFE-Cascade: Cost-Adaptive Vision-Language Routing for Chart Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19646)
*Ayush Dwivedi,Qixin Wang,Ashvi Soni,Ruoteng Wang,Han Li,Animesh Mahapatra,Neeraj Agrawal,Xintao Wu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SAFE-Cascade is a cost-adaptive chart question answering system that uses a learned router to decide whether a text-only model (via OCR) suffices or a full VLM is needed, matching full-VLM accuracy while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and cost by 9.3%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Invoking a VLM for every chart question is computationally expensive and often unnecessary, since many questions can be answered using only OCR-extracted text and lightweight language reasoning. The authors aim to reduce cost while maintaining accuracy and providing transparency into when visual grounding is truly required.

Method: SAFE-Cascade employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) OCR text extraction from chart images using Azure Document Intelligence, (2) a provisional answer from a text-only LM (gpt-5-mini), and (3) a Random Forest router trained on inference-time features that decides whether to accept the text answer or escalate to a VLM (gemini-2.5-flash-image). The system exposes all decision evidence — OCR text, routing probability, escalation decision, and cost/latency estimates — via an interactive interface where users can adjust the escalation threshold to explore the accuracy–cost trade-off.

Result: On a held-out 375-example ChartQA test split, SAFE-Cascade achieved 69.1% accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, compared to 67.7% accuracy with 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The +1.4 pp accuracy difference is statistically uncertain, so results are interpreted as matching VLM performance while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%.

Conclusion: Selective modality routing via SAFE-Cascade demonstrates that multimodal systems can be made more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware without sacrificing accuracy, by escalating to expensive VLMs only when visual grounding is genuinely needed.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are powerful for chart question answering, but invoking a VLM for every query can be unnecessarily expensive when many questions are answerable from OCR text and lightweight language reasoning. We demonstrate SAFE-Cascade, an interactive system for cost-adaptive chart question answering. Given a chart image and a natural-language question, SAFE-Cascade first extracts chart text with OCR, obtains a provisional answer from a text-only language model, and then uses a learned router to decide whether to accept the text answer or escalate to a VLM. The demo exposes this decision process to users: OCR evidence, text-only answer, routing probability, escalation decision, final answer, estimated cost, and estimated latency are shown side by side. SAFE-Cascade is designed as a transparent interface for understanding when visual grounding is actually needed. Users can upload or select charts, ask questions, inspect the evidence used by each pathway, compare text-only and VLM answers, and adjust the escalation threshold to explore the accuracy-cost frontier. The system is implemented with Azure Document Intelligence for OCR, gpt-5-mini as the text-only model, gemini-2.5-flash-image as the VLM, and a Random Forest router trained on inference-time features. On a held-out ChartQA test split of 375 examples from a 2,500-example experiment, SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% unified accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, compared with 67.7% accuracy and 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The observed +1.4 percentage-point difference is statistically uncertain, so we interpret SAFE-Cascade as matching full-VLM performance while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%. The demonstration shows how selective modality routing can make multimodal knowledge systems more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware.

</details>


### [205] [Closing the Calibration Gap in Semantic Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19719)
*Aditeya Baral,Radoslav Ralev,Iliya Sotirov Zhechev,Srijith Rajamohan,Jen Agarwal*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Semantic caching for LLMs is typically evaluated using PR-AUC, but this ranking-only metric fails to predict operational performance at fixed thresholds. The authors introduce P-CHR AUC and CRR to measure cache-aware precision and calibration retention, revealing that model selection for semantic caching is fundamentally a calibration problem, not a ranking one.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard metric for evaluating semantic caching systems, PR-AUC, only measures ranking quality and ignores threshold usability. This causes a systematic mismatch where models with top PR-AUC scores often perform worst in actual deployment, leading to poor operational choices. There is a need for metrics that bridge offline evaluation and real-world deployment quality.

Method: The authors decompose the gap between offline and deployed quality into two components: a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component determined by the dataset's positive rate. They introduce two new metrics: Precision-Cache Hit Ratio (P-CHR) AUC, which measures precision across varying cache utilization levels, and Calibration Retention Rate (CRR), which quantifies how much offline ranking quality is preserved at deployment. Experiments examine the effects of training objectives, data scale, and post-hoc calibration on closing the calibration gap.

Result: The calibration gap is primarily governed by the training objective rather than the scale of training data. Post-hoc calibration techniques only partially close this gap. Models with the best PR-AUC frequently underperform in deployment due to poor calibration, confirming that ranking metrics alone are insufficient for model selection in semantic caching systems.

Conclusion: Model selection for semantic caching should be treated as a calibration problem, not merely a ranking problem. Proper measurement using cache-aware, threshold-sensitive metrics like P-CHR AUC and CRR is essential for bridging the gap between offline evaluation and operational deployment quality.

Abstract: Semantic caching cuts LLM inference costs by serving a cached response to semantically similar queries. Standard practice evaluates these systems using PR-AUC, a metric that only measures how well scores rank and ignores whether they are usable at a fixed threshold. We show this mismatch leads to systematically poor deployment choices, as models with the highest PR-AUC are often the worst in operation. We introduce Precision-Cache Hit Ratio (P-CHR) AUC, a cache-aware metric that measures precision across cache utilization levels, and Calibration Retention Rate (CRR), which captures how much offline ranking quality survives at deployment. We decompose the operational gap between offline and deployed quality into a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component fixed by the dataset's positive rate. Our experiments show that the calibration gap is governed by the training objective rather than data scale, and post-hoc calibration only partially closes it. Ultimately, model selection for semantic caching is a calibration problem, not a ranking one, and measuring it is the first step to closing the gap.

</details>


### [206] [Stellar: Scalable Multimodal Document Retrieval for Natural Language Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19960)
*Yuxiang Guo,Zhonghao Hu,Yuren Mao,Yuhang Liu,Congcong Ge,Xiaolu Zhang,Jun Zhou,Yunjun Gao*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Stellar is a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that addresses the memory overhead problem of multi-vector retrieval by storing token embeddings on disk and loading only essential candidate embeddings into memory. It combines lexical representation-based filtering with efficient disk-backed late interaction to reduce memory and latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude without sacrificing retrieval quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art multimodal document retrieval methods use multi-vector (token-level) representations with late interaction, achieving high effectiveness but incurring substantial memory overhead that limits scalability and real-world deployment. The core challenge is reducing this memory footprint while maintaining retrieval performance.

Method: Stellar introduces two components: (1) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF) — fine-tunes an MLLM as a sparse encoder to produce lexical representations for efficient document filtering, drastically reducing the candidate set; (2) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI) — organizes on-disk token embeddings using a balanced clustering algorithm and employs a cost model to dynamically load only necessary token embeddings into memory for late interaction scoring.

Result: Experiments on four real-world benchmarks and a newly introduced large-scale dataset show that Stellar reduces memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods, without compromising retrieval effectiveness.

Conclusion: Stellar demonstrates that disk-backed, filter-then-refine strategies can make multi-vector multimodal retrieval practical for large-scale RAG deployments, overcoming the memory scalability bottleneck of late interaction methods.

Abstract: Multimodal document retrieval--selecting the most relevant multimodal document from a large corpus to answer a natural language query--plays an essential role in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. State-of-the-art methods represent each document and query with multiple token-level embeddings and use late interaction to achieve high effectiveness. However, such multi-vector representations incur substantial memory overhead during retrieval, leading to poor scalability and hindering real-world deployment. In this paper, we present Stellar, a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that stores token-level document embeddings on disk and loads only a small set of candidate embeddings into memory for late interaction. Stellar comprises two key components: (i) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF), which fine-tunes a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a sparse encoder to produce high-quality lexical representations, enabling efficient and effective document filtering to significantly reduce the candidate set; (ii) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI), which designs an on-disk token embedding storage layout guided by a balanced clustering algorithm, and dynamically loads only the necessary token embeddings into memory using a simple yet effective cost model. Extensive experiments on four real-world benchmarks and a newly presented large-scale dataset demonstrate that Stellar reduces memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods without compromising retrieval effectiveness.

</details>


### [207] [PACMS: Submodular Context Selection as a Pluggable Engine for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20047)
*Manu Ghulyani,Arunabh Singh,Karan Bharadwaj,Ankit Nath,Suranjan Goswami*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: LLM agents accumulate conversation, memory, and tool outputs in a context window. Recency-based truncation is topic-blind, discarding old but relevant facts while retaining recent but irrelevant material. Existing alternatives like RAG and context compression fail to treat all context types as a unified pool for relevance-based selection during prompt assembly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches for managing the context window of conversational and tool-using LLM agents rely primarily on recency-based truncation, which is agnostic to topical relevance. This causes critical failures: early-session facts are discarded when they become old even if the user's current query references them, while verbose but irrelevant recent material is kept. Agents designed for multi-turn memory are precisely the use case where this mechanism breaks down. Existing alternatives — RAG (which retrieves external documents but does not manage already-present context) and context compression (which operates lossily and query-blind) — fail to address the core problem: there is no mechanism that treats memory, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a unified candidate pool to be selectively retained based on relevance at prompt assembly time.

Method: This abstract primarily frames the problem space and critiques existing approaches rather than presenting a novel method. It identifies three categories of context (memory entries, conversation turns, tool outputs), critiques recency truncation as topic-blind, and positions existing alternatives (RAG, context compression) as insufficient because they operate outside the agent's assembly step and do not perform relevance-based selection over the unified context pool.

Result: The abstract does not present empirical results. It articulates a conceptual gap: recency truncation fails precisely in the multi-turn memory scenario it is meant to serve; RAG handles external retrieval but not internal context arbitration; context compression reduces token counts but is query-blind and lossy. No existing method treats all context sources as a single candidate pool for relevance-driven selection during prompt construction.

Conclusion: The paper identifies a significant gap in LLM agent design: the lack of a relevance-aware, unified context selection mechanism that operates at prompt assembly time across conversation turns, memory entries, and tool outputs. This gap is most acute for memory-dependent, multi-turn agent interactions where recency truncation is particularly ill-suited.

Abstract: Conversational and tool-using LLM agents operate over a context window that fills from several directions simultaneously. As a session proceeds, the agent accumulates user and assistant turns, entries drawn from a persistent memory store, and often largest of all, the verbatim outputs of tool calls such as file reads, search results, and API responses. Once the cumulative context exceeds the model's token budget, the framework must decide what to keep.
  The prevailing mechanism is recency truncation, sometimes paired with periodic summarization. This is topic-blind: a fact established early in a session is discarded simply because it is old, even when the current user query is about exactly that fact; conversely, verbose but irrelevant recent material is retained. Agents that must recall information across many turns, the defining case for memory, are precisely where recency truncation fails.
  Existing alternatives sit outside the agent's assembly step. Retrieval augmented generation fetches external documents into the prompt but does not arbitrate the agent's \emph{already-present} pooled context. Context-compression methods reduce token count by rewriting or pruning text, but operate query-blind and lossily. Neither treats memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a single candidate pool to be selected from by relevance at the moment the prompt is assembled.

</details>


### [208] [Generative Engine Optimization at Scale: Measuring Brand Visibility Across AI Search Engines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20065)
*Pratyush Kumar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper presents the first large-scale empirical baseline for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) by analyzing 100K+ AI search engine responses across 100+ brands. It identifies a three-tier visibility ladder based on brand stature (73% vs. 44% vs. 11% appearance rates), reveals that corporate websites dominate citations (78%), "best-of" listicles are the most-cited format (~21%), and sentiment is highly volatile. The authors propose seven protocols for causally testing GEO interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from traditional search engines to AI-powered answer engines (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini) has fundamentally altered how brands gain visibility. While SEO is well-studied, Generative Engine Optimization (GEO/AEO) lacks large-scale empirical measurement. The hard problem is visibility for non-authoritative brands — SMEs, D2C brands, creators, and startups — who cannot rely on established brand equity.

Method: The authors analyzed over 100,000 prompt responses across 100+ brands using the Ranqo tracking platform between March–May 2026. They measured: (1) brand appearance rates in AI-generated answers, (2) citation sources and formats, and (3) sentiment stability. Brands were stratified by stature into three tiers for comparative analysis across multiple AI engines.

Result: Three key findings: (1) A three-tier visibility ladder — global household names appear in 73% of relevant AI answers, mid-market brands in 44%, and niche/small brands in just 11% (~30pp drops per tier). (2) Corporate websites receive ~78% of citations; among non-corporate sources, YouTube leads, followed by Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. "Best-of" listicles are the highest-leverage format at ~21% of all citations. (3) Sentiment flips (positive/negative framing) occur ~6.7× more frequently than changes in mere mention, making it the most unstable visibility signal.

Conclusion: AI brand visibility is measurable, varies by platform, and is strongly stratified by brand maturity. The findings establish the first large-scale GEO measurement baseline. The authors propose seven v1.1 protocols for causally testing whether specific optimizations (e.g., listicle presence, YouTube coverage, sentiment management) can improve AI search visibility, particularly for lower-tier brands seeking to close the gap.

Abstract: People increasingly get answers straight from AI search engines like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini rather than scrolling search results. Brands that once focused on search engine optimization (SEO) must now optimize for how these engines represent, cite, and recommend them -- a shift variously called Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), and AI Search Visibility. We treat AEO and AI Visibility as part of GEO, and study how to measure brand visibility across AI engines: what they value when they cite a brand, which sources they rely on, and what content large language models surface. The hard case is everyone outside the already-authoritative top brands -- SMEs, D2C brands, creators, and early-stage startups.
  We analyze 100K+ prompt responses across 100+ brands tracked on Ranqo between March and May 2026. First visibility runs form a clear three-tier brand-stature ladder: global household names (e.g., Stripe, Nike) appear in 73% of relevant AI answers on their first run; established mid-market and regional brands (e.g., Olipop, Klaviyo) in 44%; niche and small brands in just 11% -- about 30 percentage points per step. When engines cite sources, about 78% go to corporate websites; among non-corporate sources YouTube leads, ahead of Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. The highest-leverage page is the ranked "best-of" listicle, the most-cited content format at about 21% of all citations. Sentiment is the unstable signal: whether a brand is framed positively or negatively flips about 6.7 times more often than whether it is mentioned at all.
  These findings provide a first large-scale baseline for measuring GEO: AI brand visibility can be measured, differs by platform, and varies strongly by brand maturity. We close by proposing seven v1.1 protocols to test whether specific recommendations can causally improve AI visibility.

</details>


### [209] [ScholarQuest: A Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark for Agentic Academic Paper Search in Open Literature Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20235)
*Tingyue Pan,Mingyue Cheng,Daoyu Wang,Yitong Zhou,Jie Ouyang,Qi Liu,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: ScholarQuest is a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for evaluating LLM-based academic paper search agents, featuring over 1,000 CS topics and four research intent types. Despite agentic methods outperforming single-shot retrieval, top agents achieve only ~0.31–0.36 recall, revealing substantial room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately evaluate LLM-based search agents in realistic, open academic literature environments. There is a need for a systematic, large-scale benchmark that supports iterative, intent-driven paper search under reproducible conditions.

Method: ScholarQuest is built from over 1,000 computer science topics organized via taxonomy, covering four research intents: method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, and scope-controlled queries. It features scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend (ScholarBase) to ensure reproducible evaluation. Both agentic methods and single-shot retrieval baselines are benchmarked using recall metrics, efficiency analysis, and failure case studies.

Result: Agentic methods consistently outperform single-shot retrieval baselines, but the best agent achieves only 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All. Analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases reveal the benchmark's capacity to provide multi-dimensional diagnostic signals.

Conclusion: ScholarQuest establishes a challenging, reproducible benchmark for agentic academic search, demonstrating that current LLM-based agents still fall well short of reliable performance and highlighting multiple dimensions for future improvement.

Abstract: Academic paper search is a core step in scientific research, and LLM-based search agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for iterative, intent-driven literature exploration. However, existing benchmarks are insufficient for systematically evaluating agentic academic search under realistic open literature environments. We propose ScholarQuest, a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for agentic academic paper search. ScholarQuest is constructed from over 1,000 computer science topics and four representative research intents, including method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, and scope-controlled queries. It further provides scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend ScholarBase for reproducible evaluation. Benchmarking results show that agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines, yet the best-performing agent only achieves 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All, indicating substantial room for improvement. In addition, analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases further highlight the benchmark's ability to provide multi-dimensional evaluation signals for academic paper search agents.

</details>


### [210] [ELVA: Exploring Ranking-Driven Universal Multimodal Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20280)
*Yuhan Liu,Pei Fu,Hang Li,Yukun Qi,Chao Jiang,Jingwen Fu,Zhen Liu,Bin Qin,Zhenbo Luo,Jian Luan,Jingmin Xin*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: ELVA is a rule-based RL framework that addresses "grain blindness" in universal multimodal retrieval by treating negative samples differently according to their similarity to positives, using RLVR to jointly optimize negative ranking and enlarge the positive-negative similarity gap, achieving SOTA results including a 13.1% gain on the newly introduced MRBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing contrastive learning approaches for Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR) suffer from "grain blindness" — the model overlooks fine-grained, grain-level information in queries because contrastive learning treats all negatives uniformly as a binary positive/negative classification, ignoring the varying information each negative carries. This hampers performance on complex, multi-grain queries.

Method: The authors propose ELVA, a rule-based RL framework that mitigates grain blindness via ranking-driven MLLMs. Key components: (1) Extending Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, enabling exploration of new ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels; (2) Using rule-based rewards to jointly optimize negative sample ranking while enlarging the similarity gap between positives and negatives. They also introduce MRBench, a benchmark for multi-grain query scenarios.

Result: ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results on standard retrieval benchmarks and delivers a notable 13.1% improvement on the newly introduced MRBench, demonstrating its effectiveness in alleviating grain blindness.

Conclusion: Treating negatives differently according to their similarity to the positive sample, operationalized through a rule-based RL framework (ELVA), effectively mitigates grain blindness in UMR, enabling MLLMs to learn distinct grain information and significantly improve retrieval performance, especially on complex multi-grain queries.

Abstract: Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) via contrastive learning has become a mainstream paradigm for improving the performance of Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR). However, previous works have ignored the grain blindness when adapting the contrastive paradigm into retrieval tasks. Grain blindness refers to the tendency of the model to overlook grain-level information contained in the query, which is crucial for effectively handling complex queries. This stems from contrastive learning treating samples as a binary classification (positive/negative), while ignoring the different information carried by each negative sample. To address this, we argue that negatives should be treated differently according to their similarity to the positive sample, enabling the model to learn distinct grain information from each negative. In this paper, we introduce a simple but effective framework, called ELVA, a novel rule-based RL framework that mitigates grain blindness through ranking-driven MLLMs. 1) Instead of relying on reward models, we extend Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
  (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, allowing the model to explore new ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels. 2) By utilizing rule-based rewards, our approach jointly optimizes the ranking of negative samples while enlarging the similarity gap between positive and negative. To more precisely measure grain blindness, we further introduce MRBench, a new benchmark specifically designed for multi-grain query scenarios. ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results across standard retrieval benchmarks, and its notable 13.1% improvement on MRBench further demonstrates its effectiveness in alleviating grain blindness.

</details>


### [211] [Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20554)
*Ruizhong Qiu,Yinglong Xia,Dongqi Fu,Hanqing Zeng,Ren Chen,Xiangjun Fan,Hong Li,Hong Yan,Hanghang Tong*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: G2Rec proposes a scalable generative recommendation framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic item tokenization, enabling semantically grounded user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth labels. It addresses limitations of existing graph-based (scalability, local-only information) and semantic tokenization (heuristic, no supervision) methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods face two key challenges: (1) graph-based integration approaches (graph serialization, GNNs) either lack scalability or capture only local graph information; (2) semantic tokenization methods rely on heuristics without explicit supervision, resulting in suboptimal semantic representations. There is a need for a unified framework that effectively injects both holistic user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts simultaneously.

Method: G2Rec is a scalable framework that combines holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization. It captures global user co-engagement patterns through graph structures while simultaneously learning semantically grounded item representations, all without requiring ground-truth user interest labels. The framework is designed for industrial-scale deployment across product surfaces.

Result: Online deployment across multiple product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that G2Rec outperforms existing methods, validating its superiority in both industrial and research settings.

Conclusion: G2Rec successfully bridges the gap between holistic graph-based behavioral modeling and semantic tokenization for generative recommendation. By unifying these two dimensions, it provides more comprehensive and accurate user behavior context modeling, proving effective at industrial scale.

Abstract: Generative recommendation is an emerging paradigm that has shown promise in industrial recommendation systems, aiming to predict users' next interactions from their historical behaviors. At the core of generative recommendation lies item tokenization, which bridges item semantics and recommendation models. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively organize and inject complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts into recommendation models simultaneously. On the one hand, existing graph-based integration methods, such as graph serialization and graph neural networks, either suffer from scalability issues or exploit only local graph information. On the other hand, existing semantic tokenization methods typically rely on heuristics and lack explicit supervision signals, which may lead to inaccurate or suboptimal semantic representations. To address these limitations in user interest context modeling, we propose G2Rec, a scalable framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization for industrial-scale generative recommendation. Overall, G2Rec enables recommendation models to capture holistic and semantically grounded user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth user interests, thereby providing more comprehensive and accurate modeling of user behavior contexts in industrial sequential recommendation. Online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of G2Rec over existing methods.

</details>

### [212] [Computational Identifiability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19361)
*Lucius E. J. Bynum,Rajesh Ranganath,Kyunghyun Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes "computational identifiability," a practical alternative to traditional theoretical identifiability. Instead of relying on asymptotic assumptions and idealized conditions, it defines identifiability through a finite computational search procedure that finds an empirical estimator within a desired error tolerance. The framework handles small samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, mixed data types, and counterfactual estimands.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional theoretical identifiability in causal inference relies on idealized assumptions (infinite data, asymptotic properties) that often fail in practice. The authors aim to bridge the gap between theoretical guarantees and practical estimation by introducing a computation-bound notion of identifiability that is empirically verifiable and sensitive to finite-sample constraints.

Method: The authors define "computational identifiability" as a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator. If the search finds an estimator within a prespecified error tolerance, identifiability is conditionally satisfied — conditional on the search procedure itself and a prior distribution over parameters. Experiments demonstrate the framework across scenarios: small finite samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, mixed observational-interventional data, and counterfactual estimands.

Result: The computational identifiability framework successfully addresses practical identification questions that theoretical identifiability cannot: it provides identifiability determinations under small samples, resolves ambiguity in graphical criteria, handles mixed observational-interventional data, and extends to counterfactual estimands. Code is released as open-source.

Conclusion: Computational identifiability offers a pragmatic, empirically-grounded complement to theoretical identifiability. By conditioning on finite computation and prior assumptions, it yields actionable identifiability judgments in realistic settings where idealized asymptotic guarantees are insufficient.

Abstract: Identification conditions describe the computability of a target query or parameter of interest as a function of the type and amount of information available. In causal identification, this information is often expressed in the form of a causal graph, and data are observed or collected for some subset of variables in the graph. Target queries may be for a single effect alone or for a class of effects in a given model. The derivation of an identification algorithm then defines mathematically the process by which the desired causal effect(s) can be uniquely determined, theoretically, in expectation. Identifiability in expectation, or 'theoretical identifiability,' generally assumes asymptotic properties, infinite data, or other mathematically idealized conditions. In this paper, we explore a fundamental distinction between this theoretical, idealized notion of identifiability and a proposed alternative that is computation-bound. The framework we propose - 'computational identifiability' - is to instead define a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator. If this process finds an estimator empirically, within a desired error tolerance, then identifiability is satisfied, conditional on the specified assumptions of the search (i.e., a prior distribution over the parameters) and conditional on the search procedure itself. Through several experiments, we demonstrate how this framework allows us to answer fine-grained, practical identification questions, such as identification with small finite samples, with ambiguous graphical criteria, with mixed observational-interventional data, and across counterfactual data and estimands. Code is available at https://github.com/lbynum/metadentify.

</details>


### [213] [When to Trust, How to Distill: Multi-Foundation Model Guidance for Lightweight, Robust Scientific Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19363)
*Rupasree Dey,Abdul Matin,Nathan Orwick,Yao Zhang,Shrideep Pallickara,Sangmi Lee Pallickara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GUARD is a knowledge distillation framework that extracts latent structural knowledge from distribution-misaligned time-series foundation models to train lightweight, specialized forecasters deployable on edge devices. It uses a Contextual Router for dynamic teacher selection and an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism to suppress distillation from overconfident teachers. Demonstrated on climate-critical domains, it outperforms fixed-weight multi-teacher baselines even when teachers perform poorly zero-shot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) possess rich universal temporal dynamics but face two critical barriers to deployment in physical sciences: (1) severe distributional misalignment when applied zero-shot to domain-specific scientific data, and (2) prohibitive computational cost for edge-computing sensor networks. The authors aim to bridge this gap by extracting useful structural knowledge from misaligned FMs to train lightweight, specialized models suitable for edge deployment.

Method: GUARD frames multi-teacher knowledge distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive components: (1) A Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher FM per input instance based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models. (2) An Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that functions as a "circuit-breaker," automatically attenuating distillation strength when a teacher's predictive confidence diverges from the target domain's reality, preventing harmful knowledge transfer.

Result: GUARD significantly reduces RMSE compared to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline. Notably, domain-misaligned teachers — despite suboptimal overall zero-shot accuracy — serve as critical correctives, outperforming globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. The framework is evaluated across four climate-critical domains: meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids.

Conclusion: Domain-misaligned foundation models can still provide valuable supervisory signal for training lightweight specialized forecasters when dynamically routed and uncertainty-gated. GUARD enables high-precision scientific forecasting on resource-constrained edge devices by adaptively distilling complementary knowledge from multiple TSFMs, even under significant distribution shift.

Abstract: The deployment of Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) in physical sciences is hindered by a critical trade-off: while these models encode rich, universal temporal dynamics, they suffer from severe distributional misalignment when applied zero-shot to specific scientific domains, and their computational cost prohibits deployment in edge-computing sensor networks. We address a fundamental challenge: How can we extract latent structural knowledge from misaligned foundation models (FM) to train lightweight, specialized forecasters? We propose Gated Uncertainty-Aware Routing for Distillation (Guard), a novel framework that reframes multiteacher distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that acts as a "circuit-breaker," automatically attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from domain reality. We evaluate our proposed lightweight framework on four climate-critical domains: meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids. Our method significantly reduces RMSE relative to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline, successfully distilling knowledge from pretrained FMs (teachers) even when they exhibit suboptimal zero-shot accuracy due to distribution shift between the original and target data domains. We demonstrate that these domain-misaligned teachers can still serve as critical correctives, outperforming the globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. Ultimately, this enables high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/RupasreeDey/GUARD-KDD2026.

</details>


### [214] [Closing the Social-Semantic Gap: SPSD for Edge-Based Prompt Compression in Cloud LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19364)
*Abhinit Sen,Ajeet Kumar,Manaranjan Pradhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SPSD is an edge-based pipeline that uses a 4-bit quantised Small Language Model to distill social scaffolding (politeness markers, repetition, rapport-building) from user prompts before sending them to a cloud LLM, achieving ~100 tokens saved per call with non-inferior response quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The prefill stage of LLM inference consumes significant cloud-scale energy. Many user prompts contain "social scaffolding" — politeness, apologies, repetition, and rapport-building language — that is important for human communication but carries low marginal information for machine reasoning. The authors term this the "Social-Semantic Gap" and seek to exploit it for energy and token cost savings.

Method: SPSD (Sentiment Preserving Semantic Distillation) deploys a 4-bit quantised Small Language Model (Gemma-2-2B-Instruct Q4_K_M) on-device to compress prompts before cloud transmission. The distilled prompts are evaluated by a cloud LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Quality is assessed via blind LLM-as-judge on a 15-point rubric. Safety-critical domains are routed through rule-based gates to passthrough without distillation. Evaluation uses a corpus of 248 prompts, with 146 distilled calls and 121 pairs subjected to blind judging.

Result: Mean input token savings of 99.9 tokens per distilled call, with all 146 distilled calls yielding positive savings. In blind LLM-as-judge scoring: 43% ties, 28% distilled wins, 29% raw wins — confirming non-inferiority within a 1-point margin on a 15-point scale. Cosine similarity between raw and distilled responses: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1% of pairs above the 0.70 threshold. Estimated per-call net energy saving: 70–270 μWh.

Conclusion: On-device prompt distillation via a quantised SLM can meaningfully reduce cloud LLM input-token costs and energy consumption while preserving response quality within a practical non-inferiority margin, demonstrating the viability of exploiting the Social-Semantic Gap at the edge.

Abstract: The prefill stage of Large Language Model (LLM) inference is a growing contributor to cloud-scale energy cost. Many consumer-support and conversational prompts contain social scaffolding: politeness markers, apologetic preamble, repetition, and rapport-building language that is important for human communication but carries low marginal information for machine reasoning. We call this discrepancy the Social-Semantic Gap. We present SPSD (Sentiment Preserving Semantic Distillation), an edge-based pipeline that compresses user prompts using a 4-bit quantised Small Language Model before transmission to a cloud-deployed LLM. Evaluation on a 248-prompt corpus using Gemma-2-2B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) as the SLM and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the cloud evaluation model yields a mean input token saving of 99.9 tokens per distilled call, with all 146 distilled calls yielding positive savings. Response quality, assessed by blind LLM-as-judge scoring across 121 pairs, is non-inferior to the raw path within a pre-specified 1-point margin on a 15-point rubric; the judge awarded 43 percent ties, 28 percent distilled wins, and 29 percent raw wins. Cosine similarity is mixed: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1 percent of pairs above the 0.70 reference threshold. Safety-critical domains are conservatively routed to passthrough via rule-based gates. Per-call net energy saving is estimated at 70-270 uWh under stated assumptions. SPSD shows that on-device prompt distillation can reduce cloud LLM input-token cost while preserving response quality within a practical non-inferiority margin.

</details>


### [215] [Human-like autonomy emerges from self-play and a pinch of human data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19370)
*Daphne Cornelisse,Julian Hunt,Zixu Zhang,Waël Doulazmi,Kevin Joseph,Jaime Fernández Fisac,Eugene Vinitsky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a self-play reinforcement learning method for autonomous driving that uses a small amount of human demonstration data (30 minutes) as a regularization objective atop a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. This achieves policies that coordinate well with humans while requiring 2500x less data than imitation learning, training in 15 hours on a single GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pure self-play RL for driving can produce effective but human-incompatible driving conventions. Prior solutions rely on extensive reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive. The authors aim to bridge this behavioral alignment gap without sacrificing the data efficiency and scalability of self-play.

Method: The method ("Spiced Self-Play") treats human demonstrations as a regularization objective layered on top of a minimal, safe goal-reaching reward — analogous to adding a small amount of spice to a stew. Only 30 minutes of human driving data is used to regularize the self-play training process.

Result: Resulting policies successfully coordinate with held-out human trajectories. The approach uses 2500x fewer human demonstrations than comparable imitation learning methods and completes training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU.

Conclusion: A little human data goes a long way: minimal human demonstration data can effectively regularize self-play RL to produce human-compatible driving policies, avoiding the need for extensive reward engineering or large-scale imitation learning datasets.

Abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning has recently emerged as a way to train driving policies without any human data. It uses cheap, large-scale simulations to substitute expensive, large-scale human driving demonstrations. A key limitation of this approach is that policies trained through pure self-play can learn effective but alien driving conventions incompatible with people. Previous works attempt to mitigate such behavioral misalignments through extensive reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive. Instead of completely discarding human demonstrations, our method treats them as a regularization objective on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. Like the spice in a good stew, we find that a little human data goes a long way: our method uses only 30 minutes of human demonstrations, 2500x fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches. Resulting policies coordinate with held-out human trajectories and complete training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. Videos and full source code are available at https://spiced-self-play.com/.

</details>


### [216] [Performance Analysis and Optimization of 3D Generative Diffusion Models across GPU Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19365)
*Jeeho Ryoo,Yongchan Jung,Muhammad Ali Khaliq,Weidong Zhang,Jiatong Han,Byeong Kil Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A performance analysis of the Med-DDPM diffusion model across three NVIDIA GPU architectures reveals that training is dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels with poor Tensor Core utilization. Two architecture-aware optimizations — TF32 Tensor Core activation and 3D channels-last layout — deliver up to 100× SM cycle reduction, 100× fewer dynamic instructions, a ~7× increase in Tensor Core utilization, and a 7% IPC improvement on A100 without degrading synthesis quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models for 3D MRI synthesis are highly effective but suffer from prohibitive GPU resource demands due to hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample and heterogeneous kernel behavior. Understanding the low-level performance bottlenecks across GPU architectures is essential for enabling practical deployment.

Method: The authors perform a comprehensive performance analysis of Med-DDPM across three NVIDIA GPU generations (V100, A100, H100), examining kernel-level runtime breakdowns, instruction-mix characteristics, memory system utilization, warp-level activities, and profiler priority-score estimates. Based on these insights, they evaluate two architecture-aware optimizations: (1) enabling TF32 Tensor Core acceleration and (2) adopting a 3D channels-last memory layout.

Result: Training is overwhelmingly dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels, with inefficiencies from poor memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and limited Tensor Core utilization. The proposed optimizations reduce SM cycles by up to 100×, cut dynamic instructions by 100×, raise Tensor Core utilization from 1.45× to 9.98×, and improve IPC by 7% on the A100, all without loss of synthesis quality.

Conclusion: Architecture-aware optimizations — specifically TF32 Tensor Core activation and channels-last layout — can dramatically improve the efficiency of medical diffusion models on modern NVIDIA GPUs, substantially lowering the computational barrier for 3D MRI synthesis without compromising output fidelity.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become essential for high-fidelity 3D MRI synthesis, yet their deployment remains constrained by substantial GPU resource demands arising from hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample and a highly heterogeneous kernel behavior. This paper performs a comprehensive performance analysis of the state-of-the-art medical diffusion model, Med-DDPM, across three generations of NVIDIA architectures to study kernel-level runtime breakdowns, instruction-mix characteristics, memory system utilization, warp-level activities, and profiler priority-score estimates. We show that training is overwhelmingly dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels, with inefficiencies arising from memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and limited Tensor Core utilization. Guided by these insights, we evaluate two architecture-aware optimizations TF32 Tensor Core activation and a 3D channels-last layout and demonstrate that they reduce SM cycles by up to 100x, cut dynamic instructions by 100x, raise Tensor Core utilization from 1.45 to 9.98x, and increase IPC by 7% on A100, all without degrading synthesis quality.

</details>


### [217] [Information Lattice Learning as Probabilistic Graphical Model Structure Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19366)
*Haizi Yu,Lav R. Varshney*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ILL learns interpretable probabilistic rules via partition lattice projections; these rules correspond to marginal constraints on quotient variables. The paper develops a PGM interpretation showing ILL constructs constraint-based factor graphs under maximum-entropy/shannon lifting, distinguishing it from Bayesian networks and positioning it as structure learning for symbolic-probabilistic models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge Information Lattice Learning (ILL) with probabilistic graphical models (PGMs), clarifying how ILL's learned rule sets — interpretable abstractions over quotient variables — correspond to marginal constraints and how lifting operations relate to maximum-entropy reconstruction, thereby providing a rigorous PGM-based understanding of ILL.

Method: The authors reinterpret ILL operations in PGM terms: a partition induces a deterministic quotient variable; a rule is its marginal law; a rule set forms marginal constraints. General lifting defines the family of joint distributions satisfying those constraints, while special lifting uses an L2 uniformity principle (closely related to maximum entropy) for maximum-ignorance reconstruction. Under Shannon-entropy lifting, constraints yield a log-linear factor graph with factors indexed by learned abstractions. The information lattice's edges encode refinement/coarsening, not conditional dependence, distinguishing it from Bayesian networks.

Result: ILL is best characterized as structure learning for interpretable, constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables — not Bayesian networks. This framing clarifies ILL's relationship to graphical models and maximum-entropy models and suggests new directions in inference, identifiability, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning.

Conclusion: ILL naturally admits a PGM interpretation as constraint-based factor graph learning, where rules are marginal constraints on interpretable quotient variables and lifting implements maximum-entropy reconstruction. This perspective opens avenues for advancing inference, identifiability, and hybrid learning paradigms.

Abstract: Information lattice learning (ILL) learns interpretable rules of a signal by alternately projecting the signal onto a partition lattice that encodes a hierarchy of abstractions and lifting selected rules back to the signal domain. When the signal is a probability mass function, we show the probabilistic rules learned by ILL admit a natural probabilistic graphical model (PGM) interpretation and develop this interpretation in detail. A partition in ILL induces a deterministic quotient variable, and a rule is the marginal law of that quotient variable. A rule set is therefore a collection of marginal constraints over interpretable abstractions. General lifting is the feasible family of all joint distributions satisfying those constraints, while special lifting chooses a maximum-ignorance reconstruction, implemented in ILL by an L2 uniformity principle closely related to maximum entropy. Under a Shannon-entropy lifting, the same constraints yield a log-linear factor graph whose factors are indexed by learned abstractions. The information lattice itself, however, is not a Bayesian network: its edges encode refinement and coarsening of abstractions, not conditional dependence. Thus ILL is best viewed as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables. This view clarifies how ILL relates to graphical models and maximum entropy models, while suggesting new directions for inference, identifiability, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning.

</details>


### [218] [Weibull Weight-Scale Parameter Evolution under AdamW Training Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19367)
*Tiexin Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes why the Weibull weight-scale parameter λ grows, overshoots, and relaxes during AdamW training by decomposing the squared weight norm dynamics into three forces: alignment, injection, and decay. On Pythia-70M, alignment dominates the growth phase (~88-94%). A spline displacement method recovers these forces from sparse checkpoints when optimizer states are unavailable. A data-coherence effect on λ peak is noted.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work established a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, but the dynamical origin of the Weibull scale parameter λ(t) — specifically, why it grows, overshoots, and then relaxes during AdamW training — remained unexplained. Understanding these dynamics is critical for mechanistic interpretability of training.

Method: The authors derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update rule: an alignment force (correlation between weights and the adaptive update direction), an injection force (adaptive step magnitude), and a decay force (decoupled weight decay). They validate this on self-trained Pythia-70M models with logged ground-truth optimizer moments. A spline displacement method is introduced to recover the alignment force from sparse checkpoints alone (without optimizer states), achieving ~92-94% accuracy. The RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset is decomposed into bridge and integration components.

Result: Alignment force dominates 88-94% of the absolute force budget during the rise phase across four random seeds and is robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the transition from growth to relaxation. The RMS-to-Weibull offset totals ~5-6% in densely sampled regions. The spline displacement method recovers alignment force about twice as accurately as a naive two-point baseline. The peak value of λ(t) varies with training-data coherence.

Conclusion: Weight-scale growth and relaxation during AdamW training are governed by a clean three-force dynamics: alignment drives growth, decay counters it, and their balance determines the λ(t) trajectory. The framework generalizes beyond toy models via the spline displacement method, and the data-coherence dependence motivates a controlled follow-up study.

Abstract: Building on a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, we study why the Weibull weight-scale parameter $λ$ grows, overshoots, and then relaxes during AdamW training. We derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update: an alignment force measuring the correlation between weights and the adaptive update direction, an injection force from adaptive step magnitude, and a decay force from decoupled weight decay. On self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments, alignment dominates the rise phase, contributing 88-94% of the absolute force budget across four random seeds and remaining robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the transition from weight-scale growth to relaxation. These force dynamics directly govern the squared-norm component underlying $λ(t)$; the remaining RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset is measurable and decomposes into bridge and integration components, totaling approximately 5-6% in densely sampled regions. To extend the analysis to real models where optimizer moments are unavailable, we introduce a spline displacement method that recovers the alignment force from sparse checkpoints with approximately 92-94% accuracy, about twice the naive two-point baseline. We further observe that the peak value of $λ(t)$ varies with training-data coherence in our experiments, suggesting a data-dependent component of weight-scale growth that we leave to a controlled follow-up study. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tiexinding/NPM-Weibull-public.

</details>


### [219] [Zero-Inflated Gaussian Distributions Enable Parameter-Space Sparsity in Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19369)
*Andreas Faust,Sven Nitzsche,Juergen Becker*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as sampling laws for estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs), enabling EDAs to operate natively on sparse parameter spaces without hand-crafted sparsity operators, and demonstrates faster convergence on the Lunar Lander benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EDAs avoid hand-designed operators by fitting distributions to elite samples, but existing EDAs only work on dense continuous spaces. For sparse problems (where most coefficients should be zero), current methods reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid — hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level alternating schemes, and arbitrary zeroing thresholds. The gap is that no principled EDA exists for sparse black-box optimization.

Method: The authors propose using multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as the sampling model within EDAs. The ZIG model uses a latent Gaussian with separate indicator and value dimensions, jointly representing sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and interactions between them — enabling hierarchy-free joint optimization. They prove latent parameter identifiability from observed samples (unlike missing-data settings) and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators that accurately recover latent correlation structures.

Result: On the Lunar Lander benchmark, the ZIG-EDA converges faster and achieves higher final returns than: (1) a dense Gaussian EDA, (2) a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and (3) an ad-hoc sparse EDA — while producing controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.

Conclusion: ZIG distributions provide a principled, assumption-free approach for extending EDAs to sparse optimization, eliminating the need for hand-designed sparsity mechanisms while achieving superior performance through joint modeling of sparsity patterns and active values.

Abstract: Estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs) are a powerful class of evolutionary methods for black-box optimization, especially when little is known about the structure of the objective. Whereas classical evolutionary algorithms rely on hand-designed mutation and crossover operators, hard to devise for unknown problem structures, and a source of bias, EDAs sidestep operator design entirely: they fit a probability distribution to the best individuals and sample the next generation from it. EDAs are well established on continuous parameter spaces, but they have not previously been generalized to sparse ones, in which most coefficients of a good solution are exactly zero. Existing sparse black-box optimizers therefore reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid: hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level schemes alternating between support set and active values, zeroing thresholds, and other baked-in assumptions. We close this gap by proposing multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as EDA sampling laws. A latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and the interactions between the two, so sparsity patterns and active values are optimized jointly, hierarchy-free. We show that the latent parameters of this model are identifiable from observed samples, unlike in the missing-data settings where related constructions originate, and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators for them. The estimators accurately recover latent correlation structures, and on the Lunar Lander benchmark the resulting ZIG-EDA converges faster and reaches higher final returns than a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while finding controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.

</details>


### [220] [Cost-Optimal LLM Routing with Limited User Feedback under User Satisfaction Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19376)
*Herbert Woisetschläger,Arastun Mammadli,Ryan Zhang,Shiqiang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SLARouter is an online LLM request routing algorithm that learns cost-optimal policies from sparse, one-sided user feedback, providing theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance, achieving up to 2.2x cost reduction over baselines without per-benchmark tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM inference costs are surging due to growing demand, while users expect high-quality responses codified in SLAs. Existing cost-aware routing methods require complete feedback, offline training, per-workload tuning, and lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity — creating a need for an online routing solution that balances cost and quality with formal guarantees.

Method: SLARouter is an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy using only sparse, one-sided user feedback (e.g., thumbs up/down) available in production systems. It operates at inference time and provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance without requiring per-benchmark tuning.

Result: Experiments across diverse LLM benchmarks show SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints and reduces operating costs by up to 2.2× compared to existing baselines, all without per-benchmark tuning.

Conclusion: SLARouter successfully resolves the cost-quality tension in LLM applications by learning from sparse feedback online, delivering provable SLA compliance and significant cost savings in a deployment-friendly manner.

Abstract: Inference costs for large language model (LLM) applications are rapidly growing, driven by surging demand and rising infrastructure cost. Users expect high-quality responses, and in commercial settings this is formally codified in Service Level Agreements (SLAs), creating a fundamental tension between cost and quality. Recent progress on cost-aware LLM request routing has shown potential to resolve this tension, but existing approaches rely on complete feedback signals, offline training, extensive per-workload tuning, and most lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity. We introduce SLARouter, an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy from the sparse, one-sided user feedback available in production systems. SLARouter provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance. Experiments across a wide range of LLM benchmarks show that SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without the need for per-benchmark tuning, reducing operating cost by up to 2.2x over existing baselines.

</details>


### [221] [ProMUSE: Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty-guided Staged Evidential Alzheimer Disease Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19371)
*Long Doan,Branden Chen,Ethan Litton,Huan Huang,Jiajing Huang,Yixin Xie,Weihua Zhou,Nandakumar Narayanan,Chen Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProMUSE is a progressive multimodal network that uses evidential uncertainty from low-cost clinical data to decide when expensive MRI/PET scans are needed for Alzheimer's diagnosis, reducing imaging usage by 50-90% while maintaining accuracy comparable to full-modality approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MRI and PET imaging are costly and not universally accessible, making full-modality AD diagnosis impractical in real-world clinical workflows. There is a need for a resource-efficient system that adaptively determines when expensive imaging is actually necessary.

Method: ProMUSE first performs evidential classification using cheap clinical data, quantifying prediction uncertainty via Dirichlet-based subjective logic. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, it progressively incorporates MRI or PET features. Multimodal fusion uses Dempster-Shafer theory to combine modality-wise belief and uncertainty for calibrated predictions.

Result: On ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS datasets across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks, ProMUSE achieves competitive or superior accuracy versus full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50-90%.

Conclusion: ProMUSE is a practical, uncertainty-aware, resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening that significantly reduces diagnostic costs without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a fatal disorder that destroys memory and cognitive skills in the elderly population. Most treatments for AD are effective in the early stage, leading to an increasing demand for early AD diagnosis. AD diagnosis increasingly relies on multimodal data such as clinical assessments, structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging. However, MRI and PET acquisition remain costly and not universally accessible, making full-modality inference impractical in real-world clinical workflows. We propose ProMUSE, a Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty Guided Staged Evidential Network that adaptively determines when additional modalities are necessary, helping reduce the overall cost of data acquisition while maintaining accuracy. ProMUSE first performs evidential classification using low-cost clinical data and quantifies uncertainty via a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, ProMUSE progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty through Dempster-Shafer theory to obtain a calibrated multimodal prediction. This staged acquisition strategy enables accurate diagnosis while minimizing reliance on expensive imaging. Experiments on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks demonstrate that ProMUSE achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50-90%, yielding substantial cost savings. These results highlight ProMUSE as a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening.

</details>


### [222] [cAPM: Continual AI-Assisted Pace-Mapping with Active Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19373)
*Dylan O'Hara,Pradeep Bajracharya,Casey Meisenzahl,Karli Gillette,Anton J. Prassl,Gernot Plank,Saman Nazarian,Roderick Tung,John L Sapp,Linwei Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces cAPM, a continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping framework that leverages a task-agnostic surrogate neural network, active learning, and continual learning to transfer knowledge across multiple ventricular tachycardia (VT) localization tasks. It dramatically reduces the number of pacing sites needed (4.5 vs. 13.7) while achieving 81% localization accuracy within 5 mm, compared to 38% for existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current active learning AI models for pace-mapping require retraining from scratch for each new VT target and cannot transfer knowledge across VTs within the same patient or across patients. This inefficiency demands a method that accumulates and reuses past pace-mapping data to reduce the number of pacing sites needed for future targets.

Method: cAPM combines three components: (1) a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that learns the mapping from pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology; (2) an active-learning strategy that selects the most informative pacing site per target to refine the surrogate; and (3) a continual learning strategy that sequentially processes targets while retaining knowledge from prior ones, with an optional replay mechanism for past data samples.
