Result: In an in-silico testbed with sequentially presented localization tasks across varying physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM achieved 81% probability of localizing within 5 mm accuracy using only 4.5 pace-mapping sites, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving 38% with 13.7 sites.

Conclusion: cAPM demonstrates strong potential for improving pace-mapping efficiency through knowledge transfer and provides a solid foundation for future in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies in catheter ablation of VT.

Abstract: Ventricular tachycardia is a life-threatening rhythm disorder and a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Pace-mapping is a clinical procedure for identifying the intervention target during catheter ablation of VT. It requires clinicians to pace different sites in the ventricles and rapidly interpret the resulting electrocardiograms to determine where to pace next or whether a target site has been identified. Active learning AI models have been proposed to guide clinicians to the next pacing site, showing promise in reducing the number of pacing sites and improving the efficiency of pace-mapping. Existing methods require retraining each target without the ability to transfer knowledge across multiple VTs within the same patient or across patients. We introduce cAPM for continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping to capture and transfer knowledge accumulated from past pace-mapping data to reduce the number of pace-mapping data needed for future target VTs. This is made possible by a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that learns the mapping from pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology, an active-learning strategy that refines this surrogate model by selecting the most informative pacing site for each target, and a continual learning strategy to do so sequentially while retaining knowledge from prior targets. Evaluated on an in-silico testbed consisting of sequentially-presented localization tasks across different physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM with and without replay of past data samples achieved an 81% probability of localizing within clinical tolerance (5 mm accuracy) using 4.5 pace-mapping sites, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving 38% probability using 13.7 pacing sites. These results provide a strong basis for preparing cAPM towards in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies where it can be used to guide pace-mapping.

</details>


### [223] [Protein Representation Learning with Secondary-Structure and Energy-Filtered Hydrogen-Bond Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19374)
*Mohamed Mouhajir,Limei Wang,El Houcine Bergou,Hajar El Hammouti,Lamiae Azizi,Dongqi Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning. Residue nodes are augmented with secondary structure labels, and edges are built from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by energetic strength. The approach consistently outperforms existing graph-based methods on standard benchmarks and yields biologically interpretable representations aligned with known structural motifs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing protein graph representations rely on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which incompletely capture the principles of protein folding. Proteins fold into 3D conformations governed by secondary structure elements (α-helices, β-sheets) and hydrogen-bond interactions, motivating a representation that explicitly encodes these structural and energetic features.

Method: The authors propose a graph neural network where (1) residue-level node features are augmented with secondary structure assignments, and (2) graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions, filtered by energetic strength. This yields a sparse, biophysically meaningful topology that captures both local structural context and long-range couplings.

Result: The proposed method achieves consistent improvements over existing graph-based approaches on commonly used protein benchmarks. The learned graph connectivity aligns with established structural motifs, offering enhanced biological interpretability.

Conclusion: Incorporating secondary structure information and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning, improving both predictive performance and interpretability. Code is publicly available.

Abstract: Graph-based representations are widely used in protein modeling, yet many existing approaches rely primarily on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which only partially reflect the principles governing protein folding. Proteins instead adopt complex three-dimensional conformations organized around secondary structure elements, such as $α$-helices and $β$-sheets, which encode recurring local motifs and stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions. In this work, we introduce a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning. Residue-level node representations are augmented with secondary structure assignments, and graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by their energetic strength. This design enables the model to capture both local structural context and long-range couplings that are central to protein stability and function. We evaluate the proposed approach on commonly used protein benchmarks and observe consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods. In addition, the resulting graph representations offer enhanced biological interpretability, as the learned connectivity aligns with established structural motifs. These findings suggest that incorporating secondary structure and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning. The code is released at https://github.com/mohamedmohamed2021/SSProNet

</details>


### [224] [Physics-Informed Discovery of Yield Functions in Plasticity via Convex Neural Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19375)
*Hyeonbin Moon,Donghyuk Cho,Jecheon Yu,Jeong Whan Yoon,Seunghwa Ryu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A physics-informed framework using convex neural networks is proposed to discover anisotropic yield functions from full-field displacement and reaction force data, without requiring stress observations, plastic strain measurements, or a prescribed parametric form. The neural yield function is embedded within elastoplastic stress integration and trained via a differentiable formulation across multiple loading cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identifying anisotropic yield functions is challenging because yielding is not directly observable in full-field measurements, directional calibration demands many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. Existing methods typically require stress-space supervision or a priori parametric assumptions, limiting their applicability.

Method: The yield function is represented by a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one, with assumed tension-compression symmetry. This neural yield function is integrated into a differentiable elastoplastic stress update and trained using a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases, using only full-field displacement and reaction force data. Validation uses FE benchmarks with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions.

Result: The framework successfully recovers yield contours matching the ground-truth models in FE benchmark studies. Assessments include yield contour agreement, sensitivity to displacement noise, identifiability via plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty quantification, and deployment as a polynomial surrogate.

Conclusion: The proposed mechanics-constrained framework enables discovery of anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data alone, keeping the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration, thus providing a principled data-driven alternative to traditional phenomenological yield function calibration.

Abstract: Identifying anisotropic yield functions remains challenging since yielding is not directly observed in full-field mechanical measurements, directional calibration can require many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. This study proposes a physics-informed framework for discovering yield functions from full-field displacement data and reaction force data, without stress observations, plastic strain measurements, direct yield surface data, or a prescribed parametric yield function. The framework identifies the yield function as a mechanically constrained constitutive component inside elastoplastic stress integration, rather than through direct stress-space supervision. The yield function is represented by a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one while imposing the assumed tension-compression symmetry, and this neural yield function is trained with a differentiable stress update and a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases. The proposed framework is validated using finite element (FE) benchmark studies with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions, assessing yield contour agreement, displacement-noise sensitivity, identifiability through plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and polynomial-surrogate deployment. This study provides a mechanics-constrained pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while keeping the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration.

</details>


### [225] [Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20493)
*Zewen Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Evaluator biases in LLM-based multi-agent systems propagate between agents. This paper formalizes "Contagion Networks" to measure bias spread, demonstrates three propagation regimes governed by spectral radius, finds homogeneous-model contagion is 3-5x weaker than cross-model contagion, and shows increasing evaluator committee size reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When LLMs act as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases can propagate through the agent network, distorting collective judgments. Prior work (MM-EPC) observed strong cross-model contagion, but the dynamics within homogeneous-model agent systems and potential mitigation strategies remain underexplored.

Method: The authors introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring evaluator bias propagation. They conduct a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), measuring the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Γ₃. Spectral radius analysis of Γ_N defines three propagation regimes. They also test committee-size scaling (k=1 to k=3) as a mitigation strategy.

Result: Evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]) even within the same model. Three propagation regimes emerge, governed by ρ(Γ_N). Homogeneous-model contagion coefficients are 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients (MM-EPC: γ ≈ 0.85–1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. Increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 yields a 72.4% reduction in effective contagion.

Conclusion: Bias contagion is a measurable, structured phenomenon in homogeneous LLM multi-agent systems, but is substantially weaker than cross-model contagion. The Contagion Network framework enables quantitative diagnostics, and committee-based evaluation provides a practical, effective mitigation strategy.

Abstract: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

</details>


### [226] [Emyx: Fast and efficient all-atom protein generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19377)
*Nicholas J. Williams,Ward Haddadin,Matteo P. Ferla,Constantin Schneider,Nicholas B. Woodall,Ruby Sedgwick,Christian D. Madsen,Andrew L. Hopkins,Edward O. Pyzer-Knapp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Emmyx is a lightweight (140M-parameter) conditional flow matching model for enzyme design that replaces heavy embedding stacks with efficient transformers, bridging flow matching with diffusion sampling via an exact reparametrisation. Despite being the smallest model and training 4× faster than competitors, it outperforms Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 on the AME benchmark across success rate, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current all-atom generative models for computational enzyme design inherit expensive, complex architectures from protein structure prediction, resulting in high training costs and limited sample diversity. The authors argue this complexity is unnecessary given that enzyme design conditions on sparse geometric constraints (catalytic residues and ligands) rather than rich co-evolutionary signals, motivating a streamlined, purpose-built generative model.

Method: Emmyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that: (1) uses standard transformer blocks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity instead of heavy embedding stacks; (2) derives an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM (Elucidating Diffusion Models) noise-level framework, enabling use of state-of-the-art diffusion sampling methods without retraining the flow matching model.

Result: Emmyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 on the AME enzyme design benchmark under strict evaluation (requiring global fold recovery, catalytic geometry accuracy, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity). It trains in only 682 GPU-hours, approximately 4× less than RFdiffusion3.

Conclusion: Streamlined architectures purpose-built for sparse geometric conditioning can surpass larger, structure-prediction-inherited models in both efficiency and enzyme design quality. The reparametrisation connecting flow matching and diffusion sampling demonstrates that training efficiency and inference-time sampling performance need not be in tension.

Abstract: Computational enzyme design requires generating proteins that scaffold catalytic residues and ligands, a task that demands both geometric accuracy and structural diversity from the underlying generative model. Current all-atom generators inherit expensive architectures from structure prediction, leading to high training costs and limited sample diversity. We argue that much of this complexity is unnecessary for generators, which condition on sparse geometric constraints rather than rich co-evolutionary signals. Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that concentrates capacity within standard transformer blocks, replacing heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity. We additionally derive an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, bridging flow matching training efficiency with state-of-the-art sampling methods designed for diffusion models without retraining. Despite being the smallest model, Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 against the AME enzyme design benchmark across success rate under strict evaluation requiring both global fold recovery and catalytic geometry accuracy, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity, while training in just $682$ GPU-hours, roughly $4\times$ less than RFdiffusion3.

</details>


### [227] [A Hybrid GNN-FEM Framework for Phase-Field Fracture Simulation. Physics-Preserving Hybridization for Generalizable Surrogate Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19378)
*Hyeonbin Moon,Yongjin Choi,Seunghwa Ryu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid GNN-FEM framework accelerates phase-field fracture simulation by using a graph neural network surrogate to replace the phase-field update in each load increment, while retaining a FEM displacement solver. This preserves history dependence and achieves strong generalization across geometries, loads, materials, and discretizations via dimensionless features, graph formulation, and physics-informed loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Phase-field fracture models are accurate but computationally prohibitive due to coupled, nonlinear, history-dependent systems solved incrementally via FEM. Existing ML surrogates struggle with physical consistency and generalization for such nonlinear, history-dependent problems. The authors aim to reduce cost while preserving the incremental, history-dependent structure and enforcing mechanical equilibrium.

Method: A hybrid staggered scheme wherein a GNN surrogate replaces the phase-field update at each load increment, while the FEM displacement solver remains intact to enforce equilibrium and boundary conditions. Key design choices include: (1) dimensionless input feature design, (2) graph-based formulation on mesh-based domains, and (3) a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field PDE. The surrogate targets the phase-field mapping at each increment rather than the full solution trajectory.

Result: Numerical experiments show reduced computational cost relative to conventional FEM while maintaining accuracy. The framework exhibits robust predictive performance and strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations.

Conclusion: Selectively replacing the phase-field solver with a GNN surrogate within an incremental FEM framework is a physically consistent and generalizable strategy for accelerating history-dependent fracture simulations, outperforming brute-force end-to-end learning approaches.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning (SciML) has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating simulations of complex physical systems, yet achieving physically consistent and generalizable predictions for nonlinear, history-dependent problems remains a central challenge. In this study, we propose a hybrid GNN--FEM framework for efficient and generalizable phase-field fracture modeling. While phase-field approaches provide a robust variational framework for simulating complex crack evolution, their high computational cost limits practical applications because they require solving coupled, nonlinear, and history-dependent systems within an incremental finite element procedure. To address this challenge, a graph neural network surrogate is integrated into the conventional staggered scheme, replacing the phase-field update at each load increment while retaining the FEM-based displacement solver to enforce mechanical equilibrium and boundary conditions. By preserving the incremental solution structure, the framework remains consistent with history-dependent fracture evolution without requiring the surrogate to approximate the full solution trajectory. This selective surrogate strategy emphasizes the identification of a physically meaningful and incrementally structured learning target, rather than relying on brute-force data generation to learn the full fracture process. The proposed framework achieves strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations through dimensionless feature design, a graph-based formulation on mesh-based domains, and a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field equation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the hybrid approach reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy compared with conventional FEM, and exhibits robust predictive performance across diverse problem settings.

</details>


### [228] [How Linear Is a Transformer Feed-Forward Block? Per-Block Linear Recoverability Is Learned, Not Architectural](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19379)
*Stuart Whipp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces R²_lin, a measure of how linearly recoverable each transformer FFN block is, computed via the closed-form least-squares linear approximation. Applied to GPT-2, Pythia-160M, and Llama-160M, it reveals highly heterogeneous, depth-varying nonlinearity profiles that are learned rather than architecturally determined. Low-rank bilinear probes cannot recover the residual nonlinearity, and the measure serves as both a compression guide and a methodological caution against under-converged linear baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer FFNs are commonly viewed as key-value stores of computation, but there is little empirical measurement of how nonlinear individual trained FFN blocks actually are. The authors seek to quantify FFN nonlinearity in a principled, optimizer-free way and understand its origins, structure, and practical implications.

Method: Each FFN block is treated as a position-wise map and decomposed into its optimal least-squares linear approximation (closed-form solution via the normal equations) plus a residual. The coefficient of determination R²_lin — the fraction of output variance explained by the linear map — quantifies linear recoverability. The residual is further probed with a low-rank bilinear model. The measure is applied across all blocks of GPT-2, Pythia-160M, and Llama-160M.

Result: R²_lin varies dramatically across blocks (from >0.99 to <0.3) in a non-monotone pattern with depth. Profiles differ sharply between same-width GELU models (GPT-2 vs. Pythia-160M), indicating nonlinearity is a learned property, not dictated by activation function or architecture. A low-rank bilinear probe of the residual recovers negligible additional variance, and the gain is uncorrelated with residual nonlinearity, suggesting the unrecovered computation involves higher-order or distributed structure. Highly recoverable blocks can be replaced with a single linear layer at 8× fewer parameters for only +0.77 perplexity, while low-recoverability blocks flag unsafe compression targets. Trained linear baselines suffer from severe under-convergence on ill-conditioned transformer activations, motivating the closed-form approach.

Conclusion: FFN nonlinearity is a learned, block-specific property that varies sharply across depth and across models, not a uniform architectural consequence. R²_lin provides a simple, optimizer-free diagnostic for model interpretability, targeted compression, and reliable linear baseline construction.

Abstract: Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs) are often treated as nonlinear stores of computation, yet how nonlinear a trained FFN block actually is has rarely been measured. We treat each FFN as a position-wise input-to-output map and split it into the exact least-squares linear approximation plus a residual. The held-out variance the closed-form linear map explains defines a block's linear recoverability (R^2_lin), an optimiser-free measure of its linearity.
  Across all twelve blocks of GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and llama-160m, R^2_lin is highly heterogeneous and non-monotone with depth, ranging from near-linear (>0.99) to strongly nonlinear (<0.3) between adjacent blocks, and is not set by the activation function: same-width GELU models GPT-2 and Pythia-160m have sharply different profiles, so recoverability is a learned property of individual trained blocks, not an architectural one. A low-rank bilinear probe of the residual recovers only a few points of R^2, with gain uncorrelated with residual nonlinearity: the unrecovered computation is not a single position-wise product but higher-order or distributed structure.
  The measurement also serves as a targeted compression signal: recoverable blocks admit large single-layer replacements (GPT-2's early FFN at 8x fewer parameters for +0.77 perplexity), while low-recoverability blocks flag where this is unsafe. It further exposes a methodological pitfall: trained linear baselines can badly under-converge on ill-conditioned transformer activations, so we report the exact closed-form least-squares ceiling throughout.

</details>


### [229] [VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19399)
*Manish Acharya,Zhenyu Liao,Yueke Zhang,Kevin Leach,Yu Huang,Yifan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VERITAS is a zero-shot framework that feeds rich verifier signals (errors, type mismatches, partial progress) back into proof search via a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling followed by critic-guided MCTS using Phase 1 failures as negative examples, achieving 40.6% on miniF2F and exposing the weakness of unguided sampling on combinatorics problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based formal provers reduce verifier feedback to a binary pass/fail signal, discarding rich diagnostic information like syntax errors, type mismatches, and partial goal progress. This impoverishes the proof search process, particularly for problems requiring iterative lemma recovery from verifier signals.

Method: A two-phase, zero-shot protocol: Phase 1 performs Best-of-N sampling to collect initial proofs. Phase 2 executes a critic-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) that ingests Phase 1 failure traces as explicit negative examples, routing all verifier signals (not just pass/fail) into tree exploration. The protocol guarantees that every theorem solved in Phase 1 is preserved, making Phase 2 gains attributable solely to feedback-driven exploration.

Result: VERITAS achieves 40.6% on miniF2F test (vs. Best-of-5 at 36.9% and Portfolio at 26.2%). On the newly released VERITAS-CombiBench (55 combinatorics theorems), VERITAS reaches 7.3% while Best-of-5 drops to 1.8% (below Portfolio's 3.6%), demonstrating that unguided sampling fails when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback.

Conclusion: Rich verifier signal routing via critic-guided MCTS substantially improves formal proof search, particularly on problems requiring iterative feedback utilization. The framework is zero-shot, preserves all Phase 1 solutions, and its gains are directly attributable to the feedback mechanism. The released CombiBench exposes a failure mode of unguided sampling in formal theorem proving.

Abstract: LLM-based formal provers often collapse rich verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress) into a binary pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that routes every verifier signal back into proof search through a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling first, then a critic-guided MCTS pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples. The protocol preserves every theorem solved by its own Phase 1 sweep, so Phase 2's additional solves are attributable to feedback-driven exploration. VERITAS reaches 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. an independently run Best-of-5 at 36.9%, Portfolio 26.2%) and 7.3% on VERITAS-CombiBench, a 55-theorem combinatorics benchmark we release on which Best-of-5 (1.8%) falls below Portfolio (3.6%), exposing that unguided sampling hurts when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback. Artifacts are available on GitHub.

</details>


### [230] [Thermodynamic Signatures of Reasoning: Free-Energy and Spectral-Form-Factor Diagnostics for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19404)
*Salim Khazem*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats attention Laplacians as Hamiltonians and extracts thermodynamic potentials and random matrix theory (RMT) features for hallucination detection in LLMs. Fes achieves state-of-the-art AUROC, improves over prior spectral methods by 2.4–6.5 points, and provides theoretical guarantees on stability, expressiveness, and PAC generalization, while also revealing that correct generations follow Wigner-Dyson statistics and hallucinations follow Poisson statistics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior attention-spectral diagnostics for hallucination detection discard most of the Laplacian spectrum by summarizing it with only a few eigenvalues or hand-crafted scalars. The authors aim to exploit the full spectral structure by drawing on statistical physics and random matrix theory.

Method: Fes treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extracts thermodynamic potentials: partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, and heat capacity, plus the RMT spectral form factor. A lightweight probe is trained on Fes descriptors. Stability (Lipschitz), expressiveness, and PAC generalization bounds are proven. An unsupervised RMT-deviation score is also evaluated.

Result: Across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, Fes outperforms LapEig by +6.5 AUROC and GoR-4 by +2.4 AUROC on average. Unsupervised RMT-deviation achieves mean AUROC 0.71. Correct generations show Wigner-Dyson spectral statistics; hallucinations show Poisson-like statistics.

Conclusion: Fes provides a richer, stable, and theoretically grounded spectral representation for hallucination detection, achieving SOTA performance without LLM updates. The RMT connection offers both a practical detector and insight into the spectral signatures distinguishing faithful vs. hallucinated generations.

Abstract: Hallucination detection in large language models (LLMs) is deployment-critical, and recent work shows that the spectrum of attention-derived graph Laplacians carries strong signal about reasoning quality. Prior spectral diagnostics, however, summarize the Laplacian spectrum by a handful of eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars, leaving most of its structure unused. We propose Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extracts its thermodynamic potentials partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity together with the random-matrix-theory (RMT) spectral form factor. We prove three results: (i)~Lipschitz stability of Fes under attention perturbation; (ii)~an expressiveness result showing that Fes enriches finite spectral summaries and approximates moment-derived spectral functionals under explicit regularity and grid-resolution assumptions; and (iii)~a finite-sample PAC bound on the AUROC of a training-free detector built from Fes. Empirically, across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, a lightweight probe on Fes descriptors achieves the strongest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, improving over LapEig by $+6.5$ AUROC points and over GoR-4 by $+2.4$ points on average, while requiring no update to the underlying LLM. In the fully unsupervised setting, an RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC $0.71$, providing a label-free but weaker detector. A complementary RMT analysis shows that correct generations exhibit more Wigner-Dyson like spectral statistics, whereas hallucinations exhibit more Poisson-like statistics. The anonymized code and config are provided in the supplementary material.

</details>


### [231] [FlexLAM: Resolving the Bottleneck Trade-off in Latent Action Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19408)
*Takanori Yoshimoto,Yang Hu,Naruya Kondo,Tatsuya Matsushima*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlexLAM replaces fixed-capacity latent action bottlenecks with variable-length codes via nested dropout, learning prefix-valid representations that capture essential transition structure first and add detail only when needed, matching or surpassing fixed-capacity LAMs across all token budgets without architectural changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity code bottleneck, creating a fundamental trade-off: tight codes discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while loose codes preserve excess variation that degrades alignment when labels are scarce. The authors aim to resolve this bottleneck trade-off without new architectures or loss functions.

Method: FlexLAM introduces variable-length latent actions using nested dropout during training. Nested dropout forces the model to learn an ordered, prefix-valid code where earlier dimensions capture the most critical transition structure and later dimensions add supplementary detail. This yields a single model that can operate at any token budget without retraining — truncating the code at inference time removes the least essential information first.

Result: A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision. Under a low-return single-task alignment stress test, FlexLAM also outperforms fixed-capacity baselines. FlexLAM improves Ego4D transition reconstruction and supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining.

Conclusion: Variable-length latent actions via nested dropout constitute a drop-in, architecture-free upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces. FlexLAM learns a fundamentally better latent-action interface rather than merely offering adjustable inference-time capacity.

Abstract: Latent actions provide a compact interface between action-free video and downstream decision-making, yet existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck. We identify a bottleneck trade-off: overly tight codes can discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while overly loose codes preserve additional transition variation that must be resolved when alignment labels are scarce or narrowly distributed. FlexLAM replaces this fixed capacity with variable-length latent actions trained by nested dropout, yielding prefix-valid codes that capture compact transition structure first and add detail only when needed, without new architectures or losses. A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision and under a low-return single-task alignment stress test, indicating that FlexLAM is not merely adjustable at inference time but learns a better latent-action interface at the same token budgets. The same model supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining, and FlexLAM improves Ego4D transition reconstruction. These results suggest that variable-length latent actions are an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces.

</details>


### [232] [Spectral DPPs via NEPv: A Scalable Continuous Relaxation of Determinantal MAP for Diversity-Aware Data Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19411)
*Richard Yi Da Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper reformulates the NP-hard DPP MAP inference (subset selection maximizing log-determinant) as a continuous optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold, revealing a novel Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv). A self-consistent field (SCF) iteration with spectral-gap convergence guarantees yields an algorithm that scales near-linearly in ground-set size n, requiring only matrix-vector products.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DPP-based subset selection is a fundamental primitive in modern ML (data curation, coreset selection, active learning, prompt selection), but MAP inference is NP-hard, and existing greedy/sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in n. This becomes prohibitive exactly in the data-centric regime where n is millions to billions, creating a need for near-linear-time algorithms.

Method: The authors recast DPP-MAP (maximizing logdet(L_S) over size-k subsets) as continuous optimization on the Stiefel manifold St(k,n). They derive first-order optimality conditions forming a Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv) of a novel form. A self-consistent field (SCF) iteration is proposed to solve this NEPv, with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee. Each iteration requires only matrix-vector products with the kernel, yielding O((ndk + nk^2)t) complexity, compatible with low-rank and feature-map kernels.

Result: The resulting algorithm, referred to as "OurMethod," achieves near-linear scaling in n (O((ndk + nk^2)t) for t iterations), dramatically improving over superlinear baselines. The paper provides the relaxation framework, solver derivation, convergence analysis via spectral gap contraction, and scaling analysis. Empirical benchmarking on real data is deferred to future work.

Conclusion: DPP-MAP can be effectively relaxed to a continuous Stiefel manifold optimization, yielding a tractable NEPv solvable via SCF iteration with local convergence guarantees. This opens the door to principled, near-linear-time diverse subset selection at scales previously intractable, with direct integration into standard ML kernel pipelines.

Abstract: Selecting a small, diverse, high-quality subset from a massive pool of candidates is a recurring primitive in modern machine learning -- data curation and coreset selection for training and fine-tuning large models, active-learning batch acquisition, prompt and exemplar selection for in-context learning, retrieval diversification, and experimental design. Determinantal Point Processes (\DPP s) give a principled, well-calibrated notion of diversity for this task, but their \emph{MAP} objective -- pick a size-$k$ subset $S$ maximizing $\logdet(L_S)$ -- is NP-hard, and the standard greedy and sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in the ground-set size $n$. This cost is prohibitive precisely in the data-centric regime where diversity matters most, where $n$ ranges over millions to billions of candidate examples, features, or embeddings. We recast \DPP-MAP as a continuous optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold, and show that its first-order optimality conditions form a \emph{Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency} (\NEPv) of a previously unstudied form. This \NEPv\ admits a self-consistent field (\SCF) iteration with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee, giving a principled iterative solver where the diversity objective drives an eigenvector-dependent operator. The resulting algorithm, \OurMethod, requires only matrix-vector products with the kernel and runs in time $O\!\big((ndk+nk^2)\,t\big)$ for a small number of iterations $t$, scaling near-linearly in $n$ and integrating directly with low-rank and feature-map kernels common in ML. This paper focuses on the relaxation, solver, and scaling analysis; full real-data benchmarking is left to a planned empirical study.

</details>


### [233] [Spectral Retrieval-Augmented Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19412)
*Huu Hiep Nguyen,Minh Hoang Nguyen,Dung Nguyen,Hung Le*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SpecReTF proposes a retrieval-augmented time series forecasting method that uses windowed frequency representations (spectrograms) with a combined amplitude-phase similarity metric and exponential moving average recency weighting to overcome spectral blindness and temporal recency bias in existing retrieval approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented time series forecasting methods suffer from two limitations: (1) spectral blindness — they operate in the time domain and fail to capture frequency-domain periodic structures, and (2) temporal recency — they treat all historical data uniformly without prioritizing recent patterns that are more relevant for non-stationary series.

Method: SpecReTF converts time series into windowed frequency representations (spectrograms), measures similarity using a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information across frequency components, and applies an exponential moving average (EMA) weighting scheme to emphasize temporally recent windows over older ones during retrieval.

Result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that SpecReTF consistently outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, yielding superior forecasting accuracy on diverse, non-stationary time series.

Conclusion: Incorporating frequency-domain representations with recency-aware weighting significantly improves retrieval quality for time series forecasting, validating SpecReTF as an effective solution to the spectral blindness and temporal recency problems.

Abstract: Time series forecasting leverages historical patterns to predict future values, but traditional methods face challenges when dealing with complex, non-stationary patterns that are difficult to memorize during training. Retrieval-augmented approaches have emerged as promising solutions by retrieving similar historical patterns to enhance predictions. However, existing retrieval methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: spectral blindness, which overlooks critical frequency-domain characteristics that capture underlying periodic structures, and temporal recency, which treats all historical data equally without emphasizing recent, more relevant patterns. In this paper, we propose SpecReTF, a novel retrieval method that addresses these issues by converting time series into windowed frequency representations, measuring similarity with a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information. To balance recency and historical context, we apply an exponential moving average weighting scheme that emphasizes recent windows. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SpecReTF outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy across diverse, non-stationary time series.

</details>


### [234] [Does Text Actually Help? Uncovering and Resolving Text Collapse in Multimodal Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19413)
*Huu Hiep Nguyen,Minh Hoang Nguyen,Dung Nguyen,Hung Le*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REST-TS identifies "text collapse" as a failure mode in multimodal time series forecasting where the text branch becomes uninformative. It addresses this by having the numerical backbone produce an independent forecast and training the text branch exclusively on the residual (i.e., the portion the numerical model cannot explain), forcing genuine textual content extraction and achieving SOTA performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal time series forecasting frameworks suffer from "text collapse": the text branch degenerates into a content-independent transformation that contributes negligible discriminative signal. This stems from a fundamental asymmetry — the numerical input is strongly autocorrelated with the output, allowing the numerical backbone to dominate, while the text branch is systematically underexploited despite carrying complementary, critical information.

Method: REST-TS (Residual-Exclusive Supervision for Text in Time Series) converts the asymmetry into a design principle. The numerical backbone independently produces its own forecast. The text branch is then exclusively supervised to predict structured components of the *residual* — the prediction gap that the numerical pathway cannot explain. Since no numerical pathway can reduce these residual losses, the text branch is compelled to extract genuine content from input descriptions.

Result: Evaluated across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures, REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance and consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization compared to existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence for the effectiveness of residual-exclusive supervision.

Conclusion: Supervising the text branch on the residual forces it to extract genuine, discriminative content from textual input. REST-TS provides a principled solution to text collapse in multimodal time series forecasting, turning the inherent numerical-textual asymmetry into an architectural advantage.

Abstract: Multimodal time series forecasting, which pairs numerical sequences with domain-relevant textual reports, promises to inject world knowledge into forecasting pipelines. However, we uncover a critical failure mode in existing frameworks that we term text collapse: the text branch converges to a content-independent transformation, contributing negligible discriminative signal regardless of the input description. We argue that text collapse is a consequence of a fundamental asymmetry in time series forecasting: the numerical input is strongly autocorrelated with the output, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant, while the text branch, despite carrying complementary and often critical information, is insufficiently utilized, leading to its systematic underexploitation. To address this, we propose \textbf{REST-TS} (\textbf{R}esidual-\textbf{E}xclusive \textbf{S}upervision for \textbf{T}ext in \textbf{T}ime \textbf{S}eries), which turns the asymmetry into a design principle: the numerical backbone produces its own independent numerical forecast, and the text branch is exclusively supervised to predict the structured components of the residual, the prediction gap that numbers cannot explain. Because no numerical pathway can reduce these losses, the text branch must extract genuine content from the input description. Evaluated across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures, REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that supervising the text branch on the residual compels it to extract genuine content from the input.

</details>


### [235] [MortarBench: Evaluating Mortgage Loan Origination Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19416)
*Matthew Toles,Yunan Lu,Manav Munjal,Bojun Liu,Yuanhao Deng,Stephanie Selig,Derek Rindner,Cheng Li,Zhou Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MortarBench is a new benchmark for evaluating AI agents in mortgage loan origination, using synthetic data with edge cases. Current LLMs perform poorly (max 77.1% accuracy) and exhibit name-based foreignness bias. The authors propose CRIT, a confidence calibration framework that boosts accuracy to 80.5% while reducing bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Firms are deploying mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers despite no public benchmark existing to evaluate their performance. This creates a need for a standardized, rigorous evaluation framework to assess LLM capabilities, uncover systematic biases, and improve risk management in loan origination.

Method: The authors present MortarBench, which employs a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples covering broad edge cases while matching real-world distributions. They evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs on this benchmark. They then introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework designed to improve accuracy, risk steering, and bias reduction.

Result: Closed-source LLMs achieve at most 77.1% exact match accuracy on MortarBench. Systematic biases were discovered in how LLMs perceive foreignness linked to non-English names. The CRIT framework raises accuracy to 80.5% and improves both risk management steering and bias mitigation.

Conclusion: Current LLMs are insufficient for reliable loan origination tasks, exhibiting both accuracy gaps and harmful biases. Confidence calibration via CRIT offers a promising direction for making AI loan agents more accurate, fair, and risk-aware, though further work is needed given the remaining performance ceiling.

Abstract: Loan origination is the process by which a lender creates a new loan, from application and underwriting through approval and funding. This process serves a critical role in evaluating the eligibility and level of risk posed by an applicant. Recently, firms have begun using mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers, despite a lack of any public benchmark. To fill this gap, we present MortarBench, a loan origination agent benchmark. MortarBench uses a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples with broad edge case coverage that match real-world distributions and questions. We find that state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) perform poorly, with closed-source models achieving at most 77.1\% exact match accuracy. We also discover systematic biases in LLM perception of foreignness related to non-English names. Noting these weaknesses, we introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. Our method increases accuracy to 80.5\% while improving risk management steering and reducing bias.

</details>


### [236] [3D-DLP: Self-Supervised 3D Object-Centric Scene Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19451)
*Ellina Zhang,Madhaven Iyengar,Amir Zadeh,Chuan Li,Deepak Pathak,David Held,Tal Daniel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: 3D-DLP extends Deep Latent Particles to 3D, decomposing RGB-D/voxel scenes into a set of 3D latent particles with disentangled attributes (position, size, appearance) learned via self-supervised reconstruction. The resulting interpretable latent space enables scene editing and improves robotic manipulation over dense or 2D baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scene representation methods either lack explicit 3D structure or use memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric decomposition. There is a need for a compact, interpretable, object-centric 3D representation that disentangles object attributes and supports downstream tasks like robotic manipulation.

Method: 3D-DLP learns a set of 3D latent particles from RGB-D or voxel observations in a self-supervised manner. Each particle encodes disentangled attributes: 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features. The model is trained end-to-end with a reconstruction objective, simultaneously learning interpretable per-particle segmentation maps without explicit supervision.

Result: On both simulated and real-world datasets, the learned latent space proved interpretable and controllable — manipulating particle positions and decoding generates novel scene configurations. For robotic manipulation, using compact 3D latent particles improved performance over baselines lacking explicit 3D information or using dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure.

Conclusion: 3D-DLP provides an effective object-centric 3D scene representation that is compact, interpretable, and beneficial for downstream robotic tasks. The disentangled latent space enables controllable scene generation and outperforms alternative representations in manipulation settings.

Abstract: We introduce 3D-DLP, a self-supervised object-centric representation learning model that decomposes scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of 3D latent particles. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, each particle encodes disentangled attributes, including 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features, and represents a distinct entity in the scene. The model learns interpretable per-particle segmentation maps through an end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective. We demonstrate on both simulated and real-world datasets that the learned latent space is interpretable and controllable: by manipulating particle positions and decoding, we can generate novel scene configurations. Furthermore, we show that leveraging these compact 3D latent particles for downstream robotic manipulation improves performance over baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or rely on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure. Code and videos are available at https://eubooks3003.github.io/3d-dlp.

</details>


### [237] [Can In-Context Learning Support Intrinsic Curiosity?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19476)
*Eric Elmoznino,Sangnie Bhardwaj,Johannes von Oswald,Rajai Nasser,Blaise Agüera y Arcas,João Sacramento,Rif A. Saurous,Guillaume Lajoie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether in-context learning (ICL) in sequence models can replace expensive gradient-based inner loops for computing intrinsic curiosity rewards. The authors prove both a negative result (ICL-derived rewards are generally biased in MDPs) and a positive result (they converge to true learning progress in non-temporal settings like active learning). Experiments validate the framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classic intrinsic curiosity methods reward agents based on learning progress—how much a new observation improves the world model. However, computing this requires costly gradient descent updates within each trajectory, making it impractical at scale. The authors ask whether the emergent in-context learning abilities of large sequence models can serve as immediate, update-free world models, eliminating this computational bottleneck.

Method: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of using ICL prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations to estimate learning progress as intrinsic rewards. It analyzes two settings: (1) general Markov decision processes, proving an impossibility result showing ICL-derived rewards either suffer from nuisance bias or are unimplementable; (2) non-temporal settings (active learning, Bayesian Experimental Design), proving that ICL-derived rewards bound and asymptotically converge to true learning progress. Controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments corroborate the theory.

Result: In general MDPs, unbiased estimation of learning progress via ICL is provably impossible—rewards either contain nuisance terms or cannot be implemented using prediction errors alone. However, for non-temporal settings like active learning and Bayesian experimental design, ICL-derived intrinsic rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to the true learning progress. Experiments confirm that the ICL-driven framework trains curious policies that explore optimally.

Conclusion: ICL can serve as an effective, update-free world model for intrinsic curiosity in non-temporal settings but fails in general sequential decision-making contexts due to fundamental theoretical limitations. The work delineates precisely when and why ICL-based exploration is viable.

Abstract: Effective machine learning depends not only on how we model data, but also on what data we choose to collect. While large sequence models have revolutionized data modeling, the problem of automated data selection, or "intrinsic curiosity", remains a significant challenge. Classic approaches incentivize exploration by rewarding an agent based on its "learning progress", which measures how much a newly acquired observation improves a world model's predictive ability. However, evaluating these rewards traditionally requires expensive inner loops of gradient descent updates within each trajectory, rendering them computationally impractical at scale. In this work, we investigate whether the emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by serving as immediate, update-free world models. Specifically, we evaluate whether an exploration policy can be trained to maximize learning progress, using solely the prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner. We first prove that in general Markov decision processes, this is in fact impossible in an unbiased way: the resulting intrinsic rewards either suffer from nuisance terms that bias their estimation of true learning progress, or they cannot be implemented using an in-context learner's prediction errors. Conversely, we prove a positive result for a broad subclass of non-temporal settings, encompassing active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design: here, ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to the true learning progress. We corroborate our theory with controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments, demonstrating that our ICL-driven framework successfully trains curious data-collection policies that explore optimally.

</details>


### [238] [Insulin4RL: Real-Time Insulin Management in the Intensive Care Unit for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19481)
*Thomas Frost,Steve Harris*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Insulin4RL, a healthcare offline RL dataset from MIMIC-IV featuring irregularly sampled real clinical trajectories for insulin titration in the ICU, addressing the artificial discretisation problem in existing ORL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current offline RL research in healthcare relies on temporally discretised EHR data (fixed regular intervals), which creates fictional clinical representations and compromises the generalisability of retrospective model evaluations. Real clinical data is inherently irregularly sampled.

Method: The authors construct Insulin4RL from MIMIC-IV, comprising over 375,000 labelled decisions across 12,209 ICU patients requiring insulin infusion titration. The dataset preserves naturally irregular inputs and actions, and the paper provides baseline performance metrics using model-free offline RL algorithms alongside a standardised fitted Q-evaluation protocol.

Result: The paper delivers a publicly available, realistic ORL benchmark dataset with baseline evaluations, demonstrating the feasibility of training and evaluating ORL models on irregularly sampled clinical data under realistic assumptions.

Conclusion: Insulin4RL enables research into ORL model performance under realistic clinical sampling assumptions and opens avenues for future work on irregular time-series RL, with suggested research directions provided.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (ORL) offers the potential to improve the quality of clinical decision-making using historical electronic health record (EHR) data. Current training and evaluative practices in this field rely heavily on EHR datasets that have been temporally discretised into fixed, regular time intervals. Discretisation creates fictional representations of complex clinical scenarios and compromises the generalisability of retrospective model evaluations. In this paper, we introduce Insulin4RL, a healthcare ORL dataset featuring naturally irregular inputs and actions from real clinical trajectories. Derived from MIMIC-IV, Insulin4RL comprises over 375,000 labelled decisions across 12,209 patients requiring insulin infusion titration in the Intensive Care Unit. The dataset can thus be used for research into ORL model performance under realistic clinical sampling assumptions. We provide a description of the dataset's structure and characteristics, baseline performance metrics using model-free offline reinforcement learning, and a standardised evaluation protocol using fitted Q-evaluation. We conclude with suggested areas for future research that could be addressed using this resource.

</details>


### [239] [Concept Flow Models: Anchoring Concept-Based Reasoning with Hierarchical Bottlenecks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19489)
*Ya Wang,Adrian Paschke*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Concept Flow Models (CFMs) replace the flat bottleneck in Concept Bottleneck Models with a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree. Each internal node focuses on a localized subset of discriminative concepts, progressively narrowing predictions. This mitigates information leakage while maintaining predictive performance and enabling transparent, auditable stepwise reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flat Concept Bottleneck Models suffer from information leakage as the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, allowing models to exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations, which undermines interpretability.

Method: CFMs construct decision hierarchies from visual embeddings, distribute semantic concepts across hierarchy levels, and train differentiable concept weights through probabilistic tree traversal. Each internal node specializes in a localized subset of discriminative concepts.

Result: CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs while substantially mitigating information leakage by reducing effective concept usage. The approach yields stepwise decision flows with hierarchical class structures.

Conclusion: Hierarchical concept-driven decision trees offer a viable alternative to flat bottlenecks, preserving interpretability and predictive accuracy while reducing vulnerability to spurious correlations through localized concept subsets.

Abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enhance interpretability by projecting learned features into a human-understandable concept space. Recent approaches leverage vision-language models to generate concept embeddings, reducing the need for manual concept annotations. However, these models suffer from a critical limitation: as the number of concepts approaches the embedding dimension, information leakage increases, enabling the model to exploit spurious or semantically irrelevant correlations and undermining interpretability. In this work, we propose Concept Flow Models (CFMs), which replace the flat bottleneck with a hierarchical, concept-driven decision tree. Each internal node in the hierarchy focuses on a localized subset of discriminative concepts, progressively narrowing the prediction scope. Our framework constructs decision hierarchies from visual embeddings, distributes semantic concepts at each hierarchy level, and trains differentiable concept weights through probabilistic tree traversal. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CFMs match the predictive performance of flat CBMs, while substantially mitigating information leakage by reducing effective concept usage. Furthermore, CFMs yield stepwise decision flows that enable transparent and auditable model reasoning with hierarchical class structures.

</details>


### [240] [Algebraic Dead Directions in LayerNorm Transformers: A Forward-Pass-Only Diagnostic at LLM Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19491)
*Tejas Pradeep Shirodkar,P. J. Narayanan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LayerNorm transformers possess a dead direction—a parameter-space direction with vanishing Fisher information—that can be read directly from the inverse-scale vector γ⁻¹/‖γ⁻¹‖ of the final LayerNorm, requiring no forward passes, backward passes, or eigendecompositions. This algebraic kernel direction matches the measured bottom singular direction at initialization, deepens by ~10³× after training, and enables classification of normalization type from parameters alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for locating dead directions (directions where the Fisher information matrix degenerates) require forward passes, eigendecompositions of activations, or sampling-based complexity estimates. None yields a direction computable solely from network parameters. This paper addresses the gap by providing a parameter-only readout for LayerNorm-based transformers.

Method: The authors analytically derive that the inverse-scale direction γ⁻¹/‖γ⁻¹‖ of the final LayerNorm affine parameter is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centered activation covariance matrix, for any input distribution. This induces a corresponding dead direction in parameter space, readable from the LN scale parameter alone. Validation is performed on 14 pretrained transformers (9 LayerNorm, 5 RMSNorm; 160M–35B parameters; language and vision objectives), comparing the predicted direction against direct SVD measurements at both random initialization and trained checkpoints.

Result: At random initialization, the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction to four decimal places on all 9 LayerNorm models and is correctly absent on all 5 RMSNorm models. On trained checkpoints, the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ~10³×, and additional dead directions emerge. Two closed-form consequences are demonstrated: (1) the residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on 13/14 transformers; (2) the kernel direction's presence classifies normalization type (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm) from parameters alone.

Conclusion: The paper provides the cheapest known dead-direction readout, specific to LayerNorm transformers, that requires only the LN scale parameter. This direction acts as a structural signature: it matches SVD ground truth at initialization, deepens with training, and serves as a diagnostic tool for normalization type classification and singular structure analysis across transformer blocks.

Abstract: Pretrained transformers sit near singular minima of the loss, where the Fisher information metric degenerates along dead directions: directions in parameter space along which the directional Fisher vanishes. Locating such a direction normally needs a forward pass and an eigendecomposition of activations, or a sampling-based complexity estimate; none returns a direction computable from the network's parameters alone. We give one, for LayerNorm transformers. The inverse-scale direction $γ^{-1}/\|γ^{-1}\|$ of the LayerNorm affine is an exact algebraic kernel of the post-final-norm centred activation covariance, for any input distribution, and induces a corresponding dead direction in parameter space. It is read from the LN scale parameter alone, with no forward or backward pass and no eigensolve: the cheapest dead-direction read, specific to LayerNorm. We test it on $14$ pretrained transformers ($9$ LayerNorm, $5$ RMSNorm; $160$M-$35$B; language and vision objectives). At random initialisation the predicted direction matches the measured bottom singular direction (one forward pass, direct SVD) to four decimal places on $9/9$ LayerNorm models, and is correctly absent on $5/5$ RMSNorm models, which lack the mean-subtraction projector that creates it. On the trained checkpoint the covariance eigenvalue along this direction deepens by ${\sim}10^3\times$ and further dead directions open; the random-init-to-trained gap is a one-forward-pass, per-checkpoint readout of singular structure along the predicted coordinate. Two consequences follow in closed form: the residual stream's smallest singular value is preserved block-to-block on $13/14$ transformers measured on their own input distribution, the one exception (Gemma$4$-$31$B) a genuine dead direction the same read pinpoints; and the kernel direction's presence classifies a transformer's normalisation from the parameters alone.

</details>


### [241] [Calibrating Generative Models to Feature Distributions with MMD Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19496)
*Nathaniel L. Diamant,Brian L. Trippe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: kCGM calibrates generative models to match target feature distributions using MMD minimization with KL regularization, outperforming direct finetuning in chemical validity and feature matching across molecules, proteins, and DNA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative models pretrained on broad data often produce samples that deviate from specific target distributions of key features (e.g., a drug-like molecule generator may not match the feature distribution of antibiotics). Direct finetuning on the target set causes overfitting and cannot control which features are matched.

Method: kCGM minimizes maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator, with KL divergence regularization to stay close to the pretrained model. It operates with only feature-level supervision and works across autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models.

Result: On 174 antibiotics, direct finetuning sacrificed chemical validity for feature-distribution matching, whereas kCGM improved target feature matching while increasing validity. Demonstrated across protein and DNA generation tasks across multiple model architectures.

Conclusion: kCGM provides a principled, architecture-agnostic framework for post-hoc distributional calibration of generative models using only feature-level feedback, maintaining sample quality while aligning feature distributions with a target set.

Abstract: Generative models can produce individually plausible samples while deviating substantially from a target set in the distribution of key features. For example, a model pretrained on broad drug-like chemical space may generate molecules whose molecular features differ from those of a therapeutic class of interest, such as known antibiotics. Correcting such distributional miscalibration is challenging: direct finetuning on the target set can overfit and does not control which features are matched. To fill this gap, we introduce kernel Calibrating Generative Models (kCGM). kCGM minimizes a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between generated and target feature distributions using an unbiased score-function estimator, with KL regularization to remain close to the pretrained model. On a target set of 174 antibiotics, direct finetuning sacrifices chemical validity for feature-distribution matching, whereas kCGM improves target feature matching while increasing validity. We further demonstrate kCGM in protein and DNA generation tasks, showing it can adapt autoregressive, continuous-space diffusion, and discrete diffusion models using only feature-level supervision. Code is available at https://github.com/smithhenryd/cgm.

</details>


### [242] [Interactive Pareto navigation for deep multi-task learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19521)
*Augustina C. Amakor,Konstantin Sonntag,Sebastian Peitz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PPE introduces a predictor-corrector framework for interactive multi-objective optimization that respects user preferences while navigating the Pareto set geometry, using Krylov subspace methods to avoid expensive Hessian computations in deep learning contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weighted-sum aggregation of losses in multi-task deep learning fails to capture decision maker preferences due to Pareto front geometry and becomes computationally prohibitive when repeated adjustments are needed. A method is needed that interactively explores the Pareto set according to user preferences without excessive computational cost.

Method: A predictor-corrector scheme operating on the Pareto-optimal manifold: predictor steps move tangentially along the Pareto set following the decision maker's preference direction, and corrector steps restore Pareto optimality at the new trade-off point. The tangent space is characterized using a Krylov subspace method requiring only matrix-vector products via automatic differentiation, circumventing explicit Hessian computation.

Result: The method is demonstrated on toy problems and deep learning examples, showing effective interactive Pareto exploration aligned with user preferences while maintaining computational efficiency and robustness.

Conclusion: PPE offers a computationally tractable, preference-aware alternative to weighted-sum aggregation for multi-task deep learning, enabling interactive Pareto front exploration without Hessian overhead.

Abstract: In multi-task learning, handling an increasing number of objectives can quickly become challenging, both in terms of the computational resources and the decision maker's capacity to choose appropriate trade-offs. A widely used approach is thus to aggregate the individual losses in a single loss function by a weighted sum. This often fails to capture either the decision maker's preferences as a result of the shape of the Pareto front, or requires multiple adjustments and computations which becomes prohibitively expensive in deep learning applications. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework, Preference Pareto Exploration (PPE), which enforces the decision maker's preferences while accounting for the geometry of the Pareto set in an interactive exploration process. PPE is based on a predictor-corrector method that performs predictor steps tangential to the manifold of Pareto-optimal solutions, following the decision maker's preference. The subsequent corrector step results in a new trade-off reflecting this preference. To avoid explicit Hessian computations when characterizing the tangent space of the manifold, we employ a Krylov subspace method that relies solely on matrix-vector products. These products can be efficiently obtained via automatic differentiation, ensuring both efficiency and robustness throughout the optimization process. The method's functionality and performance are demonstrated using both toy problems and examples from deep learning.

</details>


### [243] [Techniques for Peak Memory Reduction for LoRA Fine-tuning of LLMs on Edge Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19528)
*Hassan Dbouk,Matthias Reisser,Prathamesh Mandke,Likhita Arun Navali,Christos Louizos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes four complementary memory-saving techniques—base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization, selective activation caching with disk offloading, softmax approximation via relevant token subsets, and logits masking—to enable LoRA fine-tuning of billion-parameter LLMs on consumer hardware, achieving up to 28× peak memory reduction on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B without sacrificing quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning LLMs with LoRA on end-user data enables personalized, privacy-preserving experiences, but peak memory usage during fine-tuning exceeds the limits of consumer hardware, particularly for models with billions of parameters and long-context training data. Existing solutions address only parts of the memory bottleneck.

Method: The paper introduces four complementary techniques: (1) Quantization-aware base model storage with on-the-fly dequantization during forward/backward passes; (2) Memory-efficient checkpointing using selective activation caching (only caching activations needed for LoRA gradient computation) combined with disk offloading of remaining activations; (3) Softmax approximation that computes attention over a semantically relevant subset of tokens rather than the full sequence; and (4) Logits masking to reduce the vocabulary dimension in the output layer during training.

Result: Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B show peak memory reductions of up to 26× and 28× respectively, making fine-tuning feasible on resource-constrained devices without degrading model quality.

Conclusion: The proposed suite of complementary memory optimization techniques collectively enables practical LoRA fine-tuning of multi-billion-parameter LLMs on consumer-grade hardware, democratizing personalized model adaptation while preserving data privacy and model quality.

Abstract: Fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on an end-user's data offers personalized experiences while keeping data private, but faces severe memory constraints on consumer hardware. Peak memory during fine-tuning often exceeds device limits, especially for models with billions of parameters and long-context training data. This paper introduces a suite of complementary techniques to reduce memory footprint without sacrificing model quality: (1) base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization, (2) memory-efficient checkpointing combining selective activation caching and disk offloading, (3) softmax approximation using semantically relevant token subsets, and (4) logits masking. Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B demonstrate up to $26\times$ and $28\times$ reduction in peak memory, enabling fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices.

</details>


### [244] [Tracking Representation Dynamics in Large Language Models with Persistent Homology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19542)
*Naman Malhotra,Jay Ambadkar,Abhinav Gupta,Kushal Kasivel,Abbas Schwarz,Kamillo Ferry,Anthea Monod*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using persistent homology to track activation space topology during alignment fine-tuning, the study finds most topological reorganization occurs early in training with a transient peak followed by rapid stabilization, and that different alignment objectives produce distinguishable topological trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Little is known about how internal representations of large language models evolve during supervised fine-tuning for alignment. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a complementary, representation-level perspective beyond standard behavioral metrics.

Method: Persistent homology is applied to track the topology of activation spaces throughout fine-tuning. Experiments span four transformer models (1B–7B parameters) and three alignment objectives (helpful, harmless, mixed), using dense checkpoint analysis to capture fine-grained topological evolution.

Result: The majority of topological reorganization occurs in the earliest training stages, with a transient peak in topological activity followed by rapid stabilization. Different alignment objectives induce distinguishable topological trajectories, and instruction-tuned vs. pretrained models show qualitatively different evolution patterns. These representation-level changes are not captured by behavioral metrics alone.

Conclusion: Persistent homology offers a valuable complementary lens on alignment, uncovering structural changes in representation space that behavioral evaluations miss, and suggests that the critical phase of representational reorganization is concentrated in early fine-tuning.

Abstract: Large language models are commonly aligned through supervised fine-tuning, yet little is known about how their internal representations evolve during this process. We study alignment dynamics using persistent homology by tracking the topology of activation spaces throughout fine-tuning. Across four transformer language models ranging from 1B to 7B parameters and three alignment objectives corresponding to helpful, harmless, and mixed training data, we find that the majority of topological reorganization occurs during the earliest stages of training.
