A dense checkpoint analysis reveals a transient peak in topological activity followed by rapid stabilization. We further show that different alignment objectives induce distinguishable topological trajectories, while instruction-tuned and pretrained models exhibit qualitatively different patterns of evolution. Our results suggest that persistent homology provides a complementary perspective on alignment, revealing representation-level changes that are not apparent from behavioral metrics alone.

</details>


### [245] [Predicting Mergeability of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19549)
*Lin Tang,Wei Zhang,Jing Li,Hongyu Chen,Ming Zhao,Yuxuan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MergeProbe predicts whether LoRA adapters can be successfully merged by analyzing early-training signals (update alignment, gradient similarity, representation disturbance) within the first few percent of training, converting mergeability from a costly post-hoc trial-and-error process into an anticipatory measurement problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA enables cheap training of many task-specific adapters, but merging them often produces destructive interference that is discovered only after full training and evaluation — a costly late-feedback loop. The authors aim to predict mergeability early in training to avoid wasting compute on adapters that will conflict.

Method: MergeProbe formalizes adapter mergeability as post-merge single-task utility retention. It forecasts this from early-training signals: (1) alignment of low-rank updates across tasks, (2) gradient alignment, and (3) disturbance to shared representations. These signals are packaged into a lightweight predictor that recommends actions: direct merge, reweight, prune, or route. Evaluation uses MERGE-PEFT, a five-domain benchmark (math, code, science, instruction following, safety).

Result: MergeProbe achieves the best average and worst-case retention among interference-aware merge baselines on MERGE-PEFT, while incurring significantly less deployment overhead than full task routing.

Conclusion: LoRA merging can be reframed from a post-hoc engineering step into an anticipatory measurement problem. Early-training signals carry sufficient information to forecast adapter compatibility, enabling proactive merge decisions that save compute and improve merged-model quality.

Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes it cheap to train many domain- and task-specific language model adapters, but whether two adapters can be merged is usually discovered only after both have been fully trained and evaluated. This late feedback is costly: adapters that are strong in isolation can interfere destructively once their updates are combined. We ask whether this outcome can be anticipated. We formalize adapter mergeability as the degree to which an adapter preserves its single-task utility after merging, and show that it can be forecast from signals measured in the first few percent of training -- chiefly how the low-rank updates and their gradients align across tasks and how much they disturb shared representations. We package these signals into MergeProbe, a lightweight predictor that estimates pairwise and set-level retention and turns the estimate into a concrete decision: merge directly, reweight, prune, or route. On MERGE-PEFT, a five-domain benchmark spanning math, code, science, instruction following, and safety, MergeProbe attains the best average and worst-case retention among strong interference-aware merge baselines while adding far less deployment overhead than full task routing. This turns LoRA merging from a post-hoc engineering step into an anticipatory measurement problem.

</details>


### [246] [Displacement Is Not Direction: Evaluating Fidelity Metrics for Quantized LLM Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19558)
*Miloš Nikolić,Ali Hadi Zadeh,Enrique Torres Sanchez,Andreas Moshovos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper tests whether KL divergence (KLD) against a high-precision reference serves as a valid proxy for downstream benchmark quality in quantized LLMs. While KLD correlates strongly with benchmark scores across full quantization cohorts, this relationship collapses in the near-baseline region where practitioners actually make deployment decisions. The collapse is traced to KLD primarily measuring disagreement volume rather than direction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practitioners routinely use fidelity metrics like per-token KL divergence as cheap proxies for benchmark performance when selecting quantized model checkpoints, under the assumption that lower KLD implies better downstream quality. However, this practice has not been rigorously validated, particularly in the critical near-baseline regime where differences between quantized variants are subtle but deployment decisions are made.

Method: The authors construct two large quantization cohorts: 28 quants of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 41 quants of Devstral-Small-2-24B, spanning diverse quantization methods and bit-widths. They measure KLD against full-precision references and correlate it with downstream benchmark scores. They test 14 KLD measurement variants (aggregation methods, perplexity formulations, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, context lengths). They also evaluate per-prompt failure prediction on LiveCodeBench and cross-model routing accuracy. Finally, they structurally decompose KLD into volume-of-disagreement and direction-of-disagreement components.

Result: Over full cohorts, KLD correlates strongly with benchmark scores (ρ=−0.72 on Qwen, ρ=−0.86 on Devstral, both p<0.001). In the near-baseline silent zone, this collapses to non-significance (ρ=+0.00 and ρ=−0.24, p=0.36). The collapse persists across all 14 measurement variants. Per-prompt KLD shows only weak failure-prediction (geometric-mean ratios 1.08–1.22) and fails as a cross-model router (42.3%–49.4% accuracy). The structural decomposition reveals KLD primarily measures disagreement volume (silent-zone ρ=+0.94 on Qwen, +0.55 on Devstral), while disagreement direction is weakly and task-conditionally related to quality.

Conclusion: KLD is not a reliable proxy for benchmark quality in the near-baseline regime where quantization decisions are made. Its signal is dominated by how much the model disagrees with the reference, not the direction of disagreement, making it blind to whether errors are benign or catastrophic. Practitioners should not rely on KLD alone for model selection among similar quantized variants.

Abstract: Fidelity metrics, such as per-token KL divergence (KLD) against a high-precision reference, are often used in practice as low-cost proxies for benchmark quality. We test this practice on a 28-quant cohort of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and a 41-quant cohort of Devstral-Small-2-24B, evaluated across a suite of downstream benchmarks. We find that KLD is strongly correlated with benchmark score over the full cohort ($ρ=-0.72$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.86$ on Devstral, both with $p<0.001$). However, this relationship collapses to non-significance in the near-baseline silent zone ($ρ=+0.00$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.24$, $p=0.36$, on Devstral). This collapse persists across 14 measurement variants, including different KLD aggregations, perplexity formulations, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, and context lengths. At the per-prompt level, KLD has only weak failure-prediction power on code, with failed-vs-passed geometric-mean ratios in $[1.08,1.22]$ across five models on LiveCodeBench, and fails as a cross-model router, achieving only $42.3\%-49.4\%$ accuracy on disagreement prompts. We trace the collapse to a structural decomposition: KLD primarily measures the volume of disagreement with the reference, with silent-zone composite $ρ=+0.94$ ($p<0.001$) on Qwen and $+0.55$ ($p=0.03$) on Devstral, while its relationship to the direction of those disagreements is weak and task-conditional.

</details>


### [247] [Understanding Key Features of Time Series Foundation Models from Epidemic Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19560)
*Alireza Jafari,Judy Fox,Geoffrey C. Fox,Madhav Marathe,Aniruddha Adiga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Systematic evaluation of neural network architectures for influenza forecasting shows that mixture-of-experts models fusing pretrained forecasters achieve best performance, transformer-based numerical models are reliable, pretraining helps most at longer horizons, and LLM-based methods underperform.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the public-health importance of accurate short-term influenza forecasting, the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized, leaving practitioners without clear guidance on model selection.

Method: Systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting using ILI surveillance and hospitalization time series under temporal and spatial generalization settings for 1–4-week-ahead prediction. Compared classical neural networks, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches. Introduced a mixture-of-experts model that fuses multiple pretrained forecasters.

Result: The mixture-of-experts model achieved the strongest overall performance. Numerical transformer-based models produced reliable forecasts. Pretraining provided the largest gains at longer horizons, especially when the pretraining domain was mechanistically aligned with influenza dynamics. LLM-based time series methods underperformed relative to numerical forecasters. Hospitalization signals provided complementary improvements in selected settings.

Conclusion: The findings offer actionable guidance on model selection, pretraining strategy, and auxiliary-signal use for influenza preparedness, favoring mixture-of-experts architectures with aligned pretraining and judicious incorporation of hospitalization surveillance data.

Abstract: Seasonal influenza infects millions of people and causes substantial morbidity and mortality in the United States each year, making accurate short-term forecasting a core public-health need. Reliable forecasts of epidemic time series can inform vaccination timing, hospital staffing, and resource allocation, yet the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized. We address this gap through a systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting using influenza-like illness surveillance and influenza-associated hospitalization time series under both temporal and spatial generalization settings for 1-4-week-ahead prediction. We compare classical neural network architectures, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches. Across tasks, we demonstrate that a mixture-of-experts model that fuses multiple pretrained forecasters achieves the strongest overall performance, indicating that heterogeneous pretrained representations provide complementary predictive information. Our results further show that numerical transformer-based models produce reliable forecasts, while pretraining provides the largest gains at longer horizons, particularly when the pretraining domain is mechanistically aligned with influenza dynamics. In contrast, LLM-based time series methods underperform relative to numerical forecasters in this setting. Finally, we examine hospitalization information as both an auxiliary covariate and a pretraining source. Hospitalization signals provide complementary improvements in selected settings and clarify when additional surveillance streams enhance the robustness of multi-horizon forecasting. These findings provide actionable guidance on model selection, pretraining strategy, and auxiliary-signal use for influenza preparedness.

</details>


### [248] [Advances in Scientific Machine Learning for Coupled Fluid Flow and Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19562)
*Gabriel F. Barros,Rômulo M. Silva,Alvaro L. G. A. Coutinho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Surveys Scientific Machine Learning methods—including PINNs, β-VAEs, and Dynamic Mode Decomposition—for building efficient surrogate models of coupled incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport systems, demonstrated on turbidity currents and Rayleigh-Bénard convection, with new contributions combining these models with HPC strategies like AMR/C and data compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity simulations of coupled fluid flow and transport phenomena (e.g., turbidity currents, thermal convection) are computationally expensive due to strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior, motivating the need for efficient SciML-based surrogate models that dramatically reduce computational cost.

Method: Combines linear reduced-order techniques (SVD-based Dynamic Mode Decomposition) with nonlinear neural network approaches (Physics-Informed Neural Networks, β-Variational Autoencoders), integrated with HPC strategies including Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening and scientific floating-point data compression; new contributions apply PINNs to turbidity current surrogate modeling and β-VAEs to extract disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows.

Result: Demonstrates that SciML enables fast, accurate approximations of complex coupled systems on benchmarks (lock-exchange flows, Rayleigh-Bénard convection), substantially reducing computational cost relative to full-order simulations within the specific data regimes and modeling assumptions considered.

Conclusion: SciML methods provide viable, computationally efficient surrogates for coupled fluid flow systems, though broader capabilities like real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain active research directions whose feasibility is problem-dependent.

Abstract: This chapter reviews recent advances in Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) for modeling coupled fluid flow and transport phenomena governed by the incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport equations. Such systems, found in applications like turbidity currents and thermal convection, feature strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior that make high-fidelity simulations computationally expensive. To address this, the chapter surveys state-of-the-art SciML methods for building efficient surrogate models, including linear reduced-order techniques based on Singular Value Decomposition (such as Dynamic Mode Decomposition) and nonlinear neural network approaches like Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and $β$-Variational Autoencoders ($β$-VAEs). It first covers the authors' work combining these models with High Performance Computing strategies, including Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening (AMR/C) and scientific floating-point data compression. It then presents two new contributions: surrogate modeling of turbidity currents via PINNs, and the extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows using $β$-VAEs. Governing equations and representative benchmarks, including lock-exchange flows and Rayleigh-Bénard convection, illustrate these methodologies. The chapter is intentionally long, covering both the mathematical and physical foundations of coupled fluid flow and the computational aspects of state-of-the-art modeling. Overall, it demonstrates how SciML enables fast, accurate approximations of complex coupled systems within the specific data regimes and modeling assumptions considered, while substantially reducing computational cost relative to full-order simulations. Broader capabilities such as real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain active research directions whose feasibility depends strongly on the problem at hand.

</details>


### [249] [On the QUEST for Uncertainty Quantification via Highest Density Regions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19569)
*Sam Goring,Tom Kuipers,Nicola Paoletti,David S. Watson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces QUEST, a new uncertainty quantification framework that measures uncertainty by the volume of highest-density regions rather than pointwise predictive risk, satisfying key axioms and outperforming standard measures like variance and differential entropy in selective prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dominant scalar UQ approaches based on proper scoring rules measure uncertainty via pointwise predictive risk, which yields counterintuitive results when the target statistic is not the conditional expectation. A principled alternative is needed that better characterizes uncertainty through distributional concentration.

Method: QUEST quantifies uncertainty via the volume of the most probable subset of a distribution's support, using the concentration of Lebesgue measure at the distribution's peak(s), evaluated at one or more values of a robustness parameter α. The framework connects to information-theoretic and economic statistics and decomposes into epistemic and aleatoric components.

Result: QUEST measures satisfy axioms including monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts — properties that proper scoring rule-based alternatives lack. Selective prediction benchmarks show QUEST performs favorably against variance and differential entropy.

Conclusion: Volume-based UQ via highest-density regions provides a theoretically grounded and practically effective alternative to pointwise risk-based measures, with strong axiomatic properties and competitive empirical performance.

Abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for reliable decision-making in safety-critical applications in probabilistic machine learning. For regression problems, dominant scalar UQ approaches - notably, those based on proper scoring rules - measure uncertainty via pointwise predictive risk. This can lead to counterintuitive results when the target statistic is not the conditional expectation. We propose an alternative framework, in which uncertainty is characterised by the volume of the most probable subset of a distribution's support. QUEST (Quantifying Uncertainty via highest dEnSiTy regions) is a novel approach to UQ based on the concentration of Lebesgue measure at a distribution's peak(s), evaluated at one or more values of a robustness parameter $α$. We establish connections between our measures and classical statistics from information theory and economics. We show that, unlike popular alternatives based on proper scoring rules, QUEST measures of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty satisfy a set of axioms adapted from the UQ literature, including monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts. Selective prediction benchmarks confirm that QUEST performs favourably against standard measures such as variance and differential entropy.

</details>


### [250] [Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19594)
*Théo Saulus,Simon Lacoste-Julien,Dhanya Sridhar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of automatically learning a high-level causal abstraction directly from low-level observational data, rather than relying on the traditional hypothesis-testing approach. Leveraging insights from low-rank causal discovery, the authors prove that low-rank graphs induce latent variables forming a causal abstraction, establish identifiability results, and propose a practical learning objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on causal abstraction follows a hypothesis-testing paradigm where an expert manually proposes a candidate high-level model and then tests whether the low-level system implements it. This paper aims to invert the problem: can a high-level causal model be learned directly from low-level measurements without requiring an expert-specified candidate?

Method: The authors leverage the framework of low-rank causal discovery, where the connectivity matrix of a structural causal model admits a low-rank factorization. They (1) formally prove that observations from a low-rank SCM induce latent variables that constitute a valid causal abstraction of the low-level system, (2) derive identifiability guarantees for these latent variables, and (3) develop a practical optimization objective to recover the high-level SCM from data.

Result: The paper provides three main results: (i) a theoretical proof that low-rank graphs induce latent causal abstractions, (ii) identifiability conditions under which the high-level model can be uniquely recovered, and (iii) a tractable learning objective that enables practical discovery of high-level causal structure from low-level observations.

Conclusion: Learning high-level causal abstractions directly from data is feasible under low-rank assumptions. The proposed framework shifts causal abstraction from a hypothesis-testing paradigm to a data-driven discovery paradigm, opening new directions for automated multi-scale causal modeling.

Abstract: Causal abstractions formalize when a high-level structural causal model (SCM) captures the interventional behavior of a lower-level SCM. Existing applications of this notion largely follow a hypothesis-testing paradigm: an expert proposes a candidate high-level model and then evaluates if the low-level system implements it. We study the complementary problem of learning a high-level model directly from low-level measurements. Our contributions leverage hypotheses from low-rank causal discovery, and can be summarized as follows: (1) we show that observations generated by a low-rank graph induce latents that form a causal abstraction, (2) we provide identifiability results about these latents, and (3) we propose a practical objective to learn this high-level SCM.

</details>


### [251] [IHBench: Evaluating Post-Interruption Recovery in Voice Agents with Structured Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19595)
*Ahmad Salimi,Wentao Ma,Yuzhi Tang,Dongming Shen,Mu Li,Alex Smola*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IHBench is a new benchmark evaluating how voice agents recover after user interruptions in structured, multi-step workflows. Testing 27 audio-language models across 10 domains and 6 interruption types, it finds closed-weight models significantly outperform open-weight ones in task fulfillment, robustness to conversation length, and audio-text modality consistency. Recovery quality emerges as a distinct capability axis uncorrelated with existing speech benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing speech-capable model benchmarks focus narrowly on the timing mechanics of interruptions (barge-in detection, endpointing, turn-taking) but ignore what happens afterward: whether the agent resumes at the correct workflow step, addresses the user's interjection, and avoids repeating already-heard content. This leaves a critical gap in evaluating voice agents deployed in structured enterprise workflows (customer service, healthcare scheduling, account management).

Method: IHBench evaluates post-interruption recovery in voice agents using state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected mid-utterance at controlled points. Per-interruption evaluation rubrics are auto-generated alongside the data, scoring each interruption on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality. 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and the open-weight community are evaluated. A human study validates the LLM judge against human annotators, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge is conducted.

Result: Closed-weight models consistently outperform open-weight ones: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade approximately 3.3x more slowly as conversations grow longer, and show no audio-versus-text modality gap, while open-weight models lose ground on all three dimensions. Recovery quality depends strongly on interruption type. Cross-benchmark analysis indicates recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis from what AudioMultiChallenge measures.

Conclusion: Post-interruption recovery quality is a distinct and underexamined capability axis for voice agents, and current open-weight audio-language models lag significantly behind closed-weight counterparts in this regard. IHBench provides a structured framework for measuring and advancing this capability.

Abstract: Voice agents deployed in structured workflows (customer service, healthcare scheduling, account management) must handle frequent user interruptions while maintaining progress through multi-step procedures. Existing benchmarks for speech-capable models focus on the timing of interruptions: barge-in detection, endpointing, and turn-taking dynamics. They leave unmeasured what happens after the interruption: does the agent resume the workflow at the correct step? Does it address the user's interjection? Does it avoid re-delivering content the user already heard?
  We introduce IHBench (Interruption Handling Benchmark), a benchmark that evaluates post-interruption recovery in voice agents executing state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected at controlled points mid-utterance, with per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. Each interruption is scored on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality.
  We evaluate 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and the open-weight community. Models vary widely, and recovery quality depends strongly on the interruption type. Across our experiments, closed-weight models are consistently more robust to interruptions than open-weight ones: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade roughly 3.3x more slowly as conversations grow longer, and show no audio-versus-text modality gap, whereas the open-weight models lose ground on all three. A human study validates the LLM judge against human annotators, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge indicates that recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis.

</details>


### [252] [Comparing Linear Probes with Mahalanobis Cosine Similarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19603)
*Zhuofan Josh Ying,Peter Hase,Nikolaus Kriegeskorte*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proves that Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between a probe and a reference OOD probe linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC. This holds when class projections are Gaussian, because both metrics are sigmoid functions of signal-to-noise ratio. The theory also predicts when linearity fails, and empirical results validate this across models, layers, and concept domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work (Ying et al., 2026) empirically found that MCS to an OOD reference probe near-perfectly linearly predicts OOD AUROC (R²=0.98). However, this relationship lacked theoretical justification, and its generality across settings was unverified. The authors aim to provide a formal mathematical explanation and test the phenomenon's robustness across diverse experimental conditions.

Method: The authors extend empirical validation across multiple models, layers, and concept domains. They then provide a closed-form theoretical proof: assuming balanced classes with Gaussian-distributed projections, both OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are derived as sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data, establishing their linear relationship. The theory also identifies conditions under which linearity breaks down, and these predictions are empirically verified.

Result: Empirically, the linear MCS–AUROC relationship generalizes across different models, layers, and concept domains. Theoretically, under Gaussian class-conditional projections, both metrics are shown to be sigmoidal functions of SNR, yielding their linear relationship in closed form. The theory also correctly anticipates failure modes of the linearity, which are confirmed experimentally.

Conclusion: MCS provides a theoretically grounded, SNR-based alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes. It is both a reliable predictor of OOD performance and a principled interpretability tool, with clear conditions for its validity.

Abstract: Linear probes are widely used in interpretability research and often compared by cosine similarity. The Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between two directions, which reweights the inner product by test data covariance, is a natural task-aware refinement. Ying et al. (2026) report that a probe's MCS to a reference probe trained on the out-of-distribution (OOD) data near-perfectly linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC (R^2 = 0.98). Here, we extend this empirical finding across models, layers, and concept domains, and prove this general phenomenon in closed form: For balanced classes whose projections are Gaussian, OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are linear because both are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data. The theory also predicts when this linearity fails, which we verify empirically. MCS offers a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.

</details>


### [253] [Latent Confounded Causal Discovery via Lie Bracket Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19610)
*Sridhar Mahadevan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces two causal discovery algorithms (BRIDGE and SKFM) that detect latent confounding by analyzing the geometric properties of intervention-induced probability flows, using Lie bracket failures (Frobenius residuals) as signals of hidden structure, dramatically reducing the DAG search space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Causal discovery under latent confounding is notoriously difficult due to the super-exponential explosion of possible DAG structures. Existing methods struggle to efficiently identify when unobserved confounders are present. The authors leverage the Kan-Do-Calculus framework — which establishes a category-theoretic bi-adjunction between observation (right Kan extensions) and intervention (left Kan extensions) — to recast the problem in information-geometric terms, where latent confounders manifest as failures of integrability in intervention-induced vector fields.

Method: The paper proposes two algorithms: (1) BRIDGE (Bracket Residuals for Interventional Discovery and Geometric Estimation), which computes Lie brackets of local causal vector fields derived from Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures. Non-vanishing brackets (Frobenius residuals) flag latent confounding, producing a reduced set of admissible causal arrows for downstream discovery. (2) Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching (SKFM), which learns amortized intervention fields and performs spectral decomposition of latent curvature, directly identifying the Lie-algebraic endpoint that BRIDGE approximates. Both methods operate within the smooth statistical setting of information geometry.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that both BRIDGE and SKFM successfully discover causal models with latent confounders while reducing the super-exponential DAG search space by many orders of magnitude. The algorithms effectively identify latent-obstruction candidates through geometric screening of non-closing visible pairs.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a new paradigm in causal discovery where latent structure is inferred directly from the geometry of intervention-induced flows rather than through combinatorial search. The category-theoretic foundations of KDC, combined with information-geometric tools, provide a principled and computationally tractable approach to handling latent confounding.

Abstract: Recent work on Kan-Do-Calculus (KDC) has established that the boundary between passive observation and active intervention in causal inference is a category-theoretic bi-adjunction, with interventions modeled by left Kan extensions and conditioning by right Kan extensions. This paper introduces two causal discovery algorithms under latent confounding, building on the information-geometric and categorical consequences of KDC. In smooth statistical settings, Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures induce local causal vector fields; failures of these fields to close under Lie brackets become computable Frobenius residuals, which we interpret as witnesses of failed visible integrability and possible latent or unmodeled structure. Our first algorithm, BRIDGE (Bracket Residuals for Interventional Discovery and Geometric Estimation), combines an interventional density or Radon-Nikodym-ratio engine with a geometric screen that proposes a high-recall family of admissible arrows, identifies non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and passes the reduced family to downstream score-based or differentiable discovery routines. The second algorithmic contribution, Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching (SKFM), learns amortized intervention fields and factors latent curvature spectrally, exposing the direct Lie-space endpoint toward which BRIDGE points. A detailed set of experiments show that both algorithms are capable of discovering causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential space of possible DAGs by many orders of magnitude. This paper introduces a new paradigm in causal discovery, where latent structure is inferred directly from the geometry of intervention-induced flows.

</details>


### [254] [SEAGAN: domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19623)
*Antriksh Srivastava,Soumyashree Kar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A-Ci curve biochemical limitation-state identification is reformulated as a graph node classification problem. The proposed SEAGAN model, combining process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss, achieves F1=0.857 and accuracy=0.882, outperforming conventional and graph-based baselines, particularly near biochemical transition regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate estimation of photosynthetic parameters from A-Ci curves (net CO₂ assimilation vs. leaf intercellular CO₂ concentration) requires correctly identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each curve point. This identification remains a major source of uncertainty, as multiple interacting physiological processes overlap and their separation is difficult even with manual intervention.

Method: The authors formulate limitation-state identification as a graph-based node classification problem where curve points serve as nodes. Two graph construction strategies are employed: distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The proposed SEAGAN model integrates domain-specific process-aware node features, edge-aware graph attention over local kNN neighborhoods, and a weighted cross-entropy loss to handle class imbalance. Evaluation uses a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states, comparing against conventional learning baselines, existing graph architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark.

Result: Graph-based models consistently improve classification over conventional baselines, with the most pronounced gains near biochemical transition regions. SEAGAN achieves the best performance with an F1-score of 0.857 and accuracy of 0.882. Edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods proves to be the most effective strategy for capturing the relational structure of A-Ci curves.

Conclusion: Representing A-Ci curves as graphs significantly improves biochemical limitation-state analysis. Edge-aware graph attention over local kNN neighborhoods provides the most effective modeling strategy, suggesting that graph-based approaches are a promising direction for reducing uncertainty in photosynthetic parameter estimation from gas-exchange data.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a flexible framework for learning from scientific data linked through physical, biological, or functional relationships. One promising domain is plant physiology, where measured responses often arise from multiple interacting processes whose exact separation remains difficult even with manual intervention. In plant physiology, a key example is the A-Ci curve, which relates net CO2 assimilation rate (Anet) to leaf intercellular CO2 concentration (Ci) and is used to estimate photosynthetic parameters in leaf and crop-canopy models. However, reliable estimation requires identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each curve point, which remains a major source of uncertainty. Here, we formulate limitation-state identification along A-Ci curves as a graph-based node classification problem, with curve points as nodes. Domain-specific graph representations are created using distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The framework was evaluated against conventional learning baselines, graph-based architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark. Results on a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states show that graph-based models improve classification, particularly near biochemical transition regions. The best-performing configuration, SEAGAN (domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes), integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss, achieving an F1-score of 0.857 and an accuracy of 0.882. The results show that representing A-Ci curves as graphs improves biochemical limitation-state analysis, with edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods providing the most effective strategy.

</details>


### [255] [MassSpecGym in the Wild: Uncovering and Correcting Evaluation Pitfalls in AI-Driven Molecule Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19624)
*Hongxuan Liu,Roman Bushuiev,Ivy Lightheart,Mrunali Manjrekar,Anton Bushuiev,Magdalena Lederbauer,Filip Jozefov,Yinkai Wang,Soha Hassoun,Josef Sivic,James Taylor,Runzhong Wang,David Healey,Tomáš Pluskal,Connor W. Coley*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An audit of MassSpecGym benchmark usage reveals evaluation failures — data leakage, shortcut learning, and metric bugs — in 17 of 26 papers. The authors quantify these issues and release MassSpecGym v1.5 with fixes and generalizable recommendations for MS/MS ML benchmarking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable benchmarking is essential for progress in machine learning for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) molecule discovery, yet subtle evaluation flaws can undermine trustworthiness and lead to incorrect conclusions. The paper seeks to systematically identify, categorize, and quantify such flaws in the recent literature.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive review of model evaluation practices in 26 papers that reported MassSpecGym benchmark results within its first year. Through code replication and extensive experimentation, they isolate three failure classes: data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs/metric divergence. They use MassSpecGym as a case study to demonstrate impact.

Result: At least 17 of 26 papers (65%) exhibited evaluation issues. The three identified failure classes were shown to corrupt evaluation standards. The authors quantified the impact of each failure mode and distilled findings into generalizable recommendations.

Conclusion: Subtle evaluation flaws are pervasive in MS/MS ML benchmarks. The authors provide actionable recommendations and release MassSpecGym v1.5, a corrected benchmark suite addressing all identified failure modes, to improve future benchmarking reliability.

Abstract: Reliable benchmarking is critical for developing machine learning models for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) based molecule discovery. Subtle issues in experimental design and model evaluation procedures can degrade the trustworthiness of such benchmarks and lead to erroneous conclusions. We conduct a thorough review of model evaluation issues in the recent MS/MS machine learning literature, using the standard MassSpecGym benchmark suite as a case study to illustrate the impact of these issues. We find evaluation issues in at least 17 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in the first year of its adoption. We isolate three classes of failures: (i) data leakage, (ii) shortcut learning, and (iii) implementation bugs and metric divergence. Through extensive experimentation and code replication, we quantify the impact of these issues and show how they corrupt the evaluation standards MassSpecGym was designed to enforce. We distill our findings into recommendations generalizable to MS/MS challenges, benchmarks, and custom evaluation setups. We also release MassSpecGym v1.5, an implementation of our recommendations in the MassSpecGym benchmarking suite which addresses the failure modes identified in this audit. MassSpecGym v1.5 is publicly available at https://github.com/pluskal-lab/MassSpecGym.

</details>


### [256] [Hard or Just Unreached? Diagnosing the Sampling Blind Spot in Math-Reasoning Difficulty Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19636)
*Luca Zhou,Sajel Shah,Emanuele Rodolà,Roberto Dessì*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper reveals that pass@k, the standard difficulty metric for math reasoning benchmarks, systematically misclassifies a significant fraction of "impossible" (pass@k=0%) problems. By applying deterministic activation grafting perturbations to the residual stream, the authors recover solutions for 10.3–22.9% of examples that no sampling seed could solve, exposing a structural blind spot in how difficulty is measured and how verifiable rewards are assigned in RL training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pass@k serves as the canonical difficulty signal for math reasoning benchmarks, driving RL with verifiable rewards, data curation, synthetic curricula, and verifier training. However, the authors hypothesize that pass@k=0% examples may not be genuinely unsolvable by the model — rather, the sampling-based metric may fail to detect latent solution capacity that is structurally encoded in the residual stream but inaccessible via standard stochastic decoding. Diagnosing this blind spot is critical because misclassifying solvable problems as impossible distorts reward signals and curriculum design.

Method: The authors test four open-weight models on GSM8K and MATH (eight free-form math cells total, plus four additional cells for mechanistic verification). For each example where pass@k=0% under six sampling seeds, they apply a deterministic six-chain regime: one greedy decoding chain plus five cheap perturbations applied via activation grafting — a method that transplants residual-stream activations from one forward pass into another. Grafting is used purely as a diagnostic intervention rather than a decoding method. They measure recovery rate (fraction of pass@k=0% items solved at matched compute) and verify mechanistic distinctness of perturbations using cross-kind fix-set Jaccard (≤0.47 across all twelve cells).

Result: Across the eight primary math cells, 10.3–22.9% of pass@k=0% examples were recovered by the six-chain deterministic regime, while greedy decoding alone solved at most 6%. Recovery scaled with additional compute budget. Cross-kind fix-set Jaccard remained ≤0.47 in every setup, confirming that the perturbations activate mechanistically distinct pathways. This demonstrates that a substantial fraction of the pass@k=0% stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream, contradicting the assumption that these examples are beyond the model's capacity.

Conclusion: Pass@k has a persistent blind spot: it conflates stochastic inaccessibility with genuine incapacity. The pass@k=0% stratum contains structurally solvable examples recoverable through deterministic residual-stream interventions. This has implications for RL training signals, data filtering, and curriculum design — all of which currently treat pass@k=0% as a hard negative. The authors emphasize that activation grafting serves as a diagnostic tool, not a decoding method, and that recovery does not imply the unmodified model can reach these solutions under ordinary inference.

Abstract: Math and science reasoning benchmarks rely on pass@k, the fraction of sampled chains that reach gold, as the canonical per-example difficulty signal. The same signal drives RL with verifiable rewards, math data curation, synthetic curricula, and verifier training. We show this proxy has a persistent blind spot on its hardest stratum: on the eight free-form math cells we test (GSM8K and MATH across four open-weight models), 10.3-22.9% of the examples that no sampling seed solves in six tries are instead solved at matched compute by a six-chain deterministic regime. These are greedy decoding plus five cheap residual-stream perturbations applied via activation grafting, while greedy alone solves at most 6% on these math cells. Recovery scales with the additional budget, across perturbations whose mechanistic distinctness we verify across all twelve cells (cross-kind fix-set Jaccard <= 0.47 in every setup). Activation grafting is used as an intervention on internal representations, not a decoding method; we use it purely as a diagnostic and diversification tool, and our recovered items show that the pass@k= 0 % stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream rather than that the unmodified model reaches them under ordinary inference.

</details>


### [257] [Convex training of Lipschitz-regularized shallow neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19652)
*Chao Yin,Antoine Lesage-Landry*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a convex-restriction approach to Lipschitz-regularized training of shallow neural networks, solvable to global optimality, which improves both accuracy and adversarial robustness over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training neural networks that are robust against adversarial attacks is challenging due to the non-convex nature of the optimization problem. Existing methods often settle for local optima, potentially sacrificing both accuracy and robustness.

Method: The authors formulate a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program and then introduce a convex restriction (a convex outer approximation) of that program, which can be efficiently solved to global optimality. The method can be used as a post-processing step: a pre-trained network serves as the initial solution, and solving the convex program guarantees the resulting network is no worse than the initial one.

Result: Numerical experiments on real-world regression datasets under adversarial settings show that the proposed convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. On certain datasets, the resulting networks are both more accurate and more adversarially robust.

Conclusion: The convex restriction approach provides a tractable and certifiable way to improve adversarial robustness in shallow neural networks, offering guaranteed improvement over pre-trained initializations and outperforming existing training methods on both objective value and robustness metrics.

Abstract: In this work, we introduce a training procedure for shallow neural networks that promotes robustness against adversarial attacks. We solve a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program by introducing a convex restriction that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. Our approach can be employed as a post-processing step by taking a pre-trained network as an initial solution to then solving the convex program whose optimal network is guaranteed to be no worse than the initial one. We illustrate the improvements of our training procedure with experiments using real world datasets for regression tasks under an adversarial setting. We show numerically that solving our proposed convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. Additionally, we show that on certain datasets, networks obtained using our convex training program are both more accurate and robust with respect to adversarial attacks.

</details>


### [258] [LOKI: Memory-Free Null-Space Constrained Lifelong Knowledge Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19679)
*Masih Eskandar,Miquel Sirera Perelló,Stratis Ioannidis,Jennifer Dy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LOKI is a lifelong knowledge editing method that dynamically selects layers to update using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of model weights, eliminating the need for past knowledge access. It achieves up to 14% improvement in average accuracy over existing approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing lifelong knowledge editing methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) they update a fixed set of layers for all new knowledge, which reduces flexibility and exacerbates catastrophic forgetting, and (2) they require access to previous knowledge and extensive preprocessing to obtain data statistics, which is impractical in many real-world sequential update scenarios.

Method: LOKI employs two core mechanisms: (1) dynamic layer selection using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to identify which layers to update for each specific knowledge sample, rather than using a fixed set; (2) projecting gradient updates onto the null-space of model weights, which ensures that updates to new knowledge do not interfere with previously learned knowledge without requiring explicit access to past data.

Result: LOKI achieves superior performance compared to existing lifelong knowledge editing approaches across diverse experiments, with up to a 14% improvement in average accuracy.

Conclusion: Dynamic layer selection via HSIC combined with null-space projection of gradient updates provides a flexible, data-efficient solution to lifelong knowledge editing that mitigates catastrophic forgetting without needing access to prior knowledge, yielding significant accuracy gains.

Abstract: Lifelong knowledge editing aims to efficiently and sequentially update language models over time, as new knowledge becomes available or when the model makes mistakes, while preserving acceptable performance on past knowledge. One unresolved challenge is that existing methods modify a fixed set of layers for all new knowledge samples, reducing flexibility and increasing catastrophic forgetting. Another is requiring access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing to obtain data statistics. To address these challenges, we introduce LOKI, a novel approach that uses dynamic layer selection based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of the model weights, bypassing the requirement for previous knowledge access. We show that LOKI achieves superior performance to existing approaches across a wide variety of experiments, achieving up to a 14\% improvement in average accuracy.

</details>


### [259] [Multi-Granular Attention-Driven Reinforcement Learning Framework for Web Intelligent Enhancement Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19690)
*Navin Chhibber,Deepak Singh,Anokh Kishore,Nikita Chawla,K. Anguraj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes MGAR-WIES, a multi-granular attention-based reinforcement learning system that integrates semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive multi-agent RL to deliver personalized web services from heterogeneous data, achieving 80% accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional ML, DL, and RL models struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in dynamic, heterogeneous web environments. There is a need for a system that can handle continuously evolving structured, semi-structured, and unstructured web data while delivering personalized, context-aware services.

Method: (1) Collect and preprocess heterogeneous web data (structured, semi-structured, unstructured) to generate unified feature representations. (2) Transform representations into a dynamic semantic graph with attention-enhanced graph embeddings capturing local relevance and global contextual dependencies. (3) Deploy an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy that uses attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized web actions (content recommendation, navigation optimization, service adaptation). (4) Integrate continuous online feedback to update graph representations and learning policies in real time.

Result: The proposed MGAR-WIES achieved better results in terms of accuracy (80%) compared with existing approaches.

Conclusion: Integrating semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning yields a web intelligent enhancement system that sustains adaptability and performance through real-time feedback-driven updates, outperforming existing methods.

Abstract: From the past few years, web intelligent enhancement systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous and dynamic web data to deliver personalized, context-aware services. However, traditional machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning models often struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in continuously evolving web environments. In this research, a Multi-Granular Attention-based Reinforcement Web Intelligent Enhancement System (MGAR-WIES) is proposed to address the challenges by integrating semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Initially, heterogeneous web data comprising structured, semi-structured and unstructured sources are collected and preprocessed for generating unified feature representations. These representations are transformed into a dynamic semantic graph, where entities and their relationships are modeled by using graph embeddings enhanced by attention mechanisms for capturing both local relevance and global contextual dependencies. Subsequently, an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy leverages the attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized web actions like content recommendation, navigation optimization, and service adaptation. Finally, the continuous online feedback is further integrated to update graph representations and learning policies in real time by ensuring sustained adaptability and performance. The proposed MGAR-WIES acheived better results in terms of accuracy (80%) when compared with existing approaches.

</details>


### [260] [Efficiently Representing Algorithms With Chain-of-Thought Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19697)
*Yanhong Li,Anej Svete,Ashish Sabharwal,William Merrill*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proves that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms (the standard model for algorithm design) with only poly-logarithmic overhead, and as low as logarithmic overhead for multiplication-free flat instruction sets. This stands in stark contrast to prior CoT simulations of Turing machines, which incur quadratic overhead compared to Word RAM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing theoretical results show CoT transformers can simulate Turing machines, but Turing machines are a low-level, inconvenient model for algorithm design. Real algorithms are designed on the Word RAM model, which supports random-access memory and unit-cost operations on O(log n)-bit words, making Word RAM algorithms substantially more efficient than Turing machine implementations. The key open question is whether CoT transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms (e.g., O(n log n) sorting, Dijkstra's algorithm) without the quadratic overhead known for Turing machine simulations.

Method: The authors prove efficient simulation in three transformer settings: (1) finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, (2) continuous CoT where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than discrete tokens, and (3) a hybrid architecture with transformer layers atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. The construction shows how CoT can implement Word RAM operations (memory access, arithmetic, control flow) with poly-logarithmic step overhead, reducing to log-squared for flat instruction sets and logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions.

Result: In all three settings, CoT transformers efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only poly-logarithmic overhead in n. For a "flat" instruction set the overhead is O(log² n), and for multiplication-free flat instructions it is only O(log n). This dramatically improves upon known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.

Conclusion: CoT transformers can efficiently simulate the Word RAM model — the de facto standard for algorithm design — with minimal overhead, closing a significant gap between the theoretical expressiveness of reasoning models and practical algorithm efficiency. The results suggests that the CoT paradigm is well-suited to efficiently implementing the kinds of algorithms computer scientists actually design and use.

Abstract: The increasing popularity of \emph{reasoning} models -- language models that output a series of reasoning or thought tokens before producing an answer -- is justified, in part, by theoretical results showing that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can simulate Turing machines, and thus perform arbitrary computation. However, the Turing machine, while suitable for complexity-theoretic analysis, is not convenient, intuitive, or efficient for discussing algorithms. Algorithms are typically designed and analyzed at a higher level of abstraction, captured by the \emph{Word RAM} model with random-access memory and unit-cost operations on $\bigO(\log n)$-bit words. As a result, Word RAM algorithms can be substantially more efficient than their Turing machine counterparts, raising the question: \emph{Can CoT transformers efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms?} For instance, can they sort $n$ items in $\bigO(n \log n)$ steps or run Dijkstra's algorithm in $\bigO(E + V \log V)$ steps? We answer affirmatively, up to poly-logarithmic overhead. We first establish this for finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, then strengthen the result to two more practical settings with finite width and log-precision: \emph{continuous} CoT, where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than tokens, and a \emph{hybrid} architecture in which transformer layers sit atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In all three cases, we find that CoT \emph{can} efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only a poly-logarithmic overhead in $n$. This overhead reduces to log-square when the Word RAM has a ``flat'' instruction set, and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions -- in stark contrast to known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.

</details>


### [261] [Efficient Neural Network Model Selection for Few-Class Application Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19712)
*Bryan Bo Cao,Abhinav Sharma,Lawrence O'Gorman,Michael Coss,Shubham Jain*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "few-class distinctiveness," a data-side metric for quantifying classification difficulty on datasets with few classes, enabling 6–29× faster model selection compared to repeated training/testing, and demonstrates scaled-down models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano with comparable accuracy on resource-constrained applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most neural network benchmarking focuses on datasets with thousands of classes, yet many real-world applications involve fewer than ten classes. Existing model selection approaches are less effective in this few-class regime, and the relationship between dataset properties and efficient model choice is underexplored.

Method: The authors develop a classification difficulty measure derived from data-side properties. This metric quantifies "few-class distinctiveness" and enables direct comparison of models and datasets without repeated training and testing, accelerating model selection by 6–29×. They also extend scaled model families below the smallest published architectures to target resource-constrained settings.

Result: The proposed metric achieves 6–29× faster model selection than repeated training and testing. Scaled-down models are up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano while maintaining similar accuracy on a mobile robot task. Practical gains are demonstrated across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios.

Conclusion: Dataset properties can effectively guide efficient model selection in few-class settings, where conventional approaches fall short. The few-class distinctiveness metric enables rapid, training-free model comparison, and smaller model variants can be deployed on resource-constrained devices without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: While much effort has focused on developing and benchmarking high-performance neural networks, less attention has been given to how dataset properties, known to practitioners, can guide efficient model selection. Neural models are typically evaluated on datasets with thousands of classes, yet many real-world applications involve fewer than ten. To address this understudied but common setting, we develop a measure of classification difficulty based on data-side properties and show how it enables more efficient model selection for few-class datasets, where traditional approaches are less effective. We term this phenomenon "few-class distinctiveness". Our metric allows comparison of models and datasets 6 to 29$\times$ faster than repeated training and testing. Leveraging this insight, we extend scaled model families below the smallest published models, achieving greater efficiency at similar accuracy, for example models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano for a mobile robot task. Targeting resource-constrained applications, we demonstrate few-class model selection across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios, highlighting practical gains in efficiency without sacrificing performance.

</details>


### [262] [OnDeFog: Online Decision Transformer under Frame Dropping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19721)
*Daiki Yotsufuji,Kenta Nishihara,Shoma Shimizu,Kento Uchida,Shinichi Shirakawa*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OnDeFog extends DeFog by integrating its frame-dropping mechanisms into the Online Decision Transformer (ODT), enabling online learning that better generalizes to novel states and performs strongly under high frame-drop rates, while also outperforming DeFog on datasets with abundant low-reward trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frame dropping due to communication delays or sensor failures degrades RL performance. DeFog, an offline method, mitigates this but struggles to generalize to unseen states not in the training data. This motivates an online approach that can learn from direct environment interaction.

Method: OnDeFog combines the frame-dropping coping mechanisms from DeFog with the Online Decision Transformer (ODT), an online RL method that learns policies through direct environmental interaction rather than from a fixed offline dataset.

Result: OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments with high dropping frame rates, and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing a large amount of low-reward data.

Conclusion: Integrating DeFog's frame-dropping mechanisms into an online learning framework (ODT) yields a more robust agent that both generalizes better to novel states and handles challenging frame-dropping conditions more effectively than either approach alone.

Abstract: In challenging real-world reinforcement learning applications, communication delays or sensor failures often cause frame dropping, in which the agent cannot receive the dropped states and associated rewards. To address the performance degradation caused by frame dropping, the Decision Transformer under Random Frame Dropping (DeFog) was developed by incorporating additional mechanisms into the decision transformer to tackle frame dropping. Although DeFog can mitigate performance degradation in frame-dropping environments, since DeFog is an offline learning method, it struggles to effectively generalize to novel states not adequately represented in the training dataset. In this study, we propose OnDeFog, which integrates the mechanisms in DeFog with the online decision transformer (ODT), an online reinforcement learning method that learns policies through direct environmental interaction. Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates that our proposed OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments characterized by high dropping frame rate and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing a large amount of low-reward data.

</details>


### [263] [Federated Bilevel Performative Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19734)
*Liangxin Qian,Chang Liu,Xuanyu Cao,Jun Zhao,Kwok-Yan Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper- and lower-level objectives experience client-dependent distribution shifts induced by the deployed decisions. It defines the federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point, provides existence/uniqueness conditions, and proposes two algorithms — FBi-RRM (linear convergence) and FBi-SGD (communication-efficient stochastic method) — with theoretical guarantees, validated on strategic regression, meta strategic classification, and CNN-based tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated bilevel optimization (e.g., for hyperparameter tuning, meta-learning) traditionally assumes static client data distributions. However, in practice, deployed models can influence client behavior — a phenomenon called performativity — causing decision-dependent distribution shifts. Existing frameworks fail to account for this coupling between optimization decisions and data-generating distributions in the federated bilevel setting, creating a gap this paper aims to fill.

Method: The authors formalize the Federated Bilevel Performatively Stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective and derive sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness. They propose two algorithms: (1) FBi-RRM, a repeated risk minimization method that converges linearly under a contraction condition; (2) FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method using federated hypergradient estimation, with convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when distribution sensitivities are sufficiently small. Both operate in the federated setting with privacy and communication constraints.

Result: Experiments on strategic regression, meta strategic classification, and CNN-based classification demonstrate that: (i) the predicted stability thresholds hold empirically; (ii) the proposed methods achieve improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines; (iii) the approach scales effectively to nonconvex neural network settings, confirming practical effectiveness.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a principled framework for federated bilevel optimization under performativity, with rigorous theoretical guarantees and practical algorithms. The FBPS concept and the FBi-RRM/FBi-SGD methods effectively address the coupling between optimization and data shifts in distributed nested learning, enabling more robust federated hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning in strategic environments.

Abstract: Federated bilevel optimization is widely used for nested learning problems across distributed clients, such as federated hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning under privacy and communication constraints. Most existing formulations assume fixed client data distributions, which can be violated by performativity, where deployed decisions reshape client behavior and data collection, inducing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shift. We study federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper-level (UL) and lower-level (LL) objectives are evaluated under client-dependent, decision-dependent distributions. We formalize the federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective and provide sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. We then develop two federated methods to compute the FBPS solution: FBi-RRM, which converges linearly under a contraction condition, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method based on federated hypergradient estimation with convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when sensitivities are sufficiently small. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate the predicted stability thresholds and demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines, and CNN-based classification further demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods in nonconvex neural network settings.

</details>


### [264] [Manifold Bandits: Bayesian Curriculum Learning over the Latent Geometry of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19750)
*Darrien McKenzie,Nicklas Hansen,Xiaolong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper reframes RL problem sampling for LLMs as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity and proposes Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a hierarchical, structure-aware sampling framework. Experiments reveal that difficulty alone is insufficient; balancing productivity, diversity, and utility is critical for downstream performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adaptive curriculum learning for RL-based LLM reasoning treats problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms, ignoring the structured, heterogeneous relationships among tasks in the model's latent representation space. This overlooks how sampling decisions shape learning signal propagation across the task manifold.

Method: The authors frame problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit with endogenous non-stationarity, where problems are interrelated via the model's latent space and sampling influences learning dynamics. They propose Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), which organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree and uses Bayesian learning to guide sampling decisions in a structure-aware manner.

Result: Different sampling strategies induce tradeoffs among productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). Prioritizing difficulty alone proves insufficient for strong downstream performance.

Conclusion: Incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling is essential for effective RL-based reasoning improvement in LLMs, moving beyond simple difficulty-based heuristics.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a central approach for improving reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), where training efficiency depends critically on how problems are sampled during optimization. Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods typically prioritize prompts of intermediate difficulty, treating problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms and overlooking the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space. In this work, we frame problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity: problems are related through the model's latent representation space, and sampling decisions can steer how learning signals evolve across that space. To operationalize this perspective, we introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a structure-aware framework that organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree and applies Bayesian learning to guide sampling. Empirically, we find that different sampling strategies induce non-trivial tradeoffs between productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). These results show that prioritizing difficulty alone is insufficient for strong downstream performance, highlighting the importance of incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling.

</details>


### [265] [Learning universal approximations for partial differential equations with Physics-Informed Broad Learning System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19754)
*Zhiwen Yu,Derong Yang,Liujian Zhang,Kaixiang Yang,Peilin Zhan,Jianmin Lv,Jane You,C. L. Philip Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes PIBLS, a backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as least-squares optimization, achieving 1–3 orders of magnitude speedup over PINNs with higher accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional numerical PDE solvers are computationally expensive due to mesh dependencies, and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. There is a need for a fast, mesh-free, and stable alternative.

Method: The authors propose the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a backpropagation-free framework that casts PDE solving as direct least-squares optimization. An improved algorithm is introduced within PIBLS to efficiently handle nonlinear PDEs, and a rigorous mathematical proof of the universal approximation property is provided.

Result: Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs show PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy.

Conclusion: PIBLS offers a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, serving as a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

Abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a central role in modeling complex physical, biological, and engineering systems. While traditional numerical solvers are robust, they often incur prohibitive computational costs due to mesh dependencies, whereas recent Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative but frequently suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. To bridge this gap, this article proposes the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a novel backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization. We improved an algorithm within this framework to handle nonlinear PDEs efficiently and provide a rigorous mathematical proof establishing the universal approximation property of PIBLS for these equations. Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy. This framework provides a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, offering a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

</details>


### [266] [An Information Theoretic Framework for Graph Novelty Generation via Latent Mixture Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19770)
*Itsuki Nakagawa,Kenji Yamanishi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation that uses MDL-based mixture models in latent space, with novelty and reliability conditions grounded in description length, supported by theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph generation methods lack a principled way to generate samples that are simultaneously novel (distinct from training patterns) and structurally consistent with the global distribution. The authors aim to fill this gap with a rigorous information-theoretic formulation.

Method: Data are embedded into a latent space and modeled via finite mixture models. Novelty is operationalized by requiring generated samples to be poorly explained (high description length) by all existing components. Reliability is enforced under the MDL principle by constraining how much a new sample perturbs the overall mixture codelength. Theoretical bounds on misclassification error rates are derived.

Result: Theoretical analysis proves that with appropriate thresholds, probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero at explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets confirm the method enables principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.

Conclusion: The proposed MDL-based framework provides a theoretically grounded, principled approach to graph novelty generation, offering quantifiable guarantees on novelty and reliability that distinguish it from heuristic alternatives.

Abstract: We propose an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation, which aims to generate data that are distinct from existing patterns while preserving global structural consistency. Our approach embeds data into a latent space, models the latent distribution using finite mixture models, and generates novel samples by imposing explicit novelty and reliability conditions formulated in terms of description length. Specifically, novelty is enforced by requiring generated samples to be poorly explained by all existing mixture components, while reliability constrains their impact on the overall mixture structure under the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, with appropriate threshold choices, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero with explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enables principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.

</details>


### [267] [Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19802)
*Nicolas Zilberstein,Morteza Mardani,Santiago Segarra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Flow map models with a tunable lookahead parameter provide a continuous, single-model mechanism to traverse the entire distortion-perception tradeoff frontier in image restoration, from MMSE-optimal (blurry) to perceptually sharp reconstructions, without retraining or auxiliary models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Image restoration methods face a fundamental distortion-perception (DP) tradeoff: minimizing pixel-wise error produces blurry images, while maximizing perceptual quality yields sharp but less faithful reconstructions. Existing approaches require committing to a single operating point, paired supervision, auxiliary models, or cumbersome hyperparameter tuning. The authors aim to provide a unified, continuous, and principled way to span the full DP frontier with a single trained model.
