Method: The authors leverage flow map models — a few-step variant of flow matching that learns an average vector field. They show that the lookahead parameter t in flow maps implicitly parameterizes a family of denoisers. By varying t, the model interpolates between posterior mean (MMSE) estimation and perceptual (posterior sampling) regimes. For Gaussian targets, they prove this exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier. The mechanism is further extended to general inverse problems via a Plug-and-Play (PnP) solver, where t controls the tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency.

Result: For Gaussian targets, varying t provably recovers the optimal DP frontier. For natural images (CelebA 128×128, AFHQ 256×256) across linear and nonlinear inverse tasks, a single trained flow map matches or exceeds specialized baselines at both extremes of the DP tradeoff. The PnP extension demonstrates effective control over perceptual quality vs. data consistency without optimality guarantees.

Conclusion: Flow map models offer a simple, elegant, and unified solution to the distortion-perception tradeoff. The lookahead parameter alone enables continuous traversal of the DP frontier using a single model, eliminating the need for multiple specialized methods, retraining, or auxiliary networks, and generalizes effectively to diverse inverse problems.

Abstract: Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA ($128\times 128$) and AFHQ ($256\times 256$) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings.

</details>


### [268] [Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling for Stable RLHF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19818)
*Licheng Pan,Haocheng Yang,Haoxuan Li,Yichen Sun,Yunsheng Lu,Shijian Wang,Lei Shen,Yuan Lu,Zhixuan Chu,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UARM equips reward models with calibrated uncertainty via conformal prediction and uses heteroscedastic variance to reweight GRPO advantages, mitigating reward hacking and improving alignment quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RLHF reward models act as deterministic point estimators lacking uncertainty signals, and GRPO's uniform treatment of rewards amplifies unreliable estimates during diverse response exploration, causing severe reward hacking.

Method: UARM combines (1) quantile-based conformal prediction to endow reward models with calibrated uncertainty estimates, and (2) heteroscedastic variance decomposition to reweight GRPO advantages, downweighting high-uncertainty reward signals during policy optimization.

Result: Experiments on HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF show UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality versus standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.

Conclusion: Integrating calibrated uncertainty into both reward modeling and policy optimization effectively addresses a critical vulnerability in the RLHF pipeline, yielding more robust and reliable LLM alignment.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns large language models by training reward models on preference data and optimizing policies to maximize predicted rewards. However, this pipeline faces two fundamental challenges: (1) reward models cannot signal when their predictions are unreliable, since they usually act as deterministic point estimators; and (2) modern group-based policy optimization can amplify unreliable reward signals, as exemplified by GRPO's uniform treatment of rewards during advantage computation. As policies explore increasingly diverse responses, these two limitations create a critical vulnerability: unreliable reward estimates may be granted disproportionate influence, triggering severe reward hacking. We propose Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM), which equips reward models with calibrated uncertainty via quantile-based conformal prediction and reweights GRPO advantages through heteroscedastic variance decomposition. Experiments across HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF demonstrate that UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality compared to standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.

</details>


### [269] [Enhancing Graph Neural Networks Using Proximity Graphs for Dust Source Emission Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19825)
*Maryam Sanisales,Zahed Rahmati,Ali Darvishi Boloorani,Ali Vefghi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using proximity graphs (Delaunay, Gabriel, k-NN, Yao) as input structures for GNNs (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) to forecast dust source emissions, demonstrating significant superiority over both random-graph GNNs and LSTM models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional dust storm forecasting methods fail to capture complex spatiotemporal dynamics. There is a need for models that can effectively represent the spatial and temporal relationships inherent in dust source emission data.

Method: The authors feed various proximity graph constructions — Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph — as input structures into three GNN architectures (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) for message passing. Performance is benchmarked against GNNs using random graphs and an LSTM baseline.

Result: GNNs using proximity graphs significantly outperform GNNs using random graphs, and both GNN variants are far superior to the LSTM model for dust source emission forecasting.

Conclusion: Integrating proximity graphs with GNNs yields robust and accurate dust source emission predictions by effectively modeling intricate spatiotemporal relationships, validating the importance of geometrically meaningful graph representations over arbitrary graph structures.

Abstract: Accurate prediction of dust source emissions is critical for mitigating the significant environmental and health hazards posed by dust storms. Traditional forecasting methods often struggle to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of these phenomena.
  In this paper, we demonstrate that proximity graphs enable Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to effectively model the intricate spatial and temporal relationships between data points. Specifically, we use proximity graphs--such as Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph--as the input for GNNs (including GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Networks, and Graph Attention Networks) to perform message passing.
  Our approach highlights the effectiveness of integrating proximity graphs with GNNs for robust and accurate dust source forecasting. To emphasize the importance of proximity graph representations, we compare our method against GNNs using random graphs for message passing. The results show that GNNs with proximity graphs significantly outperform those with random graphs and are also far superior to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model in dust source emission forecasting.

</details>


### [270] [When, Where, and How: Adaptive Binning for Tabular Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19827)
*Daehwan Kim,Haejun Chung,Ikbeom Jang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive Binning introduces a self-supervised learning pretext task for medical tabular data that progressively refines per-feature discretization through a coarse-to-fine curriculum, jointly optimizing value-space concentration and representation-space coherence without manual tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical tabular data is ubiquitous but deep learning on tables remains underexplored due to costly label acquisition. While binning-based self-supervised pretexts show promise, existing methods use a fixed global quantile discretization with feature-agnostic supervision, failing to adapt to per-feature characteristics or synergize with representation learning.

Method: The method employs a training-adaptive discretization scheme coupled with a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. It detects learning plateaus to trigger progressive discretization refinement per feature, selects representation-aware split points, and uses a heterogeneity-aware objective that combines categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features. The design is motivated by spectral bias of neural networks and curriculum learning principles.

Result: Experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols demonstrate consistent gains for both linear probing and fine-tuning, without requiring dataset-specific discretization tuning. The authors also contribute a standardized medical tabular SSL benchmark for reproducible research.

Conclusion: Adaptive Binning effectively bridges the gap between tabular data characteristics and self-supervised representation learning by making discretization an integral, adaptive part of training rather than a fixed preprocessing step, advancing the underexplored field of deep learning on medical tables.

Abstract: Medical tabular data are ubiquitous in clinical research, but deep learning for tables remains underexplored because reliable labels often require costly expert adjudication, even though structured clinical variables are routinely available in tabular form. Self-supervised learning can leverage these unlabeled tables, and recent binning-based pretexts offer a promising inductive bias, but existing objectives fix a single global quantile discretization and apply feature-agnostic supervision. We propose Adaptive Binning, a training-adaptive discretization pretext for tabular SSL that couples discretization to learning through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Motivated by the spectral bias of neural networks and the principles of curriculum learning, our method progressively refines discretization per feature upon plateau detection and selects representation-aware splits to jointly improve value-space concentration and representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective unifies categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features, and experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for linear probing and fine-tuning without dataset-specific discretization tuning. We further introduce a medical tabular SSL benchmark with standardized protocols to support reproducible progress in this underexplored domain. Our code is available at https://github.com/labhai/Adaptive-Binning.

</details>


### [271] [Neural Additive and Basis Models with Feature Selection and Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19850)
*Yasutoshi Kishimoto,Kota Yamanishi,Takuya Matsuda,Shinichi Shirakawa*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: To address the computational intractability of Neural Additive Models (NAM) and Neural Basis Models (NBM) when handling feature interactions or high-dimensional data, this paper proposes integrating a feature selection layer that learns selection weights during training, reducing computational cost and model size while maintaining or improving performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NAM and NBM offer high interpretability via GAM-based architectures but become computationally intractable when using two-input neural networks (for capturing feature interactions) or when applied to high-dimensional datasets. The computational bottleneck stems from the need to train separate neural networks for each feature or feature pair.

Method: The authors introduce a feature selection layer into both NAM and NBM architectures. This layer learns selection weights during training, effectively pruning irrelevant features and feature interactions. The mechanism is simple, end-to-end trainable, and reduces the number of neural networks that need to be trained, thereby cutting computational costs and model size.

Result: The proposed models are computationally more efficient than vanilla NAM and NBM. They achieve better or comparable performance relative to state-of-the-art generalized additive models (GAMs), even when incorporating two-input neural networks to capture feature interactions in high-dimensional settings.

Conclusion: Incorporating a feature selection layer into NAM and NBM successfully resolves their computational bottlenecks, enabling scalable training with two-input NNs on high-dimensional data while preserving the interpretability advantages of the GAM framework.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit attractive performance in various fields but often suffer from low interpretability. The neural additive model (NAM) and its variant called the neural basis model (NBM) use neural networks (NNs) as nonlinear shape functions in generalized additive models (GAMs). Both models are highly interpretable and exhibit good performance and flexibility for NN training. NAM and NBM can provide and visualize the contribution of each feature to the prediction owing to GAM-based architectures. However, when using two-input NNs to consider feature interactions or when applying them to high-dimensional datasets, training NAM and NBM becomes intractable due to the increase in the computational resources required. This paper proposes incorporating the feature selection mechanism into NAM and NBM to resolve computational bottlenecks. We introduce the feature selection layer in both models and update the selection weights during training. Our method is simple and can reduce computational costs and model sizes compared to vanilla NAM and NBM. In addition, it enables us to use two-input NNs even in high-dimensional datasets and capture feature interactions. We demonstrate that the proposed models are computationally efficient compared to vanilla NAM and NBM, and they exhibit better or comparable performance with state-of-the-art GAMs.

</details>


### [272] [Physics-Informed Neural Network with Squeeze-Excitation-like Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19853)
*Yun-Fei Song,Long-Gang Pang,Fu-Peng Li,Jun-Jie Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEA-PINN introduces a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks, achieving highly stable initialization with near-zero variance on 17/20 benchmarks, competitive accuracy on high-frequency problems without specialized activation functions, and serving as an effective lightweight plug-in module that boosts nonlinear representation and convergence robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from poor initialization stability, high variance across runs, and limited capacity to model high-frequency solutions. Existing remedies like Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activation functions (e.g., TSA-PINN) add complexity. The authors seek a lightweight, general-purpose architectural enhancement that improves initialization determinism, representation power, and convergence without specialized frequency-engineering components.

Method: SEA-PINN augments standard PINN architectures with a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism that dynamically recalibrates per-neuron importance across layers. The key design includes a highly stable initialization scheme. The module is evaluated as a standalone enhancement and also integrated into TSA-PINN (a model using learnable frequencies in sinusoidal activations) to test composability. No Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activations are used in the base SEA-PINN.

Result: SEA-PINN achieved near-negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss on 17 of 20 benchmark problems, establishing a quasi-deterministic starting point. Without Fourier features or periodic activations, SEA-PINN reached 83% of the improvement relative to FNN-PINN on high-frequency case 7, versus TSA-PINN's 90% (a specialized high-frequency model). Integrating SEA-PINN into TSA-PINN further boosted performance by 42.49%.

Conclusion: SEA-PINN is an effective lightweight plug-in attention module that enhances PINNs' nonlinear representation power, promotes robust and efficient convergence, and improves overall reliability. Its strong initialization properties and compatibility with existing specialized architectures (like TSA-PINN) make it a practical general-purpose enhancement for physics-informed learning.

Abstract: We introduce SEA-PINN, a novel architecture that incorporates a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks to dynamically recalibrate the importance of neurons across layers. A key feature of SEA-PINN is its highly stable initialization. On 17 out of 20 benchmark problems, SEA-PINN exhibit nearly negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss, establishing a quasi-deterministic and favorable starting point for optimization. Notably, without employing Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activation functions, SEA-PINN attained competitive accuracy (83\% vs. 90\% improvement relative to FNN-PINN on the high-frequency case 7) as compared with TSA-PINN-a model specifically engineered for high-frequency problems via learnable frequencies in sinusoidal activations. Furthermore, integrating SEA-PINN into TSA-PINN boosted performance by 42.49\%. These results underscore SEA-PINN as a lightweight plug-in module that enhances nonlinear representation power, promotes more robust and efficient convergence, and strengthens the overall reliability of physics-informed learning.

</details>


### [273] [Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Score Matching in Gaussian Mixtures via Reverse Fisher Divergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19876)
*Alexander Tyurin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that using reverse Fisher divergence (expectation over the student distribution) instead of the standard forward Fisher divergence (expectation over the teacher distribution) for score matching yields provably better optimization properties when fitting Gaussian mixture models, including global convergence guarantees from arbitrary initialization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard score matching using forward Fisher divergence can suffer from poor, initialization-dependent convergence behavior even in simple Gaussian mixture model settings. This motivates exploring the reverse Fisher divergence as an alternative with potentially more favorable optimization properties.

Method: The authors analyze gradient descent dynamics for minimizing the reverse Fisher divergence when fitting Gaussian mixture models. They employ a Lyapunov-based analysis framework to prove global convergence guarantees. Two settings are studied: (1) a Gaussian mixture student with fixed weights and identity covariances fitting a single Gaussian teacher, and (2) both teacher and student being Gaussian mixtures, with convergence guarantees under a global random initialization and a separation assumption on the teacher means.

Result: For a single Gaussian teacher, GD converges globally from arbitrary initializations. For the Gaussian mixture teacher case, under a global random initialization and Ω̃(1)-separation of teacher means, each student component converges near its closest teacher component with high probability, and conditions are given for convergence in total variation distance.

Conclusion: The reverse Fisher divergence offers a substantially more benign optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence for score matching in Gaussian mixture models, enabling provable global convergence where the forward objective fails.

Abstract: The score matching problem is a central training objective in modern generative modeling, diffusion models, fitting unnormalized statistical models, and inverse problems. A standard approach is to minimize the forward Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the teacher distribution. However, recent results show that even in simple Gaussian mixture model settings, this objective can lead to undesirable and initialization-dependent convergence behavior. In this paper, we study an alternative objective: the reverse Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the student distribution. We analyze gradient descent (GD) for fitting Gaussian mixture models and show that this change in the objective leads to significantly better optimization properties. First, when the teacher distribution is a single Gaussian and the student is a Gaussian mixture model with fixed weights and identity covariances, we prove the global convergence of GD from arbitrary initializations. Second, we extend the analysis to the case where the teacher is also a Gaussian mixture model and prove global convergence guarantees under a global random initialization scheme and a $\widetildeΩ(1)$-separation assumption on the target means. In particular, with high probability, each student component converges near its closest teacher component, and we provide conditions under which the student distribution converges in total variation distance. Our proofs rely on a new Lyapunov-based analysis of the gradient descent dynamics, showing that the reverse Fisher divergence has a much more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence.

</details>


### [274] [On the Oracle Complexity of Interpolation-Based Gradient Descent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19878)
*Dongmin Lee,William Lu,Anuran Makur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes PPI-GD, an inexact gradient method that uses piecewise polynomial interpolation over the data domain to approximate full gradients. It achieves improved oracle complexity over several GD variants for smooth, strongly convex and non-convex ERM loss functions when data dimension is polylogarithmic in sample size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent work shows that smoothness of ERM loss with respect to training data (rather than model parameters) can be exploited to improve gradient descent oracle complexity. The authors aim to leverage this data-domain smoothness by constructing polynomial interpolants of gradient samples, reducing expensive full-gradient computations.

Method: PPI-GD queries the first-order oracle at equidistant points in the data domain, constructs tensor product polynomial interpolants over patches, and uses these to approximate the full gradient. The analysis extends bicubic spline error analysis techniques to d-variate tensor product polynomial interpolation, bounding approximation error to control convergence.

Result: PPI-GD outperforms several GD variants in key regimes when loss is sufficiently smooth and data dimension is bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples. Oracle complexity improvements are established for both strongly convex and non-convex settings.

Conclusion: Exploiting data-domain smoothness via piecewise polynomial interpolation yields a practical inexact gradient method with provably better oracle complexity. The interpolation analysis techniques developed for the d-variate case may have independent interest beyond optimization.

Abstract: Recent work on first-order optimizers for empirical risk minimization (ERM) has suggested that smoothness of ERM loss functions in the training data, rather than in the optimization parameters, can be leveraged to improve the oracle complexity of gradient descent (GD) methods. In this paper, we propose an inexact gradient method, piecewise polynomial interpolation-based gradient descent (PPI-GD), which approximates the full gradient in each iteration by querying the first-order oracle at equidistant points in the data domain to construct polynomial interpolants of the resulting gradient samples over appropriately sized patches of the data domain. We analyze the oracle complexity of PPI-GD for strongly convex and non-convex loss functions when the data space dimension is bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples, and find it to outperform several GD variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth. Furthermore, our analysis extends several techniques from the error analysis of bicubic spline interpolants to the setting of $d$-variate tensor product polynomial interpolants which may be of independent interest in interpolation analysis.

</details>


### [275] [Matching Markets meet Cumulative Prospect Theory: Towards Optimal and Adversarially Robust Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19883)
*Ananya Kunisetty,Avishek Ghosh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies competitive multi-agent multi-armed bandits in two-sided matching markets where agents' decisions follow Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT). It establishes a baseline regret bound of O(K log T (1/Δ)^(2/α)), then improves it by strategically restricting exploration to an active arm set, removing K from the dominant term. The authors also extend the framework to adversarial markets with reward corruption, proposing robust algorithms with logarithmic regret guarantees under both known and unknown corruption budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multi-agent bandit models assume rational, risk-neutral agents. However, real-world human decision-makers exhibit risk-sensitive, nonlinear preference weighting as captured by CPT. Integrating CPT into competitive matching markets creates a more realistic model of human-centric systems (e.g., online labor markets, school choice), but introduces analytical challenges due to nonlinear probability weighting. The dependence on the minimum preference gap Δ in existing regret bounds is suboptimal when K ≫ N, motivating improved exploration strategies.

Method: The authors model a multi-agent bandit with CPT-based reward distortions using an α-Hölder continuous weight function. They first analyze an existing learning algorithm under CPT distortion, yielding baseline regret. To improve this, they propose a judicious active-arm selection strategy during exploration that prunes suboptimal arms, eliminating dependence on K in the dominant regret term. For adversarial markets, they design robust algorithms handling corrupted observed rewards, separately treating cases where the total corruption budget C is known versus unknown, using CPT as a risk-sensitive measure.

Result: (1) Baseline player-optimal regret: O(K log T (1/Δ)^(2/α)). (2) Improved regret via active-arm exploration: removes K from the dominant term, achieving optimal regret when K ≫ N. (3) Robust algorithms for adversarial markets with reward corruption achieve logarithmic player-optimal regret under both known and unknown corruption budgets.

Conclusion: Incorporating CPT into competitive multi-agent bandits with matching markets yields tractable logarithmic regret. Strategic exploration pruning dramatically improves dependence on K, achieving optimality when arms outnumber players. The framework is robustly extendable to adversarial reward corruption while maintaining strong regret guarantees, making it suitable for real-world human-centric market design.

Abstract: We study a multi-agent multi-armed bandit problem in the competitive setup with two-sided matching markets under a human centric decision making model. To capture human preferences, we use cumulative prospect theory (CPT) that weighs the actions of the agent in a nonlinear fashion using a ($α$-Hölder continuous) weight function. CPT has been widely used in behavioral economics and risk sensitive machine learning to emulate human preferences. We analyze the state-of-the-art learning algorithm with CPT weight distorted rewards and obtain a player optimal regret of $\mathcal{O}(K\log T \left(\frac{1}Δ\right)^{2/α})$, where $K$ denotes the number of arms, $T$ is the learning horizon, and $Δ$ represents (suitably defined) players' minimum preference gap. Noticing the dependence on $Δ$ to be sub-optimal, we further improve this regret by judiciously selecting the active set of arms during exploration, which removes the dependence on $K$ in the dominant term and achieves an improved (optimal) regret guarantees in the setting where the number of arms $K$ is significantly larger than the number of players $N$. In addition, we consider adversarial markets where the observed rewards of the agents may be corrupted. We propose and analyze algorithms for robust markets with CPT as risk sensitive measure in both settings where the total corruption budget is known and where it is unknown, and establish logarithmic player-optimal regret guarantees in both cases.

</details>


### [276] [SL-S4Wave: Self-Supervised Learning of Physiological Waveforms with Structured State Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19888)
*Feng Wu,Harsh Deep,Eric Lehman,Sanyam Kapoor,Guoshuai Zhao,Rahul Krishnan,Gari Clifford,Li-wei H Lehman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SL-S4Wave is a self-supervised learning framework for long-sequence medical time series (ECG, EEG) that combines contrastive learning with a custom S4-based encoder featuring multi-scale global convolution, achieving SOTA on arrhythmia detection with strong label efficiency, long-sequence robustness, and cross-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SSL methods for medical time series (e.g., CNNs) fail to capture long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. Structured state space models (S4) excel at long-sequence modeling but current S4 architectures are not designed for the specific characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms.

Method: Proposes SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised contrastive learning framework with a tailored encoder built on S4. The key innovation is a multi-layer global convolution module using multiscale subkernels that captures both fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms.

Result: (1) Outperforms SOTA supervised and SSL baselines on arrhythmia detection; (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled samples (label efficiency); (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments; (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types. Also achieves superior performance on multiple EEG tasks, demonstrating cross-modality generalization.

Conclusion: SL-S4Wave effectively addresses the limitations of both CNN-based SSL methods and vanilla S4 architectures for physiological time series, demonstrating strong performance, label efficiency, long-sequence modeling capacity, and cross-domain transferability across ECG and EEG modalities.

Abstract: Modeling long-sequence medical time series data, such as electrocardiograms (ECG), poses significant challenges due to high sampling rates, multichannel signal complexity, inherent noise, and limited labeled data. While recent self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, based on various encoder architectures such as convolutional neural networks, have been proposed to learn representations from unlabeled data, they often fall short in capturing long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. Structured state space models (S4) excel at long-sequence modeling, but existing S4 architectures fail to capture the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms. In this work, we propose SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised learning framework that combines contrastive learning with a tailored encoder built on structured state space models. The encoder incorporates multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels, enabling the capture of both fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SL-S4Wave (1) consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines in a challenging arrhythmia detection task, (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples, showcasing strong label efficiency, and (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments, highlighting its capacity to model complex temporal dynamics in long sequences that most existing approaches fail to efficiently model, and (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types, underscoring its robust cross-domain generalization. We additionally evaluate SL-S4Wave on multiple EEG tasks, achieving superior performance over strong baselines, demonstrating generalizability of our approach beyond cardiac waveforms.

</details>


### [277] [Adversarial Bandit Optimization with Globally Bounded Perturbations to Convex Losses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19891)
*Zhuoyu Cheng,Kohei Hatano,Eiji Takimoto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper extends adversarial bandit optimization to settings with non-convex, non-smooth loss functions composed of a convex β-smooth base component plus an adversarial perturbation subject to a cumulative budget. The authors modify a standard bandit algorithm and provide expected regret guarantees that explicitly capture the perturbation budget's impact, reducing to standard smooth bandit convex optimization results when perturbations are absent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard bandit convex optimization assumes losses are convex and smooth, but real-world scenarios often involve adversarial perturbations applied after the learner's action is observed. Existing work on post-action perturbations focused only on linear losses. The authors aim to generalize this to the broader and more practical class of convex, β-smooth losses while maintaining explicit regret characterization in terms of the perturbation budget.

Method: The authors modify a standard bandit optimization algorithm to handle the composite loss structure. They develop a novel analysis that quantifies and bounds the additional regret incurred specifically due to adversarial perturbations, while the base algorithm otherwise operates on the underlying convex β-smooth component. The analysis explicitly tracks how the perturbation budget propagates through the regret decomposition.

Result: The paper establishes expected regret guarantees that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget for the broader class of convex β-smooth losses. In the absence of perturbations (zero budget), the guarantees recover standard regret bounds for bandit convex optimization with β-smooth losses.

Conclusion: The framework successfully extends globally-budgeted, post-action adversarial perturbations from linear losses to general convex β-smooth losses, providing regret guarantees that cleanly interpolate between perturbed and unperturbed settings. The analysis techniques developed for bounding perturbation-induced regret are the key technical contribution.

Abstract: We study adversarial bandit optimization in which the loss functions may be non-convex and non-smooth. In each round, the learner selects an action and observes only the loss incurred at that action. The loss consists of an underlying convex and $β$-smooth component and an adversarial perturbation that may be chosen after observing the learner's action. The perturbations are subject to a global budget controlling their cumulative magnitude over time.
  This framework extends the globally budgeted, post-action perturbation model from underlying linear losses to general convex and $β$-smooth losses. For this broader class, we establish expected regret guarantees that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget.
  To establish these guarantees, we modify a standard bandit optimization algorithm and develop an analysis that controls the additional regret caused by the perturbations. In the absence of perturbations, our results reduce to regret guarantees for the standard bandit convex optimization setting with $β$-smooth losses.

</details>


### [278] [Score Approximation for Diffusion Models on Arbitrary Low-Dimensional Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19894)
*Xinhe Mu,Zaijiu Shang,Zhaoqi Zhou,Chuan Zhou,Qi Meng,Guiying Yan,Zhiming Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proves a universal score approximation theorem showing that diffusion models can handle arbitrary compact distributions without requiring smoothness or manifold assumptions. The key insight is a discrete-mixture formulation where a ReLU network approximates the score function with complexity exponential only in the intrinsic (upper Minkowski) dimension d, not the ambient dimension, thus breaking the curse of dimensionality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing theoretical foundations for score-based diffusion models rely on restrictive assumptions—Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports—that are routinely violated by real-world data exhibiting singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters. The authors aim to close this gap by proving score approximation guarantees under minimal, realistic conditions.

Method: The authors propose a universal score approximation framework based on a novel discrete-mixture formulation. They prove that for any distribution supported on a compact set with upper Minkowski dimension d, the score function can be approximated using a ReLU network. The complexity scales exponentially only in d (the intrinsic dimension), not the ambient dimension, thereby avoiding the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality.

Result: The paper establishes that diffusion models readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures. Combined with existing results on solving the backward diffusion SDE for arbitrary compact distributions, this provides a theoretical explanation for why diffusion models perform well on real-world generative tasks despite their non-ideal statistical properties.

Conclusion: Diffusion models are theoretically robust to the messy, non-smooth nature of real-world perceptual data. The exponential dependence on intrinsic dimension d rather than ambient dimension explains their practical success and significantly relaxes the assumptions needed for theoretical guarantees.

Abstract: The remarkable success of score-based diffusion models has spurred significant efforts to establish their theoretical foundations. However, existing complexity bounds for score approximation rely heavily on restrictive assumptions like Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports, which are routinely violated by the singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters inherent to real-world perceptual data. This work establishes a universal score approximation theorem that works for any distribution supported on any compact set of upper Minkowski dimension $d$. Using a novel discrete-mixture formulation, we prove that the score function can be approximated with a ReLU network whose complexity grows exponentially only with $d$, thus breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality. Combined with existing theories on accurately solving the backward diffusion SDE for arbitrary compact distributions, our work shows that diffusion models readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, explaining their competence in real-world generative tasks.

</details>


### [279] [ADaPT: Token-Level Decoupling for Efficient Large Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19919)
*Tingyun Li,Zishang Jiang,Jinyi Han,Xinyi Wang,Sihang Jiang,Han Xia,Zhaoqian Dai,Shuguang Ma,Fei Yu,Jiaqing Liang,Yanghua Xiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ADaPT decouples efficiency and correctness rewards at the token level via a mode-selection token, enabling continuous control over the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier without degrading reasoning quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chain-of-thought, but uniform application incurs high computational cost. Existing methods that shorten or mix reasoning strategies degrade reasoning capability because sequence-level optimization couples efficiency and correctness signals, implicitly penalizing long but correct reasoning trajectories.

Method: ADaPT is a token-level dual-process framework that introduces a mode-selection token to control fast vs. slow reasoning. During training, efficiency-related rewards are applied exclusively to this token, decoupling efficiency from correctness optimization. At inference time, adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token enables precise, continuous movement along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance.

Conclusion: Token-level decoupling of efficiency and correctness signals via ADaPT effectively resolves the trade-off, allowing a single model to smoothly navigate the efficiency-performance spectrum without compromising reasoning capability.

Abstract: Large reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought to achieve strong performance, but applying such reasoning uniformly incurs high computational cost. Existing efficiency-oriented methods attempt to shorten or mix reasoning strategies, yet often degrade reasoning capability. We identify the root cause as sequence-level coupling between efficiency incentives and correctness optimization, which implicitly penalizes long but correct reasoning trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Adaptive Dual-Process Thinking (ADaPT), a token-level dual-process framework that explicitly decouples efficiency and correctness signals during training. ADaPT introduces a mode-selection token to control fast and slow reasoning, applying efficiency-related rewards exclusively to this token to avoid penalizing correct long reasoning while encouraging efficiency when appropriate. Moreover, ADaPT enables precise and continuous control over the efficiency-performance trade-off at inference time: by adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token, a single trained model can smoothly move along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks.

</details>


### [280] [Compositionality Emerges in a Narrow Depth-Connectivity Regime: Architecture Constraints and Solution Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19941)
*Dat H. Do,Rushi Shah,Duc V. Le,Dianbo Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Compositionality emerges only in a narrow sweet spot of network depth and connectivity sparsity; both shallower/denser and deeper/sparser networks fail to develop compositional structure. The authors introduce similarity-based pruning and a depth predictor to discover this regime, and provide theoretical justification via compositional sparsity and feature-interference bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard gradient-based training rarely yields models with compositional internal structure, despite compositionality being considered essential for generalization. The fundamental question is: how and why does compositionality form, and under what conditions can it be reliably induced?

Method: The authors systematically investigate the emergence of compositionality along two axes: (1) connectivity — varying network sparsity patterns beyond simple weight magnitude, and (2) depth — sweeping across layer counts. They introduce Similarity-based Pruning (SP) to identify and recover connectivity patterns that foster compositionality, and a heuristic depth predictor to estimate the optimal depth regime. Theoretical analysis employs compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds to explain the observed phenomena.

Result: Compositionality emerges only within a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot. Along the connectivity axis, compositionality depends on which specific connections remain, not merely on sparsity levels. Along the depth axis, compositionality peaks at specific, target-dependent depths, with both shallower and deeper networks failing. Violating either condition causes gradient descent to converge to fractured (non-compositional) solutions. The proposed SP method and depth predictor successfully recover and exploit this regime.

Conclusion: Compositionality is not an inevitable product of gradient-based learning but requires precise architectural conditions — a narrow band of depth and structured connectivity. The practical tools (SP pruning and depth prediction) and theoretical framework provide both a diagnostic and a recipe for inducing compositional representations in neural networks.

Abstract: Compositionality is believed to be the foundation for generalization, enabling models to reuse meaningful primitives in novel combinations. Yet, models trained with standard gradient-based optimization rarely, and often only weakly, exhibit compositional internal structure, and it remains unclear how or why such compositionality forms. In this work, we show that compositionality emerges in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot. Along the connectivity axis, compositionality only appears in some specifically sparse networks, heavily depends on which connections remain rather than on weights' sparsity alone. Along the depth axis, compositionality emerges within a narrow, target-dependent regime, peaking at specific depths, while both shallower and deeper networks fail. When either the depth or connectivity condition is violated, gradient descent silently converges to fractured solutions rather than compositional ones. To discover and exploit this emergence, we introduce (i) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity and (ii) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate where compositionality is most likely to appear. Finally, we support these empirical findings with a theoretical framework based on compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds, explaining why compositional solutions are reachable only in a narrow depth-connectivity regime.

</details>


### [281] [Towards Graph-Based Deep Learning for Map Generalization: Insights from Building Footprints Simplification and Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19956)
*Yanning Wang,Zhiyong Zhou,Zhouyu Liu,Mengni Yu,Yu Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First graph-based deep learning approach to map generalization, reformulating building simplification as node movement prediction and aggregation as link prediction. GraphSAGE excels at aggregation (link prediction), but precise node movement remains challenging; aggregation proves inherently harder than simplification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Map generalization — particularly simplification and aggregation of complex building footprints — is a fundamental cartographic task lacking exploration with graph-based deep learning. The authors aim to investigate whether graph neural networks can capture the spatial relationships needed for automated generalization within a unified framework.

Method: The authors reformulate building simplification as a node movement prediction task and building aggregation as a link prediction task within a unified graph learning framework. Three representative GNN architectures — GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT — are evaluated on multi-scale building datasets.

Result: GraphSAGE demonstrates relative strength in link prediction (aggregation). All architectures struggle with precise node movement prediction (simplification). Aggregation is found to be more complex and challenging than simplification, indicating that higher-level spatial relationships are difficult for current deep learning methods to capture.

Conclusion: Graph-based deep learning shows promise for automated map generalization but faces significant hurdles: data imbalance, imprecise node movement, and the intrinsic difficulty of modeling higher-level spatial aggregation. The study offers methodological insights and baselines for future work, though post-processing remains necessary.

Abstract: Map generalization remains one of the fundamental tasks in cartography, especially for the simplification and aggregation of complex building footprints. This study presents the first exploratory application of graph-based deep learning to both tasks, reformulating simplification as node movement prediction and aggregation as link prediction within a unified graph learning framework. We evaluate representative graph neural network architectures (GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE) on multi-scale building datasets, showing that GraphSAGE demonstrates relative strengths in link prediction accuracy, while also revealing persistent challenges in precise node movement prediction. Beyond quantitative performance, the results highlight that aggregation poses greater complexity and challenges than simplification, underscoring the difficulty of capturing higher-level spatial relationships in map generalization with current deep learning approaches. Although limitations such as data imbalance and the need for post-processing remain, the study provides valuable insights and methodological directions for advancing automated map generalization with deep learning approaches.

</details>


### [282] [Low-Energy Reduced RISC-V Instruction Subset Processor for Tsetlin Machine Inference at the Edge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19964)
*Chanda Gupta,Sanidhya Bhatia,Shaurya Priyadarshi,Himani Panwar,Rishad Shafik,Sudip Roy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor with a reduced instruction set tailored for Tsetlin Machine inference achieves up to 98% execution time reduction and 29.7× energy savings compared to a baseline RV32IM core, while maintaining higher accuracy than Binarized Neural Networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TM accelerator designs rely on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, limiting flexibility and programmability. There is a need for a programmable yet efficient architecture for TM inference at the edge.

Method: The authors design a domain-specific RISC-V processor with a reduced instruction subset optimized for TM inference. They use instruction profiling to identify which instructions to retain, then simplify the datapath and control path accordingly. The design is evaluated against a baseline RV32IM core and Binarized Neural Networks across multiple datasets.

Result: The TM-based approach achieves comparable or superior accuracy to BNNs (88.18% vs. 60.0% on CIFAR-2). The reduced RISC-V core reduces execution time by up to 98% and achieves an average 29.7× reduction in energy consumption compared to the baseline RV32IM core.

Conclusion: A reduced-instruction RISC-V processor tailored for TM inference successfully combines programmability with high efficiency, making it a compelling solution for edge AI systems.

Abstract: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a logic-based machine learning approach that relies on simple bitwise operations and finite-state automata, which makes it attractive for edge AI deployments. Recent work has focused on co-processor and accelerator designs based on Tsetlin Machines (TMs). Although these designs achieve high performance, they typically depend on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, limiting flexibility and ease of programming. In this work, we present a domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor architecture and design flow tailored for TM inference. Leveraging the modular structure of RISC-V, we design a reduced instruction subset processor that retains programmability while targeting improved performance and lower energy consumption for TM workloads. Instruction profiling is employed to guide instruction reduction, followed by datapath and control path simplifications tailored to TM inference. Both the baseline RV32IM core and the proposed reduced core are evaluated across multiple datasets and compared with Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs), which serve as a hardware-efficient baseline due to their reliance on bitwise operations during inference. Results show that TM achieves comparable or higher accuracy (e.g., up to 88.18% on CIFAR-2 compared to 60.0% for BNN) while reducing execution time by up to 98% across multiple datasets. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves an average $29.7\times$ reduction in energy consumption, demonstrating its effectiveness for programmable and efficient edge AI systems.

</details>


### [283] [Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19984)
*Juntian Huang,Jurgen Kurths,Ying Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KARC replaces reservoir computing's reservoir with explicit basis-function expansions from the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, creating a lightweight KAN variant that enables closed-form training while outperforming existing reservoir methods on PDE benchmarks and integrating with diffusion models for text-to-image generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional reservoir computing suffers from limited representational capacity for long-range dependencies and hyperparameter sensitivity, while next-generation reservoir computing eliminates recurrence at the cost of exploding feature dimensions. A principled approach is needed that balances expressive capacity with computational efficiency.

Method: KARC replaces the reservoir with explicit basis-function expansions based on the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, effectively constructing a lightweight KAN architecture. The method preserves KAN expressivity while enabling the efficient closed-form training (e.g., ridge regression) characteristic of reservoir computing frameworks.

Result: At comparable computational cost, KARC outperforms both conventional and next-generation reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks, including partial differential equations. The approach also successfully integrates with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation tasks.

Conclusion: KARC establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, enabling efficient, high-fidelity forecasting of dynamical systems through a lightweight design that combines KAN expressivity with reservoir computing's closed-form training advantages.

Abstract: Reservoir computing offers a lightweight framework for forecasting dynamical systems but may struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to limited representational capacity. Conventional reservoir computing recurrently uses trainable reservoirs with hyperparameter sensitivity, while the next-generation reservoir computing removes recurrence at the cost of rapidly growing feature dimensions. Here, we develop Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing (KARC), which replaces reservoirs with explicit basis-function expansions inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. We rigorously show that KARC is a lightweight design of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs), preserving the potential expressive capacity of KANs while admitting efficient closed-form training of reservoir computing. At comparable cost, KARC outperforms existing reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks including partial differential equations. It can also be integrated with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation. This work thus establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and KANs, enabling efficient and high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting.

</details>


### [284] [Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR): Function-Preserving SVD Compression for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19993)
*Nico Harder,Daniel Becking,Karsten Mueller,Wojciech Samek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AIR is an SVD-based LLM compression method that improves low-rank approximation by incorporating an influence metric via a single ALS sweep, outperforming prior SVD-based methods and composing with LoRA for further gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior SVD-based LLM compression methods like SVD-LLM(W) rely solely on activation-awareness for low-rank approximation but ignore the backward-signal influence of each weight element, leaving compression quality on the table.

Method: AIR computes an activation-aware optimal SVD initialization, then runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates an element-wise backward-signal influence metric into the low-rank factorization, with a monotone-descent guarantee.

Result: AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at ≤60% parameter retention, matches SVD-LLM(W) quality with ~90% less calibration data, exceeds ACIP standalone, and further improves when composed with LoRA. It also yields FLOP, peak-memory, and per-token latency gains.

Conclusion: AIR demonstrates that incorporating backward-signal influence into SVD-based compression via a simple, closed-form ALS step yields substantial quality improvements and practical efficiency benefits, and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods like LoRA.

Abstract: We present Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR), an SVD-based LLM compression framework that guides each weight matrix's low-rank approximation with a backward-signal influence metric. Starting from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM(W), AIR runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates influence element-wise under a monotone-descent guarantee. AIR is layer-local and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods: alone it exceeds ACIP, and AIR+LoRA outperforms it further. AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at <=60% parameter retention, matches its quality with ~90% less calibration data, and turns parameter savings into FLOP, peak-memory, and per-token latency gains.

</details>


### [285] [Connect the Dots: Training LLMs for Long-Lifecycle Agents with Cross-Domain Generalization Via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20002)
*Yanxi Chen,Weijie Shi,Yuexiang Xie,Boyi Hu,Yaliang Li,Bolin Ding,Jingren Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "Connect the Dots" (CoD), an RL framework for training LLMs to self-improve as long-lifecycle agents by interleaving task-solving with context-updating episodes, enabling progressive performance gains through accumulated environmental knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent training focuses on single-task performance rather than the meta-capability of learning from experiences across a long sequence of tasks. Long-lifecycle agents need to continuously explore, learn, and self-update their context to improve over time — a capability not addressed by standard task-by-task RL.

Method: A general framework with (1) end-to-end RL using long rollout sequences that interleave solve-task and update-context episodes, (2) a GRPO-style RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment, and (3) specially designed tasks/environments that incentivize the meta-capability rather than domain-specific skills. Training and evaluation protocols measure progressive improvement conditioned on self-updated context.

Result: End-to-end RL training in the CoD setting is empirically validated as effective. The elicited meta-capability shows out-of-distribution generalization: within training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings.

Conclusion: CoD connects multiple prior research lines and opens new opportunities for advancing LLM-based AI agents. The framework demonstrates that meta-capabilities for lifelong learning can be elicited through appropriately designed RL training. Code is open-sourced.

Abstract: This work presents a general framework for training large language models (LLMs) to "Connect the Dots" (CoD), a meta-capability required by long-lifecycle agents: as an LLM-based AI agent gets deployed in an environment, it solves a long sequence of tasks while continuously exploring the environment, learning from its own experiences, and iteratively self-updating its context about the environment, thereby achieving progressively better performance on future tasks conditioned on the updated context. Major components of the CoD framework include: (1) algorithm design and infrastructure for end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) with long rollout sequences interleaving solve-task and update-context episodes; (2) tasks and environments for incentivizing and eliciting the targeted meta-capability in LLMs during training, as well as for faithfully measuring progress during evaluation. We present proof-of-concept implementations of the CoD framework, including a GRPO-style RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment, as well as tasks and environments tailored to the targeted meta-capability (rather than domain-specific LLM capabilities or standard task-by-task RL). Empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting, and demonstrate the potential for out-of-distribution generalization -- within the training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings -- of the elicited meta-capability. Our investigation of CoD connects several lines of prior works, and opens up new opportunities for advancing LLMs and AI agents. To facilitate further research and applications, we release our implementations at \url{https://github.com/agentscope-ai/Trinity-RFT/tree/research/cod/examples/research_cod}.

</details>


### [286] [StreamKL: Fast and Memory-Efficient KL Divergence for Boosting Attention Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20005)
*Guangda Liu,Yiquan Wang,Chengwei Li,Wenhao Chen,Jing Lin,Yiwu Yao,Danning Ke,Wenchao Ding,Jieru Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StreamKL is the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates the quadratic memory cost of materializing two attention distributions. It uses a novel online one-pass forward kernel with SRAM streaming and tile-by-tile recomputation in the backward pass, achieving up to 43× forward and 14× backward speedups while reducing HBM footprint from O(N_Q N_K) to O(1).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Attention distillation via KL divergence is widely used but requires materializing both attention distributions before computing the KL reduction, incurring O(N_Q N_K) memory and IO costs. At long context lengths, this quadratic overhead becomes prohibitive, limiting the applicability of attention distillation on a single GPU.

Method: StreamKL derives a novel online formulation for coupled two-distribution KL reduction, enabling a single one-pass fused forward kernel that streams query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM without materializing full attention matrices. For the backward pass, attention probabilities are recomputed tile-by-tile, avoiding storage of quadratic intermediates. The method includes dedicated GPU kernel optimizations for efficiency.

Result: StreamKL achieves up to 43× speedup in the forward pass and 14× speedup in the backward pass over baseline methods. It reduces the extra HBM footprint of attention distillation from O(N_Q N_K) to O(1), enabling long-context distillation on a single GPU.

Conclusion: By eliminating quadratic materialization through fused online computation, StreamKL makes attention distillation practical at long context lengths on a single GPU, removing a critical memory bottleneck in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training workflows.

Abstract: Attention distillation, which trains one attention distribution to match another by minimizing their Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, is widely used in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training. However, existing approaches materialize both attention distributions before computing the KL reduction, incurring $O(N_QN_K)$ memory and IO costs that become prohibitive at long context lengths. We present StreamKL, the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates this quadratic materialization. StreamKL derives a novel online formulation for the coupled two-distribution KL reduction, enabling a single one-pass forward kernel that streams query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM. For the backward pass, StreamKL recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile, avoiding storage of quadratic intermediates. We further design and implement efficient GPU kernels with dedicated optimizations. Experiments show StreamKL delivers up to $43\times$ and $14\times$ speedups over baseline methods in the forward and backward passes, respectively. Most importantly, StreamKL reduces the extra HBM footprint of attention distillation from $O(N_QN_K)$ to $O(1)$, enabling long-context distillation on a single GPU.

</details>


### [287] [VIMPO: Value-Implicit Policy Optimization for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20008)
*Zhewei Kang,Aosong Feng,Sergey Levine,Dawn Song,Xuandong Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VIMPO is a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL, enabling dense per-token credit assignment without training a separate critic, outperforming GRPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL methods for LLM reasoning face a trade-off: GRPO-style group-relative methods avoid critic training but assign coarse trajectory-level advantage uniformly to all tokens, while actor-critic methods provide finer credit assignment but suffer from value function training instability. The authors aim to resolve this trade-off.

Method: VIMPO derives a policy-implied value function from the first-order optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL. For autoregressive generation, this yields a value recurrence expressed in policy-reference log-ratios, anchored by a terminal condition (zero future reward). A simple value loss incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards without a critic. The same derivation produces a critic-free actor advantage, enabling a PPO-style actor update that separates reward incorporation (via the value loss) from policy improvement.

Result: VIMPO outperforms GRPO on MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with particularly large gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO maintains a consistent advantage over GRPO.

Conclusion: Policy-implied value optimization (VIMPO) provides finer credit assignment than group-relative methods while retaining the practical simplicity of critic-free training, offering a compelling middle ground between GRPO and full actor-critic approaches.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a central tool for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but current methods face a trade-off between simplicity and credit assignment. Group-relative methods such as GRPO avoid training a critic, but typically assign a trajectory-level advantage to every token. Actor-critic methods provide denser learning signals, but require a learned value function with its own training instability. We introduce VIMPO, a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized reinforcement learning. For autoregressive generation, the resulting value recurrence can be written in terms of policy-reference log-ratios and anchored by the terminal condition that no future reward remains at the end of a trajectory. This gives a simple value loss that incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards without training a critic. The same derivation also yields a critic-free actor advantage, allowing VIMPO to separate reward incorporation through the value loss from policy improvement through a PPO-style actor update. On mathematical RLVR benchmarks, VIMPO improves over GRPO across MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with especially larger gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO retains a consistent advantage over GRPO, suggesting that policy-implied value optimization can provide finer credit assignment while preserving the practical simplicity of critic-free training.

</details>


### [288] [Self-Adaptive Scale Handling for Forecasting Time Series with Scale Heterogeneity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20010)
*Xu Zhang,Zhengang Huang,Yunzhi Wu,Xun Lu,Erpeng Qi,Yunkai Chen,Zhongya Xue,Peng Wang,Wei Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module to address scale heterogeneity in time series forecasting, where different series differ by orders of magnitude. AS learns adaptive scale factors via Scale Calibrating and Scaling Selection, outperforming global normalization and window-based scaling on real-world fund sales datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TSF research assumes scale-homogeneous data, but real-world industrial data (e.g., financial product sales) exhibits scale heterogeneity — different series vary by orders of magnitude yet share temporal patterns. Joint modeling is desirable, but current scaling methods either compress low-scale signals (global normalization) or destroy semantic discriminability and amplify inverse-scaling errors (window-based scaling). A method that enables effective joint modeling of scale-heterogeneous series is needed.

Method: The proposed AS module comprises two components: (1) Scale Calibrating (SC), which uses neural networks to calibrate prior mean scaling factors, and (2) Scaling Selection (SS), which adaptively decides whether to apply the calibrated factor or retain the original, preventing over-calibration. The module is model-agnostic and integrates seamlessly into existing TSF models.

Result: Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay demonstrate that AS consistently improves the performance of popular TSF models when integrated, validating its effectiveness for scale-heterogeneous forecasting.

Conclusion: AS provides an effective, plug-and-play solution for joint modeling of scale-heterogeneous time series, outperforming traditional scaling methods and advancing industrial applicability of TSF models.

Abstract: Current time series forecasting (TSF) research predominantly focuses on scale-homogeneous data, where different time series share similar numerical magnitude ranges. However, in real-world industrial scenarios such as financial product sales, different time series often differ by orders of magnitude (scale heterogeneity). Since these series share similar temporal patterns, joint modeling is desirable for better data utilization, yet existing scaling methods either compress low-scale signals (global normalization) or destroy semantic discriminability and amplify inverse-scaling errors (window-based scaling). This paper proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module that learns adaptive scale factors tailored to each input, preserving semantic discriminability while reducing inverse-scaling errors. AS consists of Scale Calibrating (SC), which calibrates prior mean scaling factors through neural networks, and Scaling Selection (SS), which decides whether to apply calibration or retain the original factor, avoiding over-calibration. Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay show that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their performance. The code and dataset are available at the link https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF.

</details>


### [289] [Hierarchical Control in Multi-Agent Games: LLM-based Planning and RL Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20014)
*Jannik Hösch,Alessandro Sestini,Florian Fuchs,Amir Baghi,Joakim Bergdahl,Konrad Tollmar,Jean-Philippe Barrette-LaPierre,Linus Gisslén*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid LLM+RL architecture uses a pretrained LLM as a strategic controller to select among specialized RL skill policies for multi-agent coordination, achieving performance competitive with hand-crafted behavior trees and superior human-likeness, without manual rule engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling RL to complex multi-agent environments is hindered by sparse rewards, vast state-action spaces, and the difficulty of learning coordinated strategies. The authors aim to leverage LLM reasoning for high-level strategic control while retaining RL for reactive low-level execution.

Method: A hierarchical architecture where a pretrained LLM serves as a centralized strategic controller, selecting among pretrained specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents. RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. Evaluated in a 2v2 King of the Hill environment against BT and Flat RL baselines, with both quantitative win-rate analysis and a human perception user study (n=15).

Result: LLM+RL achieved a 46.4% win rate vs. BT's 51.5% (statistically equivalent, p=0.103), while both significantly outperformed Flat RL. In the user study, 60% of participants rated LLM+RL agents as most human-like (p=0.027), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability.

Conclusion: Pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills for multi-agent coordination, achieving competitive task performance and superior perceived believability compared to hand-crafted and end-to-end approaches, while eliminating the need for manual rule engineering.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong performance in sequential decision-making, yet scaling to complex multi-agent environments remains challenging due to sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the difficulty of learning coordinated strategies. We propose a hierarchical architecture where a pretrained large language model (LLM) acts as a centralized strategic controller that selects among specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents, while RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. We evaluate this hybrid system in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) and \emph{``Flat''} RL (end-to-end training without skill decomposition) baselines. The LLM+RL system achieves task performance statistically equivalent to hand-crafted BT (46.4\% vs 51.5\% win rate, $p=0.103$) while both significantly outperform Flat RL trained without skill decomposition. A user study ($n=15$) reveals that 60\% of participants perceive LLM+RL agents as the most human-like ($p=0.027$), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability. These results demonstrate that pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills, achieving competitive multi-agent coordination and superior perceived believability without manual rule engineering.

</details>


### [290] [Adaptive Distance-Aware Trunk Deep Operator Learning for Long-Span Roadway Bridges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20015)
*Bilal Ahmed,Diab W. Abueidda,Waleed El-Sekelly,Tarek Abdoun,Mostafa E. Mobasher*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an adaptive-trunk DeepONet (AD-DeepONet) that uses KNN-based dynamic domain construction, distance-aware features, and stiffness-informed Schur complement reconstruction to predict localized structural responses in long-span bridges with FEM-level accuracy at up to 60x total speedup and 10,000x inference speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated full FEM analysis computationally prohibitive for influence surface generation and structural digital twin applications. Existing SciML methods fail to accurately capture these localized responses.

Method: An adaptive-trunk DeepONet framework is proposed with three key components: (1) a KNN strategy that dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain to focus on structural influence zones; (2) a trunk network enhanced with distance-aware features encoding geometric relationships between load and structural nodes; (3) a physics-based full-field reconstruction via a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation to extend predictions from adaptive nodes to the entire domain. Training data are generated using a reduced-order equivalent shell model that retains dominant global behavior at reduced cost.

Result: Validated on a benchmark bridge and the real-world Mussafah Bridge, the method achieves relative errors below 5% (FEM-level accuracy). Total response evaluation time including full-field reconstruction is reduced by approximately 60x versus FEM; excluding reconstruction, AD-DeepONet inference is up to four orders of magnitude (10,000x) faster. The framework successfully generates full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading.

Conclusion: The AD-DeepONet framework demonstrates strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications by enabling rapid, accurate prediction of localized structural responses under arbitrary loading with dramatic computational speedups while maintaining FEM-level fidelity.

Abstract: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated FE analysis computationally expensive for applications such as influence surface generation and structural digital twins. Existing SciML approaches struggle to accurately capture these localized responses. To address this challenge, this study proposes an adaptive-trunk DeepONet for localized structural response prediction in large-scale bridge systems. The framework dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain using a KNN strategy, allowing the network to focus on structural influence zones. The trunk network is further enhanced using distance-aware features that encode the geometric relationship between the load and structural nodes. A physics-based full-field reconstruction is incorporated through a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation, enabling predictions at adaptive nodes to be extended to the entire structural domain. To enable scalable training, response data are generated using a reduced-order equivalent shell model that preserves the dominant global behavior while significantly reducing computational cost. The proposed framework is validated on both a benchmark bridge model and the real-world Mussafah Bridge.
