Results show that the method achieves FEM-level accuracy with relative errors below 5%, while reducing the total response evaluation time (including full-field reconstruction) by approximately 60x; excluding the post-processing reconstruction step, the AD-DeepONet inference is up to four orders of magnitude faster than FEM. In addition, the framework enables rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading configurations, demonstrating strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

</details>


### [291] [What Makes Effective Supervision in Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Information-Theoretic Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20075)
*Xinghao Chen,Chak Tou Leong,Wenjin Guo,Jian Wang,Wenjie Li,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Latent Chain-of-Thought reasoning suffers from a dual collapse (gradient attenuation and representational drift). The authors decompose process supervision into Trajectory Supervision and Space Supervision, introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP) to measure latent–explicit mutual information, and demonstrate an Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy depends on latent information fidelity. They advocate shifting from geometric imitation to mutual information maximization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent CoT offers efficiency by internalizing reasoning in continuous hidden states, but outcome supervision yields weak learning signals, causing latent trajectories to suffer from semantic drift. The paper aims to diagnose and address this failure mode through an information-theoretic lens.

Method: The authors (1) frame Latent CoT failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in latent space; (2) decompose process supervision into Trajectory Supervision (dense stepwise signals) and Space Supervision (preserving semantic manifold structure); (3) compare rigid geometric compression against generative reconstruction as a semantic anchor; and (4) introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP) to quantify mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps.

Result: Experiments reveal an Information-Performance Binding — reasoning accuracy is directly tied to the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. Generative reconstruction outperforms rigid geometric compression as a flexible semantic anchor, better preserving information capacity.

Conclusion: Effective latent reasoning supervision requires shifting from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. The ULP and the dual-supervision decomposition provide a principled framework for future work on latent CoT.

Abstract: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) internalizes reasoning within continuous hidden states, offering a promising alternative to verbose discrete reasoning traces. However, robust latent reasoning remains difficult because outcome supervision provides weak learning signals and leaves latent trajectories prone to semantic drift. In this work, we analyze Latent CoT from an information-theoretic perspective and identify this failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in the latent space. We further decompose process supervision into two complementary dimensions: Trajectory Supervision, which injects dense stepwise reasoning signals, and Space Supervision, which preserves the semantic structure of the latent manifold. Our analysis shows that rigid geometric compression can collapse the reasoning space, whereas generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity. To measure these effects, we introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), which quantifies the mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments reveal a clear Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy depends on the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. These findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision and suggest shifting from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Supervision-in-Latent-CoT}{this repository}.

</details>


### [292] [Exploring the potential of AlphaEarth and TESSERA embeddings for Fine-scale Local Climate Zone Mapping: A case study across five cities in Switzerland](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20034)
*Htet Yamin Ko Ko,Clement Atzberger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study compares precomputed embeddings from two EO foundation models (TESSERA and AlphaEarth) against traditional Sentinel-1/2 composites for upscaling coarse ~100-m LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net across five Swiss cities. TESSERA consistently outperforms all baselines (IoU: 0.59–0.69 and 0.77–0.82), though temporal transfer across years remains challenging. Embeddings show strong potential to replace manual feature engineering for scalable fine-scale LCZ mapping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many cities rely on coarse ~100-m resolution Local Climate Zone (LCZ) maps, which are inadequate for fine-scale urban climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable design. Traditional LCZ mapping workflows involve time-consuming preprocessing and manual feature engineering. The authors investigate whether embeddings from emerging Earth Observation (EO) foundation models can simplify this pipeline and enable scalable, high-resolution (10-m) LCZ mapping.

Method: Precomputed embeddings from TESSERA (Feng et al., 2025) and AlphaEarth (Brown et al., 2025) are compared against traditional Sentinel-1/2 (S1S2) image composites as input to an attention-based U-Net architecture. Three experiments are conducted across five Swiss cities: (1) multi-city transferability assessment, (2) impact of higher-resolution reference data quality, and (3) temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. Performance is evaluated using Intersection-over-Union (IoU).

Result: All datasets achieve strong IoU of 0.59–0.69 in the first experiment and 0.77–0.82 in the second. TESSERA embeddings consistently outperform both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings. Temporal transfer of embedding-based models across different years remains an open challenge. Improving reference data quality proves to be the strongest lever for accuracy gains.

Conclusion: EO foundation model embeddings, particularly TESSERA, demonstrate promising potential to reduce preprocessing burden and manual feature engineering in LCZ mapping workflows. Combined with a simple location-aware attention U-Net, these embeddings enhance regional transferability and scalability, supporting the development of comprehensive, reproducible fine-scale (10-m) LCZ maps for global urban climate applications. Reference data quality remains the most impactful factor for further improvement.

Abstract: Understanding urban spatial morphology is critical for climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable urban design, and Local Climate Zone (LCZ) mapping provides the basic framework for this. However, many cities still use coarse ~100-m resolution LCZ records, which are unsuitable for fine-scale urban research. In this study, precomputed embeddings from TESSERA (Feng et al., 2025) and AlphaEarth (Brown et al., 2025) are compared to traditional Sentinel-1/2 (S1S2) composites in five Swiss cities to see if they can upscale coarse LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net. Three experiments assess multi-city transferability, the impact of higher-resolution reference data, and temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. We find that all datasets achieve strong performance with test data Intersection-over-Union (IoU) ranging from 0.59-0.69 and 0.77-0.82 in the first two experiments. TESSERA consistently outperforms both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings As expected, we find that the transfer of embedding-based models from one year to another remains an open challenge. Overall, however, our results demonstrate the promising potential of embeddings derived from EO foundation models to reduce time consuming preprocessing, respectively, manual feature engineering tasks and to guide a universal deep learning-based LCZ mapping workflow. When combined with a simple location-aware attention U-Net architecture, the embeddings enhance regional transferability and scalability, supporting the development of comprehensive and reproducible fine-scale LCZ maps for global urban climate applications Improving reference data quality remains the strongest lever for further accuracy gains.

</details>


### [293] [Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis using a Multimodal Approach with 3D MRI and PET](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20037)
*Loukas Ilias,Anthi-Maria Vozinaki,Christos Ntanos,Dimitris Askounis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multimodal framework for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis that combines 3D CNN feature extractors with three fusion strategies (concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit, gated self-attention) and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts classifier for input-adaptive routing. Tested on MRI and PET data across three binary classification tasks, GMU fusion achieves the best results on NC vs. MCI (80.46%) and NC vs. AD (95.47%), while gated self-attention performs best on MCI vs. AD (82.08%). Ablation confirms the MoE classifier consistently improves accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal models for AD diagnosis fuse MRI and PET using static concatenation and apply uniform computation to all subjects, which lacks robustness to patient and site heterogeneity and is computationally inefficient. The authors aim to address these limitations through adaptive fusion and conditional computation.

Method: The framework uses 3D convolutional feature extractors on MRI and PET scans, followed by one of three fusion strategies: (1) concatenation, (2) Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and (3) gated self-attention. A sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier then performs input-adaptive routing, selectively activating only the most informative experts per case. Grad-CAM is employed for visualizing disease-relevant regions to ensure interpretability.

Result: GMU fusion achieves 80.46% accuracy on NC vs. MCI and 95.47% on NC vs. AD. Gated self-attention achieves 82.08% on MCI vs. AD. Ablation studies show that removing the MoE classifier consistently degrades accuracy across all three binary classification tasks.

Conclusion: Input-adaptive multimodal modeling that leverages the complementary nature of MRI and PET, combined with sparse MoE routing, yields robust performance for AD diagnosis. The results validate the importance of dynamic fusion and conditional computation over static approaches.

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible neurodegenerative disorder and a leading cause of death worldwide. Early diagnosis plays an important part especially at the Mild Cognitive Impairment stage, where timely intervention can help slow its progression before it advances to AD. Neuroimaging data, like Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans, can help detect brain changes early by providing structural and functional brain changes related to the disease. Yet, many multimodal models still fuse MRI and PET with static concatenation and apply identical computation to all subjects, which limits robustness to patient/site heterogeneity and can waste computation. To address these limitations, we present the first study of combining 3D convolutional feature extractors with three fusion strategies - concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and gated self-attention - and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier that performs input-adaptive routing, activating only the most informative experts per case. Finally, we utilize Grad-CAM to visualize disease-related regions, ensuring model interpretability. Experiments are performed across three binary classification tasks (NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD). Results show that GMU achieves accuracies of 80.46 % (NC vs. MCI) and 95.47 % (NC vs. AD), while gated self-attention attains 82.08 % on MCI vs. AD. Ablations show that removing the MoE consistently degrades accuracy across all tasks. These findings underscore the value of input-adaptive, multimodal modeling for AD diagnosis by leveraging the complementary nature of MRI and PET.

</details>


### [294] [Comparative Study of Neural Surrogate Architectures for Autoregressive Prediction of Internal Battery States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20053)
*Gihyun Lee,Thorben Menne,Simon Olma,Jakob Hilgert,Sangyoung Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Four neural architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) are systematically compared as autoregressive surrogates for the Doyle-Fuller-Newman battery model, with U-Net achieving 3% nRMSE after 300-step rollouts and 5.38× speed-up, demonstrating that spatial inductive bias is critical for surrogate performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The DFN model accurately resolves internal Li-ion battery states but is computationally prohibitive for real-time use. Existing ML surrogates learn condition-specific solutions rather than generalizable dynamics, and no systematic comparison of architectures as autoregressive state-transition operators exists.

Method: Four architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, Fourier Neural Operator) are formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators predicting full DFN internal states. All models are trained under a unified framework with multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning to isolate the effect of spatial inductive bias in a controlled comparison.

Result: U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, with a 5.38× speed-up over the numerical solver.

Conclusion: Spatial inductive bias is a critical determinant of surrogate performance. These findings advance the development of surrogates for internal state observability in next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

Abstract: The Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model resolves internal electrochemical states in lithium-ion batteries with high fidelity. However, the numerical solution of its governing equations is computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment, limiting scalability from individual cells to pack and fleet-scale applications. While machine learning surrogates can substantially reduce inference latency through GPU acceleration, most existing approaches learn solution approximations tied to specific operating conditions rather than learning generalizable state-evolution dynamics. This work presents a systematic comparison of four neural network architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators that predict full DFN internal states across a wide range of operating conditions. To ensure a controlled architectural comparison, all models are trained under a unified framework using multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning, isolating the impact of spatial inductive bias. Results demonstrate that the U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% averaged across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, while providing a 5.38x speed-up over the numerical solver. These findings highlight spatial inductive bias as a critical determinant of surrogate performance, advancing the development of surrogates for internal state observability for next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

</details>


### [295] [PaAno+: Multiscale Encoding and Cross-Variable Attention for Time Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20055)
*Youji Zhu,Hongbing Wang,Wenchao Liu,Xiaodong Liu,Xiangguang Xiong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PaAno is a lightweight anomaly detection model using patch-oriented representation learning with multiscale convolutional encoders, cross-variable fusion attention, and a novel temporal patch-window sorting pretext task, achieving SOTA accuracy on TSB-AD while maintaining low computational cost suitable for edge deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Transformer- and large-model-based anomaly detectors are computationally prohibitive, while existing lightweight methods suffer from insufficient feature extraction and weak multivariate dependency modeling. There is a need for an efficient model that balances detection accuracy with deployability on resource-constrained terminals.

Method: PaAno employs: (1) a multiscale feature extraction encoder using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields to capture hierarchical temporal patterns; (2) cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation with residual connections for stable representation learning; (3) a cross-variable fusion attention module to explicitly model inter-variable correlations; (4) a temporal patch-window sorting pretext task to uncover intrinsic time-series structure; and (5) triplet loss to optimize the patch embedding space for enhanced discriminability.

Result: Extensive experiments on the TSB-AD benchmark show PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate tasks, with significant gains across metrics including VUS-PR, while maintaining favorable computational efficiency through its compact network design.

Conclusion: PaAno successfully bridges the gap between detection accuracy and computational efficiency, demonstrating that patch-oriented representation learning with carefully designed attention mechanisms and pretext tasks can yield a deployable, high-performance anomaly detection solution for real-time industrial and medical monitoring.

Abstract: Time-series anomaly detection has significant practical value for industrial and medical monitoring, as well as other critical domains. Current Transformer- and large-model-based detection approaches incur excessive computational overhead, while existing lightweight alternatives are constrained by insufficient feature extraction and inadequate modeling of dependencies across multivariate variables. To mitigate the above drawbacks, this study develops a lightweight, efficient anomaly detection model, dubbed PaAno, within the patch-oriented representation learning paradigm. In the encoder module, a multiscale feature-extraction backbone is constructed using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields to capture hierarchical temporal characteristics; subsequent cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation, combined with residual connection optimization, further stabilizes feature representation learning. A cross-variable fusion attention module is embedded to explicitly characterize inter-variable correlations, empowering the model to identify anomalous patterns amid intricate operational conditions. Moreover, a novel pretext task based on temporal patch-window sorting is customized to uncover intrinsic structural properties of time series, and triplet loss is leveraged to optimize the patch embedding space for enhanced feature discrimination. Extensive experiments on the TSB-AD benchmark demonstrate that the proposed PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate tasks, yielding significant performance gains across evaluation metrics, including VUS-PR, relative to the original PaAno. Leveraging a compact network design, the presented model achieves favorable computational efficiency, enabling deployment on resource-limited terminals for real-time anomaly inference.

</details>


### [296] [Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20104)
*Petr Ivashkov,Randall Balestriero,Bernhard Schölkopf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SMWM introduces a sensorimotor world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization, which simultaneously prevents representation collapse and aligns latent states with action-relevant features, enabling stable planning from offline, reward-free trajectories without complex auxiliary techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Two key challenges motivate this work: (1) perception-for-action principles suggest representations should prioritize action relevance over visual fidelity, yet most world models do not explicitly enforce this; (2) end-to-end training of JEPA-style latent world models suffers from representation collapse when the sole objective is predicting future latent states. The authors seek a unified solution that addresses both representation collapse and action-aligned representation learning with a single, simple regularizer.

Method: The authors propose the Sensorimotor World Model (SMWM), a latent world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization. The core idea is to force latent states to preserve information about the action that caused a transition between them. This is achieved by adding an inverse dynamics prediction head that predicts the action from consecutive latent states. This single regularizer serves dual purposes: it prevents the latent representations from collapsing to trivial solutions (since meaningful action information must be retained) and it biases representations toward the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment, discarding uncontrollable distractors. Training uses offline, reward-free trajectories and requires no frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or other complex latent regularizers.

Result: Empirically, SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces. The model achieves competitive planning performance on simple 2D and 3D control tasks, demonstrating that the inverse dynamics regularization alone is sufficient for stable end-to-end world model training.

Conclusion: Inverse dynamics regularization provides an elegant, minimalist solution to two longstanding problems in latent world model training: representation collapse and action-irrelevant representations. By jointly addressing these issues with a single regularizer, SMWM offers a simpler alternative to existing methods that rely on frozen encoders, EMA targets, or complex auxiliary objectives, while maintaining competitive downstream planning performance.

Abstract: Perception for action suggests that representations of the world should be shaped not by visual fidelity alone, but by their relevance for actions. At the same time, latent JEPA-style world models advocate learning compact predictive states from high-dimensional observations to facilitate the prediction of future states, but end-to-end training of these models is nontrivial because representations may collapse if our only goal is to construct a latent state that is easy to predict. We introduce a sensorimotor world model (SMWM): a latent world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization. This single regularizer addresses both issues: it prevents representation collapse and induces action-aligned representations. By forcing latent states to preserve information about the action underlying a transition, it biases the model toward the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment while discarding uncontrollable distractors. This yields stable latent world models trained from offline, reward-free trajectories, without frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers. Empirically, SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and enables competitive planning performance across simple 2D and 3D control tasks.

</details>


### [297] [Quantile of Means: A Bonus-Free Ensemble Method for Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20107)
*Asaf Cassel,Aviv Rosenberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon MDPs that achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds without requiring count-based uncertainty estimates, thereby providing theoretical justification for ensemble-based exploration in reinforcement learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimal RL algorithms rely on count-based uncertainty estimates that are theoretically sound but impractical to compute. Ensemble methods are practical and widely used, yet they lack theoretical grounding for exploration. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing theoretical justification for ensemble-based exploration.

Method: Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, the authors propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The approach is count-free and leverages ensemble statistics (quantiles) to drive exploration.

Result: The proposed method achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, matching the theoretical guarantees of count-based approaches without requiring explicit count-based uncertainty estimates.

Conclusion: Ensemble-based exploration in RL can be theoretically grounded. The quantile-based ensemble approach provides a practical and theoretically sound alternative to count-based uncertainty estimation for driving exploration in finite-horizon MDPs.

Abstract: Optimal Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms typically rely on carefully constructed count-based uncertainty estimates to drive exploration. Although theoretically sound, such estimates are hard to compute in practical settings and therefore offer limited insight for designing exploration heuristics. Meanwhile, ensembling has emerged as a practical approach, but remains without theoretical justification. Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, we propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Our simple count-free approach achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, providing theoretical grounding for ensemble-based exploration in RL.

</details>


### [298] [When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital: Federated Conformal Risk Control via Risk-Curve Shrinkage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20115)
*Nafis Fuad Shahid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A federated conformal risk control (CRC) protocol using shrinkage-regularized thresholds (with a single hyperparameter) achieves near-universal per-institution coverage guarantees on brain tumor segmentation while keeping prediction sets clinically usable, outperforming both naive pooled CRC (which violates coverage at 40% of sites) and local CRC (which inflates prediction sets 83×).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard federated CRC pools calibration scores across sites to compute a single threshold, but this only protects the average hospital and can catastrophically violate coverage at individual institutions — a critical failure for patient safety in multi-site clinical deployments. The naive alternative (per-site local CRC) restores coverage but yields impractically large prediction sets. The motivation is to develop a privacy-preserving federated protocol that provides per-institution coverage guarantees without sacrificing prediction-set efficiency.

Method: The authors propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol: each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalar values) to a central server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. The single hyperparameter n₀ trades worst-case coverage against efficiency, with selection via leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis. The method deliberately avoids transmitting patient-level images, masks, or per-volume scores. A finite-sample correction term is retained, and the authors contrast their approach against direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets.

Result: On the FeTS-2022 dataset (1,251 subjects, 20 institutions): (1) naive pooled CRC violates coverage at 8/20 (40%) institutions, with worst-case false-negative rate exceeding target by 7.8 pp; (2) local CRC inflates prediction sets by 83×; (3) the proposed shrinkage method with n₀=19 achieves only 2.7/20 violations at 2.0× stretch; (4) removing the finite-sample correction triples violations; (5) Lagrangian budget optimization concentrates risk on vulnerable hospitals and fails. Per-site coverage is validated across four target levels with three random seeds.

Conclusion: Shrinkage-based federated CRC preserves the marginal guarantee under the site-mixture assumption by construction, provides strong per-institution coverage with modest prediction-set inflation, and requires no patient-level data to leave any site — making it a practical, privacy-preserving solution for deploying conformal prediction in real-world multi-institutional medical imaging settings.

Abstract: Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees on segmentation quality by calibrating a prediction-set threshold on held-out data. In federated deployments, the standard approach pools calibration scores across sites into a single threshold. We provide the first quantification, on real multi-institutional brain tumor data (FeTS-2022, 1,251 subjects, 20 institutions), showing that this naive pooled CRC protects the average hospital but violates coverage at 40% of individual institutions, with the worst site exceeding the target false-negative rate by 7.8 percentage points. The naive alternative, per-site local CRC, largely restores coverage but inflates prediction sets by 83x, rendering them clinically useless. We propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol: each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. A single hyperparameter n0 smoothly trades worst-case coverage for prediction-set efficiency; leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis identifies n0=19, achieving 2.7/20 violations at 2.0x stretch. We further show that direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets fails, concentrating risk on vulnerable hospitals, and that the finite-sample correction term is essential: removing it triples violations. The marginal CRC guarantee is preserved by construction under the stated site-mixture assumption; per-site coverage is validated across four targets with three seeds. No patient-level images, masks, or per-volume scores leave any site.

</details>


### [299] [Multi-Modal Contrastive Learning for Implicit Earth Embeddings via Location Tying](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20167)
*Jonathan Hecht,Lukas Arzoumanidis,Ziyue Li,Youness Dehbi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes two multimodal contrastive learning architectures (MELT and SALT) for self-supervised location encoder pre-training using unpaired geospatial data. Both match the strongest two-modality baseline but reveal that the location encoder, not modality diversity, is the primary performance bottleneck.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatial prediction tasks suffer from scarce high-quality labelled data. Self-supervised contrastive learning offers a solution, but existing methods align location with only one additional modality. The authors aim to scale beyond two modalities using readily available unpaired geospatial data to improve location representations.

Method: Two architectures are proposed: MELT (Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying) ties all modality embeddings through a shared location encoder simultaneously; SALT (Sequential Alternating Location Training) alternates training between different modality pairs in sequence. Both leverage unpaired geospatial data and contrastive objectives. Evaluation is on four downstream tasks against SATCLIP and other baselines.

Result: Both MELT and SALT match SATCLIP's performance across all four downstream tasks. However, increasing modalities does not yield consistent improvement. The contrastive objective saturates early regardless of modality count or pre-training data volume, indicating the location encoder architecture is the limiting factor.

Conclusion: MELT provides more stable training than SALT and is a stronger foundation for future scaling. The key insight is that modality diversity alone cannot overcome limitations of the location encoder; future work should focus on improving the encoder architecture rather than simply adding more modalities.

Abstract: Spatial prediction tasks are often limited by a lack of high-quality labelled ground-truth observations. To overcome this challenge, self-supervised pre-training is a possible solution, with contrastive learning dominant for location encoders. Those approaches usually align geographic coordinates with just one additional modality. We propose two multimodal contrastive learning architectures: Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying (MELT) and Sequential Alternating Location Training (SALT). These architectures expand this framework beyond two modalities by utilising unpaired geospatial data. Both methods are technically viable and match the performance of the strongest two-modality baseline (SATCLIP) across four downstream tasks. However, increasing the number of modalities does not consistently improve performance, suggesting that the chosen location encoder is the main limitation - the contrastive objective reaches its peak early, regardless of modality diversity or pre-training volume. MELT provides more stable training than SALT and presents a stronger foundation for future scaling.

</details>


### [300] [Predicting gestational age at birth in the context of preterm birth from multi-modal fetal MRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20172)
*Diego Fajardo-Rojas,Megan Hall,Daniel Cromb,Mary A. Rutherford,Lisa Story,Emma C. Robinson,Jana Hutter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A machine learning pipeline using multi-modal fetal MRI data (morphological and functional) from 426 cases predicts gestational age at birth, achieving 0.77 accuracy for preterm/term classification. Cervical length and placental T2* statistics emerged as key predictive features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preterm birth carries high mortality and lifelong morbidity risks, yet its complex multifactorial etiology makes accurate prediction difficult. Current literature only addresses preterm birth as a classification problem; regression-based prediction of gestational age at birth remains unexplored.

Method: A bespoke ML pipeline combining data imputation, feature selection, and regression models was developed to predict gestational age at birth from multi-modal fetal MRI (morphological and functional) data. The pipeline was evaluated on 333 control and 93 preterm cases using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. An ablation study validated the pipeline design. Predictions were subsequently binarized into term/preterm categories for classification metrics.

Result: The pipeline achieved R² = 0.13, MAE = 2.74 weeks for regression; accuracy = 0.77, sensitivity = 0.59, specificity = 0.82 for term/preterm classification. Cervical length and placental T2* statistical features were the predominant selected predictors.

Conclusion: The confluence of fast, motion-robust multi-modal fetal MRI and ML prediction enables gestational age at birth prediction, providing a proof of concept. Future work will expand cohort size for finer preterm stratification.

Abstract: Preterm birth is associated with significant mortality and a risk for lifelong morbidity. The complex multifactorial aetiology hampers accurate prediction and thus optimal care. A pipeline consisting of bespoke machine learning methods for data imputation, feature selection, and regression models to predict gestational age (GA) at birth was developed and evaluated from comprehensive multi-modal morphological and functional fetal MRI data from 333 control cases and 93 preterm birth cases. The GA at birth predictions were classified into term and preterm categories and their accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were reported. An ablation study was performed to further validate the design of the pipeline. Performance was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The pipeline achieves an R2 score of 0.13 and a mean absolute error of 2.74 weeks. It also achieves a 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity across folds. The predominant features selected by the pipeline include cervical length and statistics derived from placental T2* values. The confluence of fast, motion-robust and multi-modal fetal MRI techniques and machine learning prediction allowed the prediction of the gestation at birth. This information is essential for any pregnancy. To the best of our knowledge, preterm birth had only been addressed as a classification problem in the literature. Therefore, this work provides a proof of concept. Future work will increase the cohort size to allow for finer stratification within the preterm birth cohort. Our code is available at https://github.com/dfajardorojas/ml-for-preterm-birth-.

</details>


### [301] [Computational Methods and Challenges in Cell-Free DNA Analysis for Multi-Cancer Early Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20174)
*Nicko Starkey,Marcin W. Wojewodzic,Krzysztof Rzecki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A review of computational methods (2022–2025) for cfDNA-based multicancer early detection, focusing on fragmentomics and epigenetic feature extraction. The paper evaluates classical ML, deep learning, and autoencoder-based approaches on biological interpretability, validation, and clinical readiness, identifying multimodal ensemble methods as most promising and calling for standardized evaluation protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) enables non-invasive, simultaneous screening for multiple cancers from a single blood draw, particularly benefiting cancers without established screening programs. However, extracting robust early-stage cancer signals from cfDNA data requires sophisticated computational methods, and the field lacks a systematic comparison of approaches developed in the recent 2022–2025 period, as well as standardized evaluation frameworks.

Method: This is a review paper. The authors survey computational methods for cfDNA-based MCED published between 2022 and 2025. They first outline the biological basis of cfDNA signals, then categorize methods into classical statistical/ML approaches and deep learning frameworks (including autoencoder-based models). Each method is assessed along three axes: biological interpretability, validation strategy, and clinical integration readiness. The paper also taxonomizes current challenges into technical, computational, and methodological categories, identifying open problems.

Result: The review finds that multimodal ensemble approaches combining multiple feature types (fragmentomics, epigenetic markers, etc.) demonstrate the highest clinical readiness and strongest integration potential. Across methods, significant heterogeneity exists in validation strategies and reporting standards, hindering fair comparison. Key open challenges span technical issues (low tumor fraction in early stages, sequencing noise), computational issues (scalability, model generalization across populations), and methodological issues (lack of standardized benchmarks and evaluation protocols).

Conclusion: Multimodal ensemble methods represent the most clinically mature direction for cfDNA-based MCED. However, the field urgently needs standardized evaluation protocols and consistent reporting practices to enable rigorous side-by-side comparison of future methods and accelerate clinical translation.

Abstract: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a promising avenue for non-invasive multicancer early detection (MCED), in that, it can enable multiple cancer detection simultaneously from a single blood draw, with particular sensitivity to cancers that currently lack established screening programs. Here we review the computational methods developed between 2022 and 2025 for cfDNA-based MCED. We focus on how fragmentomics and epigenetic features are extracted and analyzed to detect cancer at early stages. We first briefly outline the biological basis of cfDNA signals, then review classical statistical and machine learning approaches alongside deep learning frameworks including autoencoder-based models. For each method we discuss biological interpretability, validation strategy, and readiness for clinical integration. Furthermore, we categorize the current challenges into technical, computational, and methodological while outlining open problems in the field. This review shows that multimodal ensemble approaches have the strongest promise for clinical integration and the highest readiness. However, for better assessment of future work and side-by-side comparison, standardization of evaluation protocols and reporting results will be crucial.

</details>


### [302] [Effective Dimension Governs Generalization in Quantum Kernel Vision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20183)
*Jian Xu,Delu Zeng,John Paisley,Qibin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two unexplained phenomena in quantum vision models—entanglement improving generalization and noise boosting accuracy—are unified by the effective dimension of the quantum feature kernel. Entanglement structure and quantum noise both modulate effective dimension; contracting it in overfitting regimes acts as ridge-like regularization, improving test accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum vision models (quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks) exhibit two unexplained empirical phenomena: more/uniformly distributed entanglement improves generalization, and quantum noise injection improves test accuracy. These are treated as curiosities discovered by grid search without a principled theoretical account. The work aims to unify both under a single measurable principle.

Method: The authors analyze quantum-kernel vision models using spectral theory. Key techniques include: (1) an exact decomposition of the depolarized kernel K_p = (1-p)²K + p(2-p)/D · 11ᵀ with effective dimension d_eff(K_p)→1; (2) a contraction result for amplitude damping; (3) a kernel-machine capacity bound and capacity/alignment risk decomposition; (4) empirical verification of monotone contraction under entangled setups and exact kernel decomposition validated to machine precision up to 12 qubits; (5) noise injection characterized as an explicit spectral-filtering frontier.

Result: Entanglement structure and quantum noise both modulate the effective dimension d_eff of the quantum feature kernel. In overfitting regimes, contracting d_eff acts as ridge-like regularization. Amplitude damping contracts d_eff and lifts test accuracy by up to +13% along an inverted-U sweet spot; the effect sign flips between over- and under-fitting regimes. Noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier. The depolarizing family confirms the kernel decomposition to machine precision.

Conclusion: The two reported anecdotes—entanglement aiding generalization and noise improving accuracy—are manifestations of a single measurable quantity: the effective dimension of the noise-shaped quantum feature kernel. This organizes them into a principled framework for designing quantum vision models, where tuning entanglement and noise provides a controllable regularization mechanism.

Abstract: Recent quantum vision models-quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks-report two striking but unexplained empirical phenomena: (i) ansatze with more, or more uniformly distributed, entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve test accuracy rather than degrade it. These observations are currently treated as curiosities, discovered by grid search and explained, if at all, by hand. We show that both are manifestations of a single, measurable quantity: the \emph{effective dimension} $d_{\rm eff}$ of the (noise-shaped) quantum feature kernel. Working primarily with quantum-kernel vision models-a quantum feature map read out by a kernel classifier-we give a spectral account in which entanglement structure and quantum noise are two knobs that move $d_{\rm eff}$; in an overfitting regime, contracting $d_{\rm eff}$ acts as ridge-like regularization. We analyze the mechanism: an \emph{exact} decomposition of the depolarized kernel $K_p=(1-p)^2K+\tfrac{p(2-p)}{D}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ with $d_{\rm eff}(K_p)\to1$, a contraction result (and its boundary) for amplitude damping, a kernel-machine capacity bound, and a capacity/alignment risk decomposition; the monotone contraction operative in our entangled experiments is verified empirically, not proven in general. Along the one-parameter depolarizing family the collapse is instead exact by construction; we use it only to confirm the kernel decomposition to machine precision and at up to $12$ qubits, not as evidence for $d_{\rm eff}$. Amplitude damping contracts $d_{\rm eff}$ and lifts test accuracy by up to $+13\%$ along an inverted-U sweet spot; the effect's sign flips between the over- and under-fitting regimes; noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier. Our results organize two reported anecdotes into a single measurable principle for designing quantum-vision models.

</details>


### [303] [Learner-based Concept Drift Detection: Analysis and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20216)
*Md Moman Ul Haque Khan,Samira Sadaoui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a theoretical examination of concept drift characteristics and a comprehensive evaluation of drift detection algorithms across multiple categories, tested on both synthetic and real-world streaming datasets with abrupt and gradual drift patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning models in streaming environments suffer from concept drift—non-stationary data distributions that degrade predictive performance. Timely and efficient drift detection is critical for maintaining accuracy in real-world decision-making applications, yet the landscape of drift characteristics and detection algorithms lacks consolidated understanding.

Method: The authors conduct a theoretical analysis of concept drift characteristics and categorize existing drift detection algorithms. They then perform a comparative empirical evaluation of these detectors on both synthetic and real-world datasets that encompass diverse streaming scenarios, including abrupt and gradual drift types.

Result: The study presents findings on how different drift detectors behave under varying drift characteristics and streaming contexts, offering insights into their relative strengths, weaknesses, and applicability across different scenarios.

Conclusion: The work enhances understanding of concept drift characteristics and detector behavior, providing guidance on the applicability of different drift detection approaches to diverse real-world streaming contexts, thereby supporting more robust decision-making in non-stationary environments.

Abstract: Machine learning algorithms deployed for evolving streaming environments must handle the non-stationary data distributions, commonly referred to as concept drift. The presence of concept drift poses a major challenge for many real-world applications because it can severely degrade their predictive performance, hindering their ability to support robust decision-making. Consequently, the timely and efficient detection of drift events is critical for sustaining high accuracy over time. This study examines theoretically the concept drift characteristics and numerous drift detection algorithms across several categories. Furthermore, we evaluate their performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets exhibiting diverse streaming scenarios and drift characteristics, such as abrupt and gradual changes. This study aims to enhance understanding of the complex notion of concept drift characteristics and behavior of drift detectors, along with their applicability to diverse contexts.

</details>


### [304] [Boundary Embedding Shaping with Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Graph Structural Disentanglement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20283)
*Jiaqing Chen,Zidu Yin,Yichao Cai,Yuhang Liu,Zhen Zhang,Dong Gong,Javen Qinfeng Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BES is a plug-in contrastive learning module for GNNs that identifies and mitigates spurious structural noise specifically at class decision boundaries, improving node classification by an average of 3.3% over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNN performance suffers from graph structural entanglement — semantically irrelevant neighbors introduce spurious correlations into node embeddings. This problem is most severe for boundary-region nodes near class decision boundaries, where structural noise blurs separation and destabilizes predictions. Existing robust GNN methods treat all nodes uniformly, failing to address these boundary-specific vulnerabilities.

Method: The authors propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning plug-in module for GNNs. BES identifies nodes in boundary regions of the embedding space and selectively suppresses spurious structural noise through tailored contrastive objectives. The module operates with minimal parameter perturbation, making it lightweight and compatible with existing GNN architectures.

Result: Extensive experiments show BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms leading methods. BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction tasks.

Conclusion: Boundary-region structural entanglement is the primary bottleneck limiting GNN classification performance. BES effectively addresses this via adaptive boundary-aware contrastive learning, demonstrating that targeted debiasing at decision boundaries yields significant and consistent gains across tasks.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at aggregating neighbor information for classification, yet their performance is hindered by graph structural entanglement, where spurious correlations from semantically irrelevant neighbors contaminate node embeddings. This challenge is most acute for nodes near class boundaries in the embedding space, where amplified structural noise blurs decision boundaries and destabilizes predictions. Existing robust GNN methods largely treat all nodes uniformly, ignoring boundary vulnerabilities. In this paper, to improve classification performance, we tackle graph structural disentanglement by identifying boundary-region entanglement as the primary bottleneck and propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning GNN plug-in module that selectively suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries with minimal model parameter perturbation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms existing leading methods. Notably, BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction.

</details>


### [305] [Integrating national forest inventory, airborne lidar, and satellite imagery for wall-to-wall mapping of forest structure with computer vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20291)
*Luke J. Zachmann,David D. Diaz,Vincent A. Landau,Chelsey Walden-Schreiner,Tony Chang,Nathan E. Rutenbeck,Katharyn A. Duffy,Kiarie Ndegwa,Andreas Gros,Scott Conway,Guy Bayes*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VibrantForests is a satellite-based framework that generates annual, 10m-resolution maps of five forest structure attributes across the contiguous US, overcoming common saturation and regression-to-mean biases in passive-sensor models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-area forest and wildfire risk management requires wall-to-wall, annually updated maps, but current planning systems combine disparate data sources with varying vintages, purposes, and prediction quality, causing confounding behavior in operational planning.

Method: The VibrantForests framework uses a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived samples. It concurrently estimates five forest attributes — canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter — at 10-meter resolution across the contiguous United States.

Result: The model demonstrates predictive capability across the full spectrum of forest conditions (sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass). It extends the saturation range typical of comparable passive-sensor models and reduces regression-to-mean behavior, mitigating overestimation in sparse conditions and underestimation in dense conditions.

Conclusion: VibrantForests addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent, wall-to-wall estimates of management-relevant attributes at an annual cadence and 10m resolution.

Abstract: Remote sensing is increasingly relied upon to deliver actionable science for forest and wildfire risk management across large landscapes. Wall-to-wall, annually updated maps are a persistent need for effective forest management. Many planning systems and data collections combine disparate data sources with different purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, which leads to confounding behavior in operational planning systems. We introduce the VibrantForests framework, developed and applied to map forest attributes and provide a coherent foundation for effective forest and wildfire planning. VibrantForests includes a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived samples and applied across the contiguous United States to concurrently generate estimates of canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter at 10-meter resolution. We demonstrate predictive capability spanning the full spectrum of forest conditions ranging from sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass. Results show that our model extends the range at which saturation is commonly encountered in comparable passive-sensor models, and reduces regression-to-mean behavior that commonly produces overestimation of forest attributes in small/sparse conditions and underestimation in large/dense conditions. The VibrantForests framework addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent wall-to-wall estimates of management-relevant attributes at annual cadence and 10m resolution.

</details>


### [306] [Shifting-based Optimizable Linear Relaxations for General Activation Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20292)
*Philipp Kern,László Antal,Erika Ábráham,Carsten Sinz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SLiR is a general method for generating tight linear relaxations of activation functions for NN verification, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or critical points. It parameterizes relaxations by slope and computes offsets via a shifting procedure, outperforming hand-crafted relaxations by enabling verification of up to 7.8× more properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NN verification methods rely on hand-crafted linear relaxations tailored to each specific activation function. Extending these to new or state-of-the-art activation functions requires substantial manual effort, limiting scalability and broad applicability of verification tools.

Method: SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) generalizes the construction of linear relaxations by parameterizing them via slope and computing the corresponding offset through a shifting procedure. The method only needs a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points of the activation function. The shifting procedure guarantees sound upper and lower bounds across the entire input domain, enabling efficient optimization of the relaxation parameters while preserving correctness.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions. Compared to state-of-the-art hand-crafted methods, SLiR enables verification of up to 7.8× more properties.

Conclusion: SLiR eliminates the need for manual, per-activation-function relaxations in NN verification, offering a general and automated approach that matches or exceeds the tightness of specialized methods while significantly broadening the set of verifiable networks.

Abstract: The use of neural networks (NNs) is rapidly increasing, including in safety- and security-critical domains. To provide formal guarantees about NN behavior, many verification methods rely on optimizable linear relaxations of activation functions. However, existing techniques depend on hand-crafted relaxations for each activation function. Extension to state-of-the-art activation functions therefore requires substantial manual effort. In contrast, our approach SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) is broadly applicable, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points. SLiR parameterizes relaxations by their slope and computes the corresponding offset via a shifting procedure that ensures sound upper and lower bounds over the input domain, enabling efficient optimization while maintaining correctness. Our experiments show that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions and enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [307] [Recurrent neural networks approximate continuous functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20325)
*Valentin Abadie,Clemens Hutter,Helmut Bölcskei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proves that a single fixed-weight ReLU recurrent neural network (RNN) can uniformly approximate any continuous function on [-1,1] to arbitrary accuracy simply by running for longer time, eliminating the need to redesign the network when target accuracy changes. The key insight is an intermediate model called the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU), which bridges algorithmic flexibility and RNN simulatability. The authors also establish minimax lower bounds showing that runtime is a necessary resource in this fixed-network approximation regime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical neural network approximation theorems require constructing a new network whenever higher accuracy is desired. The authors challenge this paradigm by asking: can a single network with fixed architecture and weights be chosen once, with accuracy improved solely by increasing runtime? This question probes the fundamental trade-off between network complexity (size/depth) and temporal resources (runtime) in neural approximation.

Method: The authors introduce the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU), an intermediate computational model that retains sufficient algorithmic freedom to implement polynomial approximation schemes (e.g., Chebyshev or Bernstein approximations) while being rigid enough to be simulated by RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitude. They construct a fixed ReLU RNN whose time evolution simulates the TMNU executing polynomial approximation, thereby producing increasingly accurate approximations of the target continuous function as time progresses. Minimax lower bounds are derived to formalize the necessity of runtime.

Result: Every continuous function on [-1,1] can be uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU RNN with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension. The convergence rate of this approximation mirrors the underlying polynomial approximation rate. Furthermore, minimax lower bounds demonstrate that runtime is an unavoidable resource — one cannot achieve arbitrary accuracy in bounded time within this fixed-network paradigm.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a new approximation paradigm where a single, fixed-parameter RNN suffices for universal approximation, trading network redesign for increased runtime. The TMNU model provides a principled bridge between algorithmic construction and neural simulation. The lower bounds confirm that this runtime requirement is intrinsic, not merely an artifact of the construction, opening new perspectives on resource trade-offs in neural network expressiveness.

Abstract: Classical approximation theorems ask for a new neural network whenever the target accuracy is improved. This paper studies the opposite possibility: can the network be chosen once and for all, and can accuracy be bought only by letting it run longer? We prove that this is possible for every continuous function on [-1,1]. More precisely, each such function is uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension. The mechanism behind the construction is a new intermediate model, the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU). This model retains the algorithmic freedom needed to implement polynomial approximation schemes, while remaining rigid enough to be simulated by RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitude. The resulting convergence rates reflect the underlying polynomial approximation rates. We complement the construction with minimax lower bounds showing that runtime is not merely a proof artifact, but an unavoidable resource in this fixed-network approximation paradigm.

</details>


### [308] [Quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for PDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20326)
*Xiang Rao,Yuxuan Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QCPIKAN is a hybrid quantum-classical framework combining Chebyshev KAN layers with parameterized quantum circuits to solve PDEs. It embeds physical constraints via a physics-informed loss, achieves exponential convergence for high-frequency errors, and outperforms existing quantum-classical PINNs on porous media seepage problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks struggle with high-frequency error convergence and numerical dispersion when solving complex PDEs. The authors aim to leverage the approximation power of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and quantum circuits to overcome these limitations.

Method: QCPIKAN uses Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers for efficient function approximation and parameterized quantum circuits for expressive capacity. Physical laws are embedded into the training loss as constraints (physics-informed). The authors provide approximation-theoretic proofs of exponential high-frequency error convergence and numerical dispersion mitigation. Validation covers three porous-media seepage scenarios: single-phase flow, component transport, and two-phase flow.

Result: QCPIKAN surpasses existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks on global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking, and displacement front localization across all three seepage test cases.

Conclusion: QCPIKAN offers a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs, with strong theoretical guarantees and demonstrated practical advantages over existing hybrid quantum-classical approaches.

Abstract: We develop QCPIKAN, the first quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network designed to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). Built upon Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers and parameterized quantum circuits, this hybrid framework embeds physical constraints into the training loss to enforce physical consistency. Our theoretical investigations grounded in approximation theory prove that this design accelerates high-frequency error convergence to an exponential rate and effectively mitigates numerical dispersion. We validate the framework across three typical seepage scenarios in porous media, including single-phase flow, component transport and two-phase flow. Compared with existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks, QCPIKAN achieves superior performance in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking and displacement front localization. This work provides a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs.

</details>


### [309] [Constrained hybrid modelling to predict microbial dynamics and organic matter turnover in soil systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20329)
*Paul Collart,Juergen Gall,Andrea Schnepf,Holger Pagel,Lars Doorenbos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid modeling framework that uses neural networks to predict biokinetic parameters of a soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-derived genomic traits, constrained by ecological theory to ensure realistic dynamics of unobserved states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Process-based soil models are critical for predicting carbon cycling, but parameterizing microbial dynamics from data is highly challenging. Integrating genomic data offers promise, yet the relationship between genomes and biogeochemical processes remains unknown and unsolved.

Method: A hybrid framework combining a process-based soil organic matter turnover model with a neural network that predicts biokinetic parameters from metagenome-inferred functional traits (DNA sequencing data). Ecological theory and literature-based constraints are integrated to ensure realistic behavior of non-observed state variables. Evaluated on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data against multiple baselines.

Result: The hybrid approach outperforms multiple baselines, learns dynamics of unmeasurable process-based model components effectively, and performs well even with small training datasets.

Conclusion: Integrating genomic trait data via neural networks into process-based soil models is a viable and effective strategy for improving soil carbon cycling predictions, bridging the gap between metagenomics and mechanistic modeling.

Abstract: Soil microorganisms control organic matter cycling and largely determine how soil systems can cope with and mitigate climate change and environmental threats. Representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is therefore critical to predict carbon cycling in soils, albeit highly challenging to inform from data. One promising approach to improve their parametrisation is the integration of genomic data, yet modelling the complex and unknown relationship between genomes and the processes the microbes are driving is an unsolved problem. In this work, we present the first hybrid modeling framework for deriving biokinetic parameter values of a process-based soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-inferred functional traits based on DNA sequencing data. Our model predicts biokinetic parameters of the process-based model from genomic trait data with a neural network and integrates constraints from ecological theory and literature to ensure realistic behavior, even of non-observed state variables. We evaluate our method on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data, showing that our approach improves performance over multiple baselines and learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model effectively, even for small training datasets.

</details>


### [310] [Critical Percolation as a Synthetic Data Model for Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20347)
*Aryeh Brill,Tom Ingebretsen Carlson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a synthetic dataset family based on hierarchical functions over critical mean-field percolation clusters, offering sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability as a principled testbed for interpretability research. Neural network activations are shown to linearly decode the ground-truth latent variables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing synthetic datasets for evaluating interpretability methods lack the hierarchical, multi-scale structure characteristic of natural data, limiting their realism and usefulness as toy models.

Method: Construct hierarchical functions on critical mean-field percolation clusters in high-dimensional space, with latent taxonomic hierarchy variables generating target values. Leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to design a near-linear-time sampling algorithm for joint generation of random trees and hierarchical latent decompositions at arbitrary scale.

Result: Probing experiments reveal that ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations trained on this data.

Conclusion: Critical percolation clusters provide a mathematically principled, analytically tractable synthetic data model whose sparsity, self-similarity, and power-law properties make it well-suited as a testbed for interpretability research.

Abstract: Neural networks learn features that reflect the hierarchical, multi-scale structure of natural data. Synthetic datasets used to evaluate interpretability methods typically lack this structure, limiting their value as realistic toy models. To close this gap, we introduce a family of synthetic datasets consisting of hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in a high-dimensional data space. The percolation data consists of sparse, low-dimensional fractal clusters with a power-law size distribution. Latent variables modeling a taxonomic hierarchy generate each data point's target value. The data model is analytically tractable with known critical exponents that fix its properties without requiring hyperparameter tuning. We leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to propose an almost linear-time algorithm to jointly sample a random tree and its hierarchical latent decomposition, enabling data generation at arbitrary scale. Using probing experiments, we find that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations. Together, sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability make critical percolation a principled testbed for interpretability research.

</details>


### [311] [On the Variance of Temporal Difference Learning and its Reduction Using Control Variates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20357)
*Hsiao-Ru Pan,Bernhard Schölkopf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analyzes the variance of TD learning in the phased, tabular setting, showing TD reduces variance by aggregating independent trajectories. TD variance is asymptotically bounded above by MC, and shorter horizons yield lower variance. DAE is shown to be a regression-adjusted control variate with tighter variance bounds than TD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To theoretically understand the mechanisms by which temporal difference learning reduces variance compared to Monte Carlo methods, and to provide formal variance bounds that explain the empirical success of TD and related methods like Direct Advantage Estimation.

Method: The authors analyze TD learning variance using a phased setting with tabular representation. They derive asymptotic upper bounds on TD variance relative to MC estimators, examine the effect of horizon length on variance, and frame Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) as a regression-adjusted control variate to obtain tighter variance bounds in the large-sample limit. Numerical experiments in carefully designed environments validate the theoretical findings.

Result: TD variance is asymptotically bounded above by MC variance. Shorter horizon updates incur less variance for a fixed sample size. DAE, interpreted as a regression-adjusted control variate, achieves a strictly tighter variance bound than TD in the large-sample limit.

Conclusion: The variance reduction in TD stems from effectively aggregating over more independent trajectories. DAE can be understood through the lens of control variates and offers superior variance properties compared to standard TD. These insights provide a principled understanding of bias-variance trade-offs in policy evaluation.

Abstract: We analyze the variance of temporal difference (TD) learning using the phased setting with tabular representation, and show that one of the mechanisms behind its ability to reduce variance is by effectively aggregating over a larger number of independent trajectories. Based on this insight, we demonstrate that (1) the variance of TD is asymptotically bounded from above by Monte Carlo (MC) estimators, and (2) shorter horizon updates incurs less variance for a fixed number of samples. Beyond TD, we show that Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE), a method for estimating the advantage function, can be seen as a type of regression-adjusted control variate, which achieves a tighter bound on the variance compared to TD in the large-sample limit. Finally, we numerically illustrate the behaviors of these estimators with carefully designed environments.

</details>


### [312] [Train, Retrieve, or Both? A Four-Arm Head-to-Head for Correct Statutory Citation on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20359)
*Ali Asaria,Tony Salomone,Deep Gandhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fine-tuning a small LLM with retrieval (SFT+RAG hybrid) achieves zero-hallucination statutory citation on Ontario's RTA, scoring 0.481 exact-match. Retrieval is essential—pure SFT mis-recalls sections—but the cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats pipelines using larger specialized retrieval models, with no benefit from more training data. Results are preliminary on a small eval set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need accurate statutory citations to the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act (2006). The paper empirically investigates whether fine-tuning alone suffices for this task or whether hybrid retrieval-augmented generation is necessary to produce correct, hallucination-free legal citations.

Method: A four-arm head-to-head experiment using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: (1) base zero-shot, (2) LoRA supervised fine-tuning only (SFT-only), (3) retrieval-augmented generation only (RAG-only), and (4) SFT+RAG hybrid. Evaluation uses citation exact-match (section+subsection) on a small, human-verification-pending real eval set. The hybrid uses bge-small embeddings and is compared against pipelines with larger specialized embedders and cross-encoder rerankers.

Result: Base model cannot cite the RTA at all. SFT-only mis-recalls sections (hallucinates). RAG alone drives hallucination to zero by construction. The SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. SFT improves provision selection robustness under higher-recall candidate sets that degrade zero-shot RAG. The cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats larger specialized retrieval models. A larger/improved training set provides no additional benefit. Results fall short of the aspirational 0.70 target.

Conclusion: Strong statutory-citation performance does not require specialized retrieval models or more training data; a simple SFT+RAG hybrid with a small embedder suffices to eliminate hallucination entirely. However, exact-match accuracy remains moderate (0.481), leaving substantial room for improvement toward the 0.70 aspirational target. All findings are preliminary given the small eval set.

Abstract: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need to be pointed at the provision of law that actually governs a question, with a correct statutory citation. We study this task on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) and its core regulation, asking the operator's question empirically: is fine-tuning enough, or is hybrid retrieval needed? We run a four-arm head-to-head on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (base zero-shot, LoRA SFT-only, RAG-only, and an SFT+RAG hybrid), scored on citation exact-match (section+subsection) over a small, human-verification-pending real eval set. The base model cannot cite the RTA and SFT-only mis-recalls sections; retrieval is essential and drives hallucination to zero by construction; and the SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. Its edge comes from SFT making provision selection more robust to the higher-recall candidate sets that hurt zero-shot RAG. Notably, this cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats a pipeline built on bigger, specialized retrieval models (a larger embedder and a cross-encoder reranker), and a larger/improved training set does not help either: strong statutory-citation performance here does not require specialized retrieval models or more data. The artifact zeroes hallucination and clears the lift-over-base bar but does not reach the aspirational 0.70 exact-match target. All results are on a small, human-verification-pending real eval set and are reported as preliminary.

</details>


### [313] [Judging to Improve: A De-biased VLM-as-3D-Judge Protocol for Single-Image 3D Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20364)
*Ali Asaria,Tony Salomone,Deep Gandhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether a VLM-as-3D-judge can be used to specialize a strong open 3D generator (TRELLIS) for furniture assets via cheap, label-free optimization. The core contribution is hardening the judge for optimization-grade use, revealing that lightweight parameter-efficient fine-tuning on public data can match but not exceed the base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work established VLMs as reliable rankers for 3D mesh quality, but ranking alone is insufficient for optimization. The authors aim to close the loop: can a VLM judge's preferences drive generator specialization without human labels, and what breaks when a ranking judge is repurposed for training?

Method: They harden a VLM judge for optimization by: (1) separating training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) from evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to prevent circularity; (2) correcting position bias; (3) fixing three failure modes — image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs. They test six PEFT methods, two input regimes, and a severity sweep, with quality-contrastive construction to engineer learnable signal, and calibrate with clear-gap and base-vs-base win-rate baselines.

Result: Independent base samples show a 0.94 order-flip rate (nearly no learnable preference). The best method — conditioner repair under severe degradation — reaches parity (0.50 win-rate) with the base model. No method achieves the ≥65% win-rate target. The judge calibration shows clear-gap win-rates of 0.83–1.0 and base-vs-base near 0.5, confirming reliability. Clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DiT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is the locus that moves geometry.

Conclusion: Matching a strong public-data base with cheap, label-free adaptation is itself informative: exceeding it requires more than lightweight PEFT on public data. The hardened judge protocol is reusable for future 3D optimization work.

Abstract: A companion study established a de-biased, cross-model VLM-as-3D-judge that reliably ranks single-image-to-3D mesh quality where cheap geometry and CLIP proxies fall short.
