This paper asks: can that judge's preferences specialize a strong open generator, TRELLIS, on one asset class (furniture), cheaply and without human labels? Taking the judge from ranking to optimization is where the work lives. Pushing a VLM judge into the training and evaluation loop exposes failure modes ranking never triggered, so our contribution is an optimization-grade hardening of the judge: a training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) held distinct from an evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to break circularity; position-bias correction; and fixes for three failure modes (image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs), with calibration evidence (clear-gap win-rate 0.83-1.0; base-vs-base ~0.5). Using this protocol as an independent evaluator, and working only from public models and data with lightweight parameter-efficient adaptation, we find our methods match the strong base rather than exceed it. Independent base samples carry essentially no learnable preference (0.94 order-flip rate), so signal must be engineered by quality-contrastive construction. Across six adaptation methods, two input regimes, and a severity sweep, the most targeted - conditioner repair under severe degradation - reaches parity (0.50) with the base, while no method clears the >=65% win-rate target. The result is mechanistic: clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DIT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is the locus that moves geometry. Win-rates are directional at n=8 objects. Matching a strong public-data base with cheap adaptation is itself informative: exceeding it needs more than lightweight PEFT on public data, and the judge protocol is reusable.

</details>


### [314] [CRAX: Fast Safe Reinforcement Learning Benchmarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20376)
*Tristan Tomilin,Mourad Boustani,Mickey Beurskens,Thiago D. Simão*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRAX is a hardware-accelerated safety benchmark for constrained RL built on JAX/MJX, offering ~100x speedups over CPU-based alternatives. It features six environments across three difficulty levels and reveals that no single safe RL method dominates, while curriculum learning and safety transfer improve performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safe RL benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics are computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping in safety-critical domains like robotics and autonomous driving.

Method: CRAX is built on the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine, leveraging JAX-based vectorized operations and hardware acceleration (GPUs/TPUs) to achieve massive speedups. It provides six environment suites with three agent-specific tasks, each at three difficulty levels. Six popular safe RL methods (including Lagrangian-based, CPO, PPO-Lagrangian, etc.) are evaluated across these environments.

Result: CRAX achieves up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. Benchmarking reveals that no single safe RL algorithm dominates across all tasks. Curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer from easier to harder settings improve performance compared to direct training on harder tasks.

Conclusion: CRAX enables rapid, large-scale experimentation in safe RL by dramatically reducing computational bottlenecks. The benchmark highlights performance-safety trade-offs and demonstrates that curriculum learning and transfer are effective strategies for improving safe RL outcomes.

Abstract: Safety is a core concern for deploying reinforcement learning (RL) agents in real-world domains such as robotics and autonomous driving. While benchmarks have been central to progress in RL, existing safety benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics remain computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. To address this gap, we propose CRAX (Constrained RL Accelerated with JAX). Built on top of the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine with realistic 3D dynamics, CRAX leverages vectorized operations and hardware acceleration, yielding up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. The benchmark features six environment suites and three agent-specific tasks, each spanning three difficulty levels. Evaluating six popular safe RL methods shows that no single approach dominates across all tasks, and reveals the trade-offs between performance and safety. We find that curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer can improve performance over direct training in harder settings.

</details>


### [315] [Towards Modality-imbalanced Federated Graph Learning: A Data Synthesis-based Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20382)
*Zhengyu Wu,Hongchao Qin,Xunkai Li,Zekai Chen,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedMGS tackles modality-imbalanced MultiModal Federated Graph Learning by synthesizing missing modal semantics in latent representation space, using an availability-aware graph encoder, prototype-guided synthesis, and reliability-calibrated fusion, achieving up to 17.41% improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practical deployment of MM-FGL faces two granularities of modality imbalance: client-level (entire modalities missing) and node-level (individual nodes missing visual/textual attributes). Existing solutions are graph-agnostic or centralized, failing to adapt to federated graph settings directly.

Method: FedMGS formalizes the problem as implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis with three components: (1) an availability-aware graph encoder that prevents missing modalities from corrupting local structural propagation; (2) a prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer that establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities; (3) a reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism that regulates the influence of recovered latent representations before predictive readout.

Result: Extensive experiments across four tasks demonstrate that FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines with gains up to 17.41%, while maintaining the best efficiency-performance tradeoff.

Conclusion: FedMGS effectively addresses both client-level and node-level modality imbalance in MM-FGL through latent semantic synthesis, validated by significant performance gains and strong efficiency.

Abstract: MultiModal Federated Graph Learning (MM-FGL) offers a natural collaborative training paradigm, but its practical deployment is challenged by two granularities of modality imbalance. Client-level imbalance occurs when certain clients lack entire modalities, while node-level imbalance occurs when individual nodes exhibit missing visual or textual attributes. While several relevant studies exist, our investigation reveals that they predominantly target graph-agnostic or centralized scenarios, rendering them difficult to adapt directly. To address these challenges, we formalize modality-imbalanced MM-FGL as an implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis problem. This paradigm recovers missing modal semantics directly within the representation space, thereby maximizing alignment with the original data's semantic distribution and mitigating the high variance induced by missing modalities. To this end, we propose FedMGS (Federated Modality-aware Graph Synthesis), which integrates three core components. The availability-aware graph encoder prevents missing modalities from contaminating local structural propagation. The prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities. The reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism regulates the impact of recovered latent representations prior to predictive readout. Extensive experiments on four tasks show that FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines with gains up to 17.41% with best efficiency-performance tradeoff.

</details>


### [316] [The Significance of Style Diversity in Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20400)
*Zahra Abbasiantaeb,Zeno Belligoli,Omar Essam,Mohammad Aliannejadi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A fully unsupervised framework for synthetic dialogue generation for intent classification that uses only intent definitions, employs topic/style attributes for diversity, introduces two post-hoc stylization models (Univ and Exam), and demonstrates that style diversity matters more than topic diversity for synthetic data utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human-annotated seed data for intent classification is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings, creating a need for synthetic data generation methods that can operate without any human-labeled data, relying solely on intent definitions.

Method: The framework uses intent definitions to generate synthetic dialogues without human annotation. It leverages two types of topic and style attributes to improve diversity. Two novel post-hoc stylization models, Univ and Exam, transform LLM-generated utterances into varied human-like styles. An LLM-as-a-judge filtering step enhances data quality. Style attributes can be incorporated during generation or via post-hoc adaptation.

Result: The approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained with human-annotated training data on both industrial and public datasets. Style diversity proved more critical than topic diversity. Incorporating style attributes during generation outperforms post-hoc style adaptation.

Conclusion: Style diversity is the dominant factor for synthetic data utility in intent classification, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Integrating style attributes directly into the generation process is preferable to applying stylization afterward.

Abstract: Generating high-utility synthetic data for intent classification typically requires human-annotated seed data, which is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings. In this paper, we propose a framework for synthetic dialogue generation that works entirely without human-annotated data, relying solely on intent definitions. Our proposed dialogue generation framework utilizes two different types of topic and style attributes to improve data diversity. Also, we propose two novel post-hoc stylization models called Univ and Exam to transform synthetic LLM-generated utterances into more varied, human-like linguistic styles. To enhance data quality, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge filtering process. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained using human-annotated training data. Crucially, the findings reveal that style diversity is more critical than topic diversity for synthetic data utility, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Furthermore, the study shows that incorporating style attributes during the generation process is more effective than post-hoc style adaptation.

</details>


### [317] [Direct Advantage Estimation for Scalable and Sample-efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20411)
*Hsiao-Ru Pan,Bernhard Schölkopf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DAE is extended to partially observable environments and made computationally efficient via discrete latent dynamics models, demonstrating scalability and sample efficiency on the Arcade Learning Environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DAE improves sample efficiency in deep RL but suffers from two key limitations: (1) it requires full environment observability, making it impractical for realistic partially observable settings; (2) modeling transition probabilities incurs prohibitive computational cost for high-dimensional observations. The authors aim to overcome both limitations.

Method: The authors (1) extend the DAE theoretical framework to partially observable domains with minimal modifications, and (2) introduce discrete latent dynamics models to efficiently approximate transition probabilities, thereby reducing computational complexity.

Result: Evaluated on the Arcade Learning Environment, the proposed approach shows that DAE scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.

Conclusion: DAE can be successfully adapted to partially observable settings with reduced computational overhead, preserving its sample efficiency advantages and scaling well with larger function approximators.

Abstract: Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) has been shown to improve the sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning algorithms. However, its reliance on full environment observability limits its applicability in realistic settings, and its requirement to model transition probabilities incurs substantial computational overhead for high-dimensional observations. In the present work, we address both limitations. First, we extend the theoretical framework of DAE to partially observable domains with minimal modifications. Second, we reduce its computational complexity by introducing discrete latent dynamics models that efficiently approximate transition probabilities. We evaluate our approach on the Arcade Learning Environment and find that DAE scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.

</details>


### [318] [Pseudo-Feature Padding: A Lightweight Defense Against False Data Injection in Power Grids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20415)
*Farhin Farhad Riya,Shahinul Hoque,Yingyuan Yang,Jinyuan Sun,Kevin Tomsovic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A defense framework for DNNs in CPS against FDIA evasion attacks, using randomized, data-aware input padding with pseudo-features derived from statistical distributions to increase dimensionality, making adversarial perturbations computationally infeasible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DNNs deployed in CPS for FDIA detection are vulnerable to adversarial evasion attacks. The unique CPS infrastructure renders conventional defense mechanisms ineffective, creating a need for lightweight, deployable defenses that do not require architectural modifications.

Method: An additional input layer performs padding on input samples using pseudo-feature values derived from the input's statistical distribution, increasing input dimensionality in a randomized and data-aware manner. The method is model-agnostic, requires no core architecture changes, and is lightweight.

Result: Evaluated on IEEE 14-bus, 30-bus, 118-bus, and 300-bus power grid state estimation systems. The padding strategy significantly improved model robustness under adversarial settings with negligible performance impact and effectively mitigated attacks bypassing conventional defenses.

Conclusion: The proposed randomized, data-aware input padding framework is an effective, lightweight, and model-agnostic defense against adversarial FDIA evasion attacks in CPS, offering strong robustness gains without compromising baseline performance.

Abstract: Deep Neural Networks DNNs have achieved remarkable accuracy in various tasks including their application in CyberPhysical Systems CPS for detecting False Data Injection Attacks FDIA during critical operations However the unique infrastructure of CPS makes DNNs vulnerable to exploitation by attackers aiming to evade detection Additionally the distinct nature of CPS presents challenges for conventional defense mechanisms against FDIA This paper proposes an innovative defense framework that strengthens DNNs against such attacks by introducing an additional input layer that performs padding in the input samples using pseudofeature values derived from the inputs statistical distribution This padding increases the input dimensionality in a randomized and dataaware manner making adversarial attacks computationally infeasible due to the nontransferable nature of crafted perturbations and the unpredictability of the padded structure Our method is lightweight modelagnostic and requires no modifications to the core architecture making it highly deployable in realworld CPS settings We evaluated our framework on critical power grid applications such as state estimation using the IEEE 14bus 30bus 118bus and 300bus systems Experiments under adversarial settings demonstrate that our padding strategy significantly improves model robustness with negligible impact on performance and effectively mitigates attacks that would otherwise bypass conventional defenses

</details>


### [319] [On the Redundancy of Timestep Embeddings in Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20416)
*José A. Chávez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper challenges the necessity of explicit timestep embeddings in diffusion models, providing theoretical and empirical evidence that time-agnostic architectures can match or surpass conditioned counterparts on metrics like FID, precision, and recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Timestep embeddings are a ubiquitous design element in diffusion models, yet their fundamental necessity has not been rigorously examined. The authors aim to determine whether explicit temporal conditioning is truly required or merely an architectural habit.

Method: The authors provide a theoretical framework showing that under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective is achievable without explicit timestep conditioning. They conduct extensive ablation studies removing timestep embeddings from both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures, evaluating on CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets using metrics such as FID, precision, and recall.

Result: Time-agnostic models maintain high structural fidelity and can even surpass explicitly conditioned models on competitive metrics including FID, precision, and recall. The architectures appear capable of implicitly inferring noise scales from corrupted inputs, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant under the tested assumptions.

Conclusion: Explicit timestep conditioning is not strictly necessary for effective diffusion models. This finding challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms and opens the door to more efficient, structurally focused generative architectures.

Abstract: Diffusion models rely heavily on explicit timestep embeddings to modulate the denoising process across various noise scales. In this work, we challenge the necessity of these temporal signals by analyzing their impact on U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures. Beyond empirical evidence, we provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be achieved without explicit timestep conditioning. Our findings reveal a surprising robustness when timestep embeddings are completely removed. Extensive ablation studies on the CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets show that these time-agnostic models can maintain high structural fidelity and even surpass their conditioned counterparts in competitive metrics, including FID, precision, and recall. Our analysis suggests these architectures can implicitly infer noise scales from the corrupted input under specific assumptions, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant. This study challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms and paves the way for more efficient and structurally focused generative architectures.

</details>


### [320] [Neural network surrogates with uncertainty quantification for inverse problems in partial differential equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20417)
*Christian Jimenez-Beltran,Aretha L. Teckentrup,Antonio Vergari,Konstantinos C. Zygalakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DeepGaLA is a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions for Bayesian inverse problems, enabling scalable inference while maintaining accuracy comparable to Gaussian process surrogates with better scaling in high dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional numerical methods for Bayesian inverse problems involving differential equations are computationally prohibitive due to expensive likelihood evaluations in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Existing surrogates like Gaussian processes struggle with scalability as parameter dimension grows, and neural-network surrogates may yield overconfident predictions when training data are limited.

Method: The authors introduce DeepGaLA, a neural-network surrogate that quantifies predictive uncertainty, reducing overconfidence with limited data. They also propose using a short delayed-acceptance MCMC run as a diagnostic to evaluate the fidelity of surrogate-induced posterior approximations. The method incorporates differential-equation constraints, including in nonlinear settings.

Result: Across numerical experiments, DeepGaLA achieves forward-model approximation accuracy comparable to Gaussian process surrogates while maintaining better computational efficiency as parameter dimension increases. The delayed-acceptance MCMC diagnostic effectively assesses posterior approximation quality.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates like DeepGaLA can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems, bridging the gap between accuracy and computational tractability.

Abstract: Inverse problems for differential equations arise throughout science and engineering, where one seeks to infer unknown model parameters from noisy or incomplete observations. Traditional numerical methods for these problems are often computationally expensive, particularly in Bayesian settings where evaluating the likelihood becomes costly for complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces. To address this challenge, we introduce DeepGaLA, a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions, reducing overconfident inference when training data are limited. To evaluate the fidelity of the surrogate-induced posterior approximations in practice, we show that a short run of delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo can serve as an effective diagnostic. Across a range of numerical experiments, DeepGaLA delivers forward-model approximations with accuracy comparable to established Gaussian-process surrogates, while better maintaining efficiency as parameter dimension grows. Moreover, it can incorporate differential-equation constraints, including in nonlinear settings. Overall, these results indicate that uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems.

</details>


### [321] [Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting: A Mechanistic Study of Representation Retention in Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20431)
*Jan Wasilewski,Jędrzej Kozal,Michał Woźniak,Bartosz Krawczyk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled toy-world framework using synthetic generator-separator pipelines reveals that superposition (directional feature overlap) increases over time with transient dips at task boundaries, but higher superposition does not inevitably cause forgetting — representation strength and capacity allocation mediate this relationship.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world datasets entangle many factors, making it difficult to isolate the mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in continual learning systems. A controlled, observable framework is needed to test falsifiable hypotheses about how representation overlap, sparsity, and capacity interact to produce or prevent forgetting.

Method: A synthetic generator-separator pipeline defines ground-truth latent features and constructs tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap. Retention dynamics are studied by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) between retention, superposition, and exposure history. Complementary task-level analysis uses effective rank to characterize representational capacity allocation across tasks.

Result: Three main findings: (1) Superposition increases over time with transient dips at task boundaries, indicating boundary-specific interference rather than steady drift. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition but does not inevitably cause forgetting — strong representations can reduce forgetting despite overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, indicating broader capacity usage under sparse regimes.

Conclusion: The relationship between superposition and forgetting is nuanced: overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation, challenging the simplistic intuition that more superposition directly leads to more forgetting. The framework provides diagnostic tools and falsifiable hypotheses for continual learning research.

Abstract: Continual learning (CL) systems often forget previously acquired knowledge, yet the mechanisms driving forgetting remain hard to isolate in practice because real datasets entangle many factors. We present a controlled, toy-world framework that makes these mechanisms observable and testable. Using a synthetic generator-separator pipeline, we define ground-truth latent features, build tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap, and introduce measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition (directional overlap among features). We then study retention dynamics-the temporal change of representation strength by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) between retention, superposition, and exposure history. A complementary task-level analysis based on effective rank characterizes how representational capacity is allocated across tasks. Our controlled experiments yield three takeaways. (1) Superposition tends to increase over time with transient dips at task boundaries, suggesting boundary-specific interference rather than steady drift. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition yet does not inevitably cause forgetting; when representations remain strong, forgetting can be reduced despite overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, indicating broader capacity usage under sparse regimes. Together, these results nuance the common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting by showing that overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation. Our toy analysis provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for CL.

</details>


### [322] [Evolutionary Two-Stage Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20442)
*Fedor Buzaev,Dmitry Efremenko,Egor Bugaev,Andrei Ermakov,Denis Derkach,Daria Pugacheva,Fedor Ratnikov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-stage evolutionary algorithm approach for hyperparameter optimization in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). Stage 1 uses low-fidelity, truncated training runs to rapidly screen candidate configurations via black-box evolutionary search. Stage 2 fully trains only the most promising candidates with gradient-based optimizers. The method consistently outperforms standard PINN training on Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations under fixed computational budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs suffer from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and high sensitivity to architectural and optimization hyperparameters due to the non-convex, multi-term physics-informed loss. Traditional local or gradient-based hyperparameter search strategies get trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms, with population-based exploration and ability to handle mixed, non-differentiable search spaces, offer a more robust alternative for this noisy black-box optimization problem.

Method: A two-stage evolutionary optimization framework: (1) Exploration stage — low-fidelity training with truncated epochs to rapidly evaluate candidate hyperparameter configurations using evolutionary algorithms as a black-box outer-loop optimizer; (2) Exploitation stage — only the most promising configurations identified in stage 1 are fully trained with standard gradient-based optimizers (e.g., Adam/L-BFGS) to refine the PINN solution. The approach treats hyperparameter selection as an outer-loop problem over heterogeneous parameters under fixed computational budgets.

Result: Evaluated on three benchmark PDE problems — Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations — the proposed method consistently outperforms standard PINN training, achieving significantly lower mean error within the same constrained computational resources.

Conclusion: Combining evolutionary exploration with gradient-based exploitation in a two-stage pipeline effectively addresses PINN hyperparameter sensitivity, yielding more accurate and robust solutions without increasing computational budgets. The approach demonstrates that black-box evolutionary methods are well-suited to the challenging outer-loop optimization landscape of PINNs.

Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into neural network training. However, their performance suffers from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and strong sensitivity to architectural and optimization hyperparameters due to the highly non-convex and multi-term structure of the physics-informed loss. In this setting, the outer-loop hyperparameter search is a noisy and black-box optimization problem over heterogeneous parameters, where classical local or gradient-based strategies are easily trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms, with their population-based exploration and ability to handle mixed, non-differentiable search spaces, provide a more robust mechanism for discovering promising configurations. We propose and investigate a two-stage approach based on evolutionary algorithms that combines exploration and exploitation parts of PINNs training to improve solution accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets. In the first stage, we perform low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate configurations, treating hyperparameter selection as a black-box outer-loop problem. In the second stage, only the most promising candidates are fully trained with standard gradient-based optimizers to refine the solution. Evaluated on three popular problems, namely Advection, Klein-Gordon and Helmholtz equations, our method consistently outperforms standard training and achieves significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources.

</details>


### [323] [Data Bias Mitigation under Coverage Constraints & The Price of Fairness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20461)
*Bruno Scarone,Alfredo Viola,Renée J. Miller*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper extends a bias mitigation framework with coverage constraints to ensure sufficient representation of intersectional subgroups, formulates bias mitigation as an integer linear program, characterizes the price of fairness as a function of fairness tolerance, and demonstrates that coverage constraints preserve downstream ML performance while trading small bias approximation errors for data efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ML models exhibit discriminatory outcomes at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes (e.g., race × gender). Two key challenges motivate this work: (1) the lack of principled measures for quantifying potentially intersectional bias, and (2) insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. There is a need for methods that balance bias reduction with data efficiency and provide quantifiable trade-offs for legal compliance and data governance.

Method: The authors extend a prior bias mitigation framework by incorporating coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. They formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program (ILP) that optimizes over all mitigation strategies. They characterize the "price of fairness" — the minimum data modification cost — as a function of fairness tolerance, enabling practitioners to trade small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency while satisfying coverage constraints.

Result: Experiments on publicly available datasets demonstrate that: (1) the proposed bias mitigation framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers; (2) coverage constraints, while statistically motivated, are essential for preserving downstream ML performance; and (3) small approximation errors in bias enable significantly greater data efficiency.

Conclusion: Coverage constraints are essential for effective intersectional bias mitigation and downstream model performance. The ILP formulation provides a principled way to navigate fairness-accuracy-data cost trade-offs. Characterizing the price of fairness as a function of fairness tolerance is critical for legal compliance (meeting regulatory fairness thresholds) and data governance (informing data purchasing decisions).

Abstract: Machine learning models have been shown to exhibit discriminatory outcomes or degraded performance for individuals at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes, such as race and gender. This stems in part from two interrelated challenges: the lack of principled measures for quantifying bias (potentially intersectional), and insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. We extend a recent bias mitigation framework to incorporate coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. Since achieving exactly zero bias for all groups may not be data efficient (meaning it may require large amounts of data), our solution trades small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency while satisfying coverage constraints. We also formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, and characterize the price of fairness, the minimum data modification cost, as a function of fairness tolerance. This is essential both for legal compliance, where regulations may mandate specific fairness thresholds, and for data governance, enabling practitioners to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data modification (particularly, data purchasing) costs. We evaluate our techniques on publicly available datasets, demonstrating that bias mitigation via our framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers, and that coverage constraints, while motivated by statistical considerations, are essential for preserving downstream ML performance.

</details>


### [324] [Agentic Symbolic Search: Characterizing PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20467)
*Zongmin Yu,Liu Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ASYS is a prior-guided framework that combines agentic symbolic search with gradient-based optimization to automatically discover interpretable mathematical structures in PDE solutions, recovering known analytical forms and constructing novel approximations where none previously existed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mathematicians understand PDE solutions through mathematical structures, not tables of values. Traditional analysis is manual and problem-specific, while numerical simulations and neural networks fail to produce interpretable analytical forms. There is a need for automated discovery of interpretable mathematical representations of PDE solutions.

Method: ASYS uses an agent that translates PDE theory, problem constraints, and search experience into differentiable symbolic programs. These programs are refined via evolutionary search over symbolic forms while continuous parameters are optimized via gradient descent. This constitutes automated inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression.

Result: Across five problems (bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, free-boundary focusing), ASYS recovered known analytical forms and discovered novel expressions: a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up, where no closed-form descriptions previously existed.

Conclusion: ASYS demonstrates a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions that goes beyond handcrafted analysis, mesh-based numerics, and neural network approximations, by automatically producing interpretable analytical representations.

Abstract: Mathematicians understand a PDE solution through mathematical structures rather than tables of computed values. Historically, this has been the product of mathematical analysis, carried out by hand for each problem individually. Neither numerical simulation nor neural networks produce those structures directly. We propose Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), a prior-guided framework in which an agent translates PDE theory, public problem constraints, and accumulated search experience into testable differentiable symbolic programs. The mathematical forms are refined under evolutionary search, while their continuous parameters are fit by gradient-based optimization. This makes the search an automated form of inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression. For problems with known analytical forms, ASYS recovers these forms naturally; for other problems, ASYS constructs analytical approximations which can guide mathematicians toward further analysis. In our experiments, across five problems spanning bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing, ASYS produces interpretable representations, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up, in settings where no closed-form description was previously available. ASYS shows the possibility of a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions, beyond handcrafted analytical solutions, mesh-based numerical solutions, and neural network approximations.

</details>


### [325] [Fisher-Geometric Sharpness and the Implicit Bias of SGD toward Flat Minima](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20469)
*Md Sakir Ahmed,Kumaresh Sarmah,Hemen Dutta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper resolves the reparametrization-invariance critique of flatness-based generalization by grounding sharpness in the Riemannian geometry of the Fisher Information Matrix. It defines Riemannian sharpness, proves its invariance under function-preserving reparametrizations, links it to SGD noise structure, derives a PAC-Bayes bound, and validates the theory on MNIST and CIFAR-10.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Euclidean flatness measures (e.g., Hessian trace or max eigenvalue) are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, as highlighted by Dinh et al. This undermines the intuitive link between flat minima and generalization. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant foundation for the flatness–generalization connection.

Method: The authors define Riemannian sharpness using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) geometry on the statistical manifold. They prove invariance under smooth function-preserving reparametrizations, formalize mini-batch SGD gradient noise as having covariance proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the corresponding stochastic differential equation (showing exponential concentration at Riemannian-flat minima), and establish a PAC-Bayes generalization bound explicitly controlled by Riemannian sharpness.

Result: Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm that Riemannian sharpness reliably tracks generalization where Euclidean sharpness fails. The scaling of Riemannian sharpness with η/B (learning rate / batch size) matches theoretical predictions. The diagonal empirical FIM estimator inherits invariance only approximately; exact invariance requires structured estimators like K-FAC.

Conclusion: The results provide a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize, resolving the Dinh et al. critique. Riemannian sharpness, grounded in FIM geometry, successfully links SGD dynamics, generalization, and geometric flatness in a theoretically coherent and empirically validated framework.

Abstract: A widely held intuition in deep learning is that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) implicitly favors flat minima and that flat minima generalize better, but standard Euclidean measures of flatness such as the trace or maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, which undermines the theoretical foundations of this narrative. In this study we resolve this issue by grounding flatness in the Riemannian geometry of the statistical manifold induced by the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We define Riemannian sharpness mathematically and prove that it is invariant under smooth, function-preserving reparametrizations, which directly addresses the critique of Dinh et al. in the paper ``Sharp minima can generalize for deep nets''.We note that this invariance is a property of the true FIM; the diagonal empirical estimator used in practice (and in all experiments below) inherits invariance only approximately, and exact invariance under arbitrary reparametrizations would require structured estimators such as K-FAC. We formalize the gradient noise of mini-batch SGD as having a covariance structure proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the resulting stochastic differential equation, and then show that the probability mass is exponentially concentrated at Riemannian-flat minima. A PAC-Bayes generalization bound controlled explicitly by SR formally links this geometric bias to test performance. Our experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm that SR reliably tracks generalization in ways that Euclidean sharpness does not, and that its scaling with $η/B$ matches the theoretical predictions. Together these results provide a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize.

</details>


### [326] [UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20474)
*Inesh Chakrabarti,David Limpus,Aditi Ghai Rana,Bowen Bao,Spandan Tiwari,Thiago Crepaldi,Ashish Sirasao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates 4-bit KV-cache compression for multi-turn agent workloads, using rotation-based quantization methods. It proposes UltraQuant—an FP4 approximation leveraging FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, and CDNA4 native support—achieving 3.47× faster time-to-first-token and 1.63× higher throughput versus FP8 baselines on AMD GPUs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Context-heavy LLM agents with long prefixes reused across many short turns place extreme pressure on the KV cache. This creates a tension between cache residency (fitting long contexts in limited GPU memory) and serving throughput (keeping GPUs utilized under concurrency). Existing 4-bit quantization methods lack rigorous evaluation under realistic multi-round agent workloads that jointly measure task quality, cache residency, and throughput.

Method: The authors use TurboQuant-style rotation with codebook quantization as a quality reference and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment baseline. Key design choices include: asymmetric K/V treatment (aggressive V compression, milder K compression), Walsh-Hadamard rotation for outlier suppression, removal of QJL projections, and block-scale variants. The core contribution is UltraQuant: an FP4 approximation using FP8 query inputs, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group-scale factors, and native scaled-MFMA instructions on AMD CDNA4 architecture. Custom decode-attention kernels are developed for serving optimization.

Result: On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload under cache pressure, UltraQuant reduces P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47× in late rounds (2.3× across all rounds) and increases output throughput by 1.63× over the FP8 KV baseline, all while maintaining acceptable task quality.

Conclusion: 4-bit KV-cache quantization is viable for multi-round agent serving when engineered with careful design choices (asymmetric K/V, proper rotations, block scaling). UltraQuant demonstrates that an FP4 approximation path exploiting hardware-native instructions (CDNA4 scaled-MFMA) can substantially outperform FP8 baselines in both latency and throughput under realistic cache-pressure conditions.

Abstract: Context-heavy agents place unusual pressure on the key-value (KV) cache: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, while concurrency determines whether the serving system can keep GPUs utilized. We study 4-bit KV-cache compression for this setting, using TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. We report three contributions. First, we frame 4-bit KV caching around multi-round agent workloads where task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput must be measured jointly. Second, we describe the practical design choices needed to make the 4-bit path robust, including asymmetric K/V treatment, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, QJL removal, and block-scale variants. Third, we present serving optimizations on AMD GPUs, including optimized decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant, an FP4 approximation path that uses FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA support on CDNA4. On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant cuts P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47x in the cache-pressured late rounds (2.3x across all rounds) and raises output throughput by 1.63x over the FP8 KV baseline.

</details>


### [327] [Marginal Advantage Accumulation for Memory-Driven Agent Self-Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20475)
*Mingyu Yang,Keye Zheng,Congchao Cheng,Yujie Liu,Xingkang Lu,Fan Jiang,Yefei Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Batch-style trace distillation suffers from contradictory feedback across batches; this paper proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA), which enforces alignability and comparability via EMA-based signed evidence accumulation and semantic identity merging, achieving SOTA in 14/16 settings with ~75% token reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In batch-style trace distillation, a memory operation can receive inconsistent or contradictory supervisory signals across different training batches. Existing methods lack a mechanism to accumulate evidence at the operation level across batches, making it impossible to distinguish genuinely effective operations from those that succeed only by chance. The paper identifies two structural conditions—alignability and comparability—that any cross-batch evidence accumulation system must satisfy.

Method: MAA is a post-processing architecture with three components: (1) constructing differential signals that satisfy comparability across batches; (2) accumulating signed evidence per operation using Exponential Moving Average (EMA); and (3) ensuring cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging of operations. The two formal structural conditions—alignability and comparability—guide the design.

Result: MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 evaluation settings spanning 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.

Conclusion: MAA provides an effective post-processing solution for batch-style trace distillation by introducing a principled cross-batch evidence accumulation mechanism, demonstrating that structural conditions of alignability and comparability are critical for distinguishing stable operations from spurious ones, with strong empirical gains and substantial efficiency improvements.

Abstract: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation may receive contradictory feedback across different batches. Existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism, making it impossible to distinguish stably effective operations from accidental hits. This paper formalizes the requirement as two structural conditions, alignability and comparability, and proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA). MAA constructs differential signals to make them comparable across batches, accumulates signed evidence per operation via EMA, and ensures cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging. As a post-processing architecture, MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.

</details>


### [328] [Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20537)
*Liang Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlashRT introduces execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint/restore mechanism for LLM serving that snapshots the complete execution state (KV cache, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, metadata) at committed boundaries, enabling sub-millisecond GPU-resident fork, restore, and rollback. Targeting low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, it achieves 3.9x–27x TTFT speedups over cold prefill (2k–16k tokens) on RTX 5090, with byte-exact state restoration and token-identical greedy decode. This complements, rather than replaces, throughput-oriented paged/radix KV-cache systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mainstream LLM serving systems (paged/radix KV caches) optimize high-throughput, high-concurrency scenarios by reusing token-addressed KV fragments, but they only manage one positional fragment of execution state. In contrast, low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving (interactive agents, speech systems, robot policies) involves frequent branching, resetting, interrupting, and re-entering under tight responsiveness budgets — requiring complete restorable state, not just KV cache. Existing systems lack this capability.

Method: FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime with an NVIDIA CUDA backend. It runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. The live execution state is a closed set of named buffers (KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, metadata). Execution-state capsules provide graph-bound checkpoint and restore: snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the entire execution boundary atomically. This shifts reuse granularity from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries, with GPU-resident operations.

Result: On RTX 5090: capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, confirming recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot/restore are sub-millisecond. TTFT speedup over cold prefill: 3.9x at 2k tokens, 27x at 16k tokens. Correctness and structural properties also hold on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark.

Conclusion: Execution-state capsules define a complementary, latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse, distinct from high-throughput KV-cache serving. They are not a replacement for paged/radix KV-cache systems but rather address the underserved regime of low-latency, interactive, on-device physical-AI workloads where complete state integrity and fast restore are critical.

Abstract: Mainstream LLM serving systems reuse prefix work mainly through paged or radix key-value (KV) caches. This is highly effective for high-throughput, high-concurrency serving, but it manages only one positional fragment of execution state: the KV cache. We study the opposite regime: low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive LLM agents, speech systems, and robot policies repeatedly branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. We introduce execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint and restore mechanism for the complete restorable state at a committed boundary. FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime whose evaluated NVIDIA CUDA backend runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. Because the live state is a closed set of named buffers, a capsule can snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the whole execution boundary, including KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, and metadata. This moves reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries. On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, showing that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore are sub-millisecond, and TTFT speedup over cold prefill grows from 3.9x at 2k tokens to 27x at 16k tokens. On Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, the same correctness and structural properties hold. Capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse.

</details>


### [329] [Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20538)
*Qingyang Zhu,Eric Karl Oermann,Kyunghyun Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that represents priors as dataset prefixes, enabling a transformer to adapt predictions across diverse priors — matching oracle Bayesian performance with orders-of-magnitude speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing amortized Bayesian inference methods (e.g., Prior-Data Fitted networks and in-context models) are tightly coupled to their training prior and lack mechanisms to adapt to new priors at test time, resulting in poor robustness under distribution shift. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling test-time adaptation to novel priors without retraining.

Method: The authors propose a multi-task in-context learning framework where prior information is explicitly encoded as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer is trained on sequences composed of prior-describing tasks followed by target tasks, allowing it to learn how to adapt its predictive distribution across families of priors in a hierarchical Bayesian manner.

Result: The method matches oracle Bayesian predictors across evaluations of increasing difficulty — including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures — while achieving orders-of-magnitude faster inference. Practical utility is demonstrated on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-task in-context learning framework successfully decouples amortized inference from the training prior, enabling robust, fast, and accurate Bayesian predictive inference that generalizes across diverse and previously unseen priors.

Abstract: Bayesian predictive inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, data efficiency, and robust generalization. However, exact inference is often intractable, and scalable approximations may remain computationally expensive or require restrictive modeling assumptions that degrade predictive performance. Prior-Data Fitted and in-context models have recently emerged as an amortized alternative by learning to map datasets directly to predictive distributions, but existing approaches are tightly coupled to the support of the training prior and lack explicit mechanisms for adapting to new priors at test time, resulting in limited robustness under distribution shift. We introduce a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that explicitly represents prior information as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt its predictions across families of priors. On a suite of evaluations with increasing difficulty, including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures, our method matches oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. We further demonstrate its practical relevance on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/martianmartina/multi-task-bayesian-icl/.

</details>


### [330] [Predictability as a Fine-Grained Measure for Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20546)
*Linda Lu,Karthik Sridharan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces "privacy via predictability," a fine-grained privacy framework measuring leakage as an attacker's incremental predictive gain over compromised data, complementary to differential privacy. Establishes theoretical relationships with DP, provides asymptotic analysis via GMM for stationary ergodic mixing processes, and derives a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for empirical risk minimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Differential privacy's worst-case nature imposes a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff, treating all attackers uniformly regardless of their actual background knowledge. The authors argue that realistic attackers possess limited, structured prior knowledge (compromised data from a stochastic process) and target specific queries, motivating a finer-grained privacy metric that adapts to these specifics.

Method: Formalizes predictability as the incremental gain in an attacker's predictive ability for sensitive information, beyond what the compromised data already reveals. Analyzes the relationship between predictability and DP, showing incomparability generally but implication of mutual-information DP in worst-case regimes. Employs the generalized method of moments (GMM) for asymptotic analysis under stationary, ergodic, mixing data-generating processes, and derives a predictability-calibrated output perturbation mechanism for ERM.

Result: Predictability and DP are generally incomparable (each can be small while the other is large). In the worst-case regime where all but one individual is compromised and all binary queries are sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. Asymptotic predictability is characterized via GMM under mixing process assumptions. A predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for ERM is derived.

Conclusion: Predictability provides a complementary, finer-grained privacy framework tailored to specific sensitive information and attacker models. It can be deployed alongside DP to enable more nuanced privacy control, bridging the gap between worst-case guarantees and practical threat models.

Abstract: Differential privacy (DP) ensures rigorous individual-level privacy guarantees against even the most knowledgeable attackers, but its worst-case nature can impose a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. We introduce privacy via predictability, a fine-grained framework that explicitly incorporates the attacker's core knowledge, a compromised portion of the dataset generated by a stochastic process, and a specified family of queries. Predictability measures privacy leakage as the incremental gain in an attacker's ability to predict sensitive information about unknown individuals after observing the algorithm's output, beyond what can already be inferred from the compromised data. We show that predictability and DP are generally incomparable: each can be small while the other is large. However, in the worst-case regime where all but one individual is compromised, and all binary queries are considered sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. More generally, predictability provides a finer-grained privacy metric tailored to specific sensitive information and specific attacker models. We introduce a general framework, using the generalized method of moments (GMM), to analyze asymptotic predictability when the compromised data is generated by a stationary, ergodic, mixing process. Using this analysis, we derive a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for ERM. Our approach is complementary to DP and can be used alongside DP to provide fine-grained privacy control.

</details>


### [331] [The Token Is a Group Element: On Lie-Algebra Attention over Matrix Lie Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20547)
*Przemyslaw Musialski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Lie-Algebra Attention, where attention tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements. The attention score uses the closed-form negative squared Frobenius norm of the relative pose logarithm, eliminating learned kernels, irreducible representations, and Clebsch-Gordan machinery. It applies to any matrix Lie group—including non-compact, non-abelian affine groups—and matches or outperforms learned-kernel baselines with 50–80× fewer parameters while preserving exact equivariance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing attention mechanisms for geometric data either rely on vector-token representations with irreducible representations and spherical harmonics (which cannot reach affine groups with scale/shear) or on surjective exponential maps (also limited). The authors aim to construct an attention mechanism that works directly with bare group elements, is intrinsically equivariant, applies to all matrix Lie groups including non-compact non-abelian ones, and uses a principled closed-form geometric score rather than a learned kernel.

Method: Tokens are elements g_i of a matrix Lie group G. For any pair (i,j), the canonical invariant is w_ij = log(g_i^{-1} g_j). The attention score s_ij is the negative squared algebra norm under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product: s_ij = -‖log(g_i^{-1} g_j)‖_λ² / τ. Diagonal G-equivariance is tautological, and the cocycle condition holds automatically. The construction uses a chosen logarithm chart containing all relative poses and requires no learned kernel, irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, or Clebsch-Gordan products.

Result: On three sequence-completion experiments—SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2)—the closed-form Lie-algebra attention score matches a learned MLP kernel operating on the same invariant and outperforms it on SE(2), using 50–80× fewer score parameters. A vector-token baseline breaks equivariance by 5 to 12 orders of magnitude.

Conclusion: Lie-Algebra Attention demonstrates that bare group elements suffice as tokens, with a canonical, parameter-free proximity score derived from the Lie algebra norm. The approach extends attention to affine full-frame groups previously inaccessible to irrep- or surjective-exp-based methods, and achieves state-of-the-art equivariance with dramatically fewer parameters.

Abstract: We place the attention token on the group: a token is an element $g_i$ of a matrix Lie group $G$ -- a bare transformation, with no feature payload and no external action $ρ(g)$ carrying it. To our knowledge this is the first attention construction whose tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements: their score is the closed-form algebra norm of the relative pose rather than a learned kernel, and it reaches the affine full-frame groups that every irrep- or surjective-exp-based method must exclude. We call it Lie-Algebra Attention. Once tokens are group elements, the rest follows with none of the usual representation-theoretic machinery. The relative geometry of a pair is canonical, $g_i^{-1} g_j$, so the pairwise invariant $w_{ij} = \log(g_i^{-1} g_j)$ is intrinsic rather than designed; equivariance under the diagonal $G$-action is tautological, and the cocycle condition holds automatically. The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm, $s_{ij} = -\|\log(g_i^{-1} g_j)\|_λ^2/τ$: the canonical proximity kernel under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product, with no irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernel. The construction applies to any matrix Lie group on a chosen logarithm chart containing the relative poses, including the non-compact non-abelian affine groups with scale and shear that no vector-token attention method reaches: neither the irrep tradition nor surjective-exp methods. Three sequence-completion experiments, on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2), bear this out: the closed-form score matches a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant and outperforms it on SE(2), using 50 to 80x fewer score parameters, while a vector-token baseline breaks invariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude.

</details>


### [332] [Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20557)
*Georgy Noarov,Aaron Roth*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper resolves whether randomization is necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration by presenting the first deterministic algorithm achieving the minimax-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ rate, and generalizes it to outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior to this work, all multicalibration algorithms attaining the minimax-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity were randomized; deterministic predictors had substantially worse sample complexity. The necessity of randomization for optimal multicalibration was an explicit open problem posed by [CLNR26] and implicit in several earlier works.

Method: The authors construct a deterministic multicalibration algorithm that achieves the minimax-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity rate. They then generalize this algorithmic framework to produce deterministic predictors satisfying outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests, extending the technique to omnipredictors and panpredictors.

Result: The paper delivers a deterministic predictor that attains the minimax-optimal sample complexity for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration, settling the open question. The generalization yields optimal deterministic predictors for outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors, resolving open problems from [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].

Conclusion: Randomization is not necessary for achieving optimal sample complexity in multicalibration. The deterministic algorithm and its generalizations establish that optimal rates are achievable deterministically across a range of related fairness and indistinguishability frameworks, closing several open problems in trustworthy machine learning.

Abstract: A model is multicalibrated on a collection of group weights $G$ if it is calibrated -- i.e. unbiased even conditional on its prediction -- not just overall, but also after reweighting contexts by each $g \in G$. It is a useful property for many downstream applications and is a basic desideratum of trustworthy machine learning. Before this work, all predictors known to attain the minimax-optimal $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity rate for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration were randomized, while deterministic predictors were known only with substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization is necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration was explicitly asked by [CLNR26] and implicitly in several prior works.
  We resolve this open problem by giving a minimax-optimal multicalibration algorithm that outputs a deterministic predictor. We then generalize the algorithm to produce optimal deterministic predictors that satisfy outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests. As an application, this also gives deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors with optimal sample complexity, resolving open problems posed by [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].

</details>


### [333] [How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20560)
*Joshua Engels,Callum McDougall,Bilal Chughtai,Janos Kramar,Senthoran Rajamanoharan,Cindy Wu,Arthur Conmy,Asic Q Chen,Jean Tarbouriech,Min Ma,Brendan O'Donoghue,João Gabriel Lopes de Oliveira,Rohin Shah,Neel Nanda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether DiffusionGemma's continuous latent space reasoning is less transparent than autoregressive models. It decomposes transparency into variable transparency (interpretability of intermediate states) and algorithmic transparency (reconstructing the reasoning process). While DiffusionGemma initially appears 28.6X more opaque, token-bottleneck mapping reduces this to 1.1X. The paper also uncovers novel diffusion-specific reasoning phenomena and shows DiffusionGemma is similarly monitorable to Gemma 4.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM reasoning transparency is crucial for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse, and debugging. DiffusionGemma performs much of its computation in continuous latent space, raising concerns about whether this architectural choice sacrifices transparency compared to autoregressive models.

Method: The authors decompose transparency into two components: (1) variable transparency — whether intermediate computational states are interpretable, measured via "opaque serial depth"; and (2) algorithmic transparency — whether these snapshots can reconstruct the reasoning process. They map denoising-step information through an interpretable token bottleneck without performance loss, conduct interpretability case studies, and evaluate monitorability (usefulness of outputs for downstream tasks).

Result: Initial analysis showed DiffusionGemma's opaque serial depth was 28.6X higher than autoregressive Gemma 4. After applying the token-bottleneck mapping, this reduced to just 1.1X. Case studies revealed novel diffusion-specific phenomena: non-chronological reasoning, token/sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Monitorability was comparable between DiffusionGemma and Gemma 4.

Conclusion: DiffusionGemma is not inherently less transparent than autoregressive models. With appropriate interpretability techniques (token-bottleneck mapping), variable transparency approaches parity. However, algorithmic transparency remains more challenging for diffusion models due to distributed, parallel reasoning across denoising steps — requiring new interpretability methods to address.

Abstract: LLM reasoning transparency is a critical affordance for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse and misalignment, and debugging surprising model behaviors. However, DiffusionGemma performs a larger fraction of its computation in a continuous latent space; does this make its reasoning less transparent? We study this question by decomposing transparency into two components: variable transparency, whether we understand intermediate snapshots of a model's computational state; and algorithmic transparency, whether we can use these snapshots to reconstruct the process by which the model arrived at its outputs. Naively, DiffusionGemma has poor variable transparency: its opaque serial depth, the amount of serial computation that occurs in between interpretable model states, seems at first 28.6X higher than the corresponding autoregressive Gemma 4 model. However, we show that we can map the information flowing between denoising steps through an interpretable token bottleneck with no decrease in downstream performance. Treating these intermediate states as interpretable reduces the opaque serial depth to just 1.1X that of Gemma 4. Algorithmic transparency is harder for diffusion models than for autoregressive models because all token predictions in the canvas can change at every denoising step, giving the model the power to implement complicated distributed algorithms during the denoising process. To begin bridging this gap, we conduct a suite of interpretability case studies, uncovering initial evidence of novel diffusion-specific phenomena such as non-chronological reasoning, token and sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Finally, we test monitorability, a key application of transparency that measures whether model outputs are useful for downstream tasks. We find that DiffusionGemma is similarly monitorable to Gemma 4.

</details>


<div id='cs.MA'></div>

# cs.MA [[Back]](#toc)

### [334] [Mesh Inference: A Formal Model of Collective Intelligence Without a Center](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19537)
*Hongwei Xu*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper presents a formal model for "mesh inference," where independent agents with private state reach a collective conclusion without sharing internal parameters or requiring a central coordinator. The framework is built on coupled free-energy minimization, proving convergence, identification-completeness, and confidentiality guarantees, with linear-Gaussian analysis establishing O(diam²) latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated and distributed learning typically require sharing weights, gradients, or hidden states, or rely on a central coordinator. The authors ask: can a population of agents, spanning different organizations, derive a consensus answer without exposing any internal state, using only admitted typed observations? This is motivated by the energy-minimizing nature of inference in single models, generalized to a mesh.

Method: The authors model mesh inference as a coupled free-energy minimization problem, where each agent locally relaxes a free energy that is coupled to others' observations via an admission/emission policy. The coupling structure is shown to be an M-matrix, guaranteeing convergence to a unique fixed point. They analyze three formal properties (convergence, identification-completeness, observation-only confidentiality) through duality and matrix analysis. In the linear-Gaussian regime, they derive tight latency bounds and characterize the exact centralized optimum recovery conditions.

Result: (1) Mesh inference converges to a unique answer for any admission policy (symmetric or not) because the coupling is always an M-matrix. (2) It is identification-complete: it recovers the centralized optimum exactly when contributing views are carrier-connected. (3) Observation-only: no node transmits internals; confidentiality is the dual of identification. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime, every derived answer equals the centralized optimum at O(diam²) latency. One derivation corresponds to one turn of a center-free learning loop.

Conclusion: This is claimed as the first formal model of mesh inference. An open problem is posed: determining when non-linear mesh inference improves the collective answer versus producing a confident error — i.e., when "asking" upgrades rather than corrupts the collective.

Abstract: We present a formal model of mesh inference: how a population of independent agents, each holding private state and exchanging only admitted, typed observations, derives a conclusion none of them holds alone, with no central coordinator and no agent exposed. No agent shares weights, gradients, or hidden state, and the agents may span different teams, networks, and organizations. Motivated by the observation that asking a model is energy-minimizing inference, we model the mesh as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally. We show that a single admission/emission policy governs three properties. First, mesh inference converges to a unique answer for any admission, symmetric or not, because the coupling is always an M-matrix. Second, it is identification-complete: it derives the centralized optimum exactly when the contributing views are carrier-connected. Third, it is observation-only: no node transmits its internals, and confidentiality is the dual of identification. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime every derived answer is determined, hence equal to the centralized optimum, at O(diam^2) latency, the measured price of removing the center. One such derivation is one turn of a center-free learning loop, which we formalize as architecture rather than prove. The open problem we state is when asking improves the collective rather than corrupting it: whether the non-linear closure derives an upgraded answer or a confident error. To our knowledge, this is the first formal model of mesh inference.

</details>


### [335] [SIGMA: Skill-Incidence Graphs for Compositional Multi-Agent Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19758)
*Kun Zeng,Yu Huo,Siyu Zhang,Yuecheng Zhuo,Yuquan Lu,Haoyue Liu,Siyue Chen,Xiaoying Tang*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: SIGMA introduces a skill-incidence graph framework for multi-agent systems where agents are dynamically composed from reusable skills based on task requirements, rather than using fixed agents. It predicts which skills each agent should possess, builds agent embeddings from those skills, and designs the communication topology—achieving state-of-the-art performance across reasoning and coding benchmarks with improved robustness to unseen skill combinations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based MAS methods optimize communication among predefined, closed-set agents with fixed roles. This rigidity prevents them from generalizing to tasks requiring novel combinations of capabilities not seen during design, limiting adaptability and scalability.

Method: SIGMA operates in three stages: (1) given a task and a skill library, it predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix specifying which skills compose each agent; (2) it generates agent node embeddings by aggregating embeddings of their assigned skills; (3) it decodes a communication topology over these dynamically constructed agents. At execution time, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to the relevant assigned capabilities, operationalizing the incidence structure directly.

Result: Evaluated on six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance, outperforming CARD (the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline) by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points across the three LLMs. It also exhibits stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points.

Conclusion: Compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design, orthogonal to communication topology optimization. SIGMA demonstrates that building agents as task-conditioned bundles of skills significantly improves generalization and robustness in MAS.

Abstract: Existing graph-based multi-agent system (MAS) designers mainly improve collaboration by optimizing communication topologies over predefined agents, roles, or groups. However, because each node remains a closed-set entity, these methods struggle to generalize to tasks that require unseen combinations of capabilities. We propose SIGMA, a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills.
